papers.title: Generalizable Equivariant Diffusion Models for Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theory: Analytical Foundations and Numerical Scaling Tests
papers.abstract: Gauge-equivariant diffusion models can be used to generate ensembles of field configurations in non-abelian lattice gauge theories. Previously, we demonstrated the feasibility of modeling these theories by combining L-CNN-based diffusion models with the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA). Here we focus on the underlying analytical framework. In particular, we present a rigorous derivation of the reverse-time stochastic differential equation on the group manifold, discuss the gauge invariance of the denoising loss function, and provide extensive numerical benchmarks regarding the scaling behavior with respect to the lattice volume and the inverse coupling $\beta$. Full analytical expressions for arbitrarily sized Wilson loops and the topological charge susceptibility during the forward process are given as well.
papers.summary: Gauge-equivariant diffusion models can generate ensembles of field configurations for non-abelian lattice gauge theories, and this follow-up supplies the analytical framework behind an earlier approach that paired `L-CNN`-based diffusion models with the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (`MAALA`). The authors give **a rigorous derivation of the reverse-time stochastic differential equation on the group manifold** and discuss the gauge invariance of the denoising loss. They also report numerical benchmarks of how the method scales with lattice volume and inverse coupling, plus full analytical expressions for arbitrarily sized Wilson loops and the topological charge susceptibility during the forward process.

papers.title: Show Your Work: Can Small Open Models Read SEC Filings with Evidence a Machine Can Check?
papers.abstract: A fluent answer from a language model is not a verified one. We ask whether small open models that run on a single consumer GPU can extract numbers from SEC filings with evidence a machine can check: the page and a verbatim quote containing the number. We introduce Filing-Evidence, a benchmark of 1,000 questions over 90 recent 10-K and 10-Q filings of 45 US companies, with answer keys taken from the filers' inline XBRL tags. We evaluate ten instruct models from ten developers (7-21B parameters) on one RTX 4090 in three setups: plain, check-and-retry, and the model's own reasoning mode. Accuracy with checkable evidence ranges from 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup, and the best result is 84.5% (Qwen3.5-9B). An automatic checker rejects many wrong answers, but between 16 and 167 answers per 1,000 give a wrong value for an answerable question and still pass every check. In the plain setup, 57% of these are scale or unit errors and 30% take another period or column of the right line. Reasoning significantly reduces such errors for 4 of 5 models that offer it. Retrying after a failed check raises accuracy by up to 3.9 points but never reduces them. Questions, model outputs, code and protocol are public.
papers.summary: Small open models that fit on a single consumer GPU are tested on extracting numbers from SEC filings together with evidence a machine can verify: the page and a verbatim quote containing the number. The authors build `Filing-Evidence`, a benchmark of 1,000 questions over 90 recent 10-K and 10-Q filings with answer keys taken from the filers' inline XBRL tags, and evaluate ten instruct models of 7-21B parameters on one RTX 4090 in plain, check-and-retry, and reasoning setups. Accuracy with checkable evidence ranges from 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup and **peaks at 84.5% with `Qwen3.5-9B`**, yet between 16 and 167 answers per 1,000 give a wrong value and still pass every check, mostly through scale or unit errors or by reading the wrong period or column. Reasoning mode significantly reduces these errors for 4 of 5 models that offer it, while retrying after a failed check raises accuracy by up to 3.9 points but never reduces them.

papers.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
papers.abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models gain speed by committing several tokens per step, but sampling each token from its own marginal discards the dependency between them, a loss equal to the conditional total correlation of the committed set. The authors estimate this quantity for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion models from two families and ask how well rules that see only per-position marginals can predict it. On three of the four models **the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17)**, 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons among six common rules. They also show that `Dream` and `LLaDA` place a position's prediction at different logit indices, so reading the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times, and they note the results concern predicting the loss for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder would gain.

papers.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
papers.abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.
papers.summary: Many failures of deployed AI systems are attributed here to a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts, such as missing user state, repository revisions, tool traces, or sensor readings. The authors name the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling and frame a system as governed by three budgets for training, decision-time computation, and context infrastructure, arguing that **only the context-infrastructure budget targets what the system can make available before a decision**. They define an effective-context value, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. Current mechanisms are organized into a five-operation context lifecycle, with controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves proposed for evaluation.

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
papers.abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.
papers.summary: Choosing the best of several candidate answers from a language or vision-language model usually relies on model confidence, a learned judge, or a domain check, each of which can miss answers that are fluent but insecure or that quietly break a task requirement. The proposed scoring framework combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with softer checks blended into one score, using a drafting model, a configuring model that selects and weights checks per task, and scoring models for properties no grounded tool can compute. Across `CWEval`, `LIBERO` with added safety variants, `LiveCodeBench`, and `HotpotQA`, an ablation finds the gains come from pairing hard checks with candidate comparison, **lifting code-generation safety by up to +0.28 on `CWEval`** and joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 on retrieval-augmented question answering. The gain shrinks to near zero or slightly negative where the first sample is already strong, and the per-task layer that selects and weights soft checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives.

papers.title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments
papers.abstract: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.
papers.summary: A single success rate on agentic benchmarks mixes distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, not working out how its components operate, operating them in the wrong order, and failing to recover from mistakes. An early preview of `MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld` offers an interactive maze environment where key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations can be added or removed independently while the renderer, action space, and scoring stay fixed, with breadth-first search giving each instance an exact optimal action count. After fixing the protocol on 15 held-out mazes, the authors evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. The models **solve only 6 of 150 episodes**, 45 of the 50 mazes go unsolved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism is solved.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
papers.abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.
papers.summary: Detecting skilled forgeries of handwritten signatures from static images is hard because pen pressure, timing, and stroke order are missing. The authors study quantum machine learning pipelines on a public Kaggle signature corpus, pairing a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest classifiers, and propose a hybrid that uses a frozen `EfficientNetB0` feature extractor, a principal component projection down to a qubit-register-sized subspace, and a nearest neighbour rule. The hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy on a single held-out fold and **a mean of 91.26 percent under stratified five-fold cross validation**, with an ablation across six quantum variants.

papers.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
papers.abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench
papers.summary: Formalizing real mathematics requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library, whereas existing evaluations often give isolated theorem statements whose supporting theory already exists in Mathlib. `AutoformBench` is a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks from 24 advanced mathematical sources, with each target statement formalized and audited by Lean-experienced mathematicians and the proof left to the evaluated agent, which receives the informal proof but must construct the missing infrastructure. Comparing frontier models, the authors find a largely shared difficulty frontier in which **success depends less on mathematical domain than on the ability to construct missing formal infrastructure**.

papers.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis
papers.abstract: A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.
papers.summary: Reproducing a data analysis from its code does not reveal the sequence of decisions behind the result, since code mixes decisions with implementation details and manuscripts scatter or omit them. The authors propose a schema that represents an analysis as a collection of natural-language decisions from which large language models (LLMs) generate and validate analysis scripts, and which can expand one analysis into a multiverse of alternatives specified in a separate file. In a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data, **the schema reproduces the reported estimates** and a reviewer-suggested alternative is turned into code automatically. In a second application to the many-analysts football study, where no schema is provided, the workflow serves as a reproducibility check.

papers.title: Temporal Exposure to Byzantine Vulnerability Under Intermittent Participation in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of participation variability on per-round Byzantine vulnerability. We formalise Dynamic Participation Exposure (DPE), a phenomenon in which the global Byzantine fraction remains below an aggregation rule's tolerance threshold, while a participating client set violates, or approaches violation of, the assumptions required for robust aggregation. Under stochastic participation, we derive the probability of per round exposure and analyse how active-set size affects the variability of the observed Byzantine fraction. We further examine the accumulation of exposure over multiple rounds and consider adversaries that selectively participate during favourable rounds. Our analysis shows that intermittent participation does not automatically imply aggregation failure. Rather, it transforms Byzantine robustness from a static population-level property into a stochastic and temporal property. To mitigate this risk, we outline actionable design recommendations based on minimum active-set constraints, temporal monitoring, participation history, and adaptive aggregation.
papers.summary: Federated learning with intermittent client participation can expose individual rounds to Byzantine clients even when the overall Byzantine fraction stays below an aggregation rule's tolerance threshold. The authors formalise this as Dynamic Participation Exposure (`DPE`), derive the per-round exposure probability under stochastic participation, and analyse how active-set size affects variability in the observed Byzantine fraction, how exposure accumulates over rounds, and how adversaries can selectively join favourable rounds. They conclude that intermittent participation does not automatically break aggregation but **turns Byzantine robustness from a static population-level property into a stochastic and temporal one**. Recommended mitigations include minimum active-set constraints, temporal monitoring, participation history, and adaptive aggregation.

papers.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
papers.abstract: A network architecture is, in large part, a symmetry assumption: convolution ties weights across translations, attention ties them across permutations, and a fully connected layer ties nothing. When the data are only approximately symmetric, tying trades approximation error against estimation error, and the right amount of tying is a property of the dataset, not of the architecture alone. We study this trade-off in an exactly solvable model: linear maps on signals over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$, with architectures indexed by the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_d$, so that a single integer $k \mid d$ interpolates between an unconstrained layer ($k=1$, $d^2$ parameters) and a fully equivariant one ($k=d$, $d$ parameters). We derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form, show that for a generic symmetry defect the leading-order risk is affine in $1/k$, and prove that intermediate architectures are then never strictly optimal: the lattice collapses to an all-or-nothing choice with phase boundary $n^\star = \sigma^2 d(d-1)/\varepsilon^2$. Structured defects break this collapse and restore interior optima, and we give a closed-form defect profile for a graded defect. Measurements agree with the theory on $60/60$ cells of a $(\varepsilon,n)$ phase diagram and $48/48$ cells of a second phase diagram at $d=16$, recover the predicted exponent as $-1.92$ against $-2$, and exhibit the predicted $k^\star: 12 \to 4 \to 1$ ladder under graded defects; a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover. We also characterize when the affine collapse survives for non-abelian groups.
papers.summary: Weight tying in a network architecture encodes a symmetry assumption, and when data are only approximately symmetric the amount of tying trades approximation error against estimation error. The authors study this in an exactly solvable model of linear maps on signals over a cyclic group, where a single integer indexing a subgroup interpolates between an unconstrained layer and a fully equivariant one, and derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form. For a generic symmetry defect they prove that **intermediate architectures are never strictly optimal, so the choice collapses to all-or-nothing** with an explicit sample-size phase boundary, while structured defects restore interior optima. Experiments match the theory on 60 of 60 and 48 of 48 cells of two phase diagrams, and a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover.

papers.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
papers.abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.
papers.summary: Political discourse in the Bundesrat, Germany's second legislative chamber made up of state government delegates, has been hard to study because little of it is available in machine-readable form. The authors present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 plenary sessions from 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026, containing **53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals**, including written statements. Each speech carries the full German text plus the speaker's name, federal state, role, gender, contribution type, and session date and location.

papers.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem
papers.summary: Memory systems for long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents often index history by having a generative model rewrite it into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs, which is costly, non-deterministic, and discards the original turns. `MGMem` replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline that organizes recurring mentions across sessions into an incidence graph, resolves question mentions with a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and returns raw dialogue episodes to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue question answering, it **outperforms matched-protocol baselines on `LoCoMo` with no generative indexing calls**, and on the full `LongMemEval-S` it stays competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session question types among local retrieval comparisons.

papers.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
papers.abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.
papers.summary: Transformer-based automated writing scorers agree well with human scores but reveal little about which response characteristics drive their predictions. Using about 12,700 Grade 6 and 8 English Language Arts responses per prompt and `DeBERTa-v3-base` models for Expression and Conventions, the study represents each response with 61 interpretable linguistic features and compares four ways of reproducing the model's predictions before interpreting feature importance. Random Forest surrogates were the most faithful, with **held-out R2 from .81 to .95**, and SHAP analyses showed that 75% to 90% of the top 20 features were shared across traits, which differed mainly in relative weighting. Under researcher-defined mappings, correspondence with the rubric was 90%-95% for Expression but only 12%-18% for Conventions.

papers.title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.
papers.summary: Duration perception from audio in multimodal language models is measured against a human baseline using a psychophysics-style task: recognising a melody as it is progressively slowed down. Of 21 models tested, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples, and **only seven recognise melodies reliably once examples are given**, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited, since recognition peaks shift with the speed of the in-context examples, melody titles bias predictions, and supplying scientific pitch notation does not stop accuracy from declining at long note durations for most models. The authors conclude that the recognition window is largely a property of the prompt in current models, not of the perceiver as in humans.

papers.title: Geophysics-informed invertible operator network for Bayesian geophysical inversion
papers.abstract: Geophysical inverse problems are inherently ill-posed because of sparse observations and measurement noise. Classical sampling-based Bayesian inference methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), are computationally prohibitive because they require many forward simulations. Data-driven machine-learning methods often struggle to produce physically consistent solutions when training data are limited. To address these issues, we propose a geophysics-informed invertible operator network (GI-ION) that integrates an invertible neural network (INN) within a deep operator-learning framework for efficient Bayesian geophysical inversion. The INN serves as the branch network and transforms the model parameters into branch coefficients that represent the forward solution and a latent variable that captures uncertainty in the inverse problem. By learning the forward operator and enforcing statistical independence between the branch coefficients and the latent variable, GI-ION enables efficient sampling from a learned conditional approximation, even with sparse boundary observations. We validated GI-ION on three representative cases: 1D surface-wave dispersion and travel-time tomography for a 2D synthetic random-field model and a seismic-slice model. Numerical experiments demonstrate robust performance across diverse problem settings and efficient conditional sampling.
papers.summary: Bayesian inversion in geophysics is ill-posed and expensive, since sampling methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) require many forward simulations while data-driven models struggle with physical consistency when training data are limited. The geophysics-informed invertible operator network (`GI-ION`) places an invertible neural network (INN) inside a deep operator-learning framework as the branch network, mapping model parameters to coefficients that represent the forward solution and to a latent variable that captures uncertainty. By learning the forward operator and enforcing statistical independence between coefficients and latent variable, it **enables efficient sampling from a learned conditional approximation even with sparse boundary observations**. Validation covers 1D surface-wave dispersion and travel-time tomography on a 2D synthetic random-field model and a seismic-slice model.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Mesoscopic Emission Modeling
papers.abstract: Traffic-related emissions are a major contributor to urban air pollution. However, existing emission models face a fundamental trade-off: macroscopic models are computationally efficient but rely on average speeds, leading to systematic errors, while microscopic models achieve high accuracy but are computationally prohibitive for large scale simulations. To bridge this gap, this study introduces Direct Emission Prediction (DEP), a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based deep learning model. DEP was trained on over one million synthetic trips generated by coupling real-world GNSS speed profiles with the microscopic emission model MOBSim. By processing sequential link-level inputs, including vehicle characteristics, road attributes, and ambient temperature, DEP predicts CO$_2$ and NOx emissions. We integrated DEP into a MATSim-based workflow and applied it to the Ile-de-France region. DEP matches the accuracy of SPG-M, a hybrid mesoscopic-microscopic reference model, within 0.35% for CO$_2$ and 1.87% for NOx across both hot and cold-start scenarios, while reducing computational runtime to just 2.2%. Furthermore, validation against empirical remote sensing data confirms that DEP accurately reproduces real-world NOx emission levels across Euro 2-6 diesel vehicles, whereas traditional macroscopic tools like COPERT and HBEFA systematically underestimate them. Finally, DEP effectively captures the spatial distribution of cold-start emissions, identifying key hotspots in dense urban areas. This work demonstrates that deep learning-based mesoscopic frameworks can achieve microscopic accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling scalable, high-resolution urban emission modeling without relying on pre-computed emission factor databases.
papers.summary: Traffic emission models trade speed for accuracy: macroscopic models rely on average speeds and err systematically, while microscopic models are too slow for large simulations. Direct Emission Prediction (`DEP`) is a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model trained on over one million synthetic trips, built by coupling real GNSS speed profiles with the microscopic emission model `MOBSim`, that predicts CO2 and NOx from link-level sequences of vehicle, road, and temperature inputs. Integrated into a `MATSim` workflow for the Ile-de-France region, it matches the hybrid reference model `SPG-M` within 0.35% for CO2 and 1.87% for NOx while **cutting computational runtime to 2.2%**. Against remote sensing data it reproduces real-world NOx levels for Euro 2-6 diesel vehicles, which `COPERT` and `HBEFA` systematically underestimate.

papers.title: Neighbor Crowding Predicts Feature Stability in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer an approach to identify language model representations by breaking apart polysemantic features into more sparse, interpretable ones. Yet, it is challenging to identify which of the learned features are actually stable, rather than artifacts of initialization. One approach is to train multiple SAE seeds, and compare the learned features across seeds by cosine similarity, but this is notably costly. This raises the question of whether stable features can be identified without the computational expense of training multiple seeds. In this work, we examine cross-seed feature stability across differing levels of training tokens, and demonstrate that in TopK SAEs, it is highly predictable using six computationally cheap statistics derived from a single training run. Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is the strongest single predictor, with features that sit in dense regions of the unit sphere more likely to be stable than isolated ones.
papers.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model representations into sparser, more interpretable features, but telling stable features from initialization artifacts normally requires training several seeds and comparing features by cosine similarity. The authors examine cross-seed stability at different amounts of training tokens and show that in `TopK` SAEs it is highly predictable from six cheap statistics computed on a single training run. **Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is the strongest single predictor**: features in dense regions of the unit sphere are more likely to be stable than isolated ones.

papers.title: REI: Learning Ideation from Repository Evolution
papers.abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable of executing and evaluating experiments, ideation is emerging as a bottleneck in automated scientific and engineering iteration. In many real-world domains, useful ideas are sparse and their validation is costly, making direct online exploration inefficient. We observe that repository evolution provides a scalable source of reusable technical experience: code changes record concrete technical hypotheses, while subsequent revisions, adoption, and reuse provide signals about their utility. Based on this observation, we propose REI, a Repository Evolution-driven Ideation framework that learns reusable ideation policies from repository evolution, injecting domain-specific technical experience into model parameters and reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error. We further identify a hidden failure mode in quality-driven ideation optimization: semantic diversity collapse. Although generated ideas can remain lexically diverse, they increasingly concentrate in a small number of dominant method families, limiting cross-task generalization and long-tail exploration. To address this problem, we introduce Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing (SPOD), a diversity-preserving alignment mechanism that makes method identity explicit, corrects category-level reward bias, and limits redundant accumulation within the same method family while retaining strong representatives. Experiments on public benchmarks and a real-world industrial setting demonstrate improvements in ideation quality, method diversity, cross-task generalization, and long-tail exploration.
papers.summary: Idea generation is treated here as a bottleneck for automated scientific and engineering iteration, since useful ideas are sparse and costly to validate. `REI`, a Repository Evolution-driven Ideation framework, learns ideation policies from repository history, treating code changes as technical hypotheses and later revisions, adoption, and reuse as signals of their utility. The authors identify a failure mode in quality-driven optimization where **generated ideas stay lexically diverse but concentrate in a few dominant method families**, and counter it with Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing (`SPOD`), which makes method identity explicit, corrects category-level reward bias, and limits redundancy within a family. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial setting report gains in ideation quality, method diversity, cross-task generalization, and long-tail exploration.

papers.title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
papers.abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.
papers.summary: Repeated updates to an LLM agent's persistent textual memory can erode task performance, and this study tests whether statistics of the memory store give warning before held-out accuracy declines. The authors registered mean pairwise cosine similarity and 13 other geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across `ALFWorld`, `AppWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, `WebShop`, and two `ARC-AGI` settings, and found that none reliably predicted early accuracy decline. Classifiers trained on this corpus and applied unchanged to `PropWorld` runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks **falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from stable size-limited stores and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero**. Size-limited stores stayed stable in those runs, and the one failure came from unbounded whole-store prompting exceeding the model's input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

papers.title: One Neural Operator for Re-planning Low-Thrust Cislunar Transfers after Thrust Outages, at the Original or a Later Arrival
papers.abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.
papers.summary: Missed-thrust margin studies for electric-propulsion missions require thousands of exact re-plans of a trajectory after simulated thrust outages. A neural operator is trained to map a nominal trajectory plus an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and a probability that recovery exists, over 270 low-thrust transfers from near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) with an arrival slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers with zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is **1.20% versus 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner**, and it predicts recoverability with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997. Ensemble spread tracks actual error closely enough that exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages cut 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%.

papers.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
papers.abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.
papers.summary: Tuning the configuration of AI systems under a limited budget depends heavily on the decision strategy the tuner uses, and the study asks whether a general-purpose decision model can fill that role. Using `Jev` as a deployed representative, the authors test it as an optimizer, a performance predictor, and a region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight tuning tasks. **Conventional optimizers rank first in six of eight comparisons** and established predictors beat `Jev` in seven, but as a region guider it finds configurations with lower perplexity than the native tuner, at the cost of extra decision time and API fees.

papers.title: Dynamics of Collective Diversity in Human-AI Co-Creation for Creative Tasks
papers.abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed at scale to support human users in creative tasks across a variety of domains. However, as more users adopt the same AI agent, the resulting artifacts may become increasingly homogeneous, leading to a collapse in collective diversity. Prior work has documented this risk, but lacks a systematic framework for understanding how collective diversity changes as AI adoption scales across co-creation settings. In this work, we conduct a large-scale crowdsourcing study to understand and model the dynamics of collective diversity, quality, and effort in human-AI co-creation across two creative domains: Creative Hypothesis Generation and Creative Story Writing. We find that current AI agents used in co-creation can improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but at the cost of declining collective diversity as adoption increases. We further show that more fine-grained human-AI interaction, along with more diverse agent policies, can mitigate this collapse. Finally, we fit predictive models that quantify how collective diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings, providing insights for designing AI agents that aim to preserve collective diversity.
papers.summary: When many people use the same generative AI agent for creative work, their outputs may converge, and prior work lacks a systematic account of how this scales with adoption. A large crowdsourcing study measures collective diversity, quality, and effort in human-AI co-creation across creative hypothesis generation and creative story writing. Current agents improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but **collective diversity declines as adoption increases**; finer-grained human-AI interaction and more diverse agent policies mitigate the collapse. Fitted predictive models quantify how diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings.

papers.title: Formalization, Transparency, and Collusion in Open-Source Game Theory
papers.abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.
papers.summary: Collusion among AI agents can undermine alignment protocols, and whether agents collude may depend on how much they know about each other. The work builds formal foundations for open-source game theory, where programs read each other's source code and act on what they can prove: it specifies a concrete proof system, resolves an open problem about `DupocBot` and `CupodBot`, and mechanizes the resource-bounded framework in `Lean 4`. Extending the setting to partial transparency, Prisoner's Dilemma experiments show that **greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics**.

papers.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
papers.abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.
papers.summary: Large language models used as materials-property predictors usually trail specialized models and do not learn from the outcomes of their own predictions. `MatMemBench` is a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after each prediction, testing online adaptation, memory retention, and cross-task transfer. The accompanying `MatRecall` framework stores verified predictions with their evidence, outcome, and error as episodes and recalls them without retraining. It **improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model**, beat specialized models on 11 tasks, stayed useful after feedback stopped, and transferred between related tasks.

papers.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
papers.summary: Borrowing from Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), which separates the load from task difficulty from the load caused by how information is presented, the authors isolate presentation effects in large language models (LLMs). `CogLoadBench` varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families, and higher extraneous load often reduces accuracy by adding competing information or complicating the reasoning path. An activation-based metric computed at prompt time, the Extraneous Load Score (`ELS`), estimates this load and generalizes across task types and load levels. **Shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time improves average performance without changing the prompt**.

papers.title: UniMoE-CP: Unified Conditional Waveform Prediction Across Measured Optical Wireless Links
papers.abstract: Shared prediction across measured optical wireless links requires a common model to accommodate link-dependent waveform dynamics. This paper studies unified learning for underwater optical, 100-m visible-light communication and 4.3-km free-space optical links. We formulate received-waveform forecasting from historical observations and known future transmitted excitation using one shared parameter set. UniMoE-CP combines a shared pool of temporal experts, window-dependent routing and spectral covariate fusion with an autoregressive decoder. The design permits conditional specialization while reusing expert parameters across the measured links. Pooled-training benchmarks evaluate each link separately and report an aggregated result using normalized mean square error (NMSE) and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE). The reported average NMSE reductions are 29.9% for 100-m VLC, 29.1% underwater and 21.4% for 4.3-km FSO. The aggregated average NMSE decreases from 0.1645 for the best baseline to 0.1178 for UniMoE-CP.
papers.summary: A single shared model is trained to forecast received waveforms across three measured optical wireless links: underwater optical, 100-m visible-light communication, and 4.3-km free-space optical. `UniMoE-CP` predicts the waveform from past observations and the known future transmitted signal, combining a shared pool of temporal experts, window-dependent routing, and spectral covariate fusion with an autoregressive decoder. In pooled training, the **aggregated average normalized mean square error (NMSE) falls from 0.1645 for the best baseline to 0.1178**, with per-link NMSE reductions between 21.4% and 29.9%.

papers.title: Adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network for drug-drug interaction prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is essential for drug safety in combination therapy. Multimodal methods built on knowledge graphs (KGs) already combine molecular structures, substructures, targets and biomedical relations into drug representations, but they still face three problems: features are heterogeneous across modalities, fusion does not adapt to individual drug pairs, and modality-specific information is diluted during integration. We propose the adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network (AARME-GNN) to address them. A Feature Adaptive Calibration Module (FACM) reduces within-modality noise in each representation through bottleneck reparameterization and channelwise recalibration before fusion. A Multimodal Weight Router (MMWR) then sets the modality weights of each drug pair, with an entropy constraint that prevents the weights from collapsing onto one modality. A Routing-Aware Weighted Distillation (RAWD) mechanism builds a soft target from the unimodal branches, so that the fusion classifier retains the knowledge held by each modality. On Dataset 1, AARME-GNN improves precision over MKG-FENN by 3.71 and 6.57 percentage points in known drug and known new drug prediction, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by 4.53 in new drug prediction. On Dataset 2, the advantage is concentrated in the two cold-start settings and in precision.
papers.summary: Knowledge-graph-based multimodal predictors of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) suffer from heterogeneous features, fusion that does not adapt to each drug pair, and dilution of modality-specific information. `AARME-GNN` addresses these with a calibration module that denoises each modality before fusion, a router that sets per-pair modality weights under an entropy constraint, and a distillation mechanism that builds soft targets from the unimodal branches. On the first dataset it **improves precision over `MKG-FENN` by 3.71 and 6.57 percentage points** in two prediction settings and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by 4.53 in new drug prediction; on the second dataset the gains are concentrated in the cold-start settings and in precision.

papers.title: The AI Disclosure Paradox: Operational Disclosure and the Rise of Corporate AI Narratives
papers.abstract: AI-related corporate disclosure can expand while becoming less concentrated on current use. Across U.S. SEC filings from 2017 to 2025, AI-related passage intensity increased 6.3-fold between 2017-2022 and 2023-2025, whereas corrected operational-disclosure intensity increased 3.3-fold. The operational share fell from 25.76% to 13.45%; approximately 89% of the net increase in passage intensity fell outside the operational category. The decline persists within sectors and filing types and in 10-K-only analysis. These estimates combine frozen language-model predictions for 26,279 AI-related passages with an audit of 1,000 annotated passages. The findings distinguish growth in organizational attention from growth in implementation-specific claims: more operational disclosure can coexist with a substantially lower operational share. Operational disclosure was thus diluted, not displaced, by nonoperational disclosure. Reading corporate technology narratives therefore requires attention to both disclosure intensity and the organizational state described.
papers.summary: U.S. SEC filings from 2017 to 2025 are analyzed to separate how much companies talk about AI from how much they describe actual current use. Combining frozen language-model predictions on 26,279 AI-related passages with an audit of 1,000 annotated ones, the study finds AI-related passage intensity rose 6.3-fold between 2017-2022 and 2023-2025 while operational disclosure rose only 3.3-fold. The **operational share fell from 25.76% to 13.45%**, with about 89% of the net increase falling outside the operational category, a pattern that holds within sectors and filing types. Operational disclosure was therefore diluted rather than displaced by nonoperational narrative.

papers.title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has long relied on non- or weakly informative priors, on the assumption that the information needed for an informative one is rarely available. In genetics and systems biology, annotation databases now make it possible to assemble a prior DAG before learning from data. Existing informative priors are local: they score a DAG arc by arc and cannot encode how interventions propagate along its paths. Thus, we propose the local-global energy prior (LGE), a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines a local divergence from the prior DAG, the Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal one, the Structural Intervention Distance. We derive rules to calibrate its decay and the weight of the two divergences from the prior DAG alone. We quantify how much prior mass stays on the true DAG, and how much data overturn the prior, when the prior DAG is partially incorrect. In simulations, LGE improves both the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the corresponding Bayesian networks to the true distribution over non- and weakly informative priors, even when half of the arcs of the prior DAG are wrong. We also showcase LGE on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.
papers.summary: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) typically uses uninformative priors, and existing informative priors score a graph arc by arc without capturing how interventions propagate along paths. The local-global energy prior (`LGE`) is a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines the Structural Hamming Distance and the Structural Intervention Distance from a prior DAG, with calibration rules derived from the prior DAG alone. In simulations it **improves structural accuracy and distributional fit over non- and weakly informative priors even when half of the prior DAG's arcs are wrong**, and it is demonstrated on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.

papers.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
papers.abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
papers.summary: Language-model-generated Python for programmable logic controllers can import real, existing packages that are nonetheless wrong for the declared vendor or industrial protocol, a failure that existence-based checks miss. `Proteus-OT` is a label-free static verifier that checks imports against a version-pinned graph of documented vendor-protocol bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, **180 (20.4%) carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target**, and 96.6% of mismatching scripts in a balanced subset use only packages and methods that exist. A companion audit shows machine-versus-human classifiers on the same corpus reach perfect scores from artifacts such as a trailing newline, so they measure repository provenance rather than authorship.

papers.title: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA: Equilibrium Selection via Gradual Adaptation
papers.abstract: We introduce Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modification of Decentralized Q-learning in which agents maintain persistent exploration and update their acting Q-values gradually rather than switching directly to newly learned best responses when updating. We prove convergence to $\epsilon$-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. We then show, in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, that soft updating can reshape basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set. In the deterministic limit, we derive analytical basin bounds governed by the Q-value differences between actions in the target policies and show that reducing the policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria. These results suggest that soft updating is not merely a stabilization device but also a mechanism of equilibrium selection in decentralized learning.
papers.summary: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (`SDES`) modifies decentralized Q-learning so that agents keep exploring persistently and move their acting Q-values gradually instead of jumping to newly learned best responses. The authors prove convergence to epsilon-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. In the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, they show that **soft updating reshapes basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set**, and derive analytical basin bounds showing that a lower policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria.

papers.title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
papers.summary: Discrete skill vocabularies for long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) are usually built by clustering or reconstructing actions, which yields skills unrelated to what the state affords or the goal requires. The proposed quantization of action chunks instead optimizes next-state prediction conditioned on the current state and action, so skills are distinguished by the future states they lead to. The resulting vocabulary plugs into common offline RL methods by swapping the continuous actor head for a discrete one, with a trained low-level controller converting skills back to continuous actions. On benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks it shows **largely substantial and consistent improvements over continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations**.

papers.title: How Many Samples Is RL Worth? Best-of-N versus RL Post-Training for Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) on a reward that can be checked automatically has become a common last step in the training of text-to-image models. A simpler way to get more correct images is best-of-N: draw N images from the base model and keep the one that a picker prefers. We ask how many base model samples one RL sample is worth, and call this number the exchange rate. We measure it for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and its public Flow-GRPO checkpoint on 398 new prompts in the style of GenEval, the benchmark behind the RL reward, with human labels on every prompt and two automatic judges other than the reward. The answer depends on the prompt. Four fifths of the prompts do not ask for a position (for example, one object left of another). On these, the base model catches up: best-of-16 with an off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) as the picker is about as good as one RL image. A person who looks through up to 3 base images finds a correct one as often as one RL image is correct. On the prompts that ask for a position, RL is far ahead: a person finds a correct image among 8 base images for only 52% of the prompts, against 92% for one RL image. Over all prompts, our primary test, which we fixed in advance, finds best-of-16 with the VLM picker 9.3 points behind one RL image when both automatic judges must pass an image. People see a smaller gap, 5.5 and 6.5 points in two checks. FLUX.1-dev shows a similar gap in the same test. RL also solves 20 prompts that the base model misses in 128 tries, and 1,024 tries recover half of them. The automatic judges are wrong in opposite directions: a detector-based judge like the reward, as used in our primary test, reports a larger gap than people see, and VLM judges report little or none. Comparisons of RL with best-of-N should therefore check the selected images by hand.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of text-to-image models is compared against simply drawing N samples from the base model and keeping the best, measuring how many base samples one RL sample is worth. Using `Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium` and its `Flow-GRPO` checkpoint on 398 new `GenEval`-style prompts with human labels, the answer depends on the prompt: on the four fifths of prompts without a spatial relation, best-of-16 with a vision-language model (VLM) picker roughly matches one RL image. On position prompts, **a person finds a correct image among 8 base samples for only 52% of prompts versus 92% for a single RL image**. Automatic judges err in opposite directions, with detector-based judges overstating the gap and VLM judges reporting little or none, so selected images should be checked by hand.

papers.title: Diagnostically Meaningful, Privacy-aware Synthetic Chest CT via Class-Conditional Latent Sampling in Diffusion Autoencoders
papers.abstract:
Large, well-annotated datasets are essential for developing medical artificial intelligence models, yet data sharing is often restricted by privacy regulations. Synthetic images may help address this limitation if they preserve diagnostic information while reducing the risk of reproducing patient data. We developed a diffusion autoencoder-based framework for class-conditional synthetic chest CT generation that incorporates latent-space distance filtering to reduce the likelihood of regenerating training samples.
  A diffusion autoencoder was trained on the public RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) dataset. PE-positive and PE-negative images were synthesized by sampling latent representations from class-specific kernel density estimates. Samples with a nearest-neighbor latent-space distance below a predefined threshold were rejected. To assess diagnostic utility, ResNet-50 classifiers were trained across 10 independent runs using real, synthetic, or mixed real-synthetic datasets. Performance was evaluated on a held-out real test set using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
  Models trained on synthetic data achieved an AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.851-0.874), only slightly lower than models trained on real data (AUC = 0.872, 95% CI, 0.861-0.883) and mixed real-synthetic data (AUC = 0.865, 95% CI, 0.855-0.876). These differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) but small in absolute terms. A nearest-neighbor copy-detection analysis of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of real training images.
  These findings indicate that the synthetic CT images preserve diagnostically meaningful information for image-level PE classification while incorporating measures intended to enhance privacy awareness and reduce similarity to real patient data.
papers.summary: Privacy rules restrict sharing of medical images, so the authors generate class-conditional synthetic chest CT with a diffusion autoencoder trained on the `RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism` dataset. Latents are sampled from class-specific kernel density estimates, and samples too close to a training latent are rejected to avoid reproducing patient data. `ResNet-50` classifiers trained only on synthetic data reach an **area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.862 versus 0.872 for real data**, and a nearest-neighbor check of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of training images.

papers.title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $\Delta W$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters.
