The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.
papers.summary: Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods cap the update rank far below full fine-tuning and use the same rank for every input. `KiRA` instead forms the weight update as a Kronecker product of a frozen random p-by-p matrix and a trainable factor, which multiplies rank by p at no parameter cost, and adds a shared input gate that adjusts the update's rank per sample in steps of p. Because the gate changes rank discretely, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs, and the gate can be folded away at deployment when unneeded. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks it attains the highest mean score against five baselines with **8.7 to 9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation**.

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Early Rice Blast Forecasting in Sustainable Agriculture
papers.abstract: Resource-efficient artificial intelligence has become increasingly important for sustainable agriculture, where timely disease forecasting must be achieved under computational and energy constraints. Early estimation of rice blast can enhance food security by optimizing crop management practices while reducing excessive pesticide use. However, existing frameworks often suffer from high computational overhead and limited capability to model the complex spectral-temporal dependencies present in heterogeneous meteorological and remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a lightweight multimodal fusion framework comprising an attentive positional encoding-based Transformer and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-embedded gated recurrent unit (GRU) for efficient spectral-temporal representation learning. The attention-enhanced positional encoding assigns adaptive importance to sequential meteorological tokens, enabling effective modelling of temporal characteristics. In parallel, the lightweight CNN extracts discriminative spectral features, while the GRU captures temporal dynamics from remote sensing imagery acquired over two time-instances. A multimodal fusion layer integrates these heterogeneous representations to forecast rice blast risk 5-10 days before symptom manifestation across diverse agro-climatic zones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a validation accuracy of 96.93% and an F1-score of 95.79%. In addition to its predictive performance, the lightweight multimodal architecture substantially reduces computational complexity, inference latency, and carbon emissions, making it an energy-efficient solution for large-scale disease forecasting. The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for resource-efficient artificial intelligence in sustainable agriculture.
papers.summary: Forecasting rice blast disease early enough to act requires modelling heterogeneous weather and remote sensing data under tight compute and energy limits. The proposed lightweight multimodal framework pairs a Transformer with attention-enhanced positional encoding for meteorological sequences with a convolutional neural network (CNN) embedded in a gated recurrent unit (GRU) for two-date remote sensing imagery, then fuses them to predict risk 5-10 days before symptoms appear. It reports a **validation accuracy of 96.93% and an F1-score of 95.79%**, along with lower computational complexity, inference latency, and carbon emissions than competing methods.

papers.title: Sequential Testing on Complex and High Dimensional Data Streams Leveraging Unsupervised Model Errors
papers.abstract: We propose two general, distribution-free test statistics for binary Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) respectively, in streaming environments where the data (e.g., network traffic metadata) are too complicated for the exact probabilistic modeling required by conventional likelihood ratio-driven tests. Our framework also addresses the challenge of information asymmetry, where data is available only from the null/pre-change regime and not from the alternative/post-change one such as zero-day attacks or emerging disease related regimes. The proposed statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive machine learning model trained solely on null/pre-change data, relying on imperfect generalization (the model's performance will degrade when deployed on data from the alternative/post-change class). Under mild assumptions on the model's errors, we establish rigorous analytical guarantees: strict non-asymptotic error control for SHT, and explicit bounds on the Average Run Length (ARL) and the Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD. Extensive evaluations in target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world network security datasets, demonstrate that our framework consistently satisfies prescribed constraints where existing algorithms succumb to inflated missed detections and/or false alarms. Finally, because our methods operate on scalar errors without requiring online retraining or kernel evaluations, they are highly scalable.
papers.summary: Two distribution-free test statistics are proposed for Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) on data streams too complex for likelihood-ratio tests, where data exist only from the null or pre-change regime. The statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive model trained solely on that regime, relying on its performance degrading on the alternative. Under mild assumptions on the errors, the authors prove **non-asymptotic error control for SHT and explicit bounds on Average Run Length (ARL) and Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD**. Evaluations on target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and network security datasets show the prescribed constraints are met where existing algorithms produce inflated missed detections or false alarms.

papers.title: Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
papers.abstract: Educational recommenders are usually compared offline, by how well they predict the next activity in logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, where the next activity is largely decided by the platform: teachers assign problem sets, tutors draw problems until mastery, engines select questions. On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.
papers.summary: Offline evaluation of educational recommenders scores next-activity prediction on platform logs, where the next activity is mostly chosen by the platform rather than the learner. On eight public datasets from five platforms, four structural predictors that know only the last activity reach **between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95)**, compared with ten personalised recommenders and open-weight LLM rankers of 0.5 to 7 billion parameters. The LLM rankers never much exceed a word-matching baseline and stay near random against structurally plausible negatives, and a simulation shows offline accuracy ranking an oracle of learner needs below imitators of the platform. Reweighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link to usefulness, and the authors release an evaluation checklist and Python package.

papers.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.
papers.summary: Failures in large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems are hard to attribute because benchmarks entangle communication with open-domain reasoning. `CypherMAS` is a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing: agents arranged in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs must route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders, and because the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls and routing failures can be measured directly. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B parameters, **small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade as graph diameter grows, and even successful runs exceed the minimum number of LLM calls**.

papers.title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.
papers.summary: Machine-learning malware detectors are stress-tested here with the Adversarial AI Engine (`AAIE`), a platform for automated adversarial security auditing. Transfer attacks built on `EMBER2018` and aimed at a `Random Forest` target showed that **single-step `FGSM` reached a 52.9% attack success rate versus 45.2% for iterative `PGD`** (p < 0.002), which the authors attribute to iterative attacks overfitting the surrogate network and producing brittle perturbations. Attacks are also scored by transferability score, evasion rate, and a resilience index, with transferability peaking at about 0.8 under constrained perturbations.

papers.title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
papers.abstract:
The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain).
  Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined).
  We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal.
  Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.
papers.summary: The chest-pain variable in the widely used `UCI Heart Disease` benchmark is shown to be stored in reverse of its documentation: the code documented as asymptomatic actually marks typical angina patients, at all four collection sites. The evidence is that the original 1986 Cleveland study's table and regression coefficients reproduce only under the corrected reading, and that 93-96% of patients coded 4 at the other sites have all three classical angina features. In an audit of `SHAP` studies of the data, **25 of 32 papers (78%) that state a direction for a named category contradict the corrected identities**, and none of 124 readable papers identifies the reversal. Conventional models are essentially unaffected, but label-based interpretations are reversed and three open-weight zero-shot language-model classifiers lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) when given the documented labels.

papers.title: FERRETS: A Scalable Symbolic Transform for Time Series Classification
papers.abstract: Dictionary methods for time series build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. Against other families of methods, their accuracy no longer pays for their cost. We present FERRETS, a label-free dictionary transform built on WEASEL~2. It keys windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a level word of each window's mean and spread, and on multivariate data adds cross-channel words. We compare it with leading classifiers, deep networks and foundation models included, on the UCR, Multiverse and MONSTER archives. FERRETS is the fastest of the eleven methods timed on UCR under a ten-thread budget. Of the ten others, only MultiRocket-Hydra is significantly more accurate, taking 24.7 times as long. FERRETS is not significantly different from WEASEL~2, the most accurate earlier dictionary method, which takes 125 times as long, and is significantly ahead of the other dictionary methods. On the Multiverse core, it is not significantly different in accuracy from HIVE-COTE~2 and MultiRocket-Hydra, though behind both on UCR. It is also significantly more accurate than five frozen foundation models on UCR's published split. On the MONSTER problems both complete, MiniRocket takes 3.7 times as long to fit as the streaming FERRETS classifier, which is significantly more accurate.
papers.summary: Dictionary methods for time series classification build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. `FERRETS` is a label-free dictionary transform built on `WEASEL 2` that turns windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a word for each window's mean and spread, and adds cross-channel words for multivariate data. On the `UCR` archive it is the fastest of eleven timed methods and **statistically indistinguishable in accuracy from `WEASEL 2`, which takes 125 times as long**; only `MultiRocket-Hydra` is significantly more accurate, at 24.7 times the runtime. It also beats five frozen foundation models on `UCR` and matches `HIVE-COTE 2` and `MultiRocket-Hydra` on the `Multiverse` core, though it trails both on `UCR`.

papers.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
papers.abstract: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.
papers.summary: Text embedding models can treat surface similarity as factual identity, ranking a near-copy with one corrupted fact above a reworded but fact-preserving rewrite. The authors build `FOF-Bench`, an 83,263-triplet benchmark across five domains, and fine-tune `FOF-80M`, an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the altered copy. On held-out triplets the base model picks the factually altered text 99.58% of the time, and **fine-tuning raises the factual preference rate from 0.42% to only 29.37%**, although 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction. The model also penalizes omissions and transfers poorly to natural language inference and summarization, so the authors describe it as a soft factual fingerprint and not a general-purpose factuality metric.

papers.title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
papers.abstract: Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes a utility-focused approach to measuring polysemanticity by quantifying the decrease in interference-induced activation errors, which yields the practical utility of tighter prediction sets using Conformal Prediction (CP). We explicitly disentangle the polysemantic features of QPM into monosemantic concepts to create the Monosemantic QPM (MonoQPM). Because its features are disentangled, MonoQPM acts as a significantly more efficient Conformal Predictor. Additionally, we introduce CUBCars, a dataset providing ground truth information about shared concepts. Using this and other datasets, we demonstrate that polysemanticity emerges in QPM across all tested architectures, but is effectively alleviated by MonoQPM. For instance, MonoQPM guarantees 88% coverage using Adaptive Prediction Sets on ImageNet with just 66% of the frozen QPM's set size.
papers.summary: The Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (`QPM`) avoids superposition by representing classes with sparse binary assignments of a few features, yet its features remain polysemantic. The authors measure polysemanticity by its practical cost, namely interference-induced activation errors that loosen the prediction sets produced by Conformal Prediction, and split polysemantic features into monosemantic concepts to form `MonoQPM`. They also introduce `CUBCars`, a dataset with ground-truth information on shared concepts, and find polysemanticity in `QPM` across all tested architectures. On `ImageNet`, **`MonoQPM` guarantees 88% coverage with Adaptive Prediction Sets using just 66% of the frozen `QPM`'s set size**.

papers.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
papers.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.
papers.summary: Online conflict over generative AI is measured using 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, labelled by a large language model detector validated against human labels, plus the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Posts in communities devoted to the conflict are 30.0% toxic versus 4.4% in general AI communities, and the 3,312 identified anti-AI actions mainly target crawling and training data through image cloaking and data poisoning. Of code samples from a data-poisoning service, 66.5% contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet **93.6% pass a public code-curation pipeline, close to the 95.0% rate for real source code**. Crawler tarpit and poisoning output was also found in `Common Crawl`, and tarpit output in the `FineWeb` pretraining dataset.

papers.title: One Token, Many Lessons: Sliding-Window Attention within Gated Delta Networks
papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
papers.summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size recurrent state, which under the test-time regression (TTR) view is an online-learned regression model trained on key-value pairs. Instead of changing the state update rule, `SWGDN` (Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet) changes how those pairs are built, replacing the short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention that locally mixes projected queries, keys, and values by content. This makes the key-value pairs in consecutive updates more similar, letting the state reinforce associations it has already learned, and it leaves the update equations and chunkwise parallel algorithms untouched. Applied to the `GDN2` and `KDA` variants, **`SWGDN` outperforms the original Delta-Rule baselines across multiple benchmarks**.

papers.title: Fast and Scalable Abstract Interpretation for Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract:
Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together.
  We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications.
  We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out.
  Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git
papers.summary: Certifying properties of deep neural networks by abstract interpretation is expensive, partly because general implementations redo structural work for every input and property and interleave it with numerical operations. `Scepter` specializes an abstract interpreter to a fixed architecture by determining the structure of intermediate abstract values ahead of time and emitting a reusable tensor program, which is proven to compute the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. Evaluated on eight abstract interpreters and 44 networks against six baselines, it **handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest the baselines complete**, including `DeepPoly` on `ResNet50` and `VGG-16`. GPU geometric-mean speedups over `Neuton` range from 11.9x to 44.4x with a 2.60x reduction in peak memory.

papers.title: Same Tokenizer, Better Tokens: Choosing Image Tokens by MAP Inference
papers.abstract:
Discrete visual tokens encode images for reconstruction and serve as training targets for autoregressive image generators. Vector-quantized tokenizers typically assign each encoder feature its nearest code independently. The decoder uses these codes jointly, so a sequence of individually nearest codes can reconstruct an image less faithfully than an alternative assignment. A local model of the reconstruction loss yields a closest-vector problem with a decoder-dependent target and metric. Reconstruction-only search improves PSNR across the frozen tokenizers we test. Different code sequences can achieve similar reconstruction quality, leaving room to favour more predictable ones.
  We introduce RecaP (Reconstruction and Predictability), which selects codes for a frozen tokenizer by balancing how faithfully they reconstruct the image with how likely their sequence is under a pretrained autoregressive prior. On ImageNet, LlamaGen GPT-B trained on RecaP tokens achieves lower early-checkpoint FID against training images than GPT-B trained on nearest-neighbour tokens. The difference is smaller against held-out images. On an ImageNet subset, the prior improves generation at comparable reconstruction FID. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/recap
authors: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences
Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
{\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
papers.summary: Vector-quantized image tokenizers assign each encoder feature its nearest code independently, even though the decoder uses the codes jointly, so a different assignment can reconstruct the image more faithfully. `RecaP` (Reconstruction and Predictability) selects codes for a frozen tokenizer by balancing reconstruction fidelity against how likely the code sequence is under a pretrained autoregressive prior; reconstruction-only search already improves PSNR across the frozen tokenizers tested. On `ImageNet`, **`LlamaGen` `GPT-B` trained on `RecaP` tokens achieves lower early-checkpoint FID against training images than the same model trained on nearest-neighbour tokens**, with a smaller difference against held-out images.

papers.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.
papers.summary: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) can protect the weights of models deployed on edge devices from theft or manipulation, but their resource limits make running a full large network inside one impractical. `Onnx2TEE` is an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions `ONNX` models between the normal and trusted environments, using graph-aware segmentation of non-sequential feed-forward networks to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and added latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin with an Arm TrustZone TEE shows that **model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense components**. The trusted app's memory requirements depend on both the computation and the sizes of intermediate tensors.

papers.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
papers.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.
papers.summary: Guard models for mental health chatbots mostly classify harmful content categories without the context needed to choose a response. The authors propose a clinically grounded taxonomy that describes harm by what it is, who is involved, and when it occurs, and that separates harm characterization from intervention decisions so that safety policy lives in auditable clinician-written instructions outside the model weights. Relabeling public benchmarks shows they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which makes up nearly half of harm in real conversations. `MindGuard2`, a reasoning guard model trained with supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, **matches the balanced accuracy of the much larger `GLM-5.3` at roughly 10x lower median latency**.

papers.title: FrId\'eo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring
papers.abstract: Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrId\'eo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanit\'e on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.
papers.summary: Research on media framing and political communication uses outlet ideology as an explanatory variable, but France has lacked scores covering the whole press on one continuous scale. `FrIdéo` provides a composite score for 30 French news outlets by fusing nine independent families of evidence, with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. Its text-based component separates plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from qualified, distanced use, which bag-of-words methods miss, and it captures editorial change such as the Journal du Dimanche's rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. **The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single evidence family, and agrees with held-out `Media Bias Fact Check` labels**.

papers.title: JetDiffusion: Pushing the Speed Limits of Video Generation with NVFP4 Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.
papers.summary: Attention over long token sequences is the main computational bottleneck in video generation. `JetDiffusion` builds on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (`VSQA`) with custom inference kernels that combine native `NVFP4` computation and kernel fusion, giving 8-29x faster attention than `FlashAttention` at 90% sparsity. Combining sparsity with `NVFP4` linear quantization and step distillation required a staged training recipe to adapt stably to all three. On `Wan2.1-14B` the resulting model achieves a **273x end-to-end video generation speedup on an RTX 5090** with comparable video quality.

papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
papers.summary: How supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a restricted data distribution alters representations learned in pretraining is studied by pretraining transformers on the Random Hierarchy Model (`RHM`), a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, and then fine-tuning on a subset of its rules. **Generation of the deleted rules is suppressed on a fast timescale while their internal representations stay intact, and those representations are forgotten only much later** through a slow drift of the network parameters. The fast timescale is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation. Analogous results appear in a natural language setup, suggesting the separation is a general feature of fine-tuning language models.

papers.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
papers.abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.
papers.summary: Procedurally generated logic problems usually set difficulty by planting a proof of a chosen depth, but a problem may also admit shorter or unrelated proofs, so its stated depth can overstate what solving it requires. The authors compute, relative to a stated rule set, the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs, and the indispensable premises, and export certificates verified by an independent checker. Auditing eight datasets, they find that depth is forced in `ProofWriter` and `Blocksworld`, while **`FLDx2` problems labelled depth 5 require only about two specific rule applications** and `ZebraLogic` answers need no particular step. They then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, and mixtures of these certified problem types transfer better than `FLDx2`-style data when training `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 8B.

papers.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.
papers.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that AI models converge on a shared representation of the world across modalities; this work asks whether they also converge in how those representations affect outputs. Using the Jacobian lens, each word or class gets the hidden-state vector that most increases the model's tendency to produce it, and these vectors together form the model's J-space. **A single rotation fitted on a subset of words approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's**, generalizing to words and classes it was not fitted on, across vision and language models. A word vector rotated from a text-only language model changes the object a vision-language model reports in an image region, changes the object an image generator produces, and raises the matching class score in an `ImageNet` classifier trained without text.

papers.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
papers.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability per option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly, and they are ranked almost entirely in English. An evaluation of 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages finds that every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much, so that **a threshold set for 95% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil**. The loss depends on the language and base model, not leaderboard rank, and in 81 controlled fine-tuning runs a few thousand target-language items narrow large gaps without closing them. Test items translated by an LLM are answered more accurately than human-translated ones in all 23 benchmark-language pairs compared, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

papers.title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.
papers.summary: Merging many fine-tuned experts into one model reduces accuracy, and grouping is a middle ground in which the N experts are split into K groups at each layer and each task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Balanced Random Regrouping (`BRR`) independently draws equal-sized random groups at every layer or weight matrix, instead of keeping the same partners across layers or grouping similar experts. With validation-selected merge scales, **both `BRR` variants beat reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 `CLIP` settings, by 1.0-6.8 points**, and the per-matrix variant also beats the similarity-based `FlexMerge` in every setting. A first-order analysis attributes the gain to feature shifts that accumulate when partners are fixed but partly cancel when partners change, and it guides a grouping search that can outperform `BRR`.

papers.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
papers.abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.
papers.summary: Inline code suggestions in `GitHub Copilot` were previously served by separate completion, nearby-edit, and long-distance-edit models queried in a fixed sequence, which could not express one intent spanning distant locations and could need several model calls per suggestion. The replacement is a single model that predicts all three edit types as a sequence of anchored diff patches, allowing multiple edits per response that the client can serve from a cache. Training uses multi-edit supervision synthesized from single-edit data through pseudolabeling and edit history playback, with a binary LLM-graded reward and a shared patch validity taxonomy. In online A/B experiments, the first phase **cut output tokens by 58.93% and time to display by 6.77% relative to the three-model baseline**, and the full three-in-one model reduced dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06%.

papers.title: Large-scale Model Merging via Recovery-aware Task Weighting
papers.abstract: Model merging combines multiple task-specific expert models into a single model. However, merging preserves expert capabilities unevenly across tasks. This imbalance is particularly pronounced in large-scale settings, where some tasks can suffer severe capability losses even when average accuracy remains high. To address this imbalance, we introduce Recovery-aware Task Weighting (RaTW), a model merging framework that assigns larger weights to tasks whose expert capabilities are poorly retained by an initial merged model. We quantify these recovery opportunities as the fraction of a task's labeled validation samples that its expert predicts correctly but the initial merged model gets wrong, and use the resulting task weights to re-merge the experts. To evaluate merging at large scale, we construct CLIPMerge-100, a 100-task benchmark with task-specific experts on CLIP ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/32. Across eleven merging methods with 20, 50, and 100 tasks on two CLIP backbones, RaTW improves both mean accuracy and tail20 (the mean expert-normalized accuracy of the 20% worst-retained tasks) in all 33 ViT-L/14 settings and 32 of 33 ViT-B/32 settings. We further introduce ReForge++, which combines RaTW with iterative model refinement and outperforms all evaluated baselines, including a matched-budget control, in both mean accuracy and tail20 across all settings.
papers.summary: Model merging preserves expert capabilities unevenly, and at large scale some tasks lose most of their accuracy even when the average stays high. Recovery-aware Task Weighting (`RaTW`) re-merges the experts with larger weights for tasks the initial merged model retains poorly, measured as the fraction of validation samples the expert gets right but the merged model gets wrong. The authors also build `CLIPMerge-100`, a 100-task benchmark with experts on `CLIP` `ViT-L/14` and `ViT-B/32`. Across eleven merging methods at 20, 50, and 100 tasks, **`RaTW` improves both mean accuracy and the accuracy of the worst-retained 20% of tasks in all 33 `ViT-L/14` settings and 32 of 33 `ViT-B/32` settings**, and `ReForge++`, which adds iterative refinement, outperforms all evaluated baselines.

papers.title: What Does RL Post-Training Teach Text-to-Image Models? A Skill-Wise Analysis of Flow-GRPO
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become a standard way to improve text-to-image flow models: Flow-GRPO lifts the GenEval score of SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95, a gain read as the model having learned compositional generation. We ask how much of that gain the base model's own samples already contained, by measuring pass@k over shared noise seeds, one skill at a time, before and after RL, on prompts never used in training. The answer differs by skill. On four of GenEval's six skills, where 32 base samples already solve almost every prompt, the gain is sharpening: one post-trained sample is worth 4 to 10 base samples, and pass@32 barely moves. On spatial relations it is unlocking: pass@32 rises from 0.69 to 1.00, 128 base samples do not match one post-trained sample, and prompts the base model never solved in 32 samples are solved 93% of the time, as often as those it solved. The benchmark average, 31 base samples per post-trained sample, describes no skill. Relations carry 35% of the gain; of the other 65%, selecting among 8 base samples with the judge behind the reward recovers nine tenths. We propose an account of when each occurs: within a prompt, a group-relative update re-weights only the outcomes its samples contain, and a flow policy cannot widen the noise that produces them; across prompts, shared parameters let successes on some prompts repair a deficit common to many. The same anatomy applies to a text-rendering checkpoint. The account's predictions are tested with a checkpoint trained without KL, within-prompt diversity, and controlled training that holds object classes out, where sharpening comes first and transfers, and unlocking follows, on practised objects before unseen ones.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with `Flow-GRPO` raises the `GenEval` score of `SD3.5-M` from 0.63 to 0.95, and the authors ask how much of that gain was already present in the base model's own samples by measuring pass@k over shared noise seeds, one skill at a time, on held-out prompts. On four of the six skills the gain is sharpening: one post-trained sample is worth 4 to 10 base samples and pass@32 barely moves. On spatial relations it is unlocking: **pass@32 rises from 0.69 to 1.00 and 128 base samples do not match one post-trained sample**. They propose an account in which group-relative updates only re-weight outcomes already present within a prompt while shared parameters transfer successes across prompts, and test it with a checkpoint trained without KL and with controlled training that holds object classes out.

papers.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
papers.abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.
papers.summary: When evidence is spread across several LLM agents, the team can hold everything needed for a decision and still fail to use it. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, the authors study three requirements (sufficiency of what is conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of what is received) through theoretical benchmarks, controlled experiments, and message-level analyses. They find that **local probability reports can discard essential information, with the theoretical information loss closely matching the observed performance penalty**. Query-first interaction helps when the relevant evidence depends on a private query, though compact one-shot representations can remove that advantage, and agents may still fail to select or use information that was sufficiently communicated.

papers.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
papers.abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.
papers.summary: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly, so this audit measures recall and category accuracy separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On `Gemma 4 12B` without retrieval, category prompts elicit 51.0% of the brands, while a five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 of them. Among the 981 brands with separated rankings, **the error rate is 19.8%, falling to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6**. Recall across four Gemma generations is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%, and a representation-based sentiment measure shows almost no linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03).

papers.title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) adapt through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but on evolving data streams the context can become stale and rebuilding it is costly. `SAIL` is a sparse adaptation framework that **reuses the model's key-value cache between adaptation events and rebuilds the support set only when drift in the stream's structure suggests the context is inadequate**. It combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. On adaptation, the context budget is allocated in proportion to class mass and filled from the most recently updated micro-clusters.

papers.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
papers.abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.
papers.summary: Users who assume a chatbot has mental states are more prone to over-reliance and emotional dependence, yet how such mind attributions arise in conversation is poorly understood. The authors pair simulated users of varying characteristics with assistants that differ in social style and memory, and introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. **Nine of thirteen user characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant**, with relational needs such as attachment anxiety raising it as theory predicts and AI-specific characteristics raising it the least. The assistant's social style barely changed user attribution, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself, and results varied with the model playing the user.

papers.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
papers.abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.
papers.summary: Generative priors used to reconstruct medical images from incomplete measurements can erase the lesions that imaging is meant to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. Selective anchoring protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes while letting the generative model fill in unresolved structure, and is implemented as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as `AnchoredFM`, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and reach nominal interval coverage independently of the learned prior. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, deterministic anchoring raises **mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6%**, with improvements in lesion contrast preservation also reported for sparse-view CT and photoacoustic tomography.

papers.title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
papers.abstract: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.
papers.summary: Proactive autoscaling in large distributed systems needs accurate, low-latency forecasts of the immediate future rather than models of long-term trends. The described online system uses a two-stage design, a seasonality decomposition stage followed by residual correction with lightweight linear models over engineered features, and retrains for every prediction cycle so that no persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring is needed. It processes over 900K predictions per hour across heterogeneous services, and in an offline evaluation on production traffic its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6% relative to the previous production model. In production the system is estimated to have **saved 118K servers daily**.

papers.title: A Hierarchy of Risk Certificates for Representation-Based Prediction
papers.abstract: Representation-based prediction underlies many machine-learning systems. Yet a fitted predictor's failure to meet an accuracy requirement does not establish that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it. We study optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation. For blocks of $b\geq2$ independent and identically distributed (iid) observations, we minimize total squared error (normalized by $b-1$) under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. We prove that expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on optimal class risk and converge to that risk on compact metric feature spaces, although no fixed block size provides a uniform relative guarantee. Verified dual lower bounds and iid calibration observations independent of model development, with bounded targets and predictions, yield simultaneous lower confidence bounds on optimal class risk and upper confidence bounds on fitted-predictor risk. These bounds can establish that every admissible decoder exceeds a prescribed MSE threshold or that an admissible fitted predictor meets it. Controlled experiments illustrate population-risk certification; fixed PTB-XL and Bike Sharing experiments provide deterministic empirical-risk conclusions. The results support principled assessment and selection of representation-decoder configurations. Efficient certification at scale and extensions to dependent observations remain open problems.
papers.summary: A fitted predictor missing an accuracy target does not show that its representation-decoder class is incapable of meeting it. The authors study the optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation, scoring blocks of independent and identically distributed (iid) observations under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. They prove that **expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on the optimal class risk and converge to it on compact metric feature spaces**, although no fixed block size gives a uniform relative guarantee. Combined with independent calibration data, this yields simultaneous confidence bounds that can certify either that every admissible decoder exceeds an MSE threshold or that a fitted predictor meets it, illustrated on `PTB-XL` and `Bike Sharing`.

papers.title: FlowersBench: A FluidFlower-Inspired Dataset for Benchmarking Carbon Storage Surrogates Across Geological Structures
papers.abstract: Machine learning surrogates are emerging as a computationally efficient tool for uncertainty quantification in geological carbon storage (GCS). Geological structure constitutes a major source of uncertainty; however, existing benchmark simulation datasets predominantly vary petrophysical and operational parameters within a fixed geological setting. Generalisation to unseen geological structures therefore remains largely unexplored. We introduce FlowersBench, a benchmark dataset of 5,000 two-dimensional, reservoir-scale CO$_2$ storage simulations across 244 structural geometries. The geometries are sampled from an in-house structural generator inspired by the FluidFlower experiments and Case B of the 11th Society of Petroleum Engineers Comparative Solution Project (SPE11B).
