Each simulation is run with Open Porous Media (OPM) Flow over a 50-year injection period and a 500-year post-injection monitoring period. Test geometries are withheld from training to assess generalisation to unseen structural geometries. Two additional subsets support evaluation under structural shift. The first extends the parameter ranges of the structural generator beyond those used for training, and the second introduces an unseen topology of multiple parallel faults. A baseline U-Net surrogate is trained to predict CO$_2$ gas saturation. In representative test cases, the surrogate recovers the main migration pathways, including lateral spreading beneath low-permeability layers and upward flow along fault damage zones, with errors concentrated near the plume boundary. Under both structural shifts, prediction error exceeds that on the held-out geometries, and the increase in relative error is greater for the unseen fault topology. FlowersBench is publicly available and provides a common basis for evaluating GCS surrogates across geological structures.
papers.summary: Machine learning surrogates for geological carbon storage (GCS) are usually benchmarked on datasets that vary petrophysical and operational parameters within one fixed geological setting, leaving generalisation to new structures untested. `FlowersBench` provides **5,000 two-dimensional, reservoir-scale CO2 storage simulations across 244 structural geometries**, each run with `OPM Flow` over 50 years of injection and 500 years of monitoring, with test geometries withheld and two extra subsets covering extended generator ranges and an unseen multi-fault topology. A baseline `U-Net` surrogate predicting gas saturation recovers the main migration pathways, with errors concentrated near the plume boundary. Its error is higher under both structural shifts than on held-out geometries, and the relative increase is larger for the unseen fault topology.

papers.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
papers.summary: Video-language models often locate the right moment in a long video but write its timestamp incorrectly. In Temporal Weight Surgery (`TWS`), a general-purpose LLM inspects the target model's weights and activations, localises where the error arises, and edits the weights there without gradients. Three `GPT-6 Astra` sessions trace a dropped digit in `TimeLens-8B` to a single MLP layer, and the largest edit **gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more**. Two `Claude Opus 5.5` sessions trace minutes written as seconds in `Qwen3-VL-8B` to the separator token and gain 2.9 and 1.3 mIoU; every improving edit beats a random edit of the same size, and the edited models run as fast as before.

papers.title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
papers.abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.
papers.summary: LLMs asked to turn natural-language descriptions into mathematical optimization models often produce non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. The authors decompose the task into mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, build datasets targeting each component, and analyse how each relates to errors. The components are associated with different failure types, though not always strongly or consistently. Combining them improves execution reliability, but **feasible-but-incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode**, pointing to a gap between executability and correctness and to the need for data that captures constraint completeness and formulation accuracy.

papers.title: The Marauder's Map: B\'{e}zier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
papers.abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional B\'ezier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.
papers.summary: Mode connectivity links networks trained on the same task through low-loss paths or sheets, but has no analogue of the biological notion of flexible degeneracy, in which circuits gain new competencies while preserving existing function. `Nimbus` learns a high-dimensional Bézier manifold connecting N independently initialised specialist models trained on distinct tasks, forming a region of multi-task solutions. Although a naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with N, **the manifold requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders**. Across vision and language domains, ensembles sampled from these manifolds degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in negative log-likelihood and calibration error.

papers.title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
papers.abstract: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.
papers.summary: Magnetic core-loss models trade accuracy against interpretability: empirical formulas such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) are compact but imprecise, while machine learning predictors are accurate black boxes. The Symbolic Sparse Identification (`SSI`) framework builds a large library of symbolic candidate terms, selects the governing ones by sparse regression, and refines their coefficients with `AdamW` to produce an explicit analytical equation. On `Fair-Rite` 78, 79, and 95 materials it reaches **test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56% using only 10, 10, and 7 active terms**.

papers.title: Benchmarking Segmentation Models for Scalable Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-1/2 Imagery
papers.abstract: Mangroves are dynamic coastal ecosystems that contribute to carbon storage, coastal protection and biodiversity conservation, but are vulnerable to climate change. Very-high-resolution imagery such as Pl\'eiades enables detailed mangrove mapping but it is costly and have a low revisit rate. Large-scale monitoring requires free and regularly available data such as Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 but their spatial resolution poses challenges for detailed mangrove mapping. In this work, we benchmark deep learning approaches for mangrove mapping from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery using reference maps derived from very-high-resolution Pl\'eiades imagery. We compare four segmentation configurations based on CROMA and BigEarthNet-pretrained ResNet50 representations with different segmentation decoders. We construct a mangrove mapping dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amap\'a. CROMA + UPerNet achieves the best performance, with an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549. These results highlight the potential of pretrained multimodal Earth observation representations and open Sentinel data to support mangrove resilience through scalable monitoring.
papers.summary: Detailed mangrove mapping normally relies on costly very-high-resolution imagery with low revisit rates, whereas free `Sentinel-1` radar and `Sentinel-2` optical data are regularly available but coarser. Using reference maps derived from `Pléiades` imagery over French Guiana, Suriname, and Amapá, the authors build a mangrove mapping dataset and compare four segmentation configurations built on `CROMA` and `BigEarthNet`-pretrained `ResNet50` representations with different decoders. `CROMA` with a `UPerNet` decoder performs best, with **an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549**.

papers.title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
papers.abstract: Standard classification algorithms often exhibit sensitivity near decision boundaries, which can compound instability that already exists from overfitting to a subset of high-influence samples. Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers, but we show that it can destabilize those that are already stable. The well-established practice of subbagging can yield substantial improvements in stability, as we validate in the cause-of-death classification setting. However, its effect depends on the perturbation level, and for stable classifiers the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as the number of bags grows. This instability can be mitigated, though, by the recently proposed inflated argmax, which allows for multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases. We further examine the extent to which the Rashomon set, the collection of distinct models that achieve near-optimal predictive performance, can reduce instability by leveraging predictive multiplicity rather than resampling. We find that the Rashomon ensemble can stabilize unstable classifiers, but requires sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed. It is a promising direction, but not currently a general substitute for subbagging. Our results are consistent with an influence equalization interpretation of why these ensemble approaches stabilize unstable classifiers, although their failures on stable classifiers appear to have distinct sources.
papers.summary: Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers against data perturbations, and this study examines when it helps and when it hurts. Subbagging substantially improves stability in a cause-of-death classification setting, but **for classifiers that are already stable, the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as bags are added**. The recently proposed inflated argmax, which permits multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases, mitigates this. Ensembles drawn from the Rashomon set of near-optimal models can stabilize unstable classifiers but need sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed, so they are not yet a general substitute for subbagging.

papers.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Total Kinetic Energy Distributions in Neutron-Induced Fission
papers.abstract: The incident-neutron-energy dependence of post-neutron total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions, particularly their width in the multichance-fission regime, provides a sensitive test of fission calculations. We investigate how the General Description of Fission Observables (GEF) and probabilistic machine-learning models trained on GEF reproduce measured TKE distributions, emphasizing their width at high incident-neutron energies and extrapolation beyond the training range. Gaussian process regression (GPR), GPR with a white-noise kernel, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN) are evaluated on a common calculated dataset. An extended MDN/BMDN analysis uses 1,025 GEF spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Training ranges of up to 20, 40, and approximately 76 MeV are compared with matched-size controls extending to 30 or 40 MeV while preserving the number of spectra per target. Above 40 MeV, the BMDN width mean absolute error relative to experiment decreases from 5.63 MeV for training up to 20 MeV to 2.70 and 2.53 MeV for two matched-size 30-MeV controls and 1.77 MeV for the matched-size 40-MeV control. Predictive-interval coverage relative to GEF above 40 MeV rises from 52.3% to 92.3% between the 20-MeV and full training ranges. Agreement with measured mean TKE and widths is target dependent, with no uniform ordering among GEF, MDN, and BMDN. The results demonstrate the sensitivity of high-energy widths to training-energy coverage, with improvements already evident at 30 MeV. The comparatively slow variation of GEF widths at high energies limits the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to learning nontrivial energy dependence. Adequate training-energy coverage is critical for reproducing the calculated high-energy evolution, while agreement with experiment remains constrained by the underlying fission model.
papers.summary: The width of total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions in neutron-induced fission at high incident energies is a sensitive test of fission calculations. The authors compare the General Description of Fission Observables (`GEF`) code with probabilistic models trained on its output, including Gaussian process regression, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN), using 1,025 calculated spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Above 40 MeV, **the BMDN width error relative to experiment falls from 5.63 MeV when trained up to 20 MeV to 1.77 MeV with a matched-size 40-MeV training range**, showing strong sensitivity to training-energy coverage. Agreement with measurements remains target dependent and limited by the underlying fission model.

papers.title: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Self-evolving defenses protect LLM agents by learning reusable policies from observed attacks, and the authors show that this learning step is itself an attack surface. Using `SED` (Self-Evolving Defense) on the `AgentDojo` benchmark, they craft a single prompt-injection episode that makes the defense learn an over-broad policy and then refuse legitimate requests: **across 10 `Nemotron` runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task** while unrelated-task performance and the original injection defense are unaffected. The attack transfers to `gpt-oss-120b` but depends on the initial injection succeeding, and integrity-oriented attacks on the judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in the evaluated settings. Contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce over-refusal without eliminating it.

papers.title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.
papers.summary: Degraded images cause vision-language models to answer incorrectly, and this study traces which clean image-token states can still repair those answers at each stage from the vision encoder through the language model, using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light. In four encoder-based models, **12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch repair effect, whereas random orderings need four to fifteen times as many**; encoder-free `Gemma` needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair stops working at a model-specific language-model layer, and a clean-image gray-ablation crossing predicts held-out repair depth with 1.53-layer error against 3.65 for a shared-depth baseline.

papers.title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
papers.abstract: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets. We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime, and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles. On 15 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 4 points and part geometry 13, but both together add 36, from 24% to 60%. Only 7% of the coding agents' failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors, in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks. The website can be found at https://roboarc.embodied-first-exam.ai
papers.summary: Many hard manipulation tasks hinge on a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as threading a part through a narrow gap or separating interlocked pieces. `RoboARC` is a benchmark of 90 such tasks across six constraint types on three robots in `MuJoCo`, each with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution, offered in a Privileged regime (full simulator state and resets) and a Standard regime (camera images and proprioception, a single attempt). Among seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on the tasks, the strongest agent, `GPT-6 Astra` in `Codex`, **solves 86% of tasks in the Privileged regime but only 43% in the Standard regime**, and the VLA policies solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles zero-shot. On 15 puzzles failed only in the Standard regime, supplying object poses and part geometry together lifts success from 24% to 60%.

papers.title: Can a Short Video Clip Verify a Model Fix?
papers.abstract: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
papers.summary: Developers who reproduce a video model's error on a short clip may replay that clip after an update, and this study measures how often a correct clip answer means the original full-video test now passes. On 960 prespecified `CG-Bench` questions, updating from `Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct` to `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct`, the authors froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model **passed the full reference on only 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%)**, so closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved failures fixed, while requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of 67 real fixes. The short replay flags cases worth checking, but the original input is still needed to verify an individual fix.

papers.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can give wrong answers with high confidence, which makes it hard to decide which automated decisions are safe to act on without human review. A linear confidence head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen LLM to predict whether its answer is correct, with text-only metamodels trained as an alternative for closed models. On a single 2B-parameter backbone and graded answers that are about 98% `SQuAD` with the remainder `TruthfulQA`, **the confidence head beats all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest share of the workload at high accuracy targets**. Prompted confidence scores can look well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding, and transfer to unseen datasets is modest.

papers.title: Federated Learning with Uncertainty Quantification on Pseudo Label Exchange
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate federated stochastic operator learning for stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), with an emphasis on heterogeneous client data distributions and uncertainty quantification. Federated learning enables clients to collaboratively train models without exchanging their original solution data, but conventional federated averaging can suffer significant performance degradation when client distributions differ, particularly when their input function supports are disjoint. To address these challenges, we propose the Federated Stochastic Operator Network (FedSON), a two-phase framework that combines auxiliary data construction with stochastic operator learning. In the first phase, locally trained deterministic neural operators and their corresponding input functions are exchanged to generate pseudolabeled auxiliary data, enabling the federated model to learn across heterogeneous input distributions without sharing original solution trajectories. In the second phase, a stochastic operator network is trained on top of the frozen deterministic operator to characterize stochastic fluctuations and quantify uncertainty in the predicted solutions. Numerical experiments involving the heat equation, viscous Burgers' equation, and two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation demonstrate the FedSON substantially improves deterministic prediction accuracy under heterogeneous client distributions while producing uncertainty estimates comparable to those obtained through centralized training.
papers.summary: Federated averaging degrades badly when clients learning solution operators for stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) hold differently distributed data, especially when their input function supports are disjoint. The Federated Stochastic Operator Network (`FedSON`) works in two phases: clients first exchange locally trained deterministic neural operators and input functions to build pseudolabeled auxiliary data without sharing original solution trajectories, then a stochastic operator network is trained on top of the frozen deterministic operator to capture fluctuations. On the heat equation, viscous Burgers' equation, and a two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation, `FedSON` substantially improves deterministic accuracy under heterogeneous clients while **producing uncertainty estimates comparable to centralized training**.

papers.title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
papers.summary: Best-of-N test-time steering for vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies samples several candidate actions from a fixed policy and lets a verifier pick the best one. Controlled errors are injected into a `MuJoCo` trajectory verifier and the effect is measured on 60 `LIBERO-Safety` task-level cases with a `pi0.5` policy, ten repetitions each. **Increasing N does not always help when the verifier is inaccurate: the rewards of selected candidates diverge from the accurate verifier's rewards, because selection favors candidates that exploit prediction errors**, a form of reward hacking. Verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection reduce the effect in some settings.

papers.title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning
papers.abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.
papers.summary: Continual learning (CL) methods usually focus on balancing retention of old knowledge against learning new data, while the order and nature of incoming samples gets little attention. `SACK` (Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge) is a plug-in technique that breaks the model's categorical knowledge into fine-grained concepts, computes how previously learned concepts relate to new ones in each experience, and uses those relationships to prioritize new samples. Across regularization, replay, and prompt-based CL methods in class-incremental and task-incremental settings, **adding `SACK` improves accuracy and reduces forgetting**, and is also reported to handle long-tail distributions and yield better calibrated, more robust models.

papers.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
papers.abstract: Probabilistic numerical methods for partial differential equations (PDE) combines the governing physics with observations to treat solving the PDE as a Bayesian inverse problem. This allows techniques to quantify the uncertainty in the field reconstruction under model-form error. In the majority of cases, a Gaussian prior is assigned to the field of interest, and Bayes's theorem in the infinite-dimensional setting is used to derive the posterior. While Gaussians have been shown to be well-suited for linear PDEs, a similar treatment for nonlinear PDEs remains open-ended. In this work, study the use of the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for probabilistic numerics. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy about a stable solution and uncovering a Gaussian form. We then analyze the different characteristics of the resulting priors as they pertain to the inverse problem. In particular, we find that the covariance operator is given by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy whose associated Cameron-Martin space is the solution space of the PDE. We also find that the prior responds to model-form error by sharpening or flattening itself depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.
papers.summary: Probabilistic numerical methods treat solving a partial differential equation (PDE) as a Bayesian inverse problem, typically with a Gaussian prior on the field, but how to construct such priors for nonlinear PDEs remains open. The semiclassical approximation is used here to derive a Gaussian prior by expanding the PDE's variational energy or integrated square residual about a stable solution. **The resulting covariance operator is the inverse of the Hessian of the energy, with a Cameron-Martin space equal to the PDE's solution space**. The prior also sharpens or flattens under model-form error depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.

papers.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.
papers.summary: Model routing sends easy tasks to cheaper models, but a single agentic task often mixes easy and hard subtasks, so choosing one model for the whole task is inefficient. Partial routing mines past runs of a frontier lead model and a cheaper worker to identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them, then turns this into delegation guidance with a parameter delta controlling how much is delegated; the lead decides what to hand off during execution and neither model is trained. On held-out tasks with delta = 0.75, **it raises the lead's `ViBench` score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost** and its `Terminal-Bench 4.0` pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, with no worker, also cuts cost on both benchmarks and raises the `Terminal-Bench 4.0` pass rate.

papers.title: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Pursuit Game for Locomotor Agility Pretraining
papers.abstract: Agile humanoid locomotion requires controllers that can adapt to rapidly changing motion demands while remaining stable and robust. Recent locomotion controllers are typically designed with either a dense reward that is carefully shaped to encourage steps and penalize falling, or by using a reference tracking reward which teaches the controller to follow predetermined motions. Once a behavior that maximizes the reward is discovered, the controller ceases to learn. While generally stable, reference tracking methods focus on motor control separately from motion generation. Self-play has been proven as an effective technique for superhuman performance on several multiagent games like Go, Starcraft, hide-and-seek, and capture-the-flag. We train neural networks to play the game of multiagent tag in a physics simulator to study if new motion generation and control strategies can emerge through sparse feedback and competitive self-play. We present MJTag, a task suite for role-conditioned locomotion during competitive pursuit-evasion. Our model is a role-conditioned policy for a low-level locomotion controller and optional planar velocity commands. MJTag's league-based play with sparse feedback enables a locomotion controller to adopt new strategies, including dodging, sprinting, and tackling.
papers.summary: Humanoid locomotion controllers are usually trained with carefully shaped dense rewards or reference-motion tracking, and they stop learning once a reward-maximizing behavior is found. `MJTag` is a task suite for role-conditioned locomotion in competitive pursuit-evasion, in which neural networks play multi-agent tag in a physics simulator using sparse feedback and league-based self-play. The model is a role-conditioned policy for a low-level locomotion controller with optional planar velocity commands. **League play with sparse feedback leads the controller to adopt new strategies, including dodging, sprinting, and tackling**.

papers.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
papers.summary: The Audio-Visual Query Transformer (`AVQFormer`) is a video captioning architecture built on a 2.7B-parameter large language model with frozen encoders, a fixed-length 16-query semantic alignment module, and Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (`ASCST`) with entropy regularization. The base multimodal model scores 0.889 BERTScore F1, but optimizing for older captioning metrics exposes a gap that the authors hypothesize comes from global audio representations disrupting the chronological order of visual frames. **Removing audio gives 63.0 CIDEr, trailing `Qwen2.5-VL` at 67.4** but offered as a baseline for sub-3B models. The authors take this as a sign that CIDEr on datasets such as `MSR-VTT` may be biased toward visually grounded syntax.

papers.title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.
papers.summary: Low-level Internet of Things (IoT) sensor readings must be turned into semantically meaningful events before they can feed process analysis. A five-stage workflow of collaborating language models (semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction) is tested zero-shot on human activity recognition with the `CASAS Aruba` smart home dataset across eleven configurations. **Collaboration alone does not guarantee gains: general-purpose auxiliary models can degrade recognition, while complementary specialist roles improve it** and let a smaller final classifier retain much of a larger model's performance. The selected workflow reaches macro F1 of 0.643 in a 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 over one week, and trained machine learning approaches remain more accurate on this dataset.

papers.title: Temporal Selective Exploration for Reinforcement Learning-Guided Continuous-Discrete Flow Matching in 3D Molecular Design
papers.abstract: Flow matching has shown strong potential in generative tasks, while its optimization via Reinforcement Learning (RL) remains underexplored, especially in continuous-discrete mixed settings. Moreover, flow matching is formulated as an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), whose deterministic trajectories do not naturally support RL optimization. Introducing stochasticity by converting the entire trajectory into a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) is a common practice. Nevertheless, not all timesteps contribute to the final outcomes, and redundant exploration introduces additional noise. Furthermore, in multi-objective settings, some objectives may dominate the optimization while others receive insufficient updates. In this study, we propose an RL-guided continuous-discrete flow matching framework with temporal selective exploration for 3D de novo molecular design. Specifically, our method jointly optimizes continuous and discrete flow matching for atomic coordinates and molecular identities, respectively, while restricting exploration to timesteps that primarily contribute to target properties, reducing ineffective exploration. We also introduce a reward-based advantage calibration mechanism to mitigate objective dominance in multi-objective optimization. The framework is applied to design inhibitors for both the well-studied target protein EGFR and the challenging Pin1 protein. We identify some novel candidate inhibitors, supported by in silico validation.
papers.summary: Optimizing flow matching generators with reinforcement learning (RL) is awkward because their deterministic trajectories must be made stochastic to explore, and doing so at every timestep adds noise from steps that do not affect the outcome. This framework jointly optimizes continuous flow matching for atomic coordinates and discrete flow matching for atom identities in 3D de novo molecular design, **restricting exploration to the timesteps that primarily contribute to target properties**. A reward-based advantage calibration mechanism keeps one objective from dominating multi-objective optimization. Applied to inhibitor design for the proteins EGFR and Pin1, it yields novel candidates supported by in silico validation only.

papers.title: Yet Another Concept Drift Benchmark? A Principled Framework for Evaluating Drift Detectors
papers.abstract: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.
papers.summary: Evaluation of concept drift detectors for data streams relies on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. The proposed benchmark starts from an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics, using finite detection windows and repeated alarms **to separate detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability**, with a reproducible observer supplying a controlled performance signal. Normalized metrics and a composite score are defined on top of this formulation. The framework is validated by stress-testing 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.

papers.title: Scalpel and Brush: Pruning and Targeted Weight Editing of a Small Language Model by a Single LLM Agent
papers.abstract: It has recently been shown that an LLM can itself edit the weights of a language model, yet it remains unclear which part of such a result is due to the agent and which part is reproduced by a random edit of the same shape, by an instruction in the prompt, or by a standard procedure without an LLM. We unify repair and pruning as sparse weight edits to optimize a metric we specify, using BLEU as an example: three tasks -- targeted weight repair ("brush"), structured MLP neuron pruning ("scalpel", zeroing pruned weights), and layer removal with repair - are assigned to a DeepSeek Harness agent powered by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with up to 50 dev evaluations. We study Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct in three independent runs per task, with final evaluation on two hidden splits. On ordinary differential equations, changing at most 0.0084% of weights raised test BLEU by 24-32% on second-order equations and by a factor of 1.8-2.5 on equations with polynomial right-hand sides. An independent substitution check showed that higher BLEU reflects notation alignment rather than improved correctness. Masks that remove 12.5-15% of MLP neurons shrink the model by 9.4-11.2% with mean BLEU loss of at most 0.01 on both hidden splits, whereas standard pruning with equal shares per layer failed the constraint at all tested shares. On seven-class GoEmotions classification, edits raise macro-F1 from 0.100 to 0.396-0.451 on test and from 0.175 to 0.455-0.476 on holdout. A ridge-based classifier written into agent-selected weight rows yields macro-F1 of 0.424 and 0.464. Pruning search with the same evaluation limit removes 15.9% of neurons versus 14-21.4% for agent runs passing the hidden check. Standard procedures without an LLM reproduce much of the performance once given the location and form of intervention found by the agent; a comparison of agentic and non-agentic search remains open.
papers.summary: When an LLM agent edits another model's weights, it is unclear how much of the result is due to the agent versus a random edit of the same shape, a prompt instruction, or a standard non-LLM procedure. Repair and pruning are framed as sparse weight edits toward a chosen metric, and a `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` agent with up to 50 dev evaluations performs targeted weight repair, structured MLP neuron pruning, and layer removal with repair on `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct`. Changing at most 0.0084% of weights raised test BLEU on differential equation tasks by 24-32% and by a factor of 1.8-2.5, though a substitution check showed this reflects notation alignment and not improved correctness; masks removing 12.5-15% of MLP neurons shrank the model by 9.4-11.2% with BLEU loss of at most 0.01, and edits raised `GoEmotions` macro-F1 from 0.100 to 0.396-0.451 on test. **Standard procedures without an LLM reproduce much of the performance once given the location and form of intervention the agent found**, and a direct comparison of agentic and non-agentic search remains open.

papers.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
papers.abstract: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.
papers.summary: Assistants answering from supplied reference material often get material that covers only some parts of a question, yet most evaluations score one answer per question and treat partial coverage as insufficient. This small open evaluation scores each part of a three-part question separately on 30 cases, with a distinct verdict for parts answered correctly but carrying an added unsupported claim, testing `claude-haiku-4-5` and `llama3.1:8b`. Without an instruction to stay within the material both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge, and **one added sentence telling them to answer only from the material cuts unsupported-claim rates from 0.71 and 0.90 to 0.00 and 0.06**; what remains are answers that strengthen the material's claims. The added-claim verdict proved the hardest to label for both judge and author, `RAGAS` faithfulness penalises correct withholding, and a clear difference between the two models disappears when the judge model is replaced.

papers.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
papers.abstract: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.
papers.summary: Open-source layouts and predictive text dictionaries for `FUTO Keyboard` are released for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing `Divvun` Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format the keyboard uses. For prediction, **weighted dictionaries are built by combining translated Finnish lemma frequencies with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers**, which gives a way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable.

papers.title: ViCARD: Visual Credit Assignment with Reward-Gated Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Visual reasoning requires models to identify relevant visual evidence and use it to derive correct answers. Outcomebased reinforcement learning (RL) faces two key challenges in this regime: it yields no learning signal when perceptual errors cause all sampled responses to fail, and it broadcasts a uniform advantage across every token within a response. Conversely, while visual self-distillation offers dense guidance from evidence-centered image crops, student learning from token distributions alone often fails to elicit correct final answers. Motivated by an audit of training rollouts that exposes these complementary failure modes, we introduce ViCARD (Visual Credit Assignment with RewardGated Distillation), which integrates per-token visual supervision with verified correctness rewards. For each rollout group, we leverage a teacher with its input image cropped to the relevant visual area, and use this to provide per-token supervision to the student while also valuing correctness. If all sampled rollouts fail, ViCARD samples an additional crop-teacher answer and activates on-policy distillation only if that answer is correct. Together, these mechanisms provide fine-grained visual credit within informative reward groups and a learning signal for otherwise uninformative all-fail groups. Extensive comparisons across model scales demonstrate that ViCARD improves fine-grained visual reasoning performance over RL and distillation baselines, while retaining broad visual reasoning capabilities.
papers.summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) for visual reasoning gives no learning signal when perceptual errors make every sampled response fail, and it spreads one uniform advantage across all tokens of a response; visual self-distillation from evidence-centered crops gives dense guidance but often fails to elicit correct final answers. `ViCARD` (Visual Credit Assignment with Reward-Gated Distillation) combines the two: a teacher that sees the image cropped to the relevant region provides per-token supervision to the student alongside correctness rewards. When all rollouts in a group fail, it samples an extra crop-teacher answer and turns on on-policy distillation only if that answer is correct. Across model scales, **`ViCARD` improves fine-grained visual reasoning over RL and distillation baselines while retaining broad visual reasoning capabilities**.

papers.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
papers.abstract: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.
papers.summary: Representational similarity measures such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) lack realistic bounds on how estimation error depends jointly on the number of sampled neurons N and experimental conditions M. The Centered Kernel Distance (`CKD`), the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, is shown to admit an unbiased estimator, whereas CKA and several other popular measures have none. Under mild assumptions, **the estimation error of `CKD` decays in proportion to 1/M + 1/N, at a rate independent of the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions**. The results are checked on random shallow networks, trained networks, and macaque visual cortex data, and yield prescriptions for estimating similarity between neural systems efficiently.

papers.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.
papers.summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are usually post-trained with outcome reward models that supervise only the final decision, which rewards a confident answer whether or not the image supports one. `HumblePRM` is a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that splits multimodal reasoning into a perception stage, where the model factually describes the scene, and a calibration stage, where it judges whether that evidence suffices to commit, scoring each stage independently for agreement between evidence and expressed confidence. **Training with `HumblePRM` considerably increases abstention on ambiguous inputs while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged**. The improvement also transfers to the edge model `Gemma 4 E4B`.

papers.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
papers.summary: Pre-silicon hardware security verification starts by identifying security assets, and while primary assets are usually evident from a design's function, the internal signals through which they can be compromised under a given threat, called secondary assets, are much harder to find. `SecID` is a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis, bounded dynamic evaluation, and LLM reasoning, backing each asset decision with functional influence, threat features, and an explicit attack mechanism. It is demonstrated on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including `openMSP430`, `NEORV32`, and `CV32E40P`, and checked against prior work, fault simulation, formal analysis, ablations, and repeatability studies. The evaluations indicate that **`SecID` identifies highly threat-relevant secondary assets for a given primary asset**.

papers.title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation for Quantum-Enhanced Training of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.
papers.summary: Asymptotic speedup claims for quantum machine learning often hide the engineering cost of a full workflow. Realistic end-to-end resource estimates are given for training a linearized neural network with a Quantum Linear Solver, accounting for data access, computation, and readout across three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios with different sparsity-scaling assumptions. **Crossover points against classical methods appear only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements**. The analysis also identifies the bottlenecks that would have to be overcome to reach practical quantum advantage.

papers.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
papers.abstract: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.
papers.summary: Group discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives, raising the question of whether AI agents joining them can help. A framework introduces generic and persona-conditioned agents into evolving discussions; in simulations grounded in Reddit threads across four domains, AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human ones but substantially less semantically diverse, with persona conditioning narrowing that gap. In a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine threads, **AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by the human participants**, even though the agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity.

papers.title: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model
papers.abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.
papers.summary: Training controllers that track motion capture with whole-body musculoskeletal models takes hours to days of GPU time because hundreds of muscles must be coordinated through contact. The authors extend `SuperMimic`, which backpropagates through rollouts of a learned world model, to `MS-Human-700` (700 muscles) and `MyoFullBody` (354 muscles), adding observations without muscle geometry, concurrent data collection, Beta exploration noise, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090, `MS-Human-700` reaches in **6.3 minutes the held-out return that the published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours (37x sooner)**, and `MyoFullBody` trains 34x sooner without retuning. Refining actions through the world model at test time lowers position error by a further 26%.

papers.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
papers.abstract:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.
papers.summary: Quantitative sample and time complexity guarantees are sought for language generation, using a probably approximately correct (PAC) model in which a learner sees uniformly random positive examples of an unknown Boolean concept and must output a sampler close in total variation to uniform over that concept's positive set. Prior work gave an efficient algorithm assuming an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and a statistical query (SQ) learner. The authors construct **a concept class for which online learning is cryptographically hard yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient**, and give new algorithms that replace the online learner with offline empirical risk minimization oracles.

papers.title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
papers.abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.
papers.summary: World models that predict future frames in pixel or latent space do not directly represent how a 3D scene evolves. `SplatWAM` encodes unposed views into a fixed budget of 3D Gaussian tokens with a tokenizer (`SplatWAM-T`), then predicts future Gaussian states in one forward pass per action with a dynamics model (`SplatWAM-D`), so each predicted state can be rendered from any viewpoint.
