On `OGBench` Scene it renders novel views **12x faster than video world models (about 80 FPS on an RTX 5090)** with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. With a flow-matching policy head (`SplatWAM-P`), the roughly 1B-parameter model outperforms the roughly 7B `WorldVLA` and `OpenVLA` on `LIBERO`.

papers.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
papers.summary: Looped language models apply one shared block repeatedly per token, and the question here is whether that block can learn from its own predictions at greater recurrent depth. The authors retrofit `OLMo-2-1B` with a shared recurrent block, then use continuations generated at greater depth to train the block through a single pass, with no reference answers or correctness filtering, a transfer they call preference write-back. At their target depths the updated models beat a non-recurrent control matched for data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with **a mean relative accuracy gain of up to 46.2%**. On `GSM8K`, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain.

papers.title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.
papers.summary: Differentially private (DP) policy optimization is studied in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback, where trajectories are reused and rewards may depend on previously released private statistics. The algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to satisfy joint differential privacy (JDP). The high-probability regret bound keeps **the same leading order K^(3/4) dependence on the number of episodes K as the non-private bound**, with privacy adding only lower-order terms of order K^(5/8) and K^(1/2).

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.
papers.summary: Static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents are compared in security detection and response pipelines under a fixed human-analyst alert budget, across 56 experiments on an enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (`SOREL-20M`, `BODMAS`, `LANL`, `DARPA Transparent Computing`). Fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget, and rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms `GraphSAGE` without neural training. Unconstrained LLM auto-closure, tested with `Gemini` and fine-tuned `Qwen3-4B`, **removes 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases**. Post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) suppresses up to 86% of novel attacks compared with supervised fine-tuning, and adversarial cover stories in telemetry raise evasion sharply unless a deterministic policy harness gates the model.

papers.title: Memory as the Backbone: A Dual-Store Associative Memory Architecture for Visual Recognition
papers.abstract: We investigate whether explicit memory can serve as the organizing principle of a general-purpose visual backbone. Inspired by the interaction between working and long-term memory in human cognition, we introduce DuSAM (Dual-Store Associative Memory), a hierarchical memory-native visual backbone coupling image-local working memory (WM) with a fixed-capacity persistent semantic memory (PM). WM organizes local visual evidence into compact, spatially anchored states that are updated and transported across stages, then read back to refine dense features. PM consolidates semantic evidence from training images and annotated regions into prototypes, whose retrieved content enriches the same working states. With these memory operations in place of self-attention or state-space blocks, DuSAM achieves competitive performance relative to representative, similarly sized backbones on ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation. Ablations show contributions from both stores, with PM particularly benefiting class groups with fewer annotated training pixels. At $2048\times2048$, the complete DuSAM-based UPerNet segmentor achieves $2.36\times$ the throughput of the evaluated DeiT-S/16 counterpart while using $59.5\%$ less GPU memory, and $1.24\times$ the throughput of the linear-complexity VMamba-T. Memory analyses reveal spatially selective WM access and semantic associations between retrieved prototypes and training regions. Class-targeted removal and restoration further demonstrate that category-specific experience can be replenished through state updates without changing network parameters. These results establish explicit memory as a viable organizing principle for visual backbones and provide a foundation for jointly designing contextual computation and addressable semantic memory.
papers.summary: Explicit memory is tested as the organizing principle of a general-purpose visual backbone. `DuSAM` (Dual-Store Associative Memory) couples an image-local working memory, which holds compact spatially anchored states updated across stages, with a fixed-capacity persistent semantic memory of prototypes consolidated from training images, replacing self-attention and state-space blocks. It is reported as competitive with similarly sized backbones on `ImageNet-1K`, `ADE20K`, and `COCO`. At 2048x2048 resolution its `UPerNet` segmentor achieves **2.36x the throughput of the `DeiT-S/16` counterpart with 59.5% less GPU memory**, and removing or restoring class-specific memory changes behavior without changing network parameters.

papers.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
papers.abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.
papers.summary: The assumption that free, unbiased extra reward samples can only help a stochastic bandit learner is examined. The authors define a formal property of non-degradation under extra information and show that **the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (`UCB`) violates it, incurring strictly higher regret with some benign extra information than without it**. `Thompson Sampling` and `Explore-Then-Commit` appear to benefit from the same information. A proposed meta-algorithm provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms and is studied in simulations.

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries
papers.abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.
papers.summary: Existing security benchmarks focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects and largely skip closed-source binaries. `DeepBinary` has an agent analyze a Windows kernel binary with a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated virtual machines and report each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept, which is replayed on fresh machines and assessed by an LLM-based judge for validity, uniqueness, and estimated bounty value. Across 12 target binaries, models including `GPT-6 Sol`, `Claude Opus 5`, and `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash`, run through coding agents such as `Codex` and `Claude Code`, found over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including **146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities**. The authors report large differences between models in binary analysis, experimentation, and sustaining discovery over long horizons.

papers.title: The Geometry Is the Memory: Task-Density Routing for Continual LoRA
papers.abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. We propose CONTLORA, which replaces stored examples with compact class statistics for adapter selection and classification. Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select LoRA adapters, while accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Trained without retaining images or feature vectors, CONTLORA reaches 88.55% accuracy on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200. Across three benchmarks in the matched component study, its mean final accuracy differs from an independently trained stored-feature counterpart by at most 0.07 percentage points. Ablations show that improved task coverage need not improve classification and adapter composition also matters. On held-out classes, competitor-centered likelihood scores improve novelty AUROC over raw likelihood without altering routing ranks. These results support statistical memory as an alternative to example-retention approaches in the evaluated settings, while identifying task ambiguity as an ongoing limitation.
papers.summary: In continual learning with multiple frozen LoRA adapters, choosing the right adapter for a query at inference time is a failure point of its own. `CONTLORA` replaces stored examples with compact class statistics: Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select the adapter, and accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier. Without retaining images or feature vectors it reaches **88.55% accuracy on 20-task `CIFAR-100`** and 86.99% on `CUB-200`, with mean final accuracy within 0.07 percentage points of a stored-feature counterpart across three benchmarks. Task ambiguity is identified as a remaining limitation.

papers.title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
papers.abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.
papers.summary: Continuous-time physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) trained without data have so far converged to the steady symmetric solution instead of producing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder. Training over successive time windows with an analytical, divergence-free initial condition that breaks the symmetry yields shedding at Reynolds number 100, with **Strouhal number and mean drag coefficient within 0.5% of an `OpenFOAM` solution**. Pressure is discontinuous at window junctions, which the authors trace to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Imposing pressure at the junctions and adding a hidden divergence constraint to the loss makes the lift coefficient jumps 20 times smaller.

papers.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations yield either probabilities assigned to correct answers or binary correctness indicators, and using only one type excludes models or discards information. The proposed framework places both on a common scale with a two-parameter logistic item response theory (IRT) model fitted by fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood. Simulations show that **adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents**, while adding noisier binary responses to a precise probability sample can increase estimation error. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (`MMLU`) combining `Open LLM Leaderboard` and Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (`HELM`) data reveals systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols.

papers.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) usually selects evidence by semantic relevance, which can miss information needed for mandatory clauses in compliance-sensitive long documents. Constraint-Aligned RAG (`CA-RAG`) augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before retrieval. With manually annotated evidence at a budget of six passages, it raises **pooled recall from 0.5402 to 0.5950** and precision from 0.5268 to 0.5692 over standard RAG. Generation experiments show compliance and reliability gains in several model-domain settings, whereas applying constraints only at generation time gives higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are evaluated on authentic conversational African American English (AAE) using 100 six-turn segments from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (`CORAAL`), instead of synthetic or decontextualized data. `Gemini 2.5 Flash` with and without reasoning and `GPT-4.1 mini` are tested on detecting five morphosyntactic features and on generating the next conversational turn. Reasoning-enabled `Gemini` is **the strongest feature detector, with a macro F1 of 0.91**, ahead of a fine-tuned BERT-based baseline. In generation all models underproduce AAE relative to human speakers and give relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled `Gemini` producing the least AAE and the least diverse output.

papers.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
papers.abstract: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.
papers.summary: Simulated survey respondents are usually built from interviews or individual records; here an open-weight language model is instead fine-tuned on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, predicting each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it **gets the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, versus 77% for a demographic statistical model**, and is level with `Claude Opus 5` and `Claude Opus 5.5`, though those models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions its error is 12% lower than the statistical model, and it runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop.

papers.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
papers.summary: Inferring a user's persona attributes from one day of mobile activity logs on-device is limited by memory: a day yields about 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. The authors introduce `LogToPersona`, a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs, and a filtering method that keeps only behaviorally distinct log entries. Filtering **cuts the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families** and more than halves prefill time while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For `Qwen3-4B` it removes 2.5 GB.

papers.title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
papers.abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.
papers.summary: Agents are typically trained in synchronous environments where the world waits for them, so they do not learn when to act quickly and when longer reasoning is worth the delay. Real-time reasoning training (`RRT`) is introduced as a class of techniques, with three instances: training on real-time data, decoupling acting from observing, and a curriculum over time pressure. In two real-time environments, `Frogger` and `Snake`, the combination beats the strongest non-RRT baseline by **an average of 33% reward on in-distribution tasks and 55% on out-of-distribution tasks** across time pressures.

papers.title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
papers.abstract:
This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated.
  Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.
papers.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload is studied, comparing zero, shifted, and Transformer-predicted initializations of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The Transformer is trained on expert SCP solutions and its predicted control sequence is refined by the same optimizer. It cuts computation time relative to zero initialization on independently solved problems, but in closed-loop simulation **simply shifting the previous optimized control sequence gives the lowest computation time**, with similar tracking for all three. Optimization times exceed the control sampling period, so real-time operation is not demonstrated.

papers.title: Evaluation and Restoration of Safety in Reasoning-Tuned LLMs
papers.abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.
papers.summary: Open-source LLMs optimized for reasoning, such as `VibeThinker`, are widely available without external guardrails, and the question is whether stronger reasoning makes them safer. Using a new evaluation metric, the authors report that **increasing reasoning raised the unsafe rate in every model family tested**. To restore safety they propose `ESPG`, which combines evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail. Compared with alternatives such as `GRPO`, it needs no GPU memory beyond inference and works with as few as 30 training samples.

papers.title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles
papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
papers.summary: Coding agents fix a security flaw when shown the failing test but do not retain the lesson: across 14 task sequences, `Codex`, `Claude Code`, and `Qwen Code` repaired the vulnerability 85.7% of the time, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). Recording the fix in persistent context or supplying published secure coding principles did not close the gap. `PRECEPT` maintains an evolving library that starts from authoritative principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, keeping a revision only if fresh executions show more secure code with functional success preserved. On task families unseen during evolution, **its weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9%** and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.

papers.title: A Perturbation-Driven Framework for Sensitivity Analysis of Dimensionality Reduction
papers.abstract: Low-dimensional representations produced by dimensionality reduction (DR) are commonly evaluated using distortion measures such as trustworthiness and continuity. In this paper, we study the sensitivity of DR methods to plausible input variations by quantifying changes in structural preservation and visually diagnosing how these changes manifest in the resulting representations. This perspective reflects the fact that real-world datasets are finite, noisy samples of an underlying distribution, and DR should not produce substantially different structures under small data changes. We introduce a model-agnostic, perturbation-driven sensitivity evaluation framework that treats perturbations as controlled probes of plausible data variation. Across multiple perturbation families and strength levels, we repeatedly perturb the input, apply a DR method, and evaluate the resulting low-dimensional representations using a set of distortion measures to derive sensitivity profiles for each DR method. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through case studies on DR method comparison, behavior analysis, and robustness improvement. We find that methods performing well according to conventional distortion measures (e.g., t-SNE) can still exhibit substantial sensitivity, leading to instability in visually salient structures such as trajectories and clusters, while certain methods (e.g., multidimensional scaling) may exhibit improved structural preservation under specific perturbations. These results highlight the importance of sensitivity analysis for comparing DR methods, diagnosing perturbation-sensitive visual patterns, and guiding the development of more robust DR methods toward trustworthy visual analytics.
papers.summary: Dimensionality reduction (DR) methods are usually judged by distortion measures such as trustworthiness and continuity, which say little about how stable the resulting layout is when the input data changes slightly. The authors propose a model-agnostic framework that repeatedly perturbs the input across several perturbation families and strengths, re-runs the DR method, and tracks the distortion measures to build a sensitivity profile per method. In case studies, **methods that score well on conventional measures, such as `t-SNE`, can still be highly sensitive, with visually salient clusters and trajectories shifting under small perturbations**, while multidimensional scaling sometimes preserves structure better under specific perturbations.

papers.title: Deletion You Can Check: Auditing LLM Unlearning
papers.abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.
papers.summary: A membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC around 0.5) is commonly read as evidence that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record, but that reading assumes the comparison population reflects how the record should behave after a valid deletion. A controlled 2×2 study pairs the `ArxivMIA` and `BookMIA` benchmarks with `Llama-3.2-1B` and `Qwen2.5-1.5B` and uses exact retraining as the reference: it lands within the chance band on `ArxivMIA` but reaches 0.122 on `BookMIA`, and swapping in same-pool, never-fine-tuned records moves the `BookMIA`/`Qwen` reference from 0.257 to 0.523, pointing to population mismatch. Judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift, and utility, **no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (`GA+GD`), negative-preference optimization with retain training (`NPO-RT`), or teacher-student unlearning (`SCRUB`) passes** on the validated `ArxivMIA`/`Llama` axis.

papers.title: Casper: A Projection-Based Neurosymbolic Layer for Scalable & Guaranteed Constraint Satisfaction
papers.abstract: Many real-world problems demand exact constraint satisfaction to be meaningfully solved, yet existing neurosymbolic methods face a stark trade-off: those that guarantee satisfaction fail to scale, while those that scale must resort to approximation. Meanwhile, traditional deep learning approaches offer no satisfaction guarantees at all. In this paper, we propose Casper, a neurosymbolic layer that simultaneously (i) guarantees constraint satisfaction, (ii) scales at inference time, (iii) is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific engineering, and (iv) is fully differentiable, making it composable with any neural predictor both at training and at inference time. Casper casts constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the constraint-feasible region, computable in a single forward pass. Experiments across MNIST arithmetic (up to 1024 digits), Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding show that Casper is the only method that produces guaranteed-valid outputs at scale: on $30\times30$ Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while Casper produces them 100% of the time.
papers.summary: Neurosymbolic methods that guarantee exact constraint satisfaction tend not to scale, while those that scale fall back on approximation. `Casper` is a differentiable layer that treats constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the feasible region, computed in a single forward pass with no problem-specific engineering and composable with any neural predictor at training and inference time. Experiments cover MNIST arithmetic with up to 1024 digits, Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding; on 30×30 Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while **`Casper` produces valid paths 100% of the time**.

papers.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
papers.abstract: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $\Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.
papers.summary: In adversarial bandit convex optimization, a learner picks a point in a d-dimensional convex body for each of n rounds and sees only a noisy value of an adversarially chosen convex loss at that point. The authors **improve the best known regret bound from roughly d^(5/2)·sqrt(n) to d^(3/2)·sqrt(n)**, up to logarithmic factors, matching the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. in 2017 and leaving a gap of d^(1/6) to the recent lower bound of d^(4/3)·sqrt(n). The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration that uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian-smoothed loss rather than of an optimistic surrogate.

papers.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.
papers.summary: Serving large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models with Expert Parallelism (EP) is slowed by load imbalance, because every layer waits for the busiest EP rank; the bottleneck is the maximum token count per rank during compute-bound prefill and the maximum number of active experts per rank during memory-bound decode. `RankCast` keeps each token's top-p predicted experts and picks the remaining ones from a wider top-L candidate list, using per-rank prices to steer assignments toward less loaded ranks in prefill and closing experts on the busiest ranks in decode. Implemented in `SGLang` and `DeepEP` and tested on `Qwen3-235B-A22B` and `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`, it removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, **raises prefill input throughput by up to 19% and cuts decode time per output token by up to 10%**, at a quality cost below one percentage point.

papers.title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
papers.abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) struggle on mixed boundary problems where part of the boundary data is unknown. `FokasNets` pair lifted network representations, which impose Dirichlet conditions by construction, with the Global Relation from the Fokas method (Unified Transform), solved as an extra step during training to supply the missing boundary values; the construction covers elliptic and evolution PDEs and their solution operators, with error and stability analysis and a universal approximation result. Against standard and lifted PINNs and Physics-Informed `DeepONets` on manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks, **accuracy improves by multiple orders of magnitude in the solution-operator setting**, and fixed error thresholds are reached earlier in training.

papers.title: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
papers.abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.
papers.summary: Detecting AI involvement in peer review requires telling fully AI-generated reviews apart from human judgements that were merely rewritten with AI, across many models, workflows, and scientific fields. `PeerReveal` bases its decision on learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims taken from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, combined with review-level textual signals. On `PeerShift`, a new test set of 5,430 reviews spanning machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, it reaches 70.52% pooled Macro-F1, 11.48 points above the strongest baseline, and **adversarial training against a small local generator tuned to produce hard reviews raises this to 82.40%**.

papers.title: DiffER$^2$: Diffusion Ensembles for Retrosynthesis Prediction with SMILES Adapted Particle Guidance
papers.abstract: Computational retrosynthesis prediction has the potential to reduce development time for newly discovered drugs by automatically generating potential reactions for a target product. Data-driven approaches commonly treat this as a sequence-to-sequence generation task on SMILES strings. In this work, we construct ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for molecular generation and incorporate guidance mechanisms for improved output diversity. We propose an adaptation of particle guidance to SMILES sequence generation which significantly improves the number of unique molecules generated by diffusion ensembles while increasing top-k accuracy. These results further expand the efficacy of discrete diffusion for SMILES generation, and our empirical analyses offer new insights into the capabilities of diffusion models for chemical retrosynthesis.
papers.summary: Retrosynthesis prediction, which proposes reactions that could yield a target molecule, is commonly framed as sequence-to-sequence generation over SMILES strings. The authors build ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for this task and adapt particle guidance, a diversity-promoting guidance mechanism, to SMILES sequence generation. They report that the adapted guidance **increases the number of unique molecules the ensembles generate while also raising top-k accuracy**.

papers.title: FIG-MAC: A Fine-grained Inspiration Graph Empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation
papers.abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.
papers.summary: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) with large language models is held back, the authors argue, by unstructured context, a lack of traceability in how knowledge evolves, and the absence of role-specialized collaboration that covers both generation and evaluation. `FIG-MAC` builds a graph whose nodes are academic semantic units and whose edges encode heuristic relationships, follows the graph's ontology to construct reasoning paths enriched with vector-search evidence, and hands these traceable conjecture paths to a team of role-specialized agents that generate, screen, and validate hypotheses in a closed loop. Experiments report that it **outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty**.

papers.title: Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.
papers.summary: Unlearning methods such as gradient ascent try to remove backdoors from NLP models by maximizing loss on poisoned samples, but they can shift a trigger's influence to other classes instead of eliminating it. Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (`TICU`) builds pairs of clean and trigger-inserted inputs and fine-tunes the model so both produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations, while keeping a supervised loss on clean data and constraining parameter drift from the original model. Across multiple datasets, architectures, and attack settings, **`TICU` improves accuracy on triggered inputs and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts relative to existing baselines**, with limited degradation on the clean task.

papers.title: Symmetry-Aware Residual Learning of Few-Body Molecular Wave Functions
papers.abstract: Ultracold polar molecules are a highly controllable platform for engineering quantum matter, but modeling their few-body properties remains computationally challenging. Their anisotropic long-range interactions and rich internal structure lead to high-dimensional eigenvalue problems for which conventional grid-based solvers are largely restricted to two-molecule systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics-informed neural variational method that exploits known physical structure of the molecular wave function. Our key idea is to factor the wave function into analytic and neural components. The analytic component encodes rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay, while the neural residual learns the remaining intermediate-range behavior. This decomposition reduces the effective dimensionality of the problem without relying on ad hoc approximations or problem-specific discretization grids. We benchmark our method against high-accuracy two-molecule solvers and recover both ground and excited bound states with mean relative errors below 0.01%. We further demonstrate the method's applicability to three-body systems by computing field-linked trimer ground-state energies in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation. This provides a systematic route to larger molecular systems and opens opportunities to study correlations and dynamics in interacting quantum matter.
papers.summary: Few-body properties of ultracold polar molecules lead to high-dimensional eigenvalue problems that conventional grid-based solvers can mostly handle only for two molecules. The proposed physics-informed neural variational method factors the wave function into an analytic part that encodes rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay and a neural residual that learns the intermediate-range behavior. Benchmarked against high-accuracy two-molecule solvers, it **recovers ground and excited bound states with mean relative errors below 0.01%**, and it computes field-linked trimer ground-state energies for three-body systems in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation.

papers.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
papers.abstract: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
papers.summary: Retargeting human hand-object demonstrations to robots has mostly produced floating-hand motions, whereas training whole-robot policies needs arm-hand trajectories that are kinematically feasible and physically executable. `DexEngine` is a simulation pipeline that places each clip where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and corrects the result in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning; from nine human datasets it yields about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 hours) and 325,000 episodes (578 hours). It tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones, and **policies trained on the physics-corrected data far outperform those trained on the same clips without correction**, with mid-training on the data giving further gains in simulation and on a real robot.

papers.title: SEEL: Towards End-to-End 3D Sign Generation with Language Models
papers.abstract: 3D sign language generation aims to produce signing motion from written text. Motivated by the linguistic nature of sign language, recent methods combine a motion tokenizer with a language model to predict motion tokens from text. However, both components are optimized through a two-stage pipeline with mismatched objectives: the tokenizer minimizes reconstruction error in isolation, while the generator learns from rigid one-hot reference tokens. A straightforward end-to-end extension bridges discrete token selection with straight-through estimators (STE), suffering from biased gradients and codebook collapse. To address these limitations, we propose SEEL, an end-to-end framework that aligns tokenization and generation with motion quality through two complementary mechanisms. First, to overcome rigid one-hot supervision, reconstruction-aware generation decodes candidate tokens in context and converts their 3D motion errors into soft targets, guiding the generator with physical motion quality. Second, to propagate generation feedback without STE, generation-aware tokenization passes continuous codebook expectations through the frozen generator, routing generated-motion gradients to the tokenizer to prevent codebook collapse. Combining both mechanisms enables the tokenizer and generator to co-evolve, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CSL-Daily, How2Sign, and Phoenix-2014T. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.
papers.summary: Text-to-3D sign language generation typically trains a motion tokenizer and a language-model generator in two separate stages with mismatched objectives, and joining them with straight-through estimators (STE) brings biased gradients and codebook collapse. `SEEL` trains both end to end using two mechanisms: candidate tokens are decoded in context and their 3D motion errors become soft targets for the generator, and continuous codebook expectations are passed through the frozen generator so that gradients from generated motion reach the tokenizer without STE. With the tokenizer and generator co-evolving, the method reports **state-of-the-art results on `CSL-Daily`, `How2Sign`, and `Phoenix-2014T`**.

papers.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $\tau$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $\tau^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $\tau=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.
authors: Xiaoyu Li (University of New South Wales)
papers.summary: Orthogonal fine-tuning (OFT) adapts pretrained weights with an orthogonal transform, but existing methods rebuild an exact or approximate orthogonal matrix at every step, and the authors show that the approximation in `OFTv2` leaves orthogonality defects spanning five orders of magnitude at its default setting. Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (`RTOFT`) instead applies a cheap first-order update with a skew-symmetric matrix and restores exact orthogonality through a polar decomposition only when the measured drift reaches a tolerance, which bounds the defect in every forward pass by the square of that tolerance. On `GLUE`, **training time falls from 1.10-1.58× to 0.97-1.13× that of `LoRA`**, and the block-diagonal variant beats `LoRA` by 1.98±0.39 points on the six-task average; restoring after every step gives no measurable accuracy gain and costs 4.5-27.5% more per step.

papers.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.
papers.summary: Distributionally robust reinforcement learning seeks a policy that maximizes worst-case value over all transition kernels within a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence ball around a nominal model. With access to a generative model, the authors derive new upper and lower bounds on the number of samples needed to find a near-optimal robust policy, where prior results left a gap and the lower bounds covered only a limited range of uncertainty levels. The **upper bound improves on the best known one by a factor of at least min(1/p, 1/(1-gamma))**, where p is the smallest positive nominal transition probability and gamma the discount factor, the lower bound holds for any uncertainty level, and the two nearly match in several regimes.

papers.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
papers.abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for whether embedding similarity matches human judgments of meaning usually rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style ratings. `Aligned Machine` is a public platform where participants see two pairs of items (text or images) and choose which pair is more similar, feeding a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (`HASB`); the initial deployment gathered 2,875 labeled pairs from 115 participants. Evaluating 12 widely used embedding models showed only partial alignment with human judgments: **text-only models agree with humans more often than multimodal models**, and multimodal alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text, and lowest for text-text.

papers.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.
papers.summary: When a tool call or Skill fails, LLM agents replan on their own, and the recovery path can keep the task working while silently dropping the security protections the original workflow required. The authors call this workflow security downgrade, a threat that needs no change to instructions or tool definitions, and measure it through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment covering seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. Their `ARGUS` framework combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated validation of recovery plans, and execution-time enforcement; in a separate 864-run evaluation it **prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement**, while recovery assistance gives model-dependent gains in protected task completion over blocking alone.

papers.title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios.
