We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
papers.summary: LLM agents can improve over time by reusing procedural memory distilled from past trajectories, but how memories drawn from successes and from failures differ in usefulness has been little studied. Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance (`DualPM`) is a retrieval-free workflow that writes reflections from both local successes and failures within each trajectory and periodically consolidates them under a fixed memory capacity, evaluated online on heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks. The evaluation finds that **failure memory mainly broadens task coverage while success memory streamlines execution, and combining the two captures both benefits**; further tests show cross-domain generalization and portability on `EvoMemBench`.

papers.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
papers.abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.
papers.summary: Numerosity-selective units appear in deep networks trained on unrelated image tasks and even in untrained ones, leaving open what visual learning adds to this spontaneous number sense. Using a geometric framework that tracks how representations of numerosity and proportion change with training, the authors find that untrained and pretrained networks have similar unit-level selectivity and basic comparison performance, but **natural-image pretraining widens the angle between the numerosity and proportion subspaces and reduces their overlap**, supporting more robust readout when the two cues conflict. Directly manipulating these geometric properties confirms their effect on decoding, and the same separation also arises from self-supervised learning without labels and from synthetic-image training.

papers.title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
papers.abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.
papers.summary: Building computer-aided design (CAD) models of rotors for fluid machinery requires a different modeling process for each rotor type, which makes geometry hard to control through design intent and existing models hard to reuse. `VaneCraft` is an agent-driven framework in which an agent interprets design requests and invokes modeling operations over a unified analytical representation: meridional geometry and boundary angle laws act as controls, an anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps them to blade surfaces, and a geometric parameter correction (GPC) module refines controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD models back to the same controls for further editing, and experiments report that the system **outperforms representative baselines on rotor CAD generation** while supporting anisotropy control and parameter editing.

papers.title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
papers.summary: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context, so bounding it requires deciding what to keep. `State Space Attention` (`SSA`) learns that choice: a scorer rescores every stored chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory, a bounded set of past representations is kept and read with ordinary attention, and a technique called recovery generates supervised samples during training to give the scorer signal. On retrieval and reasoning benchmarks it **matches or outperforms a Transformer with about 4 times its readable budget while using constant inference memory**, and it matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language-model scale is on `RULER`.

papers.title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
papers.abstract: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.
papers.summary: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, degrades pretrained SAR models, and the authors use neuron-level interventions to study how it acts inside `SARMAE`. The model has 38 speckle-selective neurons, but restoring them to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching instead points to the first MLP layer, where **a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes**, and 96.5% of that gain remains when the speckle-selective neurons are held at noisy values. The same 64 neurons help on manipulated `Sentinel-1` and `Capella` images, whereas land-cover classification only clearly benefits from restoring the entire first MLP.

papers.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.
papers.summary: Multi-scale networks for all-in-one image restoration spend most of their compute and memory on large high-resolution feature maps. `HiGLR` (High-resolution Global-Local Restoration) is built on an analysis identifying three spatial redundancies in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks, and it replaces finest-scale self-attention with a learned input-independent kernel, uses a `Block-Routed Hybrid Attention` that shares routing indices across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and adds a `Dual-Space FFN` that mixes spatially in a compact space. The authors report state-of-the-art restoration quality with **up to a 4.24x inference speedup** over existing methods.
papers.highlight_summary:
High-resolution stages dominate the compute and memory cost of multi-scale all-in-one image restoration networks, and `HiGLR` cuts that cost by removing three measured redundancies: per-query attention readout at full resolution, per-query key routing at intermediate resolutions, and spatial mixing inside expanded feed-forward features.

- At the finest scale, attention is dropped entirely in favour of learned input-independent kernels, while the two intermediate scales use `BRHA`, which pairs dense attention over block summaries with block-sparse attention over value residuals and shares routing indices within 8×8 query blocks.
- The feed-forward block `DSFFN` runs its depthwise convolution in a compact space (rank 16 at the finest stage) and keeps the expanded path purely pointwise, so the expansion can be kernel-fused without materialising wide high-resolution features.
- With **7M parameters** it averages **31.56 dB** PSNR on `CDD-11`, **1.02 dB** above `BioIR-B` and best in all 11 degradation conditions, while its margins over the 22M-parameter `CEA-IR` on `AIO-3` and `AIO-5` are much narrower at 0.07 and 0.17 dB (33.14 and 31.30 dB).
- At 512×512 on an RTX 4090 it runs in **22.64 ms** with 294.9 MiB peak memory, which is **4.24× faster** than `CEA-IR-S` with 65.8% less memory, and block-shared routing costs only 0.02 dB against query-wise routing while speeding intermediate-stage attention by up to 5.25×.
- The efficiency figures come from a single resolution, batch size, and GPU, they rely on custom fused Triton kernels with BF16 attention cores, and the closest baseline `R2R` is already at 31.76 ms with similar memory traffic, so the headline speedup reflects the slower competitors.

papers.title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
papers.abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.
papers.summary: AI code reviewers built on reasoning models can trade cost for diligence through an effort setting, and this study measures how much effort is needed to catch patches that pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. `Claude Opus 5.5`, `Sonnet 5.5` and `Haiku 5.5` each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from `SWE-bench Verified` at low, medium and high effort, with 55 labeled wrong by strengthened `SWE-ABS` tests. High effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low in every model, and for Opus medium effort was non-inferior to high while costing 20% less, but **no setting was a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of the wrong patches**. The authors also note that for 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks, and without those patches neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

papers.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
papers.abstract: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose a model's hidden representations into sparse features, but existing cross-layer objectives do not explicitly train one layer's sparse code to predict the next layer's. Sparse-to-sparse feature learning (`S2S`) does so, anchoring the final layer with an output-distribution loss and optimizing sequentially from output back to input. Across eight language models it shows **stronger adjacent-layer feature correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines**. Feature-based interventions are compared at matched output-distribution shift to separate steering effects from reconstruction effects, with causal ablation as complementary evidence.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
papers.abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
papers.summary: Per-player feedback strategies in N-player adversarial differential games require solving a coupled, high-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system that generally lacks classical solutions. The authors approximate viscosity solutions with physics-informed neural networks inside a policy iteration scheme that uses a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. They prove **an explicit epsilon-Nash guarantee that bounds each player's regret through computable residuals**, show the method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time, and give a computable value-function error bound for two-player zero-sum games. Pursuit-evasion experiments illustrate how tight the bounds are and how the approach scales to higher dimensions.

papers.title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
papers.abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.
papers.summary: Relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases, but they are usually trained separately for each target and root entity type. Query-Conditioned Relational Pretraining (`QCRP`) is a self-supervised scheme that generates many forecasting objectives from a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor, producing a frozen encoder that is reused through lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. On large `RelBench` databases, **a single unified checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialist models** across tasks and entity types.

papers.title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
papers.abstract: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.
papers.summary: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are normally fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, even though covariance matrices for smooth kernels on noiseless data are often more ill-conditioned than double precision can resolve. Refitting a squared-exponential kernel on a clustered Bayesian-optimization design at many significand widths shows that the double-precision fit is a different model, and that **fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits**. Across 43 kernels, designs and settings the bits needed track that log condition number, and double-precision hyperparameters overstate posterior uncertainty near the cluster and can stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for posterior bias.

papers.title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
papers.abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.
papers.summary: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained once a model is trained further with reinforcement learning (RL). Using three SFT datasets with matched token budgets but different tool-call depths, the authors find similar RL training accuracy yet diverging behavior: tool initiation rises for the shallow dataset, declines for the medium one, and collapses for the deep one, whose trajectories contain much less reasoning before each call. Guided by an idealized selective-retention analysis, they keep only the deep-dataset examples with the longest pre-call reasoning, and **this filtering improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation** across multiple benchmarks.

papers.title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
papers.abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning approaches to portfolio management typically ignore tick-level intraday dynamics such as order flow imbalance and liquidity fluctuation, and their training is unstable because of high variance. The Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (`SCP`) works in two phases: it first merges market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators, then derives allocations from intermediate asset state representations using a self-supervised clipped-objective policy learner. On three major index datasets from China's A-share market, the authors report that it **balances risk and return better than the baselines they compare against**, with ablations attributing gains to each component.

papers.title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
papers.abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 {\deg}C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.
papers.summary: The `Smart Buildings Challenge` asks for a single heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, using only metadata and sensor streams. The controller gives each zone a first-order grey-box model initialized from floor-plan coefficients and updated online by recursive least squares, with a planner and closed-form mapping producing plant commands. It **scores 0.095 times the starter kit's PID baseline on a holdout set scored once**, and ablations show that either the floor-plan prior or online identification alone recovers most of what is lost without both. The result does not carry over to one office floor in a second simulator, `BOPTEST`, where the floor-plan prior alone is the least stable arm.

papers.title: SlicePlanner: Logic-Guided Agentic AI for Online QoS-Aware Network Slicing in Open RAN
papers.abstract: Adaptive network slicing in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) demands reconfiguration decisions that respond to live traffic conditions while remaining safe with respect to Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, a combination that purely data-driven controllers cannot reliably guarantee without continuous retraining. We present SlicePlanner, a logic-guided closed-loop framework that treats each RAN reconfiguration as a controlled hypothesis: proposed from live and historical KeyPerformance Indicator (KPI) evidence, filtered through explicit SLA constraints and mined RAN control rules, and committed only when post-action measurements confirm improvement. SlicePlanner comprises two cooperating agents: SliceSense, which monitors live KPIs, retrieves context-conditioned evidence, and ranks candidate RAN actions through a surrogate-guided admissibility filter; and SliceGuard, which validates post-action KPI responses, rolls back harmful configurations, and refreshes rules under distribution drift. Validated over the air using OpenAirInterface, FlexRIC, and commercial Sierra Wireless 5G devices, SlicePlanner reduces SLA latency violations by up to 86% over static slicing and 50% over Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based slicing, while maintaining comparable cell throughput and auditable decisions without online retraining.
papers.summary: Network slicing in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) must react to live traffic while staying within Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, which purely data-driven controllers cannot guarantee without continual retraining. `SlicePlanner` treats each reconfiguration as a controlled hypothesis handled by two agents: `SliceSense` monitors key performance indicators, retrieves evidence and ranks candidate actions through a rule- and SLA-based admissibility filter, while `SliceGuard` validates post-action measurements, rolls back harmful configurations and refreshes rules under drift. In over-the-air tests with `OpenAirInterface`, `FlexRIC` and commercial 5G devices it **cuts SLA latency violations by up to 86% versus static slicing and 50% versus deep reinforcement learning-based slicing**, at comparable cell throughput and without online retraining.

papers.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
papers.abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.
papers.summary: Checking LLM decomposition of sentences into propositions involves two questions: verifying that a candidate proposition belongs to a sentence, and predicting in advance how many propositions a sentence should yield. On `PropSegmEnt`, a natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy, whereas embedding geometry cannot, since cosine similarity saturates and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, token count, the `CPIDR` idea-density counter and a predicate count all reduce to length proxies, while **a linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps count signal beyond length**, ordering length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time and matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. The signal survives INT8 quantization and truncation to 256 dimensions, and the authors distill a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

papers.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is well established for autoregressive models, but its behavior for diffusion language models (DLMs) is poorly understood. A systematic study finds two failures of classical forward-KL distillation: student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and it underperforms simply training the student with the original denoising objective on the same corpus. The proposed data-free framework runs an off-policy phase on static teacher-generated data, then an on-policy phase with a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting and a trust-region anchor. On `MDLM` the **student reaches a GPT-2 perplexity of 24.75, surpassing the teacher's 27.04**, and distilling `Dream-7B` into a 93M student lowers `Qwen-2.5` perplexity from 25.23 to 19.83.

papers.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
papers.abstract:
Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee.
  In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph.
  Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs.
  Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.
papers.summary: Node-differentially private algorithms protect all records tied to an individual in a graph dataset, and the difficulty is exploiting the low degrees of realistic graphs without weakening the worst-case guarantee. The first contribution is a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable projection that leaves graphs of maximum degree D unchanged and maps any graph to a subgraph of roughly that degree; **unlike prior approaches that abstain when the degree bound is violated, it acts as degree clipping** and retains at least as many edges as a maximal D-bounded subgraph. The second is a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for total edge weight on graphs with bounded edge weights. Both are applied to node-private high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on data whose records sit on graph edges, such as email threads.

papers.title: Interactive Proofs as a Unified Framework for Evaluating and Leveraging Verifiable Proof Generation by LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in LLM-assisted theorem proving and program verification have attracted widespread attention. Beyond determining whether a proposition is true, LLM agents must produce evidence that can be independently checked by humans or formal verification tools. To evaluate the underlying, protocol-agnostic ability of LLM agents to construct verifiable proofs-rather than their proficiency with any particular proof language or verification tool, we introduce Merlin-Bench. Drawing on interactive proof systems from computational complexity theory, we cast an LLM agent as the prover: under a designated protocol, the agent interacts with a formal verifier to substantiate its claimed answer to a problem instance. We develop an automated framework for constructing test cases and use it to create 100 cases across 15 problem families, each formulated within this prover-verifier framework. Experiments with 10 frontier LLMs across multiple agent harnesses show that reliably producing verifiable proofs in accordance with specified protocols remains a substantial challenge. Our case studies further provide actionable insights into improving agents' ability to generate verifier-accepted proofs: tool use is essential for completing practical proof tasks; different forms of guidance, ranging from engineering instructions to problem-specific knowledge, substantially affect success rates on interactive-proof tasks; and proof-solving experience distilled from abstract tasks can transfer to concrete, real-world verification tasks.
papers.summary: `Merlin-Bench` measures whether LLM agents can construct independently checkable proofs regardless of any particular proof language or verification tool. Borrowing interactive proof systems from computational complexity theory, it casts the agent as a prover that must convince a formal verifier of its claimed answer under a designated protocol, with an automated framework producing 100 cases across 15 problem families. Experiments with 10 frontier LLMs across several agent harnesses show that **reliably producing verifier-accepted proofs under specified protocols remains a substantial challenge**. Case studies find that tool use is essential, that guidance ranging from engineering instructions to problem-specific knowledge strongly affects success, and that experience distilled from abstract tasks transfers to concrete verification tasks.

papers.title: Faster and Better Query (FBQ): Learning Future-Position Probes from the First Generated Token
papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.
papers.summary: When an LLM evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it has to choose what to keep before seeing the queries of later decoding steps, and drafting a continuation to approximate them costs extra autoregressive steps. Faster and Better Query (`FBQ`) builds pseudo queries from the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, by placing it at eight future positions and learning an additive offset for each of the seven positions after the first, trained to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On `LongBench` it **performs comparably to eight-step `Lookahead Q-Cache` at the same cache budget while using a single forward pass**.

papers.title: Read Before You Use: Improving Visual Memory Utilization in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal memory enables long-horizon vision-language agents to preserve and retrieve past experiences. While prior research has focused on memory construction and retrieval, effectively using the provided memory remains a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We find that VLMs often fail to answer downstream questions even when sufficient multimodal evidence is provided. To investigate why VLMs struggle, we replace memory images with reference captions and observe substantial performance gains, suggesting difficulties in reading visual evidence directly. However, model-generated captions may omit critical information, limiting this approach in practice. These limitations motivate a closer examination of memory utilization, revealing failures in both evidence reading and downstream question answering. Building on this distinction, we propose \textbf{MemRU}, a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (Read SFT) and downstream evidence utilization through Group Relative Policy Optimization (Use GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our 8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to answer questions even when a multimodal memory system supplies sufficient visual evidence. Replacing memory images with reference captions raises performance substantially, pointing to difficulty reading visual evidence directly, although model-generated captions can omit critical details. `MemRU` separates the two failure points with a two-stage recipe: supervised fine-tuning to improve evidence reading, then Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) to improve use of that evidence in downstream answers. The resulting **8B model generalizes to three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming `Qwen3-VL-32B` and approaching `GPT-5-mini`**.

papers.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
papers.abstract: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
papers.summary: Bias audits of conversational models commonly discard refusals before scoring, a filtering step rarely treated as a measurement decision. Applying seven bias-evaluation instruments, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two datasets of 360 responses each, the authors find the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one responder model, which **refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts** on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. When refusals are scored instead of dropped, no instrument identifies the refusal disparity: `Bias-Lexicon` rates refusals as clean, an apparent `HurtLex` signal traces to one lexicon entry matching the word can inside a contraction, and the judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. The authors conclude the gap is a coverage limit upstream of scoring, not a calibration problem a better lexicon or judge prompt would close.

papers.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
papers.abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.
papers.summary: Locate-then-edit methods update knowledge in large language models without retraining, but sequential versions suffer catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after a few hundred edits, while batch editing that jointly optimizes all edits supports tens of thousands. The authors present a sequential approach that is equivalent to the batch solution, closing that gap. Their analysis of weight perturbations as edits accumulate shows that existing sequential methods grow linearly or logarithmically, whereas **the batch-equivalent method has time-invariant perturbation growth, giving a theoretical guarantee of long-term stability**.

papers.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
papers.abstract:
Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.
  We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.
  The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.
papers.summary: Static agent configurations for conversational sports analytics degrade as queries, data sources, and model behavior shift. `Sports Agent` pairs an `Agentic SQL Model` and a planning and tool-orchestration harness with a Feedback Engine that scores responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and drives both model evolution (synthetic question generation, iterative supervised fine-tuning, and a later reinforcement learning stage) and bounded prompt and skill updates validated by audits, replay, and regression tests. The resulting `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`-based model is reported to outperform `Qwen3.8-Max` on sports question answering at roughly three times the inference efficiency, and 30 harness-evolution rounds raise the aggregate score by 10.8 points. In a live product, the evolved system **improves factual correctness by 10.5 points while cutting average latency by 41.3%**.

papers.title: EVA: Evidence-seeking Visual Agent for Hallucination-Resistant Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.
papers.summary: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often stem from unchecked visual assumptions, and self-reflection or multi-agent debate can reinforce them, while external visual tools can be misused or their evidence ignored. `EVA` treats multimodal reasoning as evidence acquisition and verification, combining `Iterative Tool Replanning`, which refines tool choice and parameters from intermediate observations, with `Evidence Consistency Verification`, which checks the final answer against the collected evidence. A `Selective Evidence Routing` step answers visually simple queries directly and invokes tools only for complex or high-risk cases. The authors report **improved reasoning reliability over direct vision-language model inference and multi-agent methods**, with efficiency preserved through selective tool invocation.

papers.title: P-FedSkill: A Personalized Federated Skill Learning Framework under Task Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Skill learning has become an important way to improve agent performance. However, agent trajectories often contain sensitive information and cannot be shared across clients, hindering collaborative skill learning. To tackle this issue, federated skill learning (FSL) has emerged as a solution by distilling trajectories into compact skill representations and uploading them to a central server for sharing. However, existing FSL methods typically share skills based on skill similarity without considering their contributions to heterogeneous tasks across clients, thereby degrading agent performance. To address this challenge, we propose P-FedSkill, a personalized FSL framework that comprises three key components: local skill extraction (LSE), personalized skill selection (PSS), and task-aware skill routing (TASR). Specifically, LSE first extracts skill patches (i.e., task applicability conditions and execution strategies) and task execution outcomes from trajectories. PSS then uses these outcomes to evaluate each skill patch's performance on client tasks and incorporates its task applicability condition to construct a personalized skill set for each client. Finally, TASR adaptively selects a task-relevant subset of skill patches based on their applicability conditions to guide agent execution. We further provide a theoretical guarantee for personalized skill selection in P-FedSkill, and extensive experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness.
papers.summary: Federated skill learning (FSL) lets agents share compact skills distilled from private trajectories, but existing methods share by skill similarity without checking whether a skill actually helps each client's different tasks. `P-FedSkill` extracts skill patches (applicability conditions plus execution strategies) and task outcomes locally, uses those outcomes to build a personalized skill set per client, and then routes a task-relevant subset of patches to the agent at execution time. The authors provide **a theoretical guarantee for the personalized skill selection step** and report experiments supporting the framework's effectiveness under task heterogeneity.

papers.title: PowerFix: Physics-Guided Iterative Repair for LLM-Assisted Power Converter Design
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for automated engineering design. However, repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation remains challenging: the system must identify physical causes, locate responsible design variables, and resolve violations without compromising other constraints. We introduce PowerFix, a physics-guided iterative repair framework that converts validation failures into structured diagnoses and executable patches while preserving topology and design requirements. PowerDiagGraph links failed checks to possible physical causes and constrains repair routes. An LLM prioritizes these routes, while a deterministic compiler translates selected repairs into authorized field-level edits. Candidates are validated on isolated design copies and committed only after all required engineering checks pass; failed validation can guide replanning. On our constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark, comprising injected single faults, coupled faults, and held-out natural failures from our design generator, PowerFix achieves 78.7% verified repair success rate (VRSR), compared with 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines. Three additional replanning rounds increase VRSR to 88.4%. These offline results provide pilot-stage evidence within a simulation-based design workflow, with hardware prototype validation and transfer to a second converter topology as the next steps toward deployment.
papers.summary: Repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation requires identifying the physical cause, locating the responsible design variables, and fixing violations without breaking other constraints. `PowerFix` uses a `PowerDiagGraph` to link failed checks to physical causes and constrain repair routes; a large language model (LLM) prioritizes the routes, a deterministic compiler turns them into authorized field-level edits, and candidates are committed only after all checks pass on isolated design copies. On a constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark it reaches **78.7% verified repair success rate versus 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines**, rising to 88.4% with three more replanning rounds. The results are simulation-only, with hardware validation and a second topology left for future work.

papers.title: Nepali Currency Denomination Classification Using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and MobileNetV2: An Experimental Comparison
papers.abstract: Automated currency denomination recognition is a computer vision task with applications in cash handling, financial technology, and assistive systems. This study classifies seven Nepali currency denominations (Rs. 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, and 1,000) using three configurations: a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN), MobileNetV2 with transfer learning, and MobileNetV2 with hyperparameter tuning. A compiled dataset of 16,249 images was used, comprising 10,500 training, 3,500 validation, and 2,249 independent test images. Images were resized to 128 x 128 pixels, normalized, and augmented to vary orientation, scale, illumination, and appearance. Models were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and precision-recall and ROC analysis. The hyperparameter-tuned MobileNetV2 achieved the highest validation accuracy (95\%), with precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.93, 0.91, and 0.92, but reached only 84\% accuracy on the held-out test set. MobileNetV2 with transfer learning but no additional tuning achieved 89\% test accuracy, and the conventional CNN achieved 85\%. Transfer learning therefore provided a competitive approach under the evaluated conditions, while higher validation accuracy from tuning did not yield higher test accuracy. To demonstrate practical deployment, a Flask-based web prototype using TensorFlow Lite was developed, supporting image upload and live webcam recognition with both visual and voice output. The study shows the feasibility of combining lightweight deep learning with a voice-assisted web interface for Nepali currency recognition, and highlights the need for more diverse datasets, greater robustness under uncontrolled imaging conditions, and broader real-world evaluation.
papers.summary: Seven Nepali banknote denominations are classified using three setups: a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN), `MobileNetV2` with transfer learning, and `MobileNetV2` with hyperparameter tuning, trained and evaluated on a compiled dataset of 16,249 images. The tuned model reached the highest validation accuracy at 95% but only 84% on the held-out test set, while **untuned transfer-learning `MobileNetV2` achieved the best test accuracy at 89%** and the plain CNN reached 85%. A Flask web prototype running `TensorFlow Lite` supports image upload and live webcam recognition with voice output.

papers.title: KeyDeck: Multi-Paper-to-Slide Generation via Cross-Paper Synthesis and Reference-Guided Personalization
papers.abstract: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) is the task of constructing a unified presentation from multiple research papers by selecting, organizing, and synthesizing information across sources. This task introduces two main challenges: (i) combining multiple sources into a coherent narrative requires identifying cross-paper relationships and synthesizing their content, and (ii) the desired organization and emphasis varies substantially across presenters, making personalization essential for user satisfaction. Motivated by these challenges, we propose KeyDeck, the first multi-PTSG framework that integrates per-paper and cross-paper analysis to identify relationships among sources and synthesize their contributions into a coherent narrative, and reference-guided personalization to infer presenters' narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences and adapt slide generation accordingly. To evaluate generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction, we introduce KeyBench, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations, together with a comprehensive evaluation framework. Our results demonstrate that KeyDeck outperforms existing approaches in multi-PTSG quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction.
papers.summary: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) means building one presentation from several research papers, which requires finding relationships across sources and adapting to how individual presenters like to organize and emphasize material. `KeyDeck` combines per-paper and cross-paper analysis to synthesize a coherent narrative, and uses reference-guided personalization to infer a presenter's narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences. The authors also introduce `KeyBench`, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations with an accompanying evaluation framework, and report that **`KeyDeck` outperforms existing approaches on generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction**.

papers.title: Flipping the Coins: Training Physical Simulators through Hard Switches
papers.abstract: Hybrid simulators embed learnable components such as neural networks in physical solvers and train them on reference trajectories. Many scientific solvers feature hard switches, such as a tripping power line, an igniting grid cell, or depolarizing brain tissue, where the loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, leaving standard automatic differentiation to capture only its smooth part. Existing training paradigms face a fundamentally challenging trade-off, as gradient-based relaxations smooth the switches and introduce bias across jumps, whereas derivative-free methods treat the solver as a black box and discard path gradients of the continuous dynamics. Here we introduce EventFlip, which flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the original solver, and measures the loss difference between the two runs, in effect a finite difference across the switch. By perturbing every threshold with small Gaussian noise, we cast each switch as a stochastic binary decision and derive an unbiased gradient estimator that combines the continuous path gradient with a jump term constructed from these counterfactual rollouts. EventFlip-Rand optimizes this noise-averaged objective, whereas EventFlip-Hard operates on the deterministic hard-switch simulator used at deployment and provably targets the complete discontinuous loss. Under an identical forward evaluation budget, we benchmark EventFlip against twelve baselines across a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, achieving the lowest error on every task and reducing the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4, respectively.
papers.summary: Hybrid simulators that embed neural networks in physical solvers are hard to train when the solver contains hard switches, such as a tripping power line, because the loss jumps discontinuously and automatic differentiation only sees its smooth part. `EventFlip` flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the solver, and measures the loss difference, then combines this jump term with the ordinary path gradient into an unbiased gradient estimator by treating each noise-perturbed threshold as a stochastic binary decision. Two variants are given: `EventFlip-Rand` optimizes the noise-averaged objective and `EventFlip-Hard` targets the deterministic simulator used at deployment. Against twelve baselines under an equal forward-evaluation budget on a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, it **achieves the lowest error on every task, cutting the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4**.

papers.title: Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
papers.abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.
papers.summary: Classifier-free guidance is central to diffusion and flow models yet poorly understood theoretically, because the associated transport equations are hard to solve in general. The authors attribute its effects to a mismatch in representational capacity between the conditional and unconditional distributions, and model this with a conditional Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid and an unconditional single Gaussian approximating it, which admits closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. The solution shows that guidance causes **a shift along a mean-axis direction plus a persistent skew toward and concentration around a single point**, corresponding to the conditional sample started from zero noise. The predictions are checked against pretrained large-scale image diffusion models.

papers.title: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
papers.abstract: People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation. We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice. This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes. We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost. FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in new Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth. On a real robot, success rises from 62.3\% to 74.6\% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69\,s to 31\,s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.
papers.summary: Looped models produce intermediate predictions that allow early exits, but training them to use fewer iterations with practice is hard because shared-weight updates can damage the final-loop prediction and the exit gate must track changing early-prediction quality. `FLUENT` needs no extra task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to trade off disagreement with the final prediction against computation cost. It improves shallow-depth performance in new `Crafter` worlds, raises `LIBERO` success with fewer action-head iterations, and holds language-model accuracy at lower depth. On a real robot, **success rises from 62.3% to 74.6% while mean time over successful episodes drops from 69 s to 31 s**.

papers.title: NORMCRAFT: Cultural Norm Generation for Context-Aware Language Model Alignment
papers.abstract: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.
