papers.summary: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. `NORMCRAFT` separates norm inference from response generation: one LLM is trained as a norm generator using multi-view supervision over prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios, with no downstream response labels, and its norms then guide a separate frozen responder model. With `Qwen3.5-4B` as responder it beats prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics, and on `SafeWorld` **exceeds responder SFT by 18.0 points on Coverage and 14.1 points on Faithfulness**. The same generator improves cultural alignment across fourteen frozen LLMs from 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.

papers.title: Asset4D-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Editable 3D and 4D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.
papers.summary: `Asset4D-Bench` tests whether coding agents can recover objects, motion, and interactions from visual references as editable `Blender` scenes, across 114 conditions covering image editing, video reconstruction with full or partial starter assets, and from-scratch tasks. Projects are independently reopened and measured against native reference states, yielding 228 archived scores. On 24 from-scratch tasks each model earns full dynamics credit on 14, yet three `GPT-6.1-Sol` and eight `GPT-6-Astra` reconstructions among those earn zero relation points, and **relations account for 5.15 of the 6.50-point gap in mean recovered fidelity between the two models**. The authors note that differences in execution and recovery policy across runs rule out a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.

papers.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.
papers.summary: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition forecasts on future input variables, which makes them attractive for predicting outcomes under planned actions, but their behavior is unclear when those treatment covariates fall outside anything seen in the history. The authors give an operational definition of this covariate novelty and build `CovNovBench`, 88,476 evaluation series drawn from four simulator-based and real-world datasets, covering categorical and numerical treatments and stable and trending targets. Zero-shot evaluation of six covariate-aware TSFMs finds that **no model is consistently reliable: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty**, directional accuracy changes non-uniformly, and the best model varies by dataset and metric.

papers.title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.
papers.summary: AI glasses must serve workloads ranging from simple device control to complex visual reasoning over speech, images, and video, and the simple text-based tasks have received little attention. `JOVE ICE` routes each request among the glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers using hierarchical intent classification and dynamic subagent orchestration, with new applications added as specialized subagents. Analysis of real-world requests shows simple device control makes up over 30% of interactions, which the system handles on device. On three public benchmarks it **reduces time to first token by about 13% and token usage by over 11%** compared with conventional device-and-cloud architectures while maintaining task quality.

papers.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
papers.abstract:
Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving.
  FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$).
  Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
papers.summary: Clients of closed-weight large language model (LLM) APIs cannot verify that the provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. `FlashProve-Next` generates zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual API responses without changing native floating-point serving and without revealing weights, hidden prompts, or activations, using a Reed-Solomon weight commitment, per-operator rounding contracts, and cost-weighted spot-checking; its soundness arguments are mechanized in 28 `Lean 4` modules. Calibration on five models gave zero false rejections across millions of checked blocks, and proving `Qwen3-0.6B` in the external-seed mode took 450.2 s on GPU. On a live `vLLM` deployment of `Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8`, one proof relation is **proved in 1.49 s and verified in 23.4 ms**.

papers.title: OrbACE: Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion
papers.abstract:
Accurate electronic-structure reference data are expensive, motivating interatomic potentials that learn effectively from limited training sets. We introduce OrbACE (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion), a framework that supplements an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone with inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors. On ANI-1x at the $\omega$B97X/6-31G* level, its atom-centered variant, OrbACE-A, trained on 10,000 configurations and evaluated on 442,000 held-out configurations, achieves energy and force mean absolute errors of 3.16 meV/atom and 76 meV/angstrom in direct learning, compared with 9.61 meV/atom and 146 meV/angstrom for MACE with matched backbone settings. This reduces the energy error by a factor of three and approximately halves the force error. Its energy error is also below that of the best delta-corrected MACE baseline, 5.00 meV/atom, although its force error is slightly higher. Combining OrbACE-A with a Hartree-Fock delta baseline further reduces the errors to 1.48 meV/atom and 35 meV/angstrom.
  OrbACE-A builds atom- and pair-resolved invariants from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model evaluated within the differentiable forward pass, yielding forces consistent with the predicted energy. The orbital variant, OrbACE-O, instead uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes, with scalar and equivariant electronic descriptors. Its forces are evaluated at fixed descriptors, omitting their response to nuclear motion. In direct learning on ANI-1x, its energy error is approximately three times that of OrbACE-A. The three benchmarks considered (ANI-1x, revised MD17, and 3BPA) cover neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules containing H, C, N, and O. Performance outside this domain remains to be established.
papers.summary: Interatomic potentials need to learn from small training sets because electronic-structure reference data are expensive. `OrbACE` (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion) adds inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors to an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone; the atom-centered variant `OrbACE-A` derives them from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model inside the differentiable forward pass, while `OrbACE-O` uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes. Trained on 10,000 `ANI-1x` configurations, `OrbACE-A` reaches **3.16 meV/atom energy error versus 9.61 meV/atom for `MACE` with matched settings**, and roughly halves the force error. All three benchmarks cover only neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules of H, C, N, and O, so performance elsewhere is untested.

papers.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.
papers.summary: Choosing between robot actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation, which ordinary world models trained on factual transitions do not directly provide. `WhatIf` is a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from history, with each action inducing a sparse object-factor causal graph of the physical pathways it activates. On top of it, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations while constraining the probability of harm. The authors show that **paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of 1 − ρ, where ρ is the correlation between branch outcomes**, and evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, generalization, and decision quality with paired simulator interventions.

papers.title: Tells of a Lying Machine: Analyzing LLM-Generated Strategic Dialogue in Chinese Werewolf
papers.abstract: Social-deduction games give models opposing objectives, but they also give roles different information and speaking obligations. We analyze 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese Werewolf games played by 12 models, comparing ordinary wolves with ordinary villagers so that special roles are excluded. Private knowledge and goals still differ, and no utterance is verified as true or false. After model and length adjustment, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty (coefficients +0.074 and +0.072). Emotional intensification has the largest rank-biserial effect (r = .145), but it depends on a single degree marker and correlates weakly with human-rated affect. Three annotators' ratings of 392 utterances show higher wolf scores on four behavioral dimensions, and five LLM judges reach 60.8%-70.2% accuracy on a shared evaluation set. In a generation probe that prompts six models with a wolf identity but a villager speaking goal under fixed public context, certainty (+0.164) and emotional intensification (+0.095) increase. These findings describe role-associated language rather than verified lying, and they argue for explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation. Data and code are available at https://github.com/justinchoi929/Tells-of-a-Lying-Machine
papers.summary: Social-deduction games are used to study deception in language models, but roles also differ in information and speaking obligations. The authors analyze 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese Werewolf games played by 12 models, comparing ordinary wolves with ordinary villagers. After adjusting for model and length, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty markers, human annotators rate wolves higher on four behavioral dimensions, and **five LLM judges identify wolves with only 60.8%-70.2% accuracy**. The authors stress that these results describe role-associated language rather than verified lying, and argue for explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation.

papers.title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit multi-stage verification evidence rather than a single pass/fail outcome.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can repair register-transfer level (RTL) hardware code, but passing compilation or a testbench does not show that a defect is removed, behavior is preserved, or the result is secure and implementable. `REFORGE` profiles buggy RTL, localizes failing behavior, and generates repair variants that each go through syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, behavior preservation checks, a security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis, accumulating structured evidence across iterations. In 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites, its context and diagnosis raise checked repairs on `CirFix` from 32/63 to 51/63. The evidence records show that **a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks**.

papers.title: Teaching Students to Stand on Their Own: Distilling Vision Foundation Models for Fine-Grained Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn visually similar new classes from limited images without catastrophic forgetting. Prior work typically learns strong representations on base classes or leverages vision foundation models (VFMs) directly as backbones or via knowledge distillation. However, VFM backbones incur high computational costs and do not guarantee fine-grained recognition. Although knowledge distillation reduces inference cost, our preliminary experiments reveal that distilled students still lag substantially behind their VFM teachers, particularly on new classes. To address this limitation, we propose STAND, a systematic VFM-to-student distillation design tailored for FG-FSCIL. Specifically, STAND connects the teacher and student by equipping the student with a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligning their outputs via projectors, and feeding both models composite images that combine different training images. On these composite images, relation distillation matches how the teacher and the student relate each image to other images, while difference distillation matches how this relation changes between two composite images. Finally, we freeze the student and classify new classes using length-calibrated prototypes, which restore the reduced similarity of few-shot prototypes. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that STAND achieves state-of-the-art performance across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost, while generalizing across student backbones and broader datasets.
papers.summary: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) means adding visually similar new classes from a handful of images without forgetting old ones; vision foundation models (VFMs) help but are costly as backbones, and distilled students lag their teachers, especially on new classes. `STAND` is a distillation design that gives the student a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligns outputs through projectors, and trains on composite images with relation distillation and difference distillation losses. The student is then frozen and new classes are classified with length-calibrated prototypes. The authors report **state-of-the-art results across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost**, with generalization across student backbones and broader datasets.

papers.title: TransHarness: From Benchmark Overfitting to Transferable Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: Harness evolution offers a path to improving coding agents without updating model weights. However, existing methods can overfit their evolution benchmarks, producing gains that fail to carry over to new tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce Transferable Harness Evolution (TransHarness), which evolves harness intervention policies from same-task success-failure contrasts. These policies couple execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance, enabling task-dependent checks and corrections beyond the source executions. Cross-task replay and independent semantic selection retain policies that intervene selectively and ground corrections in current-task evidence rather than source-specific solutions. We further curate an independent evolution set for cross-distribution transfer and conduct a cross-benchmark evaluation covering multiple strong models and a range of lightweight and mature harnesses. Experiments show that, with only 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, TransHarness further improves strong agents across distinct target benchmarks, demonstrating transferable harness evolution beyond benchmark overfitting. Specifically, TransHarness achieves state-of-the-art scores of 76.4% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 95.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, surpassing the strongest baseline model, GPT-6 Astra, by 2.4 and 5.6 percentage points, respectively.
papers.summary: Harness evolution improves coding agents without changing model weights, but existing methods can overfit the benchmark they evolve on. `TransHarness` learns harness intervention policies from contrasts between successful and failed runs of the same task, pairing execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance, and keeps only policies that survive cross-task replay and independent semantic selection so that corrections rely on current-task evidence. Using just 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, it improves strong agents across several models and harnesses on separate target benchmarks. It reports **76.4% on `DeepSWE v1.1` and 95.5% on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`**, exceeding the strongest baseline model, `GPT-6 Astra`, by 2.4 and 5.6 percentage points.

papers.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
papers.abstract: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.
papers.summary: Double descent, where test loss peaks near the interpolation threshold and then falls again as models grow, is analysed here through universal compression. The maximum-likelihood excess test loss is upper-bounded by four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and a gap between the maximum-likelihood and Bayes predictors. In experiments, a Gaussian-prior `SGLD` approximation to the Bayes predictor shows no pronounced interpolation peak, unlike `SGD`. With uniform random labels, **the `SGD` cross-entropy is roughly four times the `SGLD` ensemble cross-entropy at the peak**, which points to that gap as a major contributor to the peak.

papers.title: ScanAR: Parallel Row-Scan Decoding for Efficient Image Generation in Unified Autoregressive Models
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal autoregressive (AR) models represent text and images in one token sequence and generate all modalities with a shared next-token prediction head. Their image generation, however, decodes an $H\times W$ visual grid token by token in raster order, which takes $HW$ sequential steps and dominates inference time. Existing acceleration methods for visual AR generation either change the tokenizer, the prediction head, or the model interface, or keep the model but cannot reach high parallelism without losing quality, so they do not carry over to unified AR models. We propose ScanAR, a row-scan parallel decoding method that only redefines the predecessors of visual tokens. The first visual row is generated from left to right as usual, and each later row is generated in a single parallel step, with every token predicted from the vertically aligned token of the previous row. Nonvisual tokens keep the standard autoregressive rule. ScanAR reduces the visual decoding depth from $HW$ to $H+W$ without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head and without adding parameters, and it supports both training from scratch and lightweight post-training. On Emu3.5-Image-34B, ScanAR post-training reaches a GenEval score of 82.36, the best among post-training acceleration methods trained on the same data, and generates $512\times512$ images $13.8\times$ faster than raster decoding under the same inference setting. On ImageNet, ScanAR trained from scratch has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster LlamaGen. On the 34B Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 model, ScanAR preserves the overall quality of embodied scene generation, interleaved image-text generation, and video generation.
papers.summary: Unified multimodal autoregressive models generate an H-by-W image grid one token at a time, so image decoding takes HW sequential steps and dominates inference time. `ScanAR` generates the first visual row left to right and then produces each later row in a single parallel step, predicting every token from the vertically aligned token in the previous row, which cuts decoding depth to H+W without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head. After post-training on `Emu3.5-Image-34B` it reaches a `GenEval` score of 82.36 and generates 512x512 images **13.8x faster than raster decoding**. Trained from scratch on `ImageNet`, it has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster `LlamaGen`.

papers.title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
papers.abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for indoor climate control is hampered by delayed thermal responses, partial observability, and prediction errors that accumulate over long rollouts. The proposed framework trains indoor environmental world models to predict future thermal baselines and occupancy, then learns control as counterfactual advantage against those predicted futures using a `Branching Dueling Q-Network`, a `Held-Action TD-lambda` target, and a smoothness regulariser on actuator commands. On `SemiBuildingSim` and `Sinergym`, it reports **11.2% lower energy consumption**, 44.2% less occupant discomfort, and 47.3% less action fluctuation than the best-performing baselines.

papers.title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.
papers.summary: Parallel annealers produce many diverse candidate solutions, but standard post-processing refines only the best one. `Iterative Path-Relinking Polish` (`I-PRP`) is a deterministic, training-free method that explores cost-guided paths between locally optimised candidates, refines the intermediate states, and feeds improvements back into the population. The authors prove it never does worse than single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. On `MaxCut`, `MaxClique`, and graph coloring benchmarks, matched-runtime comparisons show that **exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing**.

papers.title: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information
papers.abstract: Experimental design allocates limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. Adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates, improving estimation and treatment selection. Contextual information can inform these decisions, but exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains challenging. We use large language models (LLMs) to transform complex context into proxy outcomes and propose Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE), a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that combines true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). Our methodology uses proxy outcomes in two ways: sample augmentation improves estimation precision, while observing proxies before each allocation decision provides advance information. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data suggest that estimation precision drives most gains, with smaller advance-information gains, and highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy.
papers.summary: Adaptive experimental design allocates limited measurements across treatments, but making use of unstructured or high-dimensional context is difficult. `RHOPE` (Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation) uses large language models to turn that context into proxy outcomes, then combines them with true outcomes in a Bayesian framework that treats finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic ones on `GDSC` (Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer) data suggest that **most of the gain comes from improved estimation precision**, with smaller gains from seeing proxies before each allocation decision.

papers.title: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform
papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models are increasingly deployed by selection: a practitioner picks a public checkpoint by benchmark rank and fine-tunes it on local data. The platform is fixed before the model is chosen, with little or no local data. We ask what such a checkpoint loses on a fixed platform and which part of the loss local data can buy back. We split the gap by what can repair it. A sensing gap, information the sensors do not capture, cannot be closed with their data; a latency gap, output arriving after the control loop needs it, belongs to the loop, not the weights; only a distribution gap is fine-tuning's to repair. TRIAGE turns this into feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation in five stages: gates on the sensor contract and on end-to-end latency that no score can override, probes on ten minutes of local logs, a ranking by target-relevant score among the candidates that pass, and fine-tuning that is monitored and checked in closed loop before release. On driving benchmarks, a deadline below a leading closed-loop model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes, and losing field of view moves plans 2.2 to 5.7 times more than losing resolution at equal pixels. Local frames close 75% of a stability gap but raise perturbation sensitivity at small budgets, and picking by score violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the factory camera failed the sensing gate and an added camera repaired it. The latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip. The selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips, and the closed-loop check withheld a fine-tuned model that had improved offline. TRIAGE lets organizations that cannot train foundation models from scratch find out whether a public checkpoint can run on the robot or vehicle they own, and what to fix if not.
papers.summary: Practitioners often pick a public embodied foundation model by benchmark rank and fine-tune it for a robot or vehicle whose hardware is already fixed. `TRIAGE` splits the resulting performance loss into a sensing gap, a latency gap, and a distribution gap, of which only the last can be repaired by fine-tuning, and turns this into a five-stage pipeline of hard gates on sensors and latency, probes on ten minutes of local logs, ranking among passing candidates, and monitored fine-tuning with a closed-loop check. On driving benchmarks, **a deadline below a leading closed-loop model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes**, and choosing by score alone violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, and the selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips.

papers.title: Robust Adaptive Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted mmWave Massive MIMO via a Stochastic Shannon Entropy Criterion
papers.abstract: Accurate channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems remains challenging due to the passive nature of the RIS, the high dimensionality of the cascaded channel, and the presence of non-Gaussian impulsive disturbances. This paper proposes a robust sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, termed reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy (RZA-SSE), for angular-domain channel estimation. The algorithm combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized \(\ell_1\) penalty. Both the data-driven term and the nonsmooth penalty are differentiated using exact Wirtinger calculus. An exact weight-error recursion and a mean-square energy relation are derived. Local stability is analyzed via a joint coefficient--penalty state representation, and an approximate steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD) expression is obtained. Extensive simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise demonstrate that ZA-SSE consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD.
papers.summary: Channel estimation is difficult in millimeter-wave massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems assisted by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), because the surface is passive, the cascaded channel is high-dimensional, and the noise can be impulsive and non-Gaussian. The proposed sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, `RZA-SSE` (reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy), combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized L1 penalty, and comes with a stability analysis and an approximate expression for steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD). In simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise, the authors report that **the entropy-based estimator consistently beats state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD**.

papers.title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination
papers.abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
papers.summary: Diagnosing congenital heart disease (CHD) depends on understanding spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. `CHD-Bench` defines a multi-label interactive diagnosis task over 247 CT and MRI scans covering 38 CHD types, and `CHD-Harness` is open-source software that lets a vision-language model examine scans in a `3D Slicer` environment through 22 tools. `Gemini 4 Argon` with the harness achieves the highest macro F1 across the three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43), and **interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views**.

papers.title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
papers.abstract:
Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models.
  Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
  Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios.
  Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation.
  Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.
papers.summary: `InterGenEHR+` generates synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal patient trajectories from natural-language clinical requests, so that machine learning models can be evaluated on specified scenarios. An optional large language model parser converts requests into structured constraints, after which conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records and diffusion models generate trajectories. On a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO), `Gemma 3 4B` with few-shot prompting was the best parser, and **synthetic cohorts retained predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data** across five seeds and three classifiers. The authors note that other clinical settings would need further validation.

papers.title: Multimodal Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language Models in Japanese
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Multimodal safety evaluation of vision-language models has been largely English-centric despite growing deployment in Japanese. The authors extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (`MSTS`) to Japanese with 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases plus 82 culturally localized images, and add a 5-point scale that rewards useful as well as safe responses while separating image recognition errors from safety judgment. Human evaluation of `Gemini-3-Flash`, `GPT-5`, `InternVL3`, `LLM-JP-4-VL`, and `Qwen3-VL` shows substantial variance in safety readiness. For automated judging, giving the judge model a reference answer improves agreement with humans, but **recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited**.

papers.title: ExtractBench Pro: The Long Tail of Document Extraction
papers.abstract: We present ExtractBench Pro, a schema-guided document extraction benchmark that tests six challenging modes of extraction underrepresented in existing datasets. It is created following a framework for synthetic document generation, in which deterministic document generators assemble challenging components into documents that are designed to be difficult at a level calibrated for frontier systems. We synthesize 100 realistic documents spanning a diverse range of styles. On this data, we evaluate ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations for accuracy, grounding, and their ability to perfectly extract documents. No extraction system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, Claude Code Opus 5.5 and Codex GPT-6 Astra, outperform specialized extraction APIs on both perfect-document rate and Value F1, but at a higher cost per page. Among specialized extraction APIs, LlamaExtract spans the lower-cost frontier, with Agentic Plus Max Effort approaching the strongest coding agent on both perfect-document rate and Value F1 at lower cost per page. Our analysis of coding agent traces identifies intelligent image processing and programmatic reasoning, but also failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams. We release ExtractBench Pro and these evaluation results as resources for the future development of improved frontier extraction systems.
papers.summary: `ExtractBench Pro` is a schema-guided document extraction benchmark of 100 synthetic documents, assembled by deterministic generators to stress six extraction modes that existing datasets underrepresent. Ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations are evaluated on accuracy, grounding, and error-free extraction, and **no system extracts more than 61% of documents without error**. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, `Claude Code Opus 5.5` and `Codex GPT-6 Astra`, beat specialized extraction APIs on perfect-document rate and Value F1 but cost more per page, while `LlamaExtract` covers the lower-cost frontier. Agent traces show effective image processing and programmatic reasoning alongside failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams.

papers.title: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions
papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing path costs. Most MAPF algorithms assume that each agent occupies a single vertex and that the actions of all agents are synchronized. These assumptions may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. Existing planners that get rid of both assumptions either handle only a few agents or cannot improve their solutions. Recently, a planner called LSRP* was proposed, which is scalable and anytime with asynchronous actions, but still limited by that each agent occupies a single vertex. This paper develops a new planner called LSRP*-LA for MAPF for large agents with asynchronous actions (LA-MAPF-AA), where an agent can occupy several cells. LSRP*-LA is scalable and complete, and it keeps improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP*-LA and test it against several baselines with up to 800 agents on various maps. LSRP*-LA can handle twice as many agents as baseline methods and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.
papers.summary: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) planners usually assume each agent occupies a single vertex and that all agents act in sync, which limits practical use. `LSRP*-LA` extends the scalable, anytime `LSRP*` planner to large agents that occupy several cells and act asynchronously; it is complete and keeps improving its solution until the runtime budget runs out. In tests with up to 800 agents, it **handles twice as many agents as baseline methods**, and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.

papers.title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies
papers.abstract: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement of embodied policies, in which progress is judged by evidence the improving system cannot influence.
papers.summary: Self-improving embodied policies are typically kept or discarded by a judge trained inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy it rates. `SealedLoop` adds a sealed judge that the improver cannot see or optimize against, and keeps a new policy only when a sequential test on that judge confirms the gain with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. On `LIBERO` manipulation an in-loop success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation, and on `NAVSIM` driving, policies that improved on the loop's own frames lost in an unseen city. On driving pairs with known sealed gain, **the sealed test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses**; in a real-vehicle test the reinforced policy drove further into a curve in all 6 blind pairs, though neither version completed it.

papers.title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning models can represent complex distributions but are hard to deploy on current noisy hardware because of barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and inference latency. `QPAT` (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training) uses a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior during training of a classical backbone such as an LSTM, CNN, or Transformer, with a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic `Drop-Prior` step that distils the prior's structure into the classical weights. Across six benchmarks in time-series forecasting, vision, and language, it outperforms purely classical backbones in accuracy and seed stability while **running inference entirely classically**. Ablations indicate the gains are not reproduced by random priors or a classically learned generative prior.

papers.title: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Inverse Design
papers.abstract: RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into specified target structures. Existing methods rely on learned generators that can miss exact structural matches, especially beyond their training distributions, or on costly search over a vast, multimodal sequence space. Search is further complicated by globally coupled nucleotide interactions, as correcting one pairing error can create new errors beyond a fixed repair scope. To address this, we introduce KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that learns from verifier feedback to refine sequences for exact fold-back matching. Starting from candidates generated for a target secondary structure, KnitNet uses mismatched folds to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns to predict which edits are promising. This makes search progressively more informed and compute-efficient. Crucially, KnitNet generalizes across RNA structural regimes by changing only the optimization signal to match the verifier required by each setting. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, KnitNet increases exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve. On OpenKnot57 specifically, KnitNet is the first method to achieve exact computational matches for all complex, pseudoknotted structures. Beyond 2D, KnitNet improves 3D structural self-consistency over per-target RL by 7.8% while being 39.3% faster, demonstrating generalization and effective inference-time scaling across RNA design regimes.
papers.summary: RNA inverse design looks for nucleotide sequences that fold into a given target structure, but learned generators often miss exact matches and search is expensive because nucleotide interactions are globally coupled. `KnitNet` is an inference-time framework that uses mismatched folds from a verifier to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns which edits are promising. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks it **raises exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling**, with 70% less time-to-solve, and it is reported as the first method to exactly match all pseudoknotted structures in `OpenKnot57`. For 3D design it improves structural self-consistency over per-target reinforcement learning by 7.8% while running 39.3% faster.

papers.title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
papers.abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.
papers.summary: Barrier certificates give formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems, but new obstacles or constraints after deployment can invalidate them. The authors treat this as a localized certificate repair problem, using adaptive piecewise barrier certificates that keep the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions and update only around the new unsafe regions, with a staged process that escalates from local repair to joint policy-certificate updates and local retraining. On four benchmarks with five new obstacles the method succeeds in every case within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most. Where retraining does succeed, the repair is **17.3x faster on average**, at a cost of 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

papers.title: Spectral Optimal Transport for Dynamics-Aware Sign Language Generation
papers.abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this issue, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
papers.summary: Sign language generation (SLG) turns spoken-language text into pose sequences, and flow-based models with optimal transport are a strong baseline for it. The authors argue that classifier-free guidance conflicts with pose-space optimal transport, because condition dropout during training can pair one noise sample with target motions that have incompatible dynamics. `Spectral Optimal Transport` (`SOT`) adds a spectral feature distance to the pose-space cost so that the coupling respects the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions. Quantitative and qualitative experiments are reported to show that **this improves generation when classifier-free guidance is used**, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
papers.abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.
papers.summary: An AI-predicted radiotherapy dose must still be turned into a physically deliverable plan by an optimization that balances competing objectives. `RadOncGym` lets an LLM agent iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for this dose-mimicking step, using a fast surrogate verifier for feedback and choosing when to spend one of a limited number of full planning solves. On 60 `OpenKBP` head-and-neck patients with 10 dose predictions each, a `GPT-5.6 Sol` agent with a three-solve budget reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy relative to leaving all weights at 1, and beats all evaluated non-agent tuning methods under the same budget. It stays competitive with 16-solve versions of those methods while using **75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime**.

papers.title: MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory
papers.abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Language agents on long-horizon tasks need to know which stored procedures apply and what work remains as execution proceeds. `MetaDecomp` is an in-context meta-learning framework whose outer loop builds procedural memory from successful runs, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures as directed acyclic graphs of operations, and revisits past evidence as new state distinctions are learned. At test time, with memory fixed, an inner loop refines a task decomposition and revises it from environment feedback. On `ALFWorld` and `ScienceWorld` it has the highest mean performance in four of five settings, including **an 86.3% success rate on `ALFWorld` with `Qwen3-4B`**, and uses fewer inference tokens than `ReAct` and `AutoRefine` in all five.

papers.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) can unmask tokens in any order, and one intuitive principle, here called dependency-ready decoding, says a token's dependencies should be resolved before it is unmasked. Examining a recent attention-based decoder built on this idea, the authors find that **when it beats confidence-based or future-utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to plain left-to-right**. They then define dependency without attention, as an information-theoretic score of how much revealing one masked token shifts the prediction for another, and prove that when the prediction margin is large relative to this score, no revelation can change the top prediction. `Maximum-Margin` decoding therefore already commits dependency-ready tokens in that regime, leaving potential benefit only at low-margin positions.

papers.title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
papers.abstract: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.
papers.summary: Grokking, the long delay between fitting the training data and generalizing, is analyzed by extending a signal-channel theory to connect training dissipation and evaluation transfer with population risk in preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels. The analysis separates two reasons a learned task may be invisible at evaluation (small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer) and gives conditions under which one training trajectory generalizes on one evaluation distribution but fails on another. Differences in spectral learning rates are shown to produce arbitrarily long delays followed by arbitrarily sharp accuracy transitions, all without any feature evolution. The authors also prove that **whether and when generalization occurs cannot in general be inferred from training dynamics alone**.

papers.title: FEAST: Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling for Task-Free On-Policy Learning
papers.abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which shows that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Language agents trained on their own rollouts must split a limited rollout budget across different capabilities, and prioritizing whichever capability shows the strongest learning signal can starve weaker ones, because past allocation shapes the evidence used for future allocation. The authors formalize this as the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL) and propose `FEAST`, a task-free sampler that discovers capability clusters, guarantees each continued sampling opportunities, and within each cluster's reserved budget concentrates compute on prompts with informative reward variation. On `GURU-18K` and `SMC`, `FEAST` **improves average performance over adaptive sampling baselines at matched rollout budgets while better preserving progress on weaker capabilities**.

papers.title: Learning a Whole-Body Pivot-Walking Gait for Heavy-Box Transport with a Humanoid
papers.abstract: Through pivot walking, humans can transport objects that are too heavy to lift. Previous humanoid studies have relied on planned sequences in which object manipulation and stepping are executed separately and the object is brought to rest between successive rotations. However, few studies have developed a single learned controller for humanoid pivot walking. In this paper, we propose a single reinforcement-learning policy that jointly coordinates stepping, balance control, and object manipulation. The policy is trained using rewards that promote alternating pivot motions and a phase reference that progresses according to the displacement of the object. In simulation, we confirmed that the humanoid can pivot a box. For deployment, we fine-tuned the policy into an object-blind version that follows a periodic clock instead of the progress reference. On the real robot, the deployed policy transported the box forward by more than 1 m in all five trials; each trial ended at a base-tilt safety stop. These results demonstrate that coordinated humanoid pivot walking can be learned with reinforcement learning and transferred to a physical humanoid robot without direct object-state sensing.
papers.summary: Pivot walking lets a humanoid move a box too heavy to lift by rocking it alternately on its corners, but earlier work used planned sequences that separate manipulation from stepping.
