Here a single reinforcement-learning policy coordinates stepping, balance, and box manipulation, trained with rewards for alternating pivots and a phase reference tied to the box's displacement, then fine-tuned into an object-blind version driven by a periodic clock for deployment. On the real robot, the policy **moved the box forward more than 1 m in all five trials**, although every trial ended at a base-tilt safety stop.

papers.title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
papers.abstract: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.
papers.summary: `VoroPlex` is an open-source Python package for computing two- and three-dimensional Voronoi tessellations, built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library `Voro++`. It labels each Voronoi vertex by the generator points that define it, which lets `PyTorch` compute gradients of cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to generator positions, so those quantities can be optimized by gradient descent. For one million points on 28 threads it is **46 times faster than `SciPy` in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D**, and it is demonstrated on variable-density centroidal tessellations, meshing of 2D shapes, and foam design.

papers.title: Teaching a Multilingual Translation Model Regional Varieties: Castilian and Latin American Spanish, Asturian, Aragonese and Aranese with MADLAD-400-3B-MT
papers.abstract: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: <2es_ES> for Spanish as written in Spain, <2es_419> for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian (<2ast>), Aragonese (<2an>) and Aranese (<2oc_aranes>). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from <2es>, the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. All three fine-tunes lose 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on average in thirteen other FLORES-200 directions. We release the models, data and variety classifier under open licences
papers.summary: Massively multilingual translation models typically offer one tag per language, with no control over regional varieties and weak coverage of smaller regional languages. Three fine-tunes of `MADLAD-400-3B-MT` add new target tags using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation, and replay of the base model's own translations: Spain Spanish, Latin American Spanish, and a joint model for Asturian, Aragonese, and Aranese. The Castilian model picks **Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test versus 62% for the base model**, and the Iberian model matches or beats the `TAN-IBE` Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on `FLORES+`. The authors also report a tag-collapse effect, where a new tag initialised from the parent drags the parent tag toward the new variety, and an average loss of 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on thirteen other directions.

papers.title: Can Its Own Misses Teach an MLLM to Find Small Brain Metastases?
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle to locate small abnormalities in medical images, with frontier models finding fewer than 30% of brain metastases of 0.1-1 mL at one false positive per scan. `LANTERN` (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing) turns model development into an automated loop: every missed lesion is attributed to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four pipeline levels per round, and a rule fixed in advance decides which changes are kept without touching test data. Over 15 unattended rounds, a fine-tuned 4B MLLM improves from **finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on `BraTS-MET`**, with gains holding on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%).

papers.title: The Missing Root: Geometric Imagination Without Images in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
papers.summary: Language models handle spatial questions by reasoning over words, and most multimodal approaches ground space through images, even though spatial structure is really coordinate frames, boundaries, and object relations. The proposed method interleaves continuous object tokens, combining pose and signed-distance shape embeddings, with word tokens in one transformer sequence, using control tokens to switch between text and object-state updates to a persistent workspace and an attention mask that forces answers to be read from the settled geometry. With a narrow parallel spatial stream adding 4.4% more weights to `Qwen3-1.7B`, the model in two-dimensional tests builds and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and **relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions**.

papers.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
papers.abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.
papers.summary: How well a reranker scores on its own does not determine how much it helps inside a multistage retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, so this study composes heterogeneous rerankers (lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context) without joint training. It introduces two lightweight coarse scorers, `Cache-Pointwise` and `Cache-Shapley`, which use cacheable representations, and compares cascades against stage-removal references under matched candidates and budgets. On `NoLiMa` 32K with `Gemma`, placing these scorers before `CrossEncoder` or `Provence` **raises answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while speeding up online pruning by 1.57-1.88x**. A cascade can beat its final reranker alone yet underperform its coarse selector alone, and the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration.

papers.title: ChemDeduce: Benchmarking LLMs for Unknown Chemical Identification through Interactive Simulated Experiments
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.
papers.summary: `ChemDeduce` tests whether large language models can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation, using the task of identifying an unknown chemical. Models interact with a stateful simulated laboratory that enforces instrument and operational constraints, choosing experiments, interpreting observations, and refining hypotheses over multiple steps. Across eight frontier models, 200 chemicals, and 4800 episodes, **average identification accuracy ranges from only 23.83% to 67.33%**, with weaknesses in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement despite plausible-looking plans.

papers.title: Mitigating Overgeneralization in RND via Spectral Target Design
papers.abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.
papers.summary: Random Network Distillation (RND) scores novelty in reinforcement learning by how badly a trained predictor matches a fixed random target network, but the predictor can extrapolate the target beyond the data, making novelty scores collapse on unfamiliar inputs. A kernel-theoretic analysis shows that **the novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance governed jointly by the target's covariance kernel and the predictor's kernel**, which frames overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. The authors therefore replace the random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, and report better novelty discrimination and downstream performance on offline `D4RL`, online `Atari`, and `Fetch` manipulation benchmarks.

papers.title: Contextual language representations link narrative processing to language and literacy in children
papers.abstract: Spoken narratives extensively connect moment-to-moment language processing with knowledge accumulated through language and literacy experience. This study examined that relationship using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during Cantonese story listening and contextual representations from large language model (LLM). The imaging cohort comprised 23 school-age children; 16 contributed complete standardized literacy and language assessments and served as held-out participants in a nested cross-subject encoding analysis of the same story. Contextual embeddings predicted distributed narrative responses, with prominent correspondence in temporoparietal and default-network parcels. Regional summaries of the top 25% of voxels ranked by held-out correlation yielded atlas-wide means of r=0.174 and partial R2=0.0165. A joint feature model identified negative surprisal and positive predictive-entropy coefficients across cortical and subcortical parcels, including control, salience, hippocampal and amygdalar regions. Higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance. Higher Cantonese grammar scores were associated with more negative semantic-update coefficients in parietal control, somatomotor and dorsal-attention parcels. Together, these findings connect language and literacy skills to the regional strength and direction of neural coupling with narrative context. They position naturalistic context processing as a possibly measurable link between oral comprehension and literacy in childhood.
papers.summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recorded while 23 school-age children listened to a Cantonese story is compared against contextual embeddings from a large language model, with 16 children who had full literacy and language assessments serving as held-out participants. The embeddings predicted distributed brain responses, most prominently in temporoparietal and default-network regions, with an atlas-wide mean correlation of r=0.174 among the top quarter of voxels. **Higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance**, and higher Cantonese grammar scores with more negative semantic-update coefficients in several parietal and attention regions.

papers.title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
papers.abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
papers.summary: The Normalizing-Flow World Model (`NFWM`) pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor, so a predicted distribution over latent states directly defines a distribution over future observations and the whole model can be trained by exact conditional likelihood. Agents plan in the latent space and can decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures, with an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective added for goal-conditioned control. In `Flappy Bird`, a model trained by likelihood alone supports planning that **reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games**; on `LIBERO` it selects successful action sequences more often than `LeWM` and `SMWM`, and in `Atari Boxing` training on imagined trajectories improves a behavior-cloned policy.

papers.title: Random Voronoi Networks
papers.abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods are local, simple, and interpretable, but their non-parametric form makes them memory-intensive, expensive at inference, and difficult to integrate into differentiable neural architectures. We introduce Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs), a family of structured three-layer MLPs that express nearest-neighbor geometry through sampled Voronoi comparisons. The first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from affine pairwise separators between selected training samples, the second layer aggregates these comparisons into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and the readout layer produces classification or regression predictions. We show that, when all samples and pairwise comparisons are included, step RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, while ReLU RVNs provide a violation-score realization for 1-NN that can be relaxed into a differentiable soft weighting. Subsampling yields approximate RVNs with explicit control over the number of cells and features. We study several unsupervised sampling methods that trade off random coverage, directional diversity, coordinate sparsity, and empirical feature variance. Empirically, RVFs produce a highly effective data encoding strategy, providing performance boosts to downstream methods ranging from linear to modern tabular deep learning models. Finally, we showcase that RVF provides an interpretable feature map due to its k-NN based construction and ties to pairwise local directions. These results position our Random Voronoi formulation as a bridge between nearest-neighbor rules, random features, and modern tabular models.
papers.summary: Nearest-neighbor methods are simple and interpretable but memory-hungry, slow at inference, and hard to embed in differentiable architectures. Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs) are structured three-layer networks whose first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from pairwise separators between sampled training points, whose second layer aggregates them into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and whose last layer produces predictions. With all samples and comparisons included, the step-activation version recovers exact Euclidean k-nearest-neighbors, while subsampling gives controllable approximations. Empirically, **the features work as a data encoding that boosts downstream methods from linear models to modern tabular deep learning models**.

papers.title: FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal
papers.abstract: When a guardrail rejects an LLM agent's action, its message reaches any attacker observing the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves benign users unable to recover, whereas an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message. Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.
papers.summary: When a guardrail blocks an LLM agent's action, its refusal message is also visible to an attacker: a fixed refusal leaves legitimate users unable to recover, while an explanation can hint at what to try next. `FORK` treats this as a safe-disclosure problem and co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills against an attacker that reads every public message, revising the skill library without gradients whenever a message is exploited or a decision is too permissive. Averaged over three agents on `FORK-World`, it **cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% while keeping utility above 85%**, and on the unseen `MT-AgentRisk` environments it lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

papers.title: The Gradient Difference Induced by Detaching the Denominator in QK Normalization
papers.abstract: QK normalization divides each query and key by its own RMS norm before the attention scores are computed. Treating this denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the parameter gradients. We derive a closed form for the difference between the gradient under this detached rule and the gradient under the standard rule. For a single token, this difference is parallel to the token's own query; it changes only the query norm and has no first-order effect after normalization. The queries, however, are computed by a projection matrix $W_Q$ shared across all tokens. The gradient difference on $W_Q$ therefore equals $W_Q$ right-multiplied by a weighted second moment of the inputs, and it decomposes exactly into three components: a radial component that changes only the norm of $W_Q$, a tangential component that changes the query directions of other tokens, and an upstream component that changes the gradient passed to earlier layers. Under AdamW, the radial component drives $W_Q$ to a larger equilibrium norm and reduces its angular update per step. Paired experiments on a small Transformer language model are consistent with this analysis. Detaching the query denominator consistently raises the test loss, and the gap persists across hardware, evaluation datasets and learning rates. All three components remain non-negligible throughout training, with the tangential component the largest. Norm growth and the smaller angular update appear only on the detached projection matrix, while the other projection matrix is essentially unchanged. With a learnable scale, however, we observe no resolvable loss gap.
papers.summary: QK normalization divides each attention query and key by its own RMS norm, and treating that denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the gradients. A closed-form derivation shows that the gradient difference on the shared query projection matrix `W_Q` splits exactly into a radial part that changes only its norm, a tangential part that shifts other tokens' query directions, and an upstream part that changes gradients to earlier layers; under `AdamW` the radial part inflates the matrix norm and shrinks its angular update per step. In paired experiments on a small Transformer language model, **detaching the query denominator consistently raises test loss**, although no resolvable gap appears when a learnable scale is used.

papers.title: On the Learnability of Model Reprogramming: A Reachability and Relabeling Perspective
papers.abstract: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a target task by wrapping it in a learnable input transformation from target input to the source-model input space, and an output mapping from source-model outputs to target predictions. Despite extensive empirical progress, the finite-sample learnability of the induced wrapper hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ remains underexplored. We address this for source models that expose hard source labels and analyze it through the wrapper structure: on any target samples, the input transformation selects reachable source labels that the output mapping relabels. Through this lens, we answer two questions: (1) how many target samples are needed to approach the best predictor in $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$, and (2) what gap remains between the optimum over $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ and the target Bayes risk. For (1), the wrapper structure factorizes the sample-wise complexity of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ into a reachability term counting reachable source-label patterns, and a conditional relabeling term counting their relabelings. This yields an agnostic-PAC bound on the estimation error, with sample complexity scaling additively in the two terms; this bound becomes closed-form on additive input transformations and is matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary classification construction. For (2), the same structure decomposes the approximation error exactly into the source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction with a source-conditional upper bound on this gap. We extend the approximation analysis to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound is empirically estimable. The wrapper-side analysis localizes both errors to specific components, giving a structural view of reprogramming practice.
papers.summary: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a new task by learning an input transformation into the source model's input space and an output mapping from its predictions to target labels, but how many target samples this needs has been little studied. For source models exposing hard labels, the analysis views the wrapper as selecting reachable source labels that are then relabeled, which gives **an agnostic-PAC estimation bound whose sample complexity scales additively in a reachability term and a relabeling term**, matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary construction. The same structure splits the approximation gap to the Bayes risk exactly into source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction, with an extension to logit-exposing source models where the bound can be estimated empirically.

papers.title: When Are Parallel Subagents Effective for Coding? An Empirical Study on Repository Construction
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used for long-horizon tasks such as building an entire program from a specification. Products like Codex and Claude Code let an agent delegate work to parallel subagents, multiplying run cost, yet it remains unclear whether and when delegation produces a better program. We compare a single agent with a main agent delegating to subagents on repository-construction tasks from NL2Repo and ProgramBench (which also provides an executable reference program). We compare scores at equal time and equal cost, run intervention experiments, and analyze fine-grained behavior. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent. Their gain is larger on hard tasks, where we find evidence of three mechanisms. Self-checking: with GPT-5.6 Sol, one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of this gain at a fraction of the cost; from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol, the gain shrinks as single agents check their own work more. Fresh context: in extended runs, a single agent that periodically starts a new session with an empty conversation makes faster early progress in every comparison than one that resumes its conversation. Modularity: multi-agent runs produce more modular code (more files and shorter functions), closer to the upstream source. We observe similar patterns in a smaller replication with Opus 5.5 on Claude Code. Overall, subagents help when (i) a single agent stops checking too early, (ii) a long session keeps editing with little improvement, or (iii) modular code helps on the task; otherwise, they mainly add cost.
papers.summary: Coding agents can delegate work to parallel subagents at a multiple of the cost, and this study measures when that actually yields a better program by comparing a single agent with a delegating main agent on repository-construction tasks from `NL2Repo` and `ProgramBench`, at equal time and equal cost. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents **raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent**, with larger gains on hard tasks. Three mechanisms explain the gain: self-checking (one sentence telling a single `GPT-5.6 Sol` agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of it), fresh context (periodically restarting with an empty conversation speeds early progress), and more modular code. Subagents therefore help when a single agent stops checking too early, when a long session stalls, or when modularity matters, and otherwise mainly add cost.

papers.title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
papers.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.
papers.summary: Looped language models reuse the same parameters for a variable number of passes, which already enables self-speculative decoding with shallow loops as drafters and deep loops as verifiers. `Floodgates` extends this by appending a block of mask tokens as a suffix and training, through low-rank adaptation, the shallow loops to draft several future tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, various batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, it is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, reaching **up to 7.5x acceleration**. The speedup is attributed to all-depth training of looped models and to the shallow drafter conditioning on the deep prefix cache computed during verification.

papers.title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.
papers.summary: Medical reasoning agents pair a large language model with specialized neural tools, but general-purpose models have seen little of these tools in training and the tools' uncertain outputs make choosing among them from short descriptions hard. `EATS`, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy, stores past queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback in a memory and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool choice on new queries, and **because it needs no ground-truth supervision, the memory grows with test-time experience**. Experiments on `ChestAgentBench`, `CheXbench`, `MIMIC-CXR`, and `SLAKE-VQA` with `Qwen3-VL 2B`, `Qwen3-VL 32B`, and `GPT-5.5` show consistent gains in tool selection and downstream medical reasoning.

papers.title: Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification
papers.abstract: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.
papers.summary: Trusted multi-view classification combines per-view class evidence and uncertainty estimates, but existing fusion rules treat views as independent, so highly correlated views get their shared evidence counted repeatedly while complementary evidence is diluted. Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (`CAFE`) discounts the evidence from view-private experts based on complementarity, adds a correlation-aware constraint to limit repeated contributions, and learns sample-specific weights to combine the adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. On six real-world datasets it **consistently improves both classification and calibration, with the largest gains when views are strongly correlated**.

papers.title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.
papers.summary: Medical reasoning agents that pair foundation models with imaging tools struggle to reuse past experience, because a correct final answer can hide flawed reasoning or tool use and similar-looking cases may need different diagnostic procedures. `EGSE` distills historical dialogues into conditional workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to their sources, contrasts successful and failed rollouts, and only adds or merges skills after source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference it routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question type, and disease category. On four chest X-ray benchmarks it **outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls**, with gains across seven foundation models and skill transfer across datasets.

papers.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.
papers.summary: Methods for converting autoregressive (AR) language models into diffusion generators have focused on full-attention architectures, leaving more efficient hybrid designs underexplored. `DiCALM` converts the hybrid convolution-attention `LFM2` and `LFM2.5` models to masked-diffusion generation by progressively extending the causal gated convolution to capture local context in both directions, combined with a masking warm-up and joint AR-diffusion training. In controlled experiments at the 350M and 1.2B scales it performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned AR models while running **over 1.4x faster on average and up to 1.79x faster**.

papers.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
papers.abstract: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
papers.summary: Robot world models are trained mostly on successful demonstrations, so their predictions break down when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips; across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than a static baseline that copies the first frame. `WorldReforge` builds the `Reforge` dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, and derives two training signals from the ground truth: Interaction Alignment, which focuses reconstruction on object and contact regions, and Surface Correspondence, which trains features to follow the same surface points across frames. On `Cosmos3 Nano` it **reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and 35.0% on unseen objects**, and it also improves reconstruction on `DROID` and real failure videos despite being trained only in simulation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Robot world models are trained mostly on successful demonstrations, so their predictions break down when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or dropped. `WorldReforge` post-trains these models on simulated grasp failures with exact physical ground truth, adding two auxiliary losses that focus learning on contact regions and on surface motion across frames.

- Across five pretrained action-conditioned models from three families, object-motion error is at most **10.4%** lower than a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than that baseline.
- The `Reforge` dataset holds **62k** simulated trajectories over 96 objects (about 13.6k failure-related), generated by perturbing reference grasps in translation, rotation, and closure timing, plus 300 real failure trajectories used only for evaluation.
- `Interaction Alignment` adds an area-normalized reconstruction loss over object and contact regions, while `Surface Correspondence` trains backbone features to track simulator-projected surface points across frames, and neither adds inference-time parameters.
- On `Cosmos3 Nano`, object trajectory error falls **28.2%** overall (9.07 to 6.51 px) and **35.0%** on unseen objects, the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge falls **43.3%**, and PSNR rises 1.04 dB on `DROID` and 0.68 dB on real failure videos despite simulation-only training.
- Most of the gain comes from the data rather than the losses, since base post-training alone cuts object error by 24.9% and the two losses add only about **4.4%** more, while `DreamDojo`'s object error actually worsens after post-training (9.57 to 11.62 px), and the real-world evidence covers reconstruction quality over 16-frame predictions, not motion accuracy.

papers.title: Connecting AI Agents to Live Discrete Element Simulations via the Model Context Protocol
papers.abstract: This paper describes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server through which a general-purpose AI agent operates a discrete element engine, commercial or open-source, while the simulation runs. The agent submits a long simulation to the engine and, while it computes, reads the running model, changes it, or stops it. The human modeler stays at the engine's console and graphical interface throughout, and the agent sees what the modeler does there. The tools are derived from what the agent needs to do at the engine and are held to four principles: correctness, coverage, orthogonality and simplicity. Two documentation tools let the agent search the engine's manual and browse it level by level. Five execution tools let the agent run code in the engine, submit long simulations in the background, check on them, read the running model, and stop them. A bridge inside the engine serves these tools in a commercial DEM engine, PFC, and an open-source one, YADE. In a case study, a general-purpose agent calibrated a drained triaxial model of dense Toyoura sand against laboratory data in both engines, while the modeler worked at the same engine; the agent noticed the modeler's actions at the console and acted on them. The same calibration on YADE was then given to seven language models, three sessions each and without human intervention. Twenty of the twenty-one sessions reached the targets, and nineteen of the parameter sets lie in one small region of the admissible ranges. The server and the bridge are released as two open-source packages, itasca-mcp, which also serves FLAC, 3DEC, MPoint and MassFlow, and yade-mcp.
papers.summary: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server lets a general-purpose AI agent operate a discrete element simulation engine while it runs, reading, changing, or stopping the model as a human modeler works at the same console. It exposes two documentation tools for searching and browsing the engine manual and five execution tools for running code, submitting long background simulations, checking on them, reading the running model, and stopping them, served through a bridge inside the commercial engine `PFC` and the open-source `YADE`. In a case study an agent calibrated a drained triaxial model of dense Toyoura sand against laboratory data in both engines, and when the `YADE` calibration was given to seven language models without human intervention, **20 of 21 sessions reached the targets**. The server and bridge are released as the open-source packages `itasca-mcp` and `yade-mcp`.

papers.title: Towards 360$^\circ$ Embodied UAV Tracking Without Turning
papers.abstract: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $\pi_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/
papers.summary: Drone target tracking normally ties target visibility to heading control, because targets can leave the view of a forward-facing camera; the alternative studied here uses full-spherical perception so the drone can follow a target without turning. The authors introduce `360UAV-ETrack`, a simulation benchmark with 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios, and propose `360UAV-TVLA`, a panoramic vision-language-action (VLA) framework combining persistent visual referring, compressed temporal memory, and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision. Compared with standard fine-tuning, normalized average tracking frames rise **from 22.56% to 35.28% for `pi0`** and from 25.68% to 33.64% for `pi0.5`. The benchmark also shows a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability.

papers.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.
papers.summary: Instruction-following text-to-speech must follow a free-form style instruction, pronounce the transcript correctly, and sound natural, but optimizing all three under one scalar reward with group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) is unstable because the objectives compete. The authors train three single-objective teachers with `GRPO` and fuse them using on-policy distillation (OPD), which matches the teachers' velocity fields on the student's own rollouts, after building a reward for each axis from a distilled `Qwen-Omni` judge proxy, dialect-free word error rate data, and `DNSMOS`. Because the quality target conflicts with instruction following, they add conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction opposing the primary objective. The fused model **improves over scalar-reward `GRPO` on all three objectives at once**.

papers.title: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: Many applications, especially reliability- and safety-critical ones, require accurate uncertainty quantification for the outputs of model- or learning-based measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. The errors of such systems often vary with factors such as input quality and operating conditions, and thus cannot be accurately described by a single Gaussian model. Although Gaussian mixture models and calibrated quantiles can approximate such error distributions, their unconditional forms do not capture how the error behavior depends on these factors. Hence, we propose condUQ, an approach that conditions error models on observable factors for enabling accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. condUQ is built on top of an existing system without modifying it and applies even when the system is a black box. First, condUQ maps the observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution. The QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective, without requiring quality labels. Second, for each QI, a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated on a large held-out dataset. condUQ is demonstrated on three examples: (a) GPS multipath errors conditioned on satellite elevation and signal strength, (b) relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual relative pose regression model conditioned on its internal features of the image pairs, and (c) prediction errors of a world model conditioned on the input observations and actions. In all three examples, condUQ substantially reduces the discrepancy between the modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model. Moreover, the learned QIs reveal how the underlying factors affect the error characteristics in a manner consistent with physical principles.
papers.summary: Errors of measurement, estimation, and prediction systems often vary with input quality and operating conditions, so a single Gaussian model or an unconditional mixture describes them poorly. `condUQ` sits on top of an existing, possibly black-box system and maps observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing a QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian distribution; the QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective and no quality labels, and a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated per QI on held-out data. Demonstrated on GPS multipath errors, relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual pose regressor, and world model prediction errors, it **substantially reduces the discrepancy between modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model**.

papers.title: What Does Skill Lift Actually Measure? A Source-Code-Level Audit and Noise-Aware Reanalysis of SkillsBench
papers.abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.
papers.summary: `SkillsBench` reported that human-curated agent skills (directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents) raise pass rates by about 16.6 percentage points on average but hurt some tasks, and later work has gated or removed skills based on those per-task results. A source-code audit and reanalysis of 7,554 public trials forming 1,421 paired cells found two verified cases of grader dependence, one operational definition gap, four tasks with placeholder skill directories, and a harness that added 48 built-in skills in most runs. With at most three runs per condition, **no task-level reduction reached statistical significance after multiple-testing correction**, and 58% of cells could not arithmetically have shown a decrease. A gating strategy that appeared to gain 2-3 points in the logs still gained 4-7 points after condition labels were shuffled, and showed no significant improvement on held-out runs.

papers.title: Should Service Requirements Be Scalarized or Constrained When Minimizing Costs? A Case Study on HVAC Control
papers.abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action. In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.
papers.summary: Controllers that minimize cost while meeting a service requirement can either fold the requirement into the objective with a fixed or adaptively tuned weight, or impose it as a constraint; the two are compared for heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) control of previously unseen buildings in the `Smart Buildings Challenge`. The study tests model predictive control (MPC) with hard or soft constraints, and proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) with a fixed penalty, a Lagrangian penalty, or an action projection layer. In MPC the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, and **a weight tuned on training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings** because the shadow price varies across buildings. In `PPO`, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the start and leads early, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it with longer training, and the fixed penalty never learns to satisfy the requirement.

papers.title: A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds
papers.abstract: The values of causal effects and counterfactuals are typically only partially identified from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding. With discretely-valued variables, under certain conditions, sharp bounds can be derived by solving one linear program. This is then computationally tractable for many causal questions. In this paper, for every diagram in which each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to be equal to the optimum of one linear program for every (positive) input probability table. This algorithm is implemented in a new Python package, called "partialid", that allows users to compose assumptions, queries, and data to obtain sharp bounds in a computationally tractable manner.
papers.summary: Causal effects and counterfactuals are usually only partially identified from observational data when there is unobserved confounding, and for discrete variables sharp bounds can sometimes be obtained by solving a single linear program. For every causal diagram in which each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, the authors give **necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to equal the optimum of one linear program** for every positive input probability table. The resulting algorithm is implemented in a Python package, `partialid`, which lets users combine assumptions, queries, and data to compute sharp bounds tractably.

papers.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
papers.abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD
papers.summary: Storing optimizer states at low bit widths saves memory during large-scale training, but the states are dequantized, updated, and requantized at every step, and for states updated by exponential moving averages (EMAs) the quantization errors feed back into later updates, accumulating bias and amplifying variance when the decay factor is close to 1. `BReD` (Block Replay Dithering) adapts classical subtractive dithering to this setting by combining deterministic seed replay with dither values shared across blocks, which avoids storing auxiliary random tensors or generating per-element dither. Across pretraining with five optimizers at 120M parameters and with `AdamW` and `Muon` at 1.1B and 3.4B, plus fine-tuning at 7B, **4-bit `BReD` closely matches full-precision optimizer states, with perplexity shifts of at most 0.5 in pretraining and 0.2 in fine-tuning**. A 3-bit variant also converged stably in the evaluated settings.

papers.title: DuoMI: Dual Mutual Information Regularization for Expert Reuse in Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.
papers.summary: In looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers, where two rounds of computation share one expert pool, the routers in each round may favor different expert subsets, which limits how much individual expert parameters are reused across rounds. Dual Mutual Information Regularization (`DuoMI`) adds two training penalties computed from soft routing distributions: a round-level marginal mutual information term that limits how much aggregate expert usage depends on the round, and a token-level conditional term that penalizes cross-round routing changes outside a target interval. It adds no parameters and leaves sparse Top-k routing unchanged at inference. On a looped `OLMoE` backbone with paired adjacent layers sharing experts, it raises the average score across 15 downstream tasks **from 50.08% to 51.82%**.

papers.title: PINN-Slicer: Exploiting Rotational Symmetry to Solve the Photon Orbit Equation Around a Black Hole
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically struggle with long-horizon domains, often requiring the network to be retrained as the domain grows. We present PINN-Slicer, a method for second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, $\ddot{u} = G(u, \dot{u})$, which exploits the invariance of this class of equations under translations of the independent variable. A single PINN, embedded within a solution ansatz that enforces the initial conditions explicitly, is trained on a thin slice of the independent variable using Sobol-sampled initial conditions. The PINN is then deployed recursively, slice-by-slice, across the full domain. We demonstrate PINN-Slicer on the nonlinear equation that describes photon orbits around a black hole, and reach a point-by-point root-mean-square error (RMSE) below $10^{-3}$ in $u = r_s/r$ (the inverse radial coordinate in units of the Schwarzschild radius) relative to a finite-difference reference solution. A key advantage of PINN-Slicer is that a single trained network generalizes to any orbital initial condition within the training range, without retraining. In addition, PINN-Slicer can cope with solution domains that may not be known a priori.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) struggle on long-horizon domains and often need retraining as the domain grows. `PINN-Slicer` targets second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, which are invariant under translations of the independent variable: a single network, embedded in an ansatz that enforces the initial conditions exactly, is trained on a thin slice using Sobol-sampled initial conditions and then applied recursively slice by slice across the full domain. On the nonlinear equation for photon orbits around a black hole it reaches a **point-by-point root-mean-square error below 10^-3** in the inverse radial coordinate relative to a finite-difference reference. The same trained network handles any orbital initial condition within the training range without retraining, and domains whose extent is not known in advance.

papers.title: RefMix: Expanding Endpoint Proposals for Diversity-Preserving Reward Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Online forward matching aligns flow-based generative models by repeatedly generating, rewarding, and fitting model-produced endpoints. However, this behavior creates an on-policy feedback loop: as high-reward modes become increasingly favored, alternative modes become less likely to appear in subsequent training pools, progressively reducing visual diversity. We introduce RefMix, a reference-assisted endpoint proposal strategy that addresses this limitation by injecting alternative candidates into the training pool while retaining the original task reward and forward matching objective. In particular, RefMix uses a reference model during early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes, followed by the current reward-tuned model for endpoint completion. Across state-of-the-art online forward matching methods, RefMix consistently improves visual diversity while preserving task reward performance. Controlled inference experiments further demonstrate that training-time endpoint exposure is critical to improve reward--diversity trade-offs, beyond the impact of reference-assisted inference. By rethinking how training endpoints are proposed, RefMix achieves up to 44% higher diversity over forward matching baselines at comparable reward levels.
papers.summary: Reward fine-tuning of flow-based generative models with online forward matching repeatedly generates, rewards, and fits the model's own outputs, which creates a feedback loop: high-reward modes dominate later training pools and visual diversity shrinks. `RefMix` changes how training endpoints are proposed, using a reference model for the early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes and the current reward-tuned model to complete the sample, while keeping the original reward and forward matching objective. Across several online forward matching methods it achieves **up to 44% higher diversity at comparable reward levels**, and controlled experiments indicate that the training-time exposure matters beyond what reference-assisted inference alone provides.

papers.title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes
papers.abstract: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.
papers.summary: Classical dimensional analysis specifies which dimensionless representations are admissible but not which combinations dominate, whether they change across physical regimes, or when the dependent variable needs rescaling. `AI Buckingham` is an agentic framework that takes a natural-language problem description and observational data, and couples large language model (LLM) planning with predefined symbolic and numerical tools: literature retrieval for dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering to identify regimes, and mutual information as a reparameterization-invariant criterion for selecting dominant groups. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection, and additive manufacturing, it **recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings**. For turbulent drag on rough surfaces it finds reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates.

papers.title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence.
