We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.
papers.summary: Latent reasoning lets language models reason in continuous embedding space, but deterministic inference prevents exploring diverse reasoning paths, and existing fixes inject the same amount of noise at every step and can disrupt coherence. `DLaR` works within the `GRPO` reinforcement learning framework and adds two mechanisms: Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation, which scales the perturbation at each latent step using a combined confidence and entropy signal, and Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning, which decays the base noise level on a curriculum schedule. On four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks it achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching **27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on `Llama-3.2-1B`** and 46.8%/68.2% on `Qwen2.5-1.5B`.

papers.title: Embodied-VGGT: Preserving Reliable Local Geometry for Long-Sequence Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
papers.summary: Reconstructing long sequences in 3D requires correcting accumulated drift without damaging geometry that is already locally consistent. `Embodied-VGGT` exploits regularities of vehicle and robot data capture: Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks builds on the global context memory of `Scal3R` and uses scale references from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, Superpoint Alignment balances ground and non-ground evidence to estimate translation between chunks, and Cross-Loop Optimization selects coherent chunk groups that each receive a shared Sim(3) correction preserving their internal transformations. On `KITTI Odometry` it reaches a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, **reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% relative to the state-of-the-art baseline**, with consistent improvements across five public driving benchmarks.

papers.title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
papers.abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.
papers.summary: AI-driven mathematical discovery has split between large language models (LLMs) that resolve well-specified conjectures through text reasoning and narrow models with interpretability used for open-ended exploration of mathematical data; `PatternMiner` combines the two. An LLM agent generates datasets from a broad question, trains small machine learning models on them, applies interpretability techniques to extract patterns, formulates conjectures, and then searches for counterexamples with mathematical software, using what it finds to refine the conjecture or run another round, and it may attempt a proof at any point. Applied to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics, it **proves several new theorems**, covering Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan-Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. The authors also analyze the common routes to conjecture generation and the most frequent failure modes.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
papers.abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.
papers.summary: Closed-form weight-space programming (WSP) asks whether a classifier computed without gradients on a frozen encoder can match fine-tuning: a large language model (LLM) writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads such as shrinkage discriminant analysis and kernel ridge regression, and choose among candidate heads by cross-fitting. Instantiated on `RoBERTa-large` across 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 labels, **WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning and `LoRA` at every label budget by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average** and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning, with its lead growing to 3.8 to 5.3 points at 16 labels per class. On six held-out datasets the results are weaker: it stays ahead of `LoRA` and within half a point of full fine-tuning, but no registered test passes and prompt-based fine-tuning leads by 1.30 points at 8,192 labels. The method is deterministic but needs one encoder pass per template (17 here), and the authors report all eight recipe versions and 27 ideas that did not help.

papers.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
papers.summary: Open-weight language models for register-transfer level (RTL) hardware design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which requires many verified designs and GPU training. `Kolpona` avoids gradient training with neuron programming, a form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits and keeps each edit only if testbench results on fresh tasks favor it; at inference, tool-using agents propose designs and a label-free stage selects one per task. On `Qwen3.5-4B`, edits to 16 neurons raise `VerilogEval v2` pass@1 from 31.7% to 55.4% for the model alone, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On `Qwen3.8-27B` it lifts pass@1 **from 73.1% to 94.9% on `VerilogEval v2`** and from 66.0% to 92.0% on `RTLLM v2.1` on a single 32 GB GPU, and the edits also carry over to Python, improving the 4B model on `HumanEval+` and `MBPP+`.

papers.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
papers.abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).
papers.summary: Car advertisements name the same feature in many different ways, which makes it hard to tell which of a vehicle's catalogue features an advert actually mentions. `Auto-Features` casts this as feature-conditioned named entity recognition, extracting the span that expresses one given catalogue feature, and provides a human-annotated gold layer of 430 adverts plus a silver layer of 925 adverts annotated by a search-grounded LLM whose outputs are validated, with a separate remedy for each failure type. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches **63.9% span F1** and 76.1% on the entity-linking view, against 59.0% and 74.1% for a fine-tuned encoder, with the widest gap on catalogue features never seen in training.

papers.title: Quaternion-Tucker ZigZag Networks: Halving Transformer Backbone Parameters and Enabling Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling
papers.abstract: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.
papers.summary: Standard Transformers give every feed-forward network (FFN) layer its own dense weight matrix, so parameters grow linearly with depth, while weight-tied looped Transformers avoid that but force identical updates at every layer. `QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT` treats the FFN stack as a 3D tensor and combines quaternion weight products, Tucker cores that apply depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, a reordered layer routing, and a scheme for growing width and depth without changing the loss. The authors report that a 12-layer model with a **39.0M-parameter backbone beats an 85.0M-parameter standard GPT** at all five controlled checkpoints, and that a continually scaled lineage trained on 6B tokens reaches 44.75% zero-shot accuracy across `ARC-Easy`, `HellaSwag`, `WinoGrande`, and `BoolQ`.

papers.title: MolGPAO: Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree with Speculative Decoding and Sub-Millisecond Seam Healing for 3D Molecules
papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation over adaptive 3D octrees (Uni-3DAR) offers an intrinsic $O(N \log N)$ sparsity advantage over dense $O(N^2)$ equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules, yet lags in geometric equilibrium, closed-shell valence stability, and property fidelity due to Morton-seam coordinate jumps, leaf-heavy compute with root-count trapping, and target-shortcut collapse in internal critics. We introduce MolGPAO (Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree), a standalone 3D octree architecture and single-output speculative tree-decoding engine using zero external surrogates, zero reinforcement learning, and zero inference-time MLIP relaxation. MolGPAO unifies: (1) non-trapping 6-D ScaleFreeBudgetEmbedding with L5-to-L1 covalent packing priors; (2) a FlashAttention-2 pause-and-gather speculative octree funnel ($m_{s1} \to m_{s2} \to 1$, $M_{\mathrm{out}} = 1$); (3) an anti-shortcut ground-truth TwoStageOctreeProcessCritic with 64-RBF covalent edge gating and $SO(3)$-invariant 12-channel multipole norms (blind QM9 $r = 0.9867$--$0.9989$); (4) a $<0.5$ ms 4-layer $SE(3)$ PostTreeGraphRefiner for Morton-seam healing, expected-XYZ bonded supervision, selective CFG, and zero-heavy-displacement valence reconciliation; and (5) bubble-free stride-2 GPU leaf decoding. Across GEOM-Drugs (0.49 GPU-h), disjoint 50k/50k QM9 (0.43 GPU-h), and PBE0/def2-TZVP-verified OE62 (0.56 GPU-h), MolGPAO lifts drug-scale valid-connected yield 6.78x (12.7% to 86.2%, 99.83% atom stability), runs 7.3x faster (or 1.65x faster at 2.0x yield) than 100-step FlowMol at $N=100$, beats 156 GPU-h PropMolFlow on QM9 HOMO (-12.7%) and dipole (-21.0%) at 362x lower compute, and doubles live DFT hit rate on OE62 (33.3% vs. 16.7%) at 92.8x lower compute.
papers.summary: Autoregressive generation of 3D molecules over adaptive octrees, as in `Uni-3DAR`, scales better than dense equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules but trails them in geometric quality, valence stability, and property fidelity. `MolGPAO` (Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree) adds a budget embedding with covalent packing priors, a speculative tree-decoding scheme, an internal critic designed to avoid shortcut learning, and a sub-millisecond graph refiner that repairs coordinate jumps at octree seams, without external surrogates, reinforcement learning, or inference-time relaxation. The authors report that on `GEOM-Drugs` the valid-connected yield rises from **12.7% to 86.2%**, with generation 7.3x faster than 100-step `FlowMol` at 100 atoms, and better `QM9` property targeting than `PropMolFlow` at 362x lower compute.

papers.title: Aegis-VLA: Reliability-Gated Action Refinement via a Trajectory World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object--end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72\% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44\% by 11.28 percentage points.
papers.summary: Manipulating moving objects requires a robot to stay aligned with a target that keeps moving during inference and execution, and an accurate forecast alone does not say whether changing a planned action will help. `Aegis-VLA` wraps a vision-language-action (VLA) policy with a trajectory world model that predicts object motion and its uncertainty, a refinement module that proposes bounded arm corrections, and a learned reliability gate that decides whether and how strongly to apply each correction, keeping the base action otherwise. With about 2.45M added trainable parameters, it reaches **56.72% success** over 1,800 trials on the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (`DOM`) benchmark, 11.28 percentage points above the authors' reproduced `DynamicVLA` baseline.

papers.title: The Reference Matters: Displacement Probing for Weight-Space Learning
papers.abstract: Weight-space learning predicts a model's attributes directly from its parameters, and probing-based methods do so efficiently by reading a model's responses to learned probes. Prior work shows that probing succeeds within a Model Tree -- models fine-tuned from a shared pretrained origin -- but not why. We trace this to the shared origin itself: since a tree's leaves start from the same weights, what distinguishes them is their displacement from that origin. This motivates probing the displacement rather than the raw weight, an intervention we call the DiSplacement Probe (DSProbe). We develop this idea along two axes: extending it to second-order Gram responses, whose displacement, to first order, tracks the feature changes induced by fine-tuning; and treating the reference as a design choice, learning a shared component to subtract beyond the pretrained origin. Across four architectures on the Model Jungle benchmark, the resulting Refined-DSProbe (R-DSProbe) sets a new state of the art, matches prior accuracy with substantially fewer probes, and supports a single encoder shared across Model Trees, reducing metanetwork parameters by 3.61 times. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/DSProbe.
papers.summary: Weight-space learning predicts a model's attributes directly from its parameters, and probing methods are known to work within a Model Tree, a set of models fine-tuned from one pretrained origin, without a clear explanation of why. The authors attribute this to the shared origin and propose `DSProbe`, which probes each model's displacement from that origin instead of its raw weights, then extend it to second-order Gram responses and to a learned reference that is subtracted beyond the pretrained origin. Across four architectures on the `Model Jungle` benchmark, the refined `R-DSProbe` sets a new state of the art, matches prior accuracy with fewer probes, and supports one encoder shared across Model Trees, **cutting metanetwork parameters by 3.61 times**.

papers.title: DosePET: An Open-Source Dataset with 2100 Radiation Dose Maps for PET/CT
papers.abstract: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.
papers.summary: Training AI models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine requires large sets of 3D radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy, which are hard to obtain. `DosePET` is an open dataset of **2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps** produced by Monte Carlo simulation in `GATE` on public PET/CT examinations from `ENHANCE.PET` and `PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions`, covering three radiotracers, five institutions, and seven scanner models. Each study includes a dose map, 117 organ and tissue masks generated with `TotalSegmentator`, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, and simulation metadata, alongside Python tools for selective download and conversion.

papers.title: Honest but Wrong: Formalizing Retraction in the Ethics of Speech Acts
papers.abstract: A speaker who asserts honestly may later discover that its assertion was false. Such erroneous truths are not lies, yet they raise the question of whether, and on which moral grounds, the speaker must retract them. Using the FIPA-ACL performative disconfirm, we extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism to the case of retraction. We prove that the honesty duty of deontologism, which bears on utterances when they are made, never requires retracting an erroneous truth, and add a persistent one, which forbids letting the addressee believe what the speaker no longer believes. On a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, we show that deontologism and consequentialism both require the retraction, but that consequentialism no longer does once it comes too late to prevent harm.
papers.summary: A speaker who asserts something honestly and later learns it was false has not lied, which leaves open whether and on what moral grounds they must retract the statement. Using the `FIPA-ACL` disconfirm performative, the authors extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism, and prove that **the deontological honesty duty, which applies at the time of utterance, never requires retracting an honest error**; they therefore add a persistent duty that forbids letting the addressee keep believing what the speaker no longer believes. In a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, both ethical theories require the retraction, but consequentialism stops requiring it once it is too late to prevent harm.

papers.title: CARROT: Competitive Adaptive Graph Clustering via Semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Deep graph clustering (DGC) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for unsupervised attributed graph clustering. However, existing methods often struggle with two practical challenges encountered in real-world applications: the number of clusters $K$ is unknown a priori, and cluster sizes are frequently highly imbalanced. Methods relying on a pre-specified $K$ may fail to recover the underlying clustering structure when $K$ is misspecified, while many approaches implicitly favor balanced partitions, hindering the discovery of minority clusters. We propose CARROT, a Competitive Adaptive gRaph clustering framework via semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport, which introduces semi-relaxed optimal transport into deep graph clustering to jointly address both challenges. CARROT first pre-trains node embeddings to establish a meaningful embedding space, and then jointly optimizes embeddings and cluster assignments through an Adaptive Clustering Mechanism. The mechanism combines semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities to the underlying data, a competition loss to concentrate mass onto well-supported cluster prototypes, thereby starving degenerate ones, and hard pruning to progressively eliminate them. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks demonstrate that CARROT achieves state-of-the-art NMI and ARI, accurately recovers the number of clusters without supervision, and faithfully preserves size-imbalanced community structures.
papers.summary: Deep graph clustering (DGC) methods usually assume the number of clusters is known in advance and tend to favor balanced partitions, both of which fail on real graphs with unknown and highly imbalanced communities. `CARROT` pre-trains node embeddings and then jointly optimizes embeddings and assignments using semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities to the data, a competition loss that concentrates mass on well-supported prototypes, and hard pruning that removes the degenerate ones. On five public benchmarks the authors report state-of-the-art NMI and ARI, with the method **recovering the number of clusters without supervision** and preserving size-imbalanced community structure.

papers.title: Hetero-Associative Visuomotor Memory: Soft Recall as a Base for Learned Residuals in Few-Demonstration Imitation
papers.abstract:
Retrieve-and-correct policies typically refine the nearest retrieved demonstration chunk, the
  readout that works best when executed directly. We study what a demonstration memory should
  supply to the corrector instead and find that a smooth, softmax-weighted recall over the whole
  memory is a much better base. On ALOHA cube transfer (40 human demonstrations), soft recall is
  no better to execute alone than the nearest chunk; however, with keys, candidates, and training
  fixed, correcting it raises success by 22.4 points on fresh resets with new encoders and by 7.4
  against a closed-loop-tuned top-1 corrector. On robomimic Square, it leads by 7.9 points with
  the two better operators and by 6.7 on a label-free draw of equal size. This gain holds on
  sparse, varied demonstrations under an action-aware key and leave-one-demonstration-out
  training, and fades or slightly reverses on dense, scripted, or generated data. Building on this
  finding, our hetero-associative visuomotor memory (HAVM, 14M parameters) trains offline in about
  five minutes, including a learned retrieval temperature $\beta$, and runs in 1.1 ms. Across six
  fresh ALOHA encoders, it reaches 76.4% within 24 s, comparable to a 264M Diffusion Policy
  trained for 6.7 h (78.8%) and ahead of ACT (71.7%) and fine-tuned VLAs (65.2-75.2%), while
  leading every 40-demonstration baseline within the benchmark's 8 s limit (74.6%; +6.5 over
  Diffusion Policy, +15.1 over ACT). On LIBERO, one 40-task memory reaches 92.2% and loses far
  less than SmolVLA to rewording; on a real SO-101 arm, it sustains 30 Hz control without
  stalling. Unlike pretrained foundation policies aimed at zero-shot generalization to unseen
  tasks and workspaces, HAVM trades broad out-of-distribution generalization for rapid adaptation
  to the available demonstrations.
papers.summary: Retrieve-and-correct imitation policies usually refine the single nearest retrieved demonstration chunk, and this work asks what a demonstration memory should hand to the corrector instead. The finding is that a smooth, softmax-weighted recall over the whole memory is a much better base for a learned residual even though it is no better when executed alone, raising success by 22.4 points on `ALOHA` cube transfer with 40 human demonstrations, with gains that hold on sparse, varied demonstrations and fade on dense, scripted, or generated data. The resulting hetero-associative visuomotor memory (`HAVM`, 14M parameters) trains offline in about five minutes and runs in 1.1 ms, reaching **76.4% on `ALOHA`, comparable to a 264M-parameter `Diffusion Policy` trained for 6.7 hours (78.8%)**, and 92.2% on `LIBERO` with a single 40-task memory.

papers.title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement
papers.abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.
papers.summary: Stories that different LLMs write from the same prompt can resemble each other, and that similarity may come from the prompt's constraints or from shared writing tendencies of the models. Using 51,240 stories from five models on 10,248 common prompts in the `StoryScope` corpus, the study compares cross-model distances over 213 narrative features for same-prompt stories against stories from different but semantically matched prompts, and applies a semantic relevance mask to discount features tied to prompt content. The mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) is **.409 without masking and .406 with it**, indicating measurable cross-model narrative convergence beyond what the matched-prompt baseline explains.

papers.title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting
papers.abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.
papers.summary: Whether a language model produces normative Ukrainian is measured here with a released set of 1,444 minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government, and calques from Russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control. Each pair is scored both by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences and by prompting the model directly with the sentences in both orders, so that answer-position effects are measured separately. Across 19 models, order consistency falls below 0.05 for ten of them, with instruction tuning and not scale separating the usable models, and the vocative case is systematically inverted at **0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control**; Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces that deficit.

papers.title: Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping
papers.abstract: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are important for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results showed that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type mapping when using TabPFN. However, AEF embeddings yielded comparable results, achieving accuracies of 0.91 for agricultural LULC and 0.85 for irrigation-type mapping, while reducing the need for extensive data processing and manual feature engineering typically required for satellite products. Spatial LULC mapping using TabPFN achieved comparable overall accuracies (0.85-0.86) across the three feature configurations, but revealed substantial differences in mapped tree cover, ranging from 14.57% for surface reflectance to 29.79% for AFE. Physical probing revealed that AEF embeddings strongly encode spectral indices (A30-SWIR: rho=0.58-0.67), (A38-NDMI: rho=-0.72), vegetation (A49-NDVI: rho = 0.72-0.73), and SAR structure (A25-VH: rho = 0.71). Future research should focus on enhancing the interpretability of embedding-based approaches by incorporating physical knowledge to develop more transparent and trustworthy AI systems for agricultural applications.
papers.summary: Mapping agricultural land use and irrigation type in water-scarce Morocco is used to test whether `AlphaEarth` Foundation (AEF) embeddings can replace conventional satellite features. The embeddings are compared against single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using `XGBoost`, `CatBoost`, and `TabPFN` classifiers, and are probed for the physical quantities they encode. Multi-temporal feature time series perform best with `TabPFN` at 0.93 accuracy for land use and 0.87 for irrigation type, while the embeddings come close at **0.91 and 0.85** with far less data processing and feature engineering, and individual embedding dimensions correlate strongly with spectral indices, vegetation indices, and radar structure.

papers.title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
papers.abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.
papers.summary: Rubric-based medical benchmarks such as `HealthBench` grade LLM answers against physician criteria that assume the institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region, so machine translation alone can penalize answers that are appropriate elsewhere. `JHealthBench-L` adapts 79 patient-facing consultations and 1,022 criteria to Japan through source-cited LLM drafting, specialist revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Across 18 LLMs, translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings but **flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria**, against 7.3% re-grading noise, and context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain the main weaknesses.

papers.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
papers.abstract:
Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture.
  By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.
papers.summary: Because larger `EfficientNet` architectures were grown from smaller ones, the authors hypothesize that a smaller variant can hold the knowledge of a larger one. They propose a transfer learning method that uses knowledge distillation to pass knowledge from larger to smaller `EfficientNet` models. The method improves every `EfficientNet` variant tested, and **several smaller models outperform larger ones trained with standard transfer learning**.

papers.title: Counter-DECEIVR: Counterfactual Explanations for Deepfake Detectors using Detector-Guided Rectified Flow Inversion
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples. Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. It also leverages the detector's explanation maps to concentrate editing to salient regions, turning low-level feature importance into localised counterfactual edits. A single parameter controls the strength of the edits. Across two deepfake detectors and two widely used forensics datasets, Counter-DECEIVR outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones. Code will be made available upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Deepfake detectors are often black boxes, and region-based explanations become less useful as generated images improve, so the authors turn to counterfactual examples that show the minimal change needed to flip a detector's decision. `Counter-DECEIVR` is a **training-free** framework that steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf detectors, and uses the detector's explanation maps to concentrate edits on salient regions, with one parameter controlling edit strength. Across two detectors and two forensics datasets, it outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including ones that require training.

papers.title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes
papers.abstract: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
papers.summary: Strategy-following multi-agent deep reinforcement learning lets a manager steer teams through regional instructions, but in the `sfDA7-X` architecture the number of instruction combinations grows exponentially with team and instruction size, making training costly and transfer poor. The authors introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture so that one trained policy can be replicated across agents in teams of other sizes, and also test warm-start retraining from the pre-trained policy. In an object collection game, a policy trained with four agents transfers to three- and five-agent teams without substantial degradation, and warm-start retraining beats training from scratch while **cutting required training episodes by up to 90%**.

papers.title: Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models via Agentic Model Editing
papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation transfers pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to new domains using a small set of labeled images. Most methods fit prompts, representations, or classifiers within an adaptation procedure specified in advance. Yet the visual distinctions needed for recognition can differ substantially across domains, motivating the question: Can an LLM agent use few-shot examples and model observations to design the adaptation procedure itself? We propose Agentic Model Editing (AME), an agentic framework that jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting as an executable, domain-customized adaptation program. The agent inspects images, class semantics, model parameters, intermediate representations, and activations to formulate hypotheses about the target task. It implements and tests candidate programs on the support set, with aggregate validation accuracy guiding refinement and selection. Each program fits a complete domain model that is fixed before testing. The agent and its tools are shared across domains, while each domain receives its own adaptation program. Across eleven datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME achieves the highest average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with back-propagation among the compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate applicability across VLM backbones and LLM agents.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) normally fits prompts, representations, or classifiers inside a procedure fixed in advance, although the visual distinctions that matter differ across domains. Agentic Model Editing (`AME`) has an LLM agent inspect images, class semantics, model parameters, and activations, then write and test an executable, domain-specific adaptation program covering input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting, with support-set validation accuracy guiding refinement. Across eleven datasets with `CLIP ViT-B/16`, it achieves the highest average accuracy among compared methods, **81.2% without back-propagation** and 81.9% with it.

papers.title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
papers.abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.
papers.summary: LLM-based learner simulators used for teacher training and tutoring research are supposed to hold an assigned level of knowledge and misconceptions, but they can display skills beyond that profile, which the authors call competence leakage. An analysis of 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner transcripts identifies over-competence as a prominent form of misalignment, and previously observed leakage cases are then re-tested under four protocols ranging from isolated questions to multi-turn interaction across five model configurations. **Violations recur more often under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering**; more capable models generally leak less, while higher reasoning effort does not consistently help.

papers.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.
papers.summary: LLM-based user simulators used to evaluate conversational assistants can drift from their assigned goals or skip specified options, producing errors that get blamed on the assistant. A benchmark of 500 workflows expressed as Hierarchical Task Networks (HTN) tests simulators on sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, and shows that fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, that goal drift causes the majority of failures, and that scores vary with the assistant's response style. `ReUST` (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a prompting strategy that maintains state across dialogue turns, **improves goal success rate by more than 12 points** for mid-sized and large models and reduces sensitivity to response style.

papers.title: Decentralized Clustered Federated Learning for Cellular Traffic Forecasting over LEO Constellations
papers.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are positioned to act as orbital edge-compute nodes in emerging 6G non-terrestrial networks, supporting forecasting and control tasks for ground cellular infrastructure. However, training such models is challenged by heterogeneous ground-cell traffic patterns, intermittent links to ground stations, and the satellites' own orbital motion, which continuously shifts the data each satellite observes. In this work, we extend Decentralized Federated Clustering (DFCA) to the LEO setting and apply it to cellular internet-traffic forecasting on the Telecom Italia Milan+Trentino dataset. Satellites cooperate exclusively through $k$-nearest inter-satellite gossip with no ground-side aggregator, while zero-shot head selection lets each satellite specialize to the latent traffic regime of the ground cell currently beneath it. Averaged over $K{=}20$ post-training orbital snapshots, our extension reduces forecasting Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) by $15.3\%$ over a decentralized FedAvg baseline of equivalent capacity, with cluster recovery accuracy of $85.3\%$. The results indicate that clustered specialization yields measurable gains under the structural heterogeneity inherent to realistic cellular-over-LEO scenarios.
papers.summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites acting as edge-compute nodes must train forecasting models despite heterogeneous ground-cell traffic, intermittent ground links, and orbital motion that keeps shifting the data each satellite sees. The authors extend Decentralized Federated Clustering (`DFCA`) to this setting, with satellites cooperating only through gossip among nearest neighbors and no ground aggregator, while zero-shot head selection lets each satellite specialize to the traffic regime of the cell beneath it. On the `Telecom Italia` Milan and Trentino dataset, the approach **reduces forecasting Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) by 15.3%** against a decentralized `FedAvg` baseline of equal capacity, with 85.3% cluster recovery accuracy.

papers.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
papers.abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
papers.summary: Gated DeltaNet-2 (`GDN-2`), a linear-attention architecture with independent channel-wise control over erasing and writing its recurrent state, fails to train on long contexts. The authors trace this to an asymmetry between the reading and modification directions during erasure, which lets directional gains accumulate across tokens and makes the state grow exponentially even without new writes. Their stabilized variant uses symmetric erasure and decay-regulated residual writing, with a proven O(sqrt(T)) bound on state growth while keeping chunkwise parallel computation. On models of about 1.6B parameters it trains stably and **raises the average 128K `RULER` score by 6.80 points over `GDN-2` in the recurrent setting**, plus 0.62 points of average accuracy across nine downstream tasks in the hybrid setting.

papers.title: CARE-WM: Same-Horizon Self-Conditioning with Constraint-Adaptive Regularization for Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Planning with latent world models requires both accurate multi-step predictions and latent distances that reflect physical proximity to the goal. However, models are typically trained on ground-truth observations but must rely on their own imaginations during planning, while closer latent distances do not necessarily correspond to better task outcomes. Existing methods resort to auxiliary training objectives or additional task-cost readouts, which respectively incur extra training overhead or leave the latent geometry itself misaligned with task cost. We introduce CARE-WM, a drop-in training method that meets both requirements without additional supervision, a separate cost model, or any change to LeWM's architecture and Euclidean-cost planner. CARE-WM trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates the strength of latent regularization. With a single hyperparameter configuration, CARE-WM improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds the best results of other LeWM-family methods on most tasks. Further analyses show lower open-loop latent prediction error and closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.
papers.summary: Latent world models used for planning are trained on ground-truth observations but must roll out their own predictions at planning time, and distances in their latent space do not always track real task cost. `CARE-WM` is a drop-in training method that trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates the strength of latent regularization, with no extra supervision, separate cost model, or change to the `LeWM` architecture and its Euclidean-cost planner. With a single hyperparameter configuration it **improves mean planning success over `LeWM` on every evaluated continuous-control task** and matches or exceeds the best other `LeWM`-family methods on most tasks. Further analysis shows lower open-loop latent prediction error and closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.

papers.title: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
papers.abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.
papers.summary: Six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters are given bid landscapes, meaning the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, built from eBay closing prices and the simulated advertising market `AuctionNet`, and their bids are scored against an exact calculator. Two failures belong to the models themselves: they skip the best option even when their own trace ranks it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid, costing 7-17% of the calculator's surplus on eBay at 768 forced tokens. Two more come from operator choices: a token cap truncates traces, and asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it, so that **closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay**. An audit that overrides bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay.

papers.title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
papers.abstract: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.
papers.summary: Finding one distribution that balances several targets is cast as Pareto multiobjective optimization of Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures. The proposed multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (`MWPG`) method and its accelerated version (`MWAPG`) use implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and rely on a Hilbert-space lifting that represents each measure as the pushforward of a fixed base measure, turning the problem into a constrained composite one over transport maps. **`MWAPG` decreases a Pareto merit function at rate O(1/k^2) for convex smooth potentials**, with a linear rate in the strongly convex case, giving the discrete-time guarantees that the earlier accelerated method `A-MWGraD` lacks. Particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks need no score estimation, and in experiments `MWAPG` needs far fewer iterations than `MWPG` while matching or outperforming `A-MWGraD` in Bayesian multi-task learning.

papers.title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
papers.abstract: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.
papers.summary: Image-to-3D services screen uploaded images for policy violations, but the inspector sees only the visible input, so a benign-looking image can still be crafted to produce restricted 3D geometry. `PTA3D` is a targeted adversarial attack built on two components: Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA), which aligns only the early diffusion-transformer outputs where the core geometry forms, and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO), which optimizes across diverse image transformations so the attack transfers between services. The authors also give a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound. On three open-source models and three online services, the attack reaches **41.5%-88.5% success on online services** and 90.8%-94.6% in white-box settings, outperforming existing attacks.

papers.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation
papers.abstract: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.
papers.summary: Building a coherent, explorable 3D world from scattered images with little or no visual overlap defeats geometry-aware methods, while image- and video-based generators fill in unseen regions but with inconsistent geometry across views. `WorldBridge` encodes the scattered references into a global scene context that guides geometry and appearance generation, adds a temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism for references on and off the target trajectory, and applies a plug-and-play reprojection-guided test-time optimization to improve reference fidelity. The authors also introduce the `WorldBridge` benchmark suite for low-overlap references. They report that the method **surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in coherent, controllable 3D world generation** in both qualitative and quantitative comparisons.

papers.title: Feature Engineered Reinforcement Learning for S-pair Selection in Buchberger's Algorithm
papers.abstract: Selecting the order in which to process S-pairs is a crucial decision in Buchberger's algorithm for computing Groebner bases: this choice can change the cost by orders of magnitude. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning agents viewing exponent vectors of the polynomials outperform classical heuristics on binomial ideals. We extend this line of work to general polynomial ideals by using statistical features. We introduce a 17-dimensional feature vector to describe a polynomial and use PPO to train policies on five distributions of random ideals. We find that using S-polynomial features significantly outperforms S-pair features on all five distributions. The new policies also outperform the retrained RL baseline on all five distributions, reducing algorithmic work by 41--53\% relative to the degree heuristic on four distributions where learning helps. The additional cost of the feature engineering means that wall-clock cost remains similar to the baseline, but our new approach benefits from easier transfer to unseen distributions.
papers.summary: The order in which S-pairs are processed in Buchberger's algorithm for computing Groebner bases can change its cost by orders of magnitude, and earlier reinforcement learning work on this choice covered only binomial ideals. Here each polynomial is described by a 17-dimensional statistical feature vector, and `PPO` policies are trained on five distributions of random general polynomial ideals. Features of the S-polynomial outperform S-pair features on all five distributions, and the new policies **reduce algorithmic work by 41-53% relative to the degree heuristic** on the four distributions where learning helps. The cost of computing features leaves wall-clock time similar to the baseline, but the approach transfers more easily to unseen distributions.

papers.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.
papers.summary: Researchers who describe AI with cognitive terms such as understanding and believing, and critics who reject this as wishful anthropomorphism, are argued to share the same flawed approach: asking whether AI systems fall under concepts built for humans. The author proposes instead that **anthropomorphic language should be disciplined rather than discouraged**, by separating the inferential connections bundled into each cognitive concept and deciding which to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. That discipline comes from the human needs that give the concepts their point and from empirical, especially mechanistic, evidence. The resulting conceptions of understanding and belief are claimed to be potentially richer and better fitted to AI than thinned-out versions of the human ones.

papers.title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting.
