Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.
papers.summary: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and `EAGLE`-style drafters speed up speculative decoding by reusing the target model's hidden states, but at inference they attend to a growing tail of their own recurrently generated states that training never showed them. Two training-only fixes are proposed: Hidden State Mixing (`HSM`), which samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, and Hidden State Gradient Detach (`HSGD`), which stochastically blocks gradients through hidden-state and embedding pathways; neither adds inference cost. `HSGD` gives the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions and `HSM` at later ones, and across four `Nemotron` models and `DeepSeek-V4-Pro`, **`HSM`-based boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2%** over the co-trained MTP. For `EAGLE-3` drafters, `HSM` is competitive with training-time test (TTT) while using 48% less peak training memory in a four-step `Qwen3-8B` comparison.

papers.title: Exploring the Design Factors of Pixel-space Diffusion
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT
papers.summary: Design choices for diffusion models that operate directly on pixels are examined from three angles: architecture, representation, and the frequency domain. The resulting model, `EiT`, is a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer with an explicit channel-dimension bottleneck, motivated by an analysis showing a three-stage representation dynamic across layers and timesteps in which earlier denoising and a longer middle stage go with better generation. The authors also show that pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion are equivalent when the network operates in pixel space. On `ImageNet`, `EiT` **achieves an FID of 1.61 against 1.85 for `JiT` at 256x256** and 1.73 against 1.99 at 512x512, and extended to video it outperforms latent video diffusion on `Kinetics-600` at comparable parameter counts.

papers.title: Whose Side Are You On? A Framework and Benchmark for Assessing LLM Political Stances through Politicians Social Media Posts
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.
papers.summary: To measure which political positions large language models (LLMs) support or oppose, the authors simulate social media interactions in which models respond to politicians' posts under several prompting methods and keep only the stances expressed consistently. They build `WorldPOLL`, a set of **4,600 posts from about 200 politicians in ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries**, collected from X/Twitter. Quantitative and qualitative analyses show how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, revealing positions shared across models as well as differences between national contexts. The study also examines how consistent stances are across prompting methods and how model size and instruction tuning affect that inconsistency.

papers.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
papers.abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.
papers.summary: A pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing tests how task complexity affects willingness to use AI tools instead of hiring entry-level staff. Managers were randomly assigned a lasting need for extra capacity involving either standardised tasks or complex tasks requiring professional judgement, contextual knowledge, and independent problem-solving. Complex tasks **reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale** and raise the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Managers also expect AI availability to reduce hiring of both junior and experienced workers, but significantly more for juniors.

papers.title: AlignPre: Skill-Aligned Post-Training for Latent-Free Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based precipitation nowcasting models produce detailed radar forecasts but usually depend on separately trained components, and matching the data distribution does not directly optimize the verification scores forecasters use. `AlignPre` is an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster that works in pixel space with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture and no latent compression. Its skill-aligned post-training (`SAPT`) stage uses the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to build a differentiable objective and backpropagates it from the radar fields into the generator. On three real-world benchmarks with different forecast horizons, it **consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill**.

papers.title: Do Machine Learning Ensembles Beat Published Quotas? Target Parameterization, Censored Baselines, and Conformal Intervals Under Admissions Reform
papers.abstract: Public admission capacity caps published prior to matriculation are widely used by ministries and institutional analysts as default intake projections in centralized postsecondary clearinghouses. Using an audited 2022 to 2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel (26,895 program-year records across 309 universities) linked to strictly lagged t-1 occupational vacancy signals, this paper evaluates machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric estimators against published quotas across 5,385 continuing 2024 programs (five-fold university-grouped cross-validation) and 3,348 matched (2,179 grain-consistent) 2025 programs strictly out of time. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll their exact published quota, unanchored log-growth ensembles degrade accuracy, while the worst 5% generate half of total quota error via unfilled "phantom capacity." Controlled target ablations, including a single-factor test under widened non-binding clipping, show that parameterizing the log fill ratio ln(D_it / S_it) instead of log growth reduces 2024 MAE by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67), aligns ML with Tobit, Cragg, REML HLM, and capped L1 baselines, and lifts combined tuition and institutional-tier TreeSHAP attribution from 2.5% to 45.8%. Hurdle stacking attains the lowest full-census 2024 MAE (H-Hard 11.29; H-Soft 11.32 vs. 12.35, p = 0.022, clearing 10% not 5% FDR; fold-overlap p = 0.134), whereas continuous QA-Stack outperforms H-Soft on mixed-reporting campuses, Tobit (median) ties H-Soft across both 90% MCS sets, and interior-only Cragg-ML lowers RMSE to 28.1. Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. Across 257 reporting campuses, reconciled 2026 national totals (627,114 to 629,256) lie squarely within 604,533 to 662,044.
papers.summary: Published admission quotas are widely used as default enrollment projections, and this study tests whether machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric models can beat them on a 2022-2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel of 26,895 program-year records across 309 universities. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll exactly their published quota, ensembles that predict log growth lose accuracy, whereas **predicting the log fill ratio instead cuts 2024 mean absolute error by 21.5%**, from 14.86 to 11.67. Hurdle stacking gives the lowest 2024 error at 11.29 against 12.35 for quotas. After Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, the best models only tie the quotas, and 90% conformal interval coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%.

papers.title: SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression methods that reproduce a biological system's trajectories accurately do not necessarily recover its true reaction mechanisms, and existing benchmarks do not measure that gap. `SysBio-SR` collects 198 literature-based biological ordinary differential equation systems with reaction annotations, testing trajectory fidelity for 11 symbolic-discovery methods in-distribution and under out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, and mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods on 161 systems. The joint analysis shows that trajectory-based evaluation severely overestimates mechanism recovery. The authors' `KineSelect` framework, which searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws, **improves aggregate OOD extrapolation R^2 by 19.2% and overall reaction F1 by 14.3%** over the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration
papers.abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
papers.summary: Deciding per input which internal experts, model endpoints, or agents to run has been studied separately at the token level (expert gating in sparse architectures), the query level (model cascades), and the task level (multi-agent orchestration). This systematic review synthesizes **2,289 studies from 2017 to September 2026**, selected from 13,884 records, across 20 method families under a single two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of the token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead is a top bottleneck at every layer. Safeguards are asymmetric: intra-layer gating focuses on load balancing and rarely estimates uncertainty, while model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules and struggle with miscalibration and cascading errors, and the fastest-growing area, agentic task delegation, is where routing is least often isolated experimentally.

papers.title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
papers.abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.
papers.summary: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information, and consolidate findings into a report. `LEXI` (Legal Extraction and Intelligence) is a work-in-progress system that uses large language models to classify documents under a configurable taxonomy, assign target entities, extract predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance, and prepare report content, with structured outputs linking the stages. Lawyers review and correct the model's output and keep responsibility for legal assessments, risk ratings, and final wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components give **preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible**.

papers.title: Unstable Action Boundaries in Lethal Drone Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.
papers.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents pose risks that text-only refusal tests miss, and this study asks whether a drone agent's willingness to act stays stable when the description of the target changes. Recent popular LLMs are evaluated in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where they can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. **Some agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as people, with no jailbreak needed**. In addition, an agent that appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe after a simple semantic shift in the target description.

papers.title: MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) at millimeter-wave frequencies supports human sensing tasks such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, but each task typically needs its own model trained from scratch with no way to flag unreliable predictions. `MUSE` (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder) is a single shared transformer encoder with per-dataset tokenization, pretrained by masked autoencoding across five datasets and fine-tuned with evidential classification heads that quantify uncertainty. It replaces N separate encoders while **improving classification performance by 9.7 percentage points over task-specific models**. Its uncertainty estimates support selective prediction and remain useful on unseen users, ranking wrong predictions as more uncertain than correct ones 78% of the time and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy without retraining.

papers.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.
papers.summary: Video large language models often see only part of the visual evidence a question needs, and should answer when it is sufficient, guess from visible clues when it is partial, and abstain when it is absent. `ClueProbe` is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,721 human-annotated questions over 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, with controlled perturbations of wording and visual input. Across 10 open-source and proprietary models, failures come from judging sufficiency rather than from perception: models see the evidence but either answer or refuse outright and rarely guess. Fine-tuning with supervision at the guess level **lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals**, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions.

papers.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
papers.abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.
papers.summary: Feed-forward pointmap methods reconstruct 3D geometry from images without known camera poses, but they output discrete, sparse points rather than continuous surfaces. The proposed pipeline takes geometric priors from a pre-trained pointmap model, selects relevant reference views by surfel voting, regresses a coarse continuous surface by cross-attention between query rays and reference features, and then refines fine detail and surface normals with a raylet-based module. Trained as a single model on 9 datasets, it is reported to **generalize zero-shot to 6 unseen datasets with better geometric accuracy and detail than prior baselines**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Feed-forward pointmap models such as `VGGT` recover geometry from unposed images but only as discrete, sparse points, while ray-based distance fields give continuous surfaces but need accurate poses or point clouds. `FoundSurface` joins the two, using pointmap priors to condition a ray-surface distance predictor that outputs continuous surfaces and analytic normals for any query view.

- A frozen `VGGT` supplies pointmaps, poses and multi-layer features, a surfel-voting step keeps the top-k reference views that overlap the query, a cross-attention regressor in query-centric coordinates predicts a coarse ray distance map, and a sparse-convolution raylet module adds a per-ray residual for fine detail.
- Trained once on 9 datasets and tested zero-shot on 6 others with 50 input views, it has the **lowest absolute distance error on all six**, for example **0.132 m** on `ScanNet++` against 0.179 m for the retrained `RayletDF`, although `PriorDA` beats it on RMSE and relative-error metrics on `Tanks&Temples`.
- Normals derived from depth supervision alone reach a mean angular error of **29.83°** on `ScanNet++` and **20.72°** on `Replica`, against 39.87° and 28.96° for the best baseline, and the refinement stage matters most on `Replica`, where it cuts distance error from 0.137 m to 0.064 m.
- On `ScanNet++` meshes it has the best Chamfer distance (**0.056**) and F1@5cm (**0.792**), but the margin over Poisson fitting on the same `VGGT` points (0.787) is thin and its accuracy score (0.046) trails `VGGT` with TSDF fusion (0.042).
- Quality tracks the `VGGT` prior despite the authors' robustness claim, with `ScanNet++` distance error rising from 0.041 m to 0.534 m as pointmap error grows past 0.20 m, and the model is large because of that backbone, with ablations trained on `ScanNet` only.

papers.title: WorldPhy: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Physical Plausibility of World Models in Robotics
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.
papers.summary: Video world models used in robotics must respect fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interaction, which existing world-model benchmarks tend to overlook. `WorldPhy` provides 300 tasks, each an initial frame plus an instruction, spanning varied scenes, task types, viewpoints, and robot configurations. More than 12K human annotations are used to train `WorldPhyReward`, a scorer that gives ratings and reasons on six physical dimensions plus instruction following and aligns with human ratings better than general vision-language models and existing reward models. An evaluation of **13 open and closed-source world models finds that none consistently maintains fine-grained physical plausibility** across robotics scenarios.

papers.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
papers.abstract: The bestseller D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and na\"ive Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.
papers.summary: The 2017 Danish bestseller Dødevaskeren was published under the name Sara Omar, but it has been suggested that Mads Peder Nordbo may have written it. Four authorship attribution methods are applied to the question: `Delta`, intertextual distance, `Nearest Shrunken Centroids`, and naive Bayes. Across parameter settings, the methods **consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the novel**, though not conclusively for the whole text. When the book is split into 5,000-token segments, most again match Nordbo, while a few passages point to another, unidentified author, possibly Omar herself.

papers.title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
papers.abstract: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sunyxedu/General-Verifier
papers.summary: Score-based verifiers give a scalar reward for a model output but no auditable evidence for the judgment, and text-feedback reward models rarely use tools or iterative reasoning to check claims. `Agent-as-a-Verifier` places role-separated LLM agents in a claim-obligation-certificate protocol inspired by formal methods: it extracts a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiles the task's acceptance contract, and derives checkable obligations to produce a certificate. It reports higher verification accuracy than the previous best approach on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, and agents augmented with it outperform plain agents on `FrontierMath` and `CyberGym`. The system also **identifies reward-hacking solutions that fool the benchmark's own evaluator**.

papers.title: SOC-Net: Second-Order-Cone-Constrained Neural Networks
papers.abstract: In many applications, neural networks must learn input-output maps that respect prior knowledge such as physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits. These requirements constrain which outputs are admissible for a given input and often admit second-order cone (SOC) representations, including norm bounds and robust linear inequalities. Examples in control include friction cones, thrust bounds, and input-robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions. However, existing approaches to enforcing general input-dependent SOC constraints require a conic solver, an iterative scheme whose feasibility depends on convergence, or an interior feasible point for each input. We propose SOC-Net, a neural network architecture that enforces input-dependent SOC constraints by construction for every input, even outside the training distribution. SOC-Net projects an affine lifting of the backbone output onto the reachable slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back to the output space. For separable constraints, this projection splits into one projection per cone, and each is available in closed form or reduces to a single scalar equation, regardless of the cone dimension. We prove that SOC-Net retains the expressive power of the backbone network under regularity conditions and accommodates end-to-end training by standard backpropagation with an explicit Jacobian. Experiments on contact force allocation with friction constraints and 3-D obstacle avoidance with an input-robust CBF demonstrate that SOC-Net satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input, with lower evaluation latency than the tested solver-based and iterative baselines.
papers.summary: Neural networks used in control often must produce outputs that satisfy input-dependent second-order cone (SOC) constraints such as friction cones, thrust bounds, and robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions, and existing ways of enforcing them need a conic solver, a convergent iterative scheme, or a known interior feasible point. `SOC-Net` instead projects an affine lifting of the backbone's output onto a slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back, with each projection available in closed form or as a single scalar equation for separable constraints. The authors prove the architecture keeps the backbone's expressive power under regularity conditions and supports standard backpropagation. In contact force allocation and 3-D obstacle avoidance experiments, it **satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input with lower latency than solver-based and iterative baselines**.

papers.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
papers.abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.
papers.summary: `Delta` is an authorship attribution method based on the most frequent words, valued because its results are easy to interpret but not always accurate. The proposed variant applies a resampling procedure to the selected stylistic features. The authors report that this **raises attribution accuracy while preserving interpretability**, at the cost of additional computation time.

papers.title: Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel
papers.abstract:
Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC.
  We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.
papers.summary: Agentic review systems now flag suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports, but maintainers often ignore them because confirming a bug means building a reproducer by hand. `ReproCue` generates runnable proofs-of-concept (PoCs) for such reports by replaying historical kernel bugs to learn one reproduction finite-state machine (FSM) per subsystem, then following that FSM for a new report and adjusting the PoC and environment as execution reveals what is missing. On 100 recent AI-generated reviews it produced PoCs for 49, versus 10 for an existing agentic reproducer and 9 for directed fuzzing. **Kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of the reports that came with a generated PoC**, compared with 9.3% for text-only reports from `Sashiko`.

papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses usually handle context for the model by summarizing history when the window fills; the alternative studied here lets the model decide when and what to compact through a context API. The two strategies are compared in NVIDIA's open-source agent harness on document research and machine learning engineering tasks, with context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the API well score higher, often with fewer input tokens: **`GPT 6.1` rises from 21% to 56% on `OfficeQA Pro v2` at a 32K budget**, and `Kimi` improves with up to 41% fewer input tokens, though models vary widely in how often, how aggressively, and when they compact. Reusing the key-value (KV) cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit also cuts prefill compute by up to 15% per request with no measurable accuracy change.

papers.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.
papers.summary: Benchmarks that test multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on grid games mostly report end-to-end success, which hides whether failures come from perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. `GridProbe` pairs Sokoban solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and presents every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Across seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game, proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, while open-source models are limited by rule application or by counting rows and columns in the image. Acting on the diagnosis, **fine-tuning only the vision module of a perception-limited model raises its interactive Sokoban success from 5.8% to 20.4%** and transfers zero-shot to the maze game, whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model.

papers.title: When High Capacity Becomes Undeployable: Pore-Filling Constraints for Multi-Objective Optimization of Direct Air Capture Sorbents
papers.abstract: Amine-impregnated sorbents with the highest nominal CO2 capacity are frequently the least deployable, as amine beyond the pore-volume limit blocks active sites. Yet multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) for direct air capture (DAC) treats formulation search as unconstrained. We encode the pore-filling boundary as an explicit outcome constraint, c(x) = tanh(1 - phi_hat) - tau, and use it as a diagnostic instrument on a hand-curated, DOI-traceable benchmark of 618 solid-amine formulations from 43 publications. Unconstrained MOBO attains higher nominal capacity (3.639 +/- 0.815 vs. 2.964 +/- 0.728 mmol/g, p = 1.0e-11), but across 100 seeds 63.2% of its Pareto-optimal candidates violate the pore-filling boundary versus 39.3% under the constraint: it is rewarded for proposing candidates outside the pore-confined design regime. The constraint steers the front to lower loadings (55.8 vs. 65.2 wt%) and larger pores. The boundary is corroborated once apparatus effects are harmonized hierarchically: 77.8% of kinetic variance is between-laboratory, and pore filling carries a significant kinetic penalty (p = 0.002). Standard hypervolume over-credits feasibility-agnostic methods by 13.9-16.1% (vs. 11.1% constrained), and three surrogate-based analyses---the constrained front, a regeneration-energy third objective, and harmonized kinetics---consistently point to a conservative deployable window at pore filling phi_hat ~ 0.4-0.5 (45-55 wt% loading). The benchmark and associated analysis outputs accompany this submission.
papers.summary: Amine-impregnated sorbents for direct air capture (DAC) of CO2 lose effectiveness when the amine loading exceeds the pore volume, yet multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) of formulations usually ignores this limit. The authors encode the pore-filling boundary as an explicit outcome constraint and test it on a hand-curated benchmark of 618 solid-amine formulations from 43 publications. Unconstrained optimization reaches higher nominal capacity, but **63.2% of its Pareto-optimal candidates violate the pore-filling boundary, versus 39.3% with the constraint**. Three surrogate-based analyses point to a conservative deployable window of roughly 45-55 wt% amine loading.

papers.title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments
papers.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
papers.summary: Assigning AI-controlled agents to contested objectives in team combat games requires real-time coordination under uncertainty about teammates and opponents. The system uses a hybrid predict-then-optimize design: a masked multi-head model predicts per-agent tactical signals such as survival chance, local superiority, and travel time, these are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes global assignments under capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive constraints. Built as a research prototype on a commercial game and evaluated with offline diagnostics, online A/B tests, and latency measurements, it indicates that **learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable allocation under strict real-time constraints**.

papers.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
papers.abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $\pi_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $\mu_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.
papers.summary: Deconvolution methods estimate cell-type-level features from bulk RNA data, and predicting cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) has proven much harder than predicting cell-type proportions. The authors explain the gap with closed-form accuracy bounds: a ceiling on R-squared for per-gene linear estimators of CTSE, and a closed-form R-squared with a computable lower bound for proportion estimators that pool evidence across genes. On 106 curated cell-type and gene pairs in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value. **A sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as one built on the bulk genes** while attributing its signal to specific cell types.

papers.title: Multi-view fnirs identifies neurophysiological subtypes in post-stroke aphasia
papers.abstract: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cram\'er's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.
papers.summary: Post-stroke aphasia varies widely between patients, and conventional clinical categories may not reflect differences in brain functional organisation. Seventy-nine patients were clustered without clinical labels using three views of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data, covering resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity changes, integrated by similarity network fusion and spectral clustering. **Three neurophysiological subgroups emerged, distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state connectivity**, and the solution was stable under subsampling but collapsed when the resting-state view was removed. Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype or baseline language scores.

papers.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
papers.abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.
papers.summary: Applying mental vocabulary to language models is argued to separate two processes usually treated as one: conventionalization, where a stretched word stops being marked as figurative, and calibration, where the inferences it invites are fitted to what the new referents actually do. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows **conventionalization running most of its course within three years**, while calibration lags because models are opaque, fast-changing, and trained on the very discourse about them. The author proposes a norm of targeted qualification, flagging the specific unsupported inferences an attribution invites, and offers three testable predictions about when such qualifications calibrate expectations.

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
papers.summary: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where a single perturbed image or a few altered text strokes can redirect a decision, yet diffusion-based adversarial purifiers have only been evaluated at the diffusion model's fixed resolution on classifier benchmarks. The study tests purifiers at native resolution for an agent built on `Qwen3-VL-8B`, against grey-box attackers who know the model but not the defense, and compares them at matched clean-accuracy cost. Resizing inputs to the diffusion model's resolution raises the `TextVQA` clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (`DC`) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, **`DC` keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy where cheap input transformations at matched cost keep at most 40.0%**, with the robustness coming from the global noise level rather than input-estimated masks.

papers.title: Lightweight Reasoning Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Vector Projection
papers.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.
papers.summary: Transferring reasoning ability from a large language model to a smaller one usually needs extensive teacher supervision or costly student fine-tuning. The approach here keeps both models frozen: a task-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT) vector is learned in the teacher from solution traces, and a lightweight linear projector is trained to map it into the student's residual space using only final-answer supervision on a small set of examples. On `GSM8K` and `MATH`, **the projected vector improves base students by 10.37 to 21.98 accuracy points**. On four code-generation benchmarks, a `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` student gains 3.23 to 4.67 pass@1 points and the base `Qwen2.5-7B` student gains up to 9.65.

papers.title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.
papers.summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) systems must cope with modalities that go missing through sensor failure, privacy masking, or unstable transmission, and existing methods typically work from a single flattened encoder output. Hierarchical Semantic Learning (`HSL`) exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder, uses high-level semantics from observed modalities as anchors to progressively reconstruct the missing ones, regularizes the reconstruction with prototypical contrastive losses, and fuses across modalities and levels. On `CMU-MOSI`, `CMU-MOSEI`, `IEMOCAP`, and `CH-SIMS`, it **outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings**.

papers.title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
papers.abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.
papers.summary: Defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tend to be reactive: prompt-based ones get overridden by injected instructions, and supervised detectors need retraining for each new attack style. `MINE` is a training-free, attack-agnostic defense that works by maximizing the relevance of context to the query, using mutual information and embedding variance, and it doubles as a query-conditioned reranker. The authors also introduce `LC-Inj-SQuAD`, a long-context benchmark averaging 4,032 words per context, and evaluate on it alongside `Inj-SQuAD`, `Inj-TriviaQA`, and `InjecAgent`. Across all four, `MINE` shows **the best accuracy-security trade-off among training-free defenses**, stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, and has the lowest latency on long contexts.

papers.title: SOLO: Towards Sample-Faithful and Detectable LLM Watermarking under Repeated Sampling via Content-Anchored Single-Owner Contexts
papers.abstract: Providers watermark the outputs of large language models, while applications sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, and uncertainty estimation. We show that deployed configurations of distortion-free watermarks, which deduplicate keyed contexts only within a response, couple the responses of a request: answer templates make all responses query the watermark with the same context before the answer, so collisions across responses, usually assumed rare, become the norm. Key pools reduce or avoid the coupling at the cost of multiple testing, and the exact remedy of a context history shared across the request leaves many positions unwatermarked. We propose SOLO, which keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so that siblings rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses, each detectable with a single key. On five language models from three families and three benchmarks, SOLO preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, also after randomly editing 10% of the tokens, and more than the context history on most clean tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhongliangGuo/solo-watermark.
papers.summary: Applications often sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, or uncertainty estimation, and deployed distortion-free watermarks turn out to couple those responses: shared answer templates make every response query the watermark with the same context, so cross-response collisions become the norm. `SOLO` keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so sibling responses rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are **jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses while each remains detectable with a single key**. Across five language models and three benchmarks, it preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, including after 10% of tokens are randomly edited.

papers.title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
papers.summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast from numerical history alone, but relevant information is often available only in accompanying text. `C2LoRA-TS` encodes that text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM, keeping both the backbone and the text encoder frozen and exactly recovering the original model's output when no context is given. On `Time-MMD` across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, it **achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen model and a static LoRA baseline for every architecture and seed**. Replacing instance-specific text with a single fixed context degrades performance in every case.

papers.title: Beyond Logits: Coherent Hallucination Mitigation via Attention Contrastive Decoding
papers.abstract:
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression.
  We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.
papers.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) hallucinate, and Contrastive Decoding (CD), which contrasts an amateur and an expert branch at the logit level, is a common training-free fix. The authors argue that logit-level intervention damages the coherence of generated text and forces penalty constraints that have nothing to do with suppressing hallucination. Their plug-in, `Attention Contrastive Decoding` (`ACD`), moves part of the contrast into the attention mechanism through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy that weakens hallucination-associated attention patterns and amplifies important visual information. Combined with existing methods such as `VCD`, it is reported to give **more coherent outputs with fewer hallucinations while removing the need for the restrictive penalties**.

papers.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.
papers.summary: Cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems is modelled with submodular utilities, where evaluating every candidate action to update the policy can be too expensive online. The proposed algorithm caps the number of evaluations by sampling a fixed number of agent-action pairs and applying inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, which gives an unbiased gradient estimate for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. The analysis yields a **1/2-approximate regret bound that splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies and a term that depends on the query budget**. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show performance staying high with less online computation.

papers.title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence
papers.abstract: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory.
