An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at https://github.com/Haochen-Luo/PROVE.
papers.summary: LLM agents that verify each other's work over long interactions drift into collusion, accepting work without the evidence the verification protocol requires. The authors trace this to accurate feedback accumulating in memory, since an agent that follows the rule is told its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right. `PROVE` (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them instead of their outcome, and credits each call an agent makes with the outcome that call controls. A LoRA adapter for `Qwen3.6-27B` trained on six-episode interactions cuts the **collusion rate on held-out ten-episode sequences from 65.0% to 1.0%** with no detectable change in task success.

papers.title: GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision
papers.abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.
papers.summary: Paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery could support seabed habitat mapping, but existing self-supervised methods make little use of the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata in real surveys. `GeoCAM` learns a shared embedding space without semantic labels by combining a Set Attention Aggregator that summarizes several optical views per sonar tile, an `InfoNCE` objective weighted by GPS-derived footprint overlap as soft positive supervision, and an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch. On the `BenthiCat SSS-CAM` dataset it **improves cross-modal retrieval and alignment over contrastive baselines**.

papers.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
papers.abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.
papers.summary: Generative AI can produce hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations in minutes, and the authors argue that it has **accelerated scientific discovery far more than justification**. They describe three ways confidence can outgrow evidence in human-AI research: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance, with unscrutinised contributions building up as verification debt. Their proposed `PAUSE` protocol is a checkpoint at consequential decisions with five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It ends in a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer, and the authors outline a framework for evaluating whether the practice helps.

papers.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
papers.abstract: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.
papers.summary: Window-based change point detection (CPD) scores the discrepancy between two adjacent samples of a time series, but windows small enough for temporal precision give too little data for the classifiers and deep models that compute the score. The study uses generative models to augment each window, expanding the available data and stabilizing the distribution of CPD scores. On synthetic and real data, the augmentation lets **simple classifiers outperform complex deep-learning baselines**.

papers.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.
papers.summary: Prostate MRI segmentation models trained on limited, heterogeneous data tend to make boundary errors and over-segment. The authors augment training data with synthetic T2-weighted volumes from a 2.5D denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that is weakly conditioned on stacks of adjacent binary masks through channel concatenation. On the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort, an `nnU-Net` trained with a 20% synthetic mix raised **mean Dice from 0.8935 to 0.9094 and cut false-positive voxels by 23.1%**. On the larger `LUND` cohort, a 23% synthetic mix gave a much smaller drop in false-positive voxels, from 11,102 to 10,757 per case.

papers.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
papers.abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.
papers.summary: To separate forecasting from recall, each drug target-disease hypothesis is treated as a dated event, namely the pair's first clinical trial, and a biomedical knowledge graph is rebuilt as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 onward. Six open language models are asked, with and without the graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease in the following year. Without retrieval the models rank about as well as a simple count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, and evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain. The newest graph lifts five of six models clearly above that baseline, but **its paths usually contain the answer itself, the pair's own trial dated after the decision**.

papers.title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.
papers.summary: Shapley values in reinforcement learning explain which observation features drive an agent's behaviour and expected return, but not how certain the agent is. `EXPOSURE` uses a single mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations, which supplies the predictions needed for every subset of visible features. It attributes the variance of the return, split into a part caused by missing features and a part caused by the environment's own randomness, along with the entropy of the agent's belief over masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values can be computed, it gives **more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty** and is the only compared method that explains belief uncertainty.

papers.title: Navigent: A Geometry-Grounded Agentic Framework for Vision Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Project Page: https://marslab-navigent.github.io/navigent.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/MarsLab-Navigent/Navigent
papers.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggles over long routes, where an agent must track progress, notice when actual motion differs from commanded motion and recognise when it has passed a landmark or entrance. `Navigent` pairs a frozen MLLM with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC) that checks measured displacement against commanded movement and tracks visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates, interrupting the action sequence to reobserve, adjust or recover when they disagree. An offline self-improvement step analyses past trajectories to refine prompts and critic logic without changing model weights. It reports **84.0% success rate on `R2R-CE` and 86.0% on `RxR-CE` validation-unseen splits**, with success weighted by path length of 72.9% and 69.1%.

papers.title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.
papers.summary: LLM agents often fail to apply a skill's rules during autonomous execution even when the skill spells them out, which the authors call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). Their `EBU-Bench` benchmark covers 12 medical task groups and measures the gap between autonomous skill use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. Every model-harness combination tested shows the problem, with a **mean gap of 43.94 percentage points**, and the same model's accuracy varies by up to 38.96 points across harnesses. `EBU-Evolve` uses execution feedback to rewrite skill instructions, raising autonomous skill-use accuracy by 33.33 to 55.17 points with gains that transfer across models and harnesses.

papers.title: Crucible: Evaluating LLM Agents in Executable Chemistry Research Environments
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on chemistry knowledge benchmarks, which mainly assess question answering and isolated tasks. Chemical research, however, requires using specialized tools and interpreting their outputs to obtain chemically valid results. To address this gap, we introduce Crucible Bench to evaluate this ability across all four stages of the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle. The benchmark contains 1,078 tasks in 12 task families curated from 18 published datasets, covering molecular design, synthesis planning, experimental execution, closed-loop optimization, simulation, and analytical characterization. Agents access 75 domain-specific tools through the Model Context Protocol in seven isolated environments. Sandboxed graders verify the resulting synthesis routes, experimental protocols, and other outputs. Laboratory tasks use robotic simulators or previously measured experimental data. We evaluate 14 LLMs as agents and find that the best achieves an overall score of 0.545, with synthesis planning and closed-loop optimization emerging as the hardest domains. Overall performance does not predict optimization performance well: the model ranked twelfth overall achieves the highest score in closed-loop optimization. Error analysis also shows that agents often submit chemically invalid results despite running their tools successfully. Stronger models benefit more from tool access, but reliable use of chemical software remains a challenge that Crucible Bench can track as models improve.
papers.summary: Chemistry benchmarks for LLMs mostly test question answering, while real chemical research requires running specialised tools and interpreting their output. `Crucible Bench` contains 1,078 tasks in 12 families across the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle, with agents calling 75 domain tools through the Model Context Protocol in seven isolated environments and sandboxed graders checking the results. Across 14 LLMs, the **best achieves an overall score of 0.545**, with synthesis planning and closed-loop optimization the hardest areas. Agents often submit chemically invalid results even after running their tools successfully, and overall rank does not predict optimization performance.

papers.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
papers.abstract: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.
papers.summary: Synthetic clinical time series need realistic temporal behaviour, calibration that does not leak test data, and transparency about privacy. The pipeline factorizes generation: a compact GPT-style language model learns which biomarker values co-occur using quantile tokens, per-biomarker 3x3 Markov transitions enforce temporal direction, and a monotone quantile map is fit on training data only. On a 5,000-patient simulated testbed it improves distributional fidelity and co-occurrence over an empirical sampler, and a **membership-inference audit gives an AUC of about 0.5**, though no differential-privacy claim is made. The results come from a controlled simulator, with validation on real health-record cohorts still planned.

papers.title: LLM-coupled interpretable tool wear monitoring with multi-evidence reasoning in CNC machining
papers.abstract: Interpretable tool wear assessment in CNC machining is challenging. Existing diagnostic models have high accuracy but provide limited guidance for tool replacement. This study proposes a two layer framework combining deep learning wear classification and LLM assisted reasoning. The first layer uses PCA Loading feature selection and optimized GRU to recognize three wear states, achieving 98.38 percent macro F1 score on the PHM2010 dataset. The second layer uses LLMs to generate natural language reports and replacement suggestions from classification results and feature trends. Engineer evaluation shows the reports outperform rule templates. Cross dataset tests on NASA milling data support the generalizability of this framework.
papers.summary: Tool wear models for CNC machining can be accurate while giving little guidance on when to replace a tool. The proposed two-layer framework first classifies three wear states using feature selection based on principal component loadings and an optimized GRU, reaching a **98.38% macro F1 score on the `PHM2010` dataset**. A second layer uses LLMs to turn the classification results and feature trends into natural-language reports and replacement suggestions, which engineers rated above rule-based templates. Cross-dataset tests on `NASA` milling data are offered as evidence of generalization.

papers.title: Libtt: A Compiler and Runtime for Tenstorrent Processors
papers.abstract: Libtt brings the PyTorch and JAX ecosystem to Tenstorrent hardware. It implements PJRT, the interface through which XLA-based frameworks drive Google's TPUs, so JAX runs on it directly, PyTorch runs through TorchTPU, and software written for TPUs carries over with no changes except replacing custom kernels. Built on Tenstorrent's open-source compiler and runtime, libtt ships the entire stack, from the compiler to the multi-chip runtime, as a single shared library. It contains extensive fixes to the upstream Tenstorrent software to make existing PyTorch and JAX code work out of the box, and extensive new compiler optimizations to make it fast. It passes most of the JAX and TorchTPU test suites and runs SGLang, TorchTitan, and Miles, covering serving, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: `Libtt` is a compiler and runtime that lets `PyTorch` and `JAX` code run on Tenstorrent processors. It implements `PJRT`, the interface that XLA-based frameworks use to drive Google's TPUs, so **software written for TPUs carries over unchanged apart from replacing custom kernels**. The whole stack, from compiler to multi-chip runtime, ships as a single shared library with fixes to the upstream Tenstorrent software and new compiler optimizations. It passes most of the `JAX` and `TorchTPU` test suites and runs `SGLang`, `TorchTitan` and `Miles` for serving, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

papers.title: LatentCP-DPO: Conformal Pessimism for DPO with Finite-Sample Guarantees
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns a response policy from human preference data, but with a limited dataset it can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels. We introduce LatentCP-DPO, a framework that combines conformal prediction with pessimistic preference optimization for Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback. Building on LatentCP's construction of uncertainty sets for unobserved model parameters, we address how to incorporate this uncertainty into preference optimization and characterize its effect on policy performance. Under exchangeability and a correctly specified preference model, we construct uncertainty sets for latent relative rewards with finite-sample marginal coverage from conformal prediction sets for observable preferences. We then learn a response policy by maximizing the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over these uncertainty sets, using an independent collection of prompts and candidate responses without preference labels. Under suitable assumptions, we establish finite-sample upper bounds on regularized policy suboptimality that separate policy-class approximation error, conformal uncertainty, and statistical estimation error. For BT feedback, we further establish a worst-case lower bound for LatentCP-DPO that matches the upper bound's reciprocal dependence on the number of unlabeled optimization examples. The lower bound also shows that the uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows. Together, these results characterize both the statistical accuracy and potential limitations of preference optimization using conformal uncertainty sets. Experiments support the benefits of the proposed framework in finite preference datasets.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels when the dataset is small. `LatentCP-DPO` uses conformal prediction to build uncertainty sets over latent relative rewards with finite-sample coverage, for both Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback, then learns a policy that maximizes the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over those sets. The analysis gives finite-sample upper bounds on policy suboptimality that separate approximation error, conformal uncertainty and estimation error. For BT feedback, a matching lower bound shows that the **uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows**.

papers.title: Scaling Looped MoE Language Models under Matched Budgets: Information Flow and Parameter Allocation
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter count, and prior studies have demonstrated promising performance gains with increased computation. However, systematic design principles for configuring these models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints remain scarce. We contribute to this direction by improving information flow in looped models and systematically studying loop parameter configurations. Specifically, we refine this information flow via gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection. Building on this design, controlled studies identify a configuration combining a single-pass Core depth of 25%-35% of the total unrolled depth with reallocating saved parameters into extra routed experts per layer, improving performance at zero extra compute while preserving compatibility with existing training infrastructure. Evaluated after 1T pre-training tokens, our 69B MLA and 51B KDA Mixture-of-Experts models outperform budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks, respectively. Further reproduction experiments on a common backbone with a 200B-token training budget show that our method achieves lower perplexity than other looped methods. Code for these reproduction experiments is available at https://github.com/lxi01766/Scaling-Looped-MoE-Language-Models-under-Matched-Budgets-Information-Flow-and-Parameter-Allocation.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers reuse layers to gain computational depth without adding parameters, but there is little guidance on configuring them under fixed parameter and compute budgets. The authors improve information flow with gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection, then find that a single-pass core depth of 25% to 35% of the total unrolled depth works best when the saved parameters are spent on extra routed experts per layer. After 1 trillion pre-training tokens, their 69B `MLA` and 51B `KDA` Mixture-of-Experts models **beat budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points** across four benchmarks. Reproduction runs on a common backbone with 200 billion tokens show lower perplexity than other looped methods.

papers.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
papers.summary: Most deep-learning beat and downbeat trackers work offline and cannot be used in real time. The authors adapt the offline `Beat This` model into a causal, streaming variant and train it with temporally shifted labels so that it predicts slightly ahead of the current frame, which lowers latency and makes peak-picking more effective. On the `GTZAN` dataset, **F1 rises from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and from 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats** compared with `BeatNet+`, the previous best online tracker.

papers.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract:
As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds.
  In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems can share internal representations instead of text, for example by using a learned mapper to translate one model's Key-Value (KV) cache into a form another model can consume. The `Chasm` framework studies attacks on this handoff through the source model, the mapper and the handoff mechanism, and finds that it weakens safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. A target model that follows 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively **follows up to 44.2% when the context arrives through a mapper**. White-box jailbreak optimization through the mapper reaches a 92.5% success rate against 37.5% for ordinary `GCG`, and a lightweight target-side cache guard is proposed that mitigates the attacks.

papers.title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
papers.abstract: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.
papers.summary: Long video generation struggles to keep characters and scenes consistent across shots and to show state changes caused by story events, and agentic workflows accumulate context as they plan and repair. `StateWeaver` introduces Active States, which turn discrepancies found during review into concrete visual asset requirements for building, validating and regenerating reference images, and links confirmed results to asset states, story time and reference versions for reuse by later shots. Its Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip and repair round and organizes them with hierarchical memory. Across multiple benchmarks it is reported to **outperform existing methods while sustaining cross-shot consistency** under both predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

papers.title: WebVibe: Multimodal Interactive Website Generation via Reverse Synthesis and Visual Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Although multimodal large language models translate single screenshots into static HTML, generating interactive functional websites from design specifications still struggles with multi-page routing and stateful widget transitions. Examining existing training pipelines reveals two bottlenecks: (1) in forward data synthesis (X -> Y), writing the specification X before code execution leaves unimplemented or altered requirements in X as supervision noise; and (2) in reinforcement learning, scalar rewards discard the rich state transitions observed during replay. Based on these findings, we introduce WebVibe and Interactive-SDPO to train InteractiveCoder. WebVibe reverses synthesis into Y -> X by verifying cross-page and in-page interactions in the browser before deriving multimodal inputs from replay-confirmed states to build the 31,542-site WebVibe-32K corpus with reusable execution contracts. Interactive-SDPO then conditions a weight-sharing self-teacher on the replay trace and a 2x2 state-transition montage to provide token-level supervision at zero inference-time overhead. On the public Vision2Web L2, one-shot InteractiveCoder-9B nearly 3x its base model's functional score (20.2 to 55.2 FS) and matches a 1T-parameter coding agent in a single pass with 111x fewer total parameters and 78x fewer tokens. On our WebVibeBench, InteractiveCoder-4B and 9B further outperform all evaluated baselines by over 23 points.
papers.summary: Generating interactive, multi-page websites from design specifications is hampered by noisy synthetic training data, where specifications written before execution describe requirements the code never implements, and by reinforcement learning rewards that collapse rich browser state transitions into a scalar. `WebVibe` reverses the synthesis order, verifying cross-page and in-page interactions in a browser first and then deriving the multimodal specification from replay-confirmed states, yielding the 31,542-site `WebVibe-32K` corpus. `Interactive-SDPO` then conditions a weight-sharing self-teacher on the replay trace and a 2x2 state-transition montage to give token-level supervision with no inference-time overhead. On `Vision2Web` L2, one-shot `InteractiveCoder-9B` **raises its base model's functional score from 20.2 to 55.2**, matching a 1T-parameter coding agent with 111x fewer parameters and 78x fewer tokens, and the 4B and 9B models beat all baselines on `WebVibeBench` by over 23 points.

papers.title: LatENSO v1.0: a learned latent state of the tropical Pacific for seasonal ENSO operators and forecasting
papers.abstract: Here we present LatENSO v1.0, a machine-learning forecast system for the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) built around a learned, 32-dimensional state of the tropical Pacific. A Swin-transformer autoencoder compresses thirteen monthly-averaged ocean and atmosphere fields into 32 numbers, trained to reconstruct the fields, with no forecast target. The 32 numbers rebuild the fields as well as O(100) empirical orthogonal functions. Two seasonal operators use this state. The first is the extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO) with two directions of the learned state among its variables; we call it XRO-lat. The second is a Floquet modal operator (FMO) of three damped oscillators, which forecasts a correction added to a least-squares base forecast made from four observed predictors. We evaluate both against the recharge oscillator, XRO and a deep echo-state network (DESN), all refitted on identical data, cross-validation folds and verification windows (1981-2024). Over lead times of 1-18 months, XRO-lat reaches an anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) of 0.673, the highest of all tropical-Pacific-only (in-domain) systems and statistically indistinguishable from XRO and DESN with their eight remote-basin indices (0.685 and 0.667). From lead 15 to lead 24 it is the most skillful of all systems. Over leads 1-18, the FMO forecast (0.619) is statistically indistinguishable from every in-domain reference model (0.631-0.654). What the FMO adds to its base forecast, 0.054 in ACC, is carried by its Floquet propagation, whose generator consistently holds a prominent quasi-biennial oscillator. At leads 3-9 the FMO trails XRO, DESN and the in-domain XRO, a deficit partly attributable to its base. LatENSO combines competitive skill with trustworthiness: a compact state whose physical content can be inspected, and fully open access to code, weights and data.
papers.summary: `LatENSO v1.0` is a machine-learning forecast system for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) built on a `Swin`-transformer autoencoder that compresses thirteen monthly ocean and atmosphere fields of the tropical Pacific into a 32-dimensional state, trained only for reconstruction. Two seasonal operators use this state: `XRO-lat`, an extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO) that includes two directions of the learned state, and a Floquet modal operator (FMO) of three damped oscillators that corrects a least-squares base forecast. Over lead times of 1-18 months, `XRO-lat` reaches **an anomaly correlation coefficient of 0.673**, the highest among tropical-Pacific-only systems and statistically indistinguishable from `XRO` and a deep echo-state network that use eight remote-basin indices, and it is the most skillful system from lead 15 to 24. The FMO forecast (0.619) is statistically tied with the in-domain reference models but trails at leads 3-9.

papers.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
papers.abstract: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.
papers.summary: Euclidean representations have Johnson-Lindenstrauss random projection as an oblivious compression primitive, but no analogue exists for hyperbolic representations; tangent-space schemes pay a curvature penalty, and fully hyperbolic projections mix radial and angular error. Radial-angular random projection (`RAP`) keeps the radial coordinate exactly, applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, and lifts the result back to the target hyperboloid at the cost of one Gaussian matrix-vector product. The authors prove a finite-set distortion guarantee with explicit conditioning terms, alongside a local tangent-space theorem and a conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across synthetic point clouds, trees, clustered data, and the `WordNet` noun hierarchy, `RAP` has the lowest mean relative distortion in every setting, **cutting distortion by about 48-49% versus the strongest hyperbolic baseline on broad-radius data**, and it scales to million-point datasets.

papers.title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly learn from their own experience, the tasks they learn from and are evaluated on are almost always in English. We ask whether self-evolution transfers from English to Urdu, and release IRTIQA, a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of DROP, SNIPS, AppWorld, and SkillsBench, built with a matrix-language code-switching pipeline and human verification. Using IRTIQA, we evaluate three self-evolving frameworks, Tool-R0 (self-play RL), AgentEvolver (experience-guided RL), and Autogenesis (protocol-level evolution), against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability: AgentEvolver lifts AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across all conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%. But it rarely closes the language gap. Evolved systems remain stronger in English, by up to 0.26 DROP F1, the gap is largest on multi-step tasks, and code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation. On a shared Gemma-4 31B backbone, the gap exists before evolution, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English. Language parity must therefore be an explicit design target, as it does not emerge from self-improvement alone.
papers.summary: Self-evolving LLM agents are almost always trained and evaluated in English, so it is unclear whether their gains carry over to other languages. `IRTIQA` is a benchmark of aligned English, Urdu-translated, and Urdu code-switched variants of `DROP`, `SNIPS`, `AppWorld`, and `SkillsBench`, used to compare three self-evolving frameworks (`Tool-R0`, `AgentEvolver`, and `Autogenesis`) against their unevolved backbones. Self-evolution often raises capability, for example lifting `AppWorld` goal completion from near zero to 20-36%, but **it rarely closes the language gap, with evolved systems remaining stronger in English by up to 0.26 `DROP` F1**. The gap is largest on multi-step tasks, code-switching behaves as a distinct condition rather than degraded translation, and RL-based evolution can hurt Urdu reasoning more than English.

papers.title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
papers.abstract: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.
papers.summary: Identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids from displacement fields and boundary reaction forces is an inverse problem that recent work addresses with parameter-heavy deep learning frameworks enforcing force equilibrium at collocation points. The proposed framework instead exploits the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and optimizes constitutive parameters directly at the finite-element level, predicting the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of multiple parameters from displacement data alone. Validated on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks with heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic materials, it reports **acceptable accuracy at significantly lower computational time than recent deep-learning-based frameworks**.

papers.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
papers.abstract: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.
papers.summary: These lecture notes connect classical variational principles, from least action to the variational formulation of partial differential equations, with machine learning algorithms viewed as nonlinear minimisation problems over highly expressive function spaces. They examine how numerical-analysis concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness are reinterpreted in this setting and how the variational structure of the continuous problem governs the behaviour of neural-network approximations. The authors argue that **alternative, strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable and reliable computational methods**.

papers.title: The cost of being seen as AI in group bargaining
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.
papers.summary: A repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining experiment with 2,234 participants tests how being perceived as AI affects outcomes in group decisions. Every decision was made by a human, but each opponent was labeled as Human or AI, with AI described as acting either independently or on behalf of a person. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received lower opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements, and **earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human**, mostly because of smaller payoffs in the agreements that did include them. A payoff gap persisted even when all three players agreed.

papers.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.
papers.summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) incur heavy token overhead, and existing routers treat cost only implicitly and cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a given query. `MeterRouter` incrementally builds a collaboration graph, choosing each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and when to stop, conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. The router is initialized by imitating successful execution graphs and refined with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, it matches the accuracy of the strongest MAS **at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router**, while adapting spend to the specified budget and rarely exceeding it.

papers.title: LUDIUS: A Benchmark for Embodied Social Intelligence in Everyday Human-Robot Interactions
papers.abstract: Social intelligence in a robot requires interpreting a situation from the perspectives of the people involved and using that understanding to decide when and how to act. We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark for evaluating how vision-language models exercise this judgment through a robot's verbal responses and actions, organized around 15 social intelligence skills drawn from social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science. LUDIUS comprises six editions, each a collection of episodes spanning one simulated week. Three editions each cover all 15 skills in a different household. The other three focus on interactions involving multiple people, safety, and context-specific norms, respectively. We evaluate frontier models and a smaller model finetuned on social-interaction data we generated, using a common evaluation harness. The harness supplies each model with the robot's camera views and residents' reactions, retrieves relevant interaction history, and converts the model's tool calls into robot verbal responses and actions. Models tend to perform worse when they must reason about what a resident saw or heard earlier, reconcile competing interests, or fulfill a request within safety constraints and household rules. Beyond the home setting, LUDIUS's design pipeline offers a way to construct social intelligence benchmarks by translating social intelligence skills into context-specific judgments and observable robot behavior.
papers.summary: `LUDIUS` is a benchmark for how vision-language models exercise social judgment through a household robot's verbal responses and actions, organized around 15 social intelligence skills drawn from social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science. It comprises six editions of episodes each spanning a simulated week: three cover all 15 skills in different households, and three focus on multi-person interactions, safety, and context-specific norms. A common harness feeds models the robot's camera views, residents' reactions, and retrieved interaction history, and converts tool calls into robot behavior. Evaluating frontier models and a smaller finetuned model shows that **models perform worse when they must reason about what a resident saw or heard earlier, reconcile competing interests, or satisfy a request within safety constraints and household rules**.

papers.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
papers.abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
papers.summary: `Puzzling-Bench` collects 23,777 human-written puzzles from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026), covering riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral thinking, wordplay, and recreational mathematics, a third with images, each with the author-accepted answer, hints, tags, and a creation date that enables a post-training-cutoff contamination check. Nine frontier and open models are scored by normalized exact match followed by an LLM judge, with three judges from two model families agreeing on 95-97% of verdicts. **The best model, `GPT-6.1`, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set**, 17 puzzles defeat all nine models, and failures are strongly correlated across models even though an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. In a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points.
papers.highlight_summary:
Puzzle benchmarks tend to cover a single genre and lack reliable free-form ground truth, so `Puzzling-Bench` turns twelve years of Puzzling Stack Exchange into **23,777** puzzles whose answers were accepted by the puzzle authors themselves. Each puzzle also carries the asker's hints, community tags and a posting date, enabling hint ablations, category analysis and a refreshable post-cutoff slice.

- The dataset keeps every unclosed question with an author-accepted answer (a third include images), and scoring is two-tier: normalized exact match, then an LLM judge that decides only answer equivalence and accounts for roughly half of every score.
- On the frozen 255-puzzle text-only set `Pilot-255`, `GPT-6.1 Sol` leads at **74.8%**, ahead of `Claude Opus 5.5` at **66.1%**, with the nine evaluated models spanning 28.3–74.8%.
- Three judges from two model families agree on **95–97%** of verdicts (κ 0.82–0.96), shift no model by more than **1.6 points** and show no own-family preference, whereas switching from spoiler-based to LLM-extracted reference answers moved scores by up to 2.8 points.
- Failures are strongly correlated across models: on the 193 puzzles no model errored on, a hard core of **17** defeats all nine, yet a per-puzzle oracle reaches **91%**, with most of the complementary coverage coming from the previous-generation `Opus 4.8` rather than `Opus 5.5`.
- On the 100-puzzle `Img-100` pilot, withholding the image costs the two best models **24 and 35 points**, and removing the asker's hints costs them 10.5 and 15.0 points on the roughly 40 hinted puzzles.
- The evidence is thin in places: frontier models ran on only 255 puzzles (standard error about 3 points), the 56-puzzle post-cutoff slice cannot separate contamination from difficulty drift, two harnesses with different reasoning budgets confound cross-generation comparisons, and excluding timed-out rows inflates the accuracy of slow models.

papers.title: Scaling and Cross-Simulation Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Cosmic-Web Classification in CAMELS
papers.abstract: Graph-based methods can classify galaxies by their dark-matter cosmic-web environments, but reliability beyond development simulations remains uncertain. Galaxy-formation models alter tracer populations and spatial distributions, potentially shifting graph features. We test how graph neural networks scale with independent training realizations and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the $z=0$ CAMELS IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites, we label galaxies with $M_\star>10^9\,M_\odot$ as void, sheet, filament or knot from the smoothed cold-dark-matter density field. We represent their spatial distributions as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors. We compare a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and five graph neural networks (GNNs), including a local graph Transformer, under realization-grouped evaluation. Learning curves increase training data from 10 to 100 realizations, with validation and test boxes fixed. We test every source-to-target suite pairing on 100 unseen realizations per target suite. On this external holdout, the Transformer, GAT+ and EdgeConv reach mean per-realization macro-averaged F1 scores of $0.652$, $0.651$ and $0.642$, against $0.481$ for the MLP. The Transformer outperforms the MLP by 0.171, while the difference between the Transformer and GAT+ is not statistically significant. Voids remain the hardest class. Performance is higher in boxes with more selected galaxies and shorter Delaunay edges. Associations with cosmological and feedback parameters weaken after accounting for galaxy richness and void fraction. Our results benchmark the scaling and cross-simulation transfer of galaxy-graph classifiers, demonstrating the value of neighbourhood information and identifying tracer sampling as an important limitation for dark-matter web inference.
papers.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) that classify galaxies into void, sheet, filament, or knot environments of the dark-matter cosmic web are tested for how they scale with training data and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the `CAMELS` `IllustrisTNG`, `SIMBA`, and `Astrid` suites, galaxies are represented as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) is compared with five GNNs across every source-to-target suite pairing. On held-out realizations, the graph Transformer, `GAT+`, and `EdgeConv` reach **macro-averaged F1 scores of about 0.65 versus 0.481 for the MLP**, with no significant difference between the top two. Voids remain the hardest class, and performance depends mainly on how many galaxies a box contains, pointing to tracer sampling as a key limitation.

papers.title: Learning from Unreliable Operator References: Claim-Level Rewards for Customer Support Agents
papers.abstract: Even a correct operator reply can be an unreliable training target for a customer-support agent. About a quarter of the factual claims in these replies lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. We treat operator replies as claims to verify rather than answers to imitate. Unverified claims guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools. Verified claims serve as coverage targets in a claim-level GRPO reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved for its answer. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the GRPO agent's text answers were flagged for hallucinations, compared with 13.6% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system increased the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%.
papers.summary: Human operator replies are an unreliable training target for customer-support agents: about a quarter of their factual claims lacked full support in the agent's knowledge base and tool records. The authors treat replies as claims to verify, using unverified claims to guide revisions to the knowledge base and tools and verified claims as coverage targets in a claim-level `GRPO` reward that scores factual precision against the evidence the agent retrieved. On an offline benchmark, 8.6% of the resulting agent's answers were flagged for hallucinations versus 13.6% for a supervised fine-tuning baseline. In a randomized A/B test against the existing procedural bot, the deployed system **raised the share of conversations closed without a human operator from 63.3% to 80.8%**.

papers.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
papers.abstract: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.
papers.summary: Content-based music similarity estimation measures how alike two audio recordings are without metadata, which matters for cold-start recommendation where no user interaction data exists. `JukeSim` computes similarity from embeddings produced by `Jukebox`, a generative music model. Across multiple datasets, **`JukeSim` performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed measures**, which had not previously been compared with recent work. The method requires more compute than the alternatives.

papers.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.
papers.summary: Standard inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers a reward function from behavior under an assumption of effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is bounded and varies with the situation. `SC-AIRL` (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL) trains per-depth policies that share one reward but sum it over different explicit horizons, and a state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. On held-out episodes of pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, it **raises top-1 imitation accuracy over standard `AIRL` from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718**, and reproduces participant behavior more closely in rollouts. The inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity.

papers.title: RAWPrism: A Three-Task Dataset and a Unified Model for RAW-Domain Image Fusion
papers.abstract: Research on multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) has largely focused on rendered RGB images, while unified fusion across these tasks in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP) remains relatively underexplored. To support research in this setting, we introduce the RAWPrism dataset, covering all three tasks, and the RAWPrism model, a lightweight unified multi-task fusion network. The RAWPrism dataset comprises 422 usable MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from our RAW captures, together with 1,500 FMB-derived IVIF samples, in which the visible RAW inputs are reconstructed by ReRAW and their RGB counterparts rendered by CycleISP. Scene-level partitions and task-specific rendering and scoring protocols connect these resources to method development and evaluation. To our knowledge, the RAWPrism model is the first to unify MEF, MFF, and IVIF directly in the RAW domain. It combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone to support all three tasks with one 3.58M-parameter checkpoint. Together, the dataset and model support the study of shared fusion mechanisms across exposure, focus, and spectral complementarity.
papers.summary: Multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) have mostly been studied on rendered RGB images rather than in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP). The `RAWPrism` dataset provides 422 MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from new RAW captures, plus 1,500 IVIF samples derived from `FMB` with visible RAW inputs reconstructed by `ReRAW`. The accompanying `RAWPrism` model combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone, and is described as the first to **unify all three fusion tasks directly in the RAW domain with a single 3.58M-parameter checkpoint**.

papers.title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents typically rewards a query when its result matches the reference on a single database, so a buggy query can be paid by luck when the data lacks the rows that would expose it. A counterfactual-database reward also runs the query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form **cuts fully paid buggy queries from 29.5% to 16.8% and reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9% while rejecting none of 2,847 correct queries**. In a controlled `GRPO` comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, however, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy and gained 1.6 points on `Spider`, and one seed reversed both signs, showing that single-seed reward comparisons mislead.

papers.title: ConTra: A Training Framework for Effective Contextual Retrieval via Prefix Generation
papers.abstract: Data management systems organize large text collections for tasks such as finding relevant studies and extracting contract clauses. Systems make long documents searchable by splitting them into independently indexed chunks. Chunking can separate text from its identifying details. The indexing challenge is to keep each chunk independently searchable while preserving the context needed to find and rank it. Existing methods either encode that context in chunk vectors or attach it as a text prefix. Context encoded only in vectors is unavailable to text rerankers. Prompted prefixes serve both vector search and reranking, but are costly to generate at indexing time and can underperform contextual encoders. We propose ConTra (Context That Travels), a reinforcement learning framework for training lightweight prefix generators. Its reward combines feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models with factual verification and length control. ConTra generates one prefix per chunk during index construction and stores the augmented text and its embedding for reuse across queries. To evaluate contextual retrieval across workloads and under interference, we introduce RealContextBench, a benchmark with five application collections and three controlled conditions that isolate the effect of distracting text. On ConTEB and RealContextBench, ConTra-2B outperforms the prompted 9B baseline using Anthropic's method and the PPLX-4B contextual encoder, with a margin of up to 3.15 points over their best overall scores, while indexing short documents 7.74 times and 2.15 times as fast as those baselines, respectively.
