Post-trained only on ConTEB, it leads the standalone methods on RealContextBench after reranking and is less sensitive than the prompted 2B baseline to random and topically similar distractors. Code, datasets, and trained models are available at https://github.com/SStan1/ConTra.
papers.summary: Splitting long documents into independently indexed chunks can strip away the context needed to retrieve and rank them; encoding that context only in vectors hides it from text rerankers, while prompting a large model to write a prefix for each chunk is costly at indexing time. `ConTra` (Context That Travels) uses reinforcement learning to train lightweight prefix generators, with a reward combining feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models, factual verification, and length control. The authors also introduce `RealContextBench`, with five application collections and three controlled conditions isolating the effect of distracting text. On `ConTEB` and `RealContextBench`, `ConTra-2B` **beats a prompted 9B baseline and the `PPLX-4B` contextual encoder by up to 3.15 points while indexing short documents 7.74 and 2.15 times as fast**, and it is less sensitive to distractors than a prompted 2B baseline.

papers.title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
papers.abstract: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.
papers.summary: Influence functions aim to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output, but evaluations at LLM pretraining scale have assumed rather than tested that they work. This study checks whether supposedly influential examples actually carry properties relevant to the output by retraining on controlled data splits, comparing three Hessian approximation methods (`GradSim`, `TrackStar`, `K-FAC`) on linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge in `GPT-2`-type models trained on 68M to 5.6B tokens. **On average the influential examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target property directly**, and the proportion and kind of relevance vary by setting.

papers.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
papers.abstract: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.
papers.summary: Training spiking neural networks with backpropagation through time requires computing weight updates through every step of a simulated device, which becomes costly and unstable for fine-grained or long simulations. `ChronoProp` decouples the clock of learning from that of computing, calculating weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. It reaches similar image-classification accuracy to backpropagation through time with **about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested**, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks it is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and the resulting networks tolerate simulated hardware defects better.

papers.title: Plausible Is Not Proven: Testing Failure Explanations in Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: Failure analyses of monocular depth models often name a cause for each error, such as an occluding boundary, a thin object or a reflective surface, but such labels are rarely tested. We present the Vision Error Observatory (VEO), an audit that finds regions failing the $\delta_1$ criterion on sensor-measured pixels, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then subjects the labels to four tests: agreement with object annotations on data the label model never saw, agreement with blinded human raters, response to targeted image edits, and value as a training signal. We apply it to eight models on NYU Depth V2, DIODE and iBims-1, with labels also checked on Hypersim, and fix most decision rules before their results. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on NYU, 0.81 on Hypersim, 0.69 on iBims-1), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, and most boundary failures of the strongest model vanish under a 2-pixel tolerance. The reflection label does not transfer to synthetic data, the textureless label is near chance against annotations, and only one of four edit tests, an exploratory one, supports its label. Evaluated against five blinded raters, VEO's labels matched the human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.05). In addition, an increase in the weight on the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning led to an increase in the error on targeted pixels at every weight tested. The architecture-specific failure fingerprint claimed by an earlier version of this project also failed to replicate across the datasets. Plausible failure explanations, in short, need to be tested before they are trusted; we release the protocol, code, ratings and every result file.
papers.summary: Failure analyses of monocular depth models routinely attribute errors to causes such as occluding boundaries, thin objects, or reflective surfaces without testing those labels. The Vision Error Observatory (`VEO`) finds failing regions, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then tests the labels against held-out object annotations, blinded human raters, targeted image edits, and their value as a training signal, across eight models on `NYU Depth V2`, `DIODE`, and `iBims-1`. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on `NYU Depth V2`), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, while the reflection and textureless labels fail to hold up. **Against five blinded raters the labels matched human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's kappa = 0.05)**, and upweighting the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning increased error on the targeted pixels at every weight tested.

papers.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) merges separately trained domain specialists into one model, but existing methods start the student from a base model or multi-domain fine-tuned checkpoint and leave integration to distillation. `Uni-MOPD` instead initializes the student with a training-free uniform merge of specialists sharing a base model, then refines it with a short distillation run using uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, **the uniform merge alone matches what the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates**, and the simple recipe matches or exceeds every tested sampling strategy and divergence. It also outperforms `Open-MOPD` at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than that method's released code.

papers.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
papers.abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.
papers.summary: Learning skills individually does not guarantee they can be combined, a concern for agents that build reusable skill libraries. The authors study independently trained soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, supplying the skill identities and execution order, across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models. **Composing two skills in a single call reaches at most 7.6% mean accuracy, versus 88.2% to 100% when split over two calls** with an explicit intermediate output. Skills trained alongside specific partners also fail when those partners are swapped for independently learned blocks of the same operation, with median accuracy on two `Qwen` bases dropping from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, and repairing a composition can damage the original skill.

papers.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.
papers.summary: Existing streaming benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents use short or mostly independent task sequences, so they reveal little about whether agents reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier ones. `EvoLink-Bench` provides long-horizon interdependent task streams over office work, multi-turn dialogue, and research-style workflows with persistent workspaces, split into a level for acquiring and revising language-expressible knowledge and a level for building task capabilities through execution and feedback. Evaluating five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations and three persistence conditions (19,635 scored task slots), the authors find that **no framework is consistently best across both levels**. Retries recover only a limited share of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve later performance.

papers.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
papers.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
papers.summary: Nested multi-precision quantization lets one checkpoint serve several bit-widths by reading only the leading bits of each weight, but existing methods offer only integer bit-widths and degrade badly at 2 bits. `Any-Rate` serves 2 to 8 bits from a single checkpoint, with half-bit steps between 2 and 4 bits, by restricting some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords over 8-weight blocks and encoding all precisions jointly with a separate target for each. Across four LLMs it gives the best accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, **retaining 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits**, and stays within one point of the best at 4 bits. Decoding speed is comparable to existing kernels, and an energy model estimates up to 27% less memory energy at equal accuracy.

papers.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.
papers.summary: Neural driving policies lack guarantees that the vehicle stays collision-free at all future times. The authors define policy recoverability, meaning whether a vehicle can return in finite time to the set of states where the original policy is safe, and edit the policy's outputs only in states that are unsafe in the long run but still recoverable, handing control back to the original policy once recovered. In closed-loop simulation on `nuPlan` urban scenarios, the method yields a **48% reduction in safety incidents** relative to the original policy while largely preserving driving performance.

papers.title: Agentic Waterfall: An Intent-Driven Information Discovery Framework for Reclaiming User Control in the Attention Economy
papers.abstract: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.
papers.summary: Recommendation feeds typically give users little direct control over what they see. The authors formalize a feed in which users actively direct recommendations through explicit requests while the system also adapts to browsing behavior, and build `Agentic Waterfall`, where a language-model controller keeps persistent user state and coordinates retrieval, ranking, and state updates. They contribute the `Agentic Waterfall Dataset`, combining real content metadata with simulated interaction histories, plus a replay-based evaluation protocol. The system stays competitive with strong baselines on five public recommendation benchmarks and beats the strongest baseline on the new dataset by **up to 16.1% relative improvement**.

papers.title: SemProxy: Semantic 3D Proxies for Controllable Agentic 3D Modeling
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable of generating 3D models, yet enabling users to effectively control the modeling process remains challenging. Existing workflows rely primarily on text prompts and reference images, which often struggle to convey precise spatial intentions and require iterative corrections. We introduce SemProxy, a lightweight intermediate representation that bridges intuitive human interaction and agentic 3D modeling. Instantiated as labeled 3D bounding boxes, semantic 3D proxies allow users to directly specify object parts and spatial arrangements while leaving geometric details to coding agents. These proxies can be serialized into structured text and rendered as images, making them directly accessible to existing coding agents without additional training or modifications. We further develop ProxyStudio, a user interface that integrates text, image references, and interactive 3D proxy editing into agentic modeling workflows. We demonstrate the versatility of SemProxy across object- and scene-level modeling tasks with different coding agents, and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting controllable human-agent collaborative 3D modeling through a user study.
papers.summary: Coding agents can generate 3D models, but text prompts and reference images convey spatial intent poorly and lead to repeated corrections. `SemProxy` introduces labeled 3D bounding boxes as an intermediate representation: users place and name object parts and arrangements, and the agent fills in the geometric detail. Because the proxies serialize to structured text and render as images, **they work with existing coding agents without any training or modification**. The authors also build `ProxyStudio`, an interface combining text, image references, and interactive proxy editing, and report demonstrations on object- and scene-level tasks with different coding agents plus a user study.

papers.title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
papers.abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.
papers.summary: Robots working in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty about the scene while also lacking some of the skills a task needs. `CHASE` treats curiosity as choosing investigations that both reduce task uncertainty and expand what the robot can execute, linking dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. Its planner weighs information value, skill reuse, and acquisition and execution cost, and a missing skill triggers bounded exploration with held-out checks before the skill is admitted. In simulation and real-robot experiments it reaches **50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps**, with 70-90% evidence resolution.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
papers.abstract: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.
papers.summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve because scenario trees grow exponentially with the horizon and value functions are non-convex. The authors propose a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework in which a neural network scores the part of the decision that drives state transitions, trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems using a Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers. Applied to power network repair scheduling on a synthetic 5-bus network and the `IEEE 14-bus` network, **DFL is the cheapest policy under a binding repair budget, 14% to 23% below the next best**, and lands within 1.8% of the exact optimum on the 5-bus case. Without the budget it does not beat a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline on the 14-bus network, though it computes decisions orders of magnitude faster than MPC.

papers.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
papers.abstract: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization
papers.summary: Vision-language models for multi-page documents encode each page separately, so visual tokens are formed with no knowledge of adjacent pages. `DocSEAM` is a lightweight module placed between the vision encoder and the language model that groups each page with its two neighbors, fuses neighbor information through center-anchored masked self-attention with directional gates, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens so the token count is unchanged. The resulting 9B-parameter model achieves **the best results among evaluated open-weight models up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document question-answering benchmarks**. Under controlled re-pagination it is also less sensitive to where page boundaries fall and better at localizing spans that cross pages.
papers.highlight_summary:
Page-wise document VLMs encode every page in isolation, so content that continues across a page break (a paragraph, a table) is represented without its other half and accuracy shifts with where the breaks fall. `DocSEAM` is a small module between the vision encoder and the language model that enriches each page's visual tokens with context from its two neighbouring pages, leaving the token count unchanged.

- For each page it runs two masked self-attention layers over the (previous, current, next) triplet, where a center-anchored mask blocks direct previous-to-next attention and four learned send/receive gates per token decide which tokens exchange cross-page information, adding about **235M parameters** (roughly 2.6% of the 9B backbone) and under 7% of forward-pass FLOPs on a 20-page document.
- Training is two-stage: the zero-initialised module is first warmed up alone on 74k cross-page boundary examples from `MP-DocStruct1M`, then frozen while the rest of the model is LoRA fine-tuned, and this boundary-focused warm-up is worth +4.4 / +5.3 points over warming up on the downstream mixture.
- On `Qwen3.5-9B` it scores **63.0** on `DUDE`, **89.2** on `MP-DocVQA`, **87.1** on `SlideVQA`, **58.3** on `MMLongBench-Doc` and **62.9** on `LongDocURL`, the best among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters, though `Gemini 3 Pro` remains ahead on the three benchmarks where it is reported.
- Gains over the matched fine-tuned baseline range from +1.7 to **+20.1** points, but the largest are inflated by that baseline falling well below zero-shot `Qwen3.5`, against which the gains are +1.2 on `MMLongBench-Doc` and +8.4 on `LongDocURL`.
- Cross-page span localization rises from 65.0% to **85.8%** and the penalty for page breaks that cut through tables and paragraphs drops to 0.8 / 0.7 points (from 1.2 / 1.6), but the three-page window helps less on non-adjacent evidence (+5.9 versus +11.5 for adjacent pages, over zero-shot) and truncated-table merging at 62.9 TEDS stays far behind rule-based pipelines at 83.1–88.1.

papers.title: A Head-Level Investigative Study of Self-Supervised Backbones for Synthetic Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech backbones are the standard frontend for synthetic-speech detection, and layer-wise probing has established which layers carry the most signal. But analysis stops there: which of a layer's twelve attention heads compute the spoof decision is unknown. We present the first head-level study of two frozen backbones, WavLM-base and Wav2Vec2-base, on ASVspoof 5. Per-head ablation shows that only a few heads carry the decision while others actively oppose it; removing those heads lowers equal error rate (EER) with no retraining, by 13% relative in WavLM and 22% in Wav2Vec2. We also find a probe-free signature: spoofed speech draws more focused attention than genuine speech, and this gap alone separates the two almost as well as the full representation, peaking at each backbone's most discriminative layer. Finally, attack identity is decodable from every head, yet heads differ in what they do, not in what they know.
papers.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech backbones are the standard front end for detecting synthetic speech, and prior analysis has identified which layers matter but not which attention heads. A head-level study of frozen `WavLM-base` and `Wav2Vec2-base` on `ASVspoof 5` finds that only a few heads carry the spoof decision while others actively oppose it. **Removing the opposing heads lowers equal error rate (EER) without retraining, by 13% relative in `WavLM` and 22% in `Wav2Vec2`**. Spoofed speech also draws more focused attention than genuine speech, and that gap alone separates the two almost as well as the full representation.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.
papers.summary: Pipelines that check an LLM's atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard hallucination fix for medical question answering (QA), yet evaluations usually treat the verifier's verdict as ground truth. The authors test that assumption with 160 questions over four ESC cardiology guidelines and a five-stage verify-and-revise pipeline, manually auditing all 606 claims the verifier refuted on first pass. **Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations**, single-run recall of true hallucinations was 35.6-41.2%, and 35% of the genuine errors remaining at the end were introduced by the correction step itself. The final genuine-error rate was 1.7% of answers, and the authors conclude that verifier reliability rather than generation is the limiting factor.

papers.title: Calibration of Neuromusculoskeletal Models Using Differentiable Physics: Recommendations for Improving Model Accuracy
papers.abstract: Differentiable physics has shown potential to usher in a new paradigm in human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) model calibration. Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.
papers.summary: Differentiable physics speeds up calibration of human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) models, but the modules proposed in separate studies have never been compared side by side. The authors test muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable wrap-object geometry, and constraint torque in 16 configurations on one differentiable upper-limb model, scoring each by the mismatch between forward- and inverse-dynamics joint torques on 9 test movements across 4 subjects. **Using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activity cut torque loss by 23.6% on average**, and optimizing bone dynamic parameters cut it by 10.9%, so both are recommended for calibration pipelines.

papers.title: One Representation to Rule Them All -- Open-Vocabulary Change Detection from Text or Visual Examples
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) aims to localise user-specified changes without retraining for predefined categories. Existing approaches typically rely on textual descriptions and combine separate models for region proposal, semantic recognition, and temporal comparison. This limits how target concepts can be expressed and makes detection dependent on several intermediate predictions. We introduce OVTSID3, a training-free framework that unifies region grouping, concept identification, and temporal comparison in the representation space of DINOv3. OVTSID3 supports two complementary modes of concept specification: zero-shot textual queries or one-shot visual prompting through a masked reference pair. OVTSID3 outperforms all prior training-free OVCD methods on two building and two natural-disaster benchmarks, raising the average F1 by 8.9 points. OVTSID3 also supports semantic change detection and achieves state-of-the-art on SECOND. These results demonstrate the flexibility of a unified representation for text- or example-guided change detection without task-specific model training.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) localizes user-specified changes between images without retraining for fixed categories, but existing systems depend on text descriptions and chain separate models for region proposal, recognition, and temporal comparison. `OVTSID3` is a training-free framework that performs all three steps in the representation space of `DINOv3` and accepts either a zero-shot text query or a one-shot visual prompt given as a masked reference pair. It outperforms prior training-free methods on two building and two natural-disaster benchmarks, **raising average F1 by 8.9 points**, and also reaches state-of-the-art semantic change detection on `SECOND`.

papers.title: Evaluating Aviation Safety Knowledge Extraction with SmolLM2: From Zero-Shot to Retrieval-Grounded Prompting
papers.abstract: Aviation accident narratives contain safety knowledge that is difficult to capture using structured occurrence fields alone. This study evaluates prompting-based knowledge extraction across four dimensions: concept accuracy, verbatim evidence grounding, structural compliance, and directed relation extraction. SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct was evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting using 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives from 2000-2020, containing 3,763 reference concepts and 467 directed relations. Evaluation combined structural checks, verbatim evidence matching, expert-reviewed semantic matching, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. No prompting strategy performed best across all dimensions. Retrieval-grounded prompting achieved the highest concept micro-F1 of 32.27%, although its advantage over fixed few-shot prompting was uncertain (95% CI: -0.92 to 2.40 percentage points). One-shot prompting achieved the highest relation F1 of 6.95%, identifying directed relation extraction as the principal SmolLM2 bottleneck. Compared with fixed few-shot prompting, retrieval improved verbatim grounding (59.45% vs. 54.02%) but reduced complete structural compliance (33.3% vs. 42.7%). Verbatim matching establishes source presence rather than evidential relevance. An exploratory comparison using 35 benchmark narratives showed that Qwen3-8B achieved higher concept micro-F1 across all prompting conditions and higher relation F1 under demonstration-based prompting, reaching 51.37% and 34.62%, respectively, under one-shot prompting. The small subset limits generalization. These findings support evaluating semantic correctness, source traceability, structural reliability, and directed relation accuracy separately.
papers.summary: Aviation accident narratives contain safety knowledge that structured occurrence fields miss. The study evaluates `SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct` on extracting concepts and directed relations from 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting, scoring concept accuracy, verbatim evidence grounding, structural compliance, and relation extraction separately. No strategy won on every dimension: retrieval-grounded prompting gave the top concept micro-F1 of 32.27% with an uncertain edge over few-shot, while **relation F1 peaked at just 6.95%**, making directed relation extraction the main bottleneck. In an exploratory 35-narrative comparison, `Qwen3-8B` reached 51.37% concept micro-F1 and 34.62% relation F1 with one-shot prompting.

papers.title: Most of the Way There: Turning a Strong Video Prior into an Action-Conditioned World Model
papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.
papers.summary: Video generators produce plausible futures but do not reliably show the physical consequences of specific robot actions, which action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) need for policy evaluation. `Dianjing` adapts `MiniMax H3`, a 33B video foundation model, by freezing the backbone and adding unified action conditioning, native history conditioning, and training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout are decided. It **trains only 0.34% of the parameters on about 65 hours of robot video** across two embodiments, with no robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Ablations indicate that how training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network, and on `WorldOracle` the model takes the best score on four of five evaluation tracks.

papers.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
papers.summary: Improving LLM agents with reinforcement learning requires expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, which makes it hard to apply at test time. Verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (`vSFT`) closes a loop in which a supervisor writes natural-language feedback on the agent's failed trajectories and a hypernetwork converts that feedback into low-rank weight updates for the agent. Using `Qwen3-4B`, the method **beats `GRPO` and `Reflexion` by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on `ALFWorld`**, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on `WebShop`. The authors report that this in-parameter test-time adaptation outperforms both in-context alternatives and common reinforcement learning methods.

papers.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) can give human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems neural evidence for event recognition and action preparation, but its usefulness varies from sample to sample and existing fusion methods do not decide when it helps. `VECTA` separates producing an EEG-informed fusion prediction from deciding whether that prediction should replace the base one, using a signed-value learner to estimate the per-sample loss reduction and prioritize high-value fusion outputs under a budget. In cross-subject tests on three HRC datasets, **estimated gains tracked realized gains with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612**, and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.708-0.842. The method reduced Brier loss and harmful fusion adoption, and it also worked as a post-hoc decision layer on three external multimodal datasets without retraining.

papers.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
papers.abstract: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.
papers.summary: Second-order optimizers increasingly outperform first-order ones when training physics-informed neural networks to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), yet convergence theory has covered essentially only first-order methods. The authors analyze regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton training and show that, as network width goes to infinity, the dynamics converge with explicit rates to a deterministic limit governed by a Newton neural tangent kernel operator tied to the PDE. Although that operator has no spectral gap, they prove **the PDE residual vanishes during training and, under mild assumptions, the network converges to the PDE solution**. A small regularization parameter acts as a spectral filter that lifts the convergence rate of high-frequency components toward that of low-frequency ones, mitigating the spectral bias of gradient descent.

papers.title: ProxyGenBench: Benchmarking Proxy-Guided Video Generation
papers.abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.
papers.summary: Structural proxies such as animated 3D blockouts let users steer video generators by specifying layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order, but they are coarse and can contain artifacts that should not be copied. `ProxyGenBench` tests whether generators preserve the intended structure, complete missing content while correcting proxy artifacts, and bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events, using 312 cases from 60 scenes with controlled variation in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. Evaluating five video generators with verified case-specific checklists shows that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, yet **more detailed proxies can coincide with worse completion, and strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding**.

papers.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.
papers.summary: Smart glasses and similar wearables let computer tasks arise from what a user is doing in the physical world, but first-person views are partial and user intent can shift as new observations arrive. `EgoUseBench` evaluates agents in three settings: plain `Computer-Use` with explicit instructions, `Offline Ego Use` with prerecorded first-person context, and `Online Ego Use` with continuous observations. It contains 693 tasks built from over 74 hours of real recordings, grouped by whether the user revises requirements (`Graft`), new observations arrive (`Refresh`), or the agent must ask for information (`Clarify`). Advanced models show **average success rates 26.3% lower in the online setting than in ordinary computer use**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Smart glasses let computer tasks originate from what a wearer sees and does, but first-person views are partial and user intent shifts mid-task, so an agent may need to undo earlier browser actions. `EgoUseBench` tests this by replaying real first-person footage and changing requests while the agent works on a website.

- The benchmark has **693 tasks** built from over **74 hours** of first-person recordings (293 `Online Ego Use`, 200 `Offline Ego Use`, 200 `Computer-Use`), run on local simulations of Amazon, YouTube and Google Maps and scored only on whether the final website state matches a verified goal set.
- Online tasks change through three mechanisms: `Graft` revises the user's request, `Refresh` delivers new footage that may invalidate an earlier choice, and `Clarify` requires the agent to ask which of several plausible objects is meant.
- Mean success across six models is **86.1%** in `Computer-Use`, **64.2%** in `Offline Ego Use` and **63.4%** in `Online Ego Use` (a **26.3%** relative drop from `Computer-Use`), with Online scores ranging from **87.0%** for `GPT-6.1 Terra` to **39.0%** for `Kimi K2.6`.
- The weakest spot is revising a choice from new visual evidence alone: `Refresh`-Replace shows the largest average Offline-to-Online decline (`Kimi K2.6` scores **6.7%**), and agents often find the correct new item but leave the outdated selection in place, while scene-change alerts help modestly and longer visual history gives no consistent benefit.
- Caveats include simulated websites, one run per task per condition, fixed rather than generated clarification replies, small `Refresh` and `Clarify` subsets (30 and 28 tasks), and a human review in which both reviewers accepted **90%** of a 40-task sample.

papers.title: DiversePlace: Diversity-Seeking Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Macro Placement
papers.abstract: Macro placement is a critical early-stage decision in physical design because macro locations strongly constrain subsequent implementation stages. The task is difficult because these high-impact discrete decisions must be made before downstream quality can be measured accurately, forcing training to rely on fast but imperfect training-time oracles such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Existing RL-based placers therefore mostly optimize single HPWL-driven solutions, and their long sequential horizons often require heavy search assistance or offline expert data while leaving little room to preserve multiple competitive layouts. We address this gap by making quality-controlled diversity an explicit objective for macro placement. Instead of relying on a single proxy-optimal solution, we maintain a compact archive of HPWL-competitive yet meaningfully different placements for downstream selection. We realize this idea in DiversePlace, a curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that combines a quality-gated diversity reward with an expanding placement horizon, enabling from-scratch RL optimization while keeping exploration inside competitive HPWL regions. On the ISPD2005 benchmarks, DiversePlace consistently improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity and achieves lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs with better efficiency. Code: https://github.com/William030422/NIPS2026-DiversePlace.
papers.summary: Macro placement in chip physical design has to be decided before downstream quality can be measured, so reinforcement learning placers train against a fast but imperfect proxy, half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), and usually return a single proxy-optimal layout. `DiversePlace` instead keeps a compact archive of HPWL-competitive but meaningfully different placements for later selection, using curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a quality-gated diversity reward and an expanding placement horizon, trained from scratch. On the `ISPD2005` benchmarks it improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity while achieving **lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs**, with better efficiency.

papers.title: Noise threshold for learning with quantum memory
papers.abstract: A quantum memory can reduce exponentially the number of experiments needed to learn a physical process, but real memories are noisy. Here we show that, for Pauli memory noise with eigenvalues $\lambda_X,\lambda_Y,\lambda_Z$, the advantage is governed by $\lambda_X^2+\lambda_Y^2+\lambda_Z^2$. We prove that no protocol with an entangled probe gains an exponential advantage when this sum is at most one, reduce the general case to the additivity of a R\'enyi-2 coherent information, and find coded memories that retain a growing advantage within 1% of this threshold. On a superconducting processor, nine simultaneously operated Bell pairs show an advantage that grows or shrinks exponentially with system size, reversing where a parameter-free model predicts. A three-qubit repetition code turns a shrinking advantage into a growing one with all processor and readout errors included, and under dephasing its memory performs better than Bell sampling in any memory frame on a perfect processor.
papers.summary: A quantum memory can exponentially cut the number of experiments needed to learn a physical process, but real memories are noisy. For Pauli memory noise, the authors prove that **no entangled-probe protocol gains an exponential advantage when the sum of the squared noise eigenvalues is at most one**, and they find coded memories that keep a growing advantage within 1% of that threshold. On a superconducting processor, nine simultaneously operated Bell pairs show an advantage that grows or shrinks exponentially with system size, flipping where a parameter-free model predicts. A three-qubit repetition code turns a shrinking advantage into a growing one with all processor and readout errors included.

papers.title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
papers.abstract: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.
papers.summary: Gradient-based training can be viewed as a damped particle moving in the potential defined by the loss, and the authors use the Bateman-Galley doubling of degrees of freedom to write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method, and Nesterov's accelerated gradient as Hamiltonian systems. Treating network activations as phase-space coordinates and the layer equations as constraints, they show that **backpropagation is exactly the Dirac-bracket evolution of this constrained system**, with the backpropagated errors appearing as Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints. The inverse constraint matrix contains both forward and reverse modes of automatic differentiation. The claims are checked numerically to machine precision, and a network is trained by integrating the Dirac flow with no backward pass.

papers.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
papers.abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
papers.summary: Short-video moderation classifiers fuse video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision, and fairness across language communities is usually judged from a single accuracy score that can hide errors concentrated in one group. A post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier applies one significance standard at three stages: what the classifier is allowed to read, what its branches encode, and what it decides, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is **significant at the input stage and in the text branch but undetectable at the decision stage**, where the smallest subgroup leaves only twelve items to test. At the input stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one because of segmentation rather than verbosity.

papers.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth language models produce each token by iterating a shared block of layers until the hidden state converges, and existing inference methods only decide when to stop, with every token starting from random noise. `FlyingStart` is a linear warm start, fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costing under 5% of one loop, that predicts a token's fixed point from the state where the previous token stopped. On `Huginn-0125` it matches the strongest training-free baseline's accuracy with **14-19% fewer decoding layers**, raises batched throughput by 16-18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10-14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the loops saved on all four models studied and shows the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

papers.title: Auditing Identity and Timing Signals in Operational Logs
papers.abstract: Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in ICU records or failures in hard drives, can score well by recognizing which patient or drive a record came from, or when it was recorded, instead of predicting the event. I introduce two simple audits that measure how much of this information a dataset carries before any event-prediction model is trained, and apply them to seven public datasets in six domains. One asks whether a classifier can tell that two records came from the same unit; the other asks which of two records from the same unit came later. Under the stated nulls, both have expected AUC 0.5. In ICU data, the identity audit flags a common preprocessing step: carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993. On a 12-hour sepsis forecasting task, carrying forward makes a model look 0.163 AUC better than raw values when a patient's hours are split between training and test, but only 0.046 better when patients are held out. The exaggeration under patient overlap also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a chronological control with complete follow-up, in which training sees only a patient's earlier, resolved hours, shows no positive mean overlap gap. Timing is a strong predictor: with complete follow-up, hour of stay and measurement counts alone, with no clinical value, score 0.761 on held-out patients, and adding the raw clinical values changes that by +0.018. Outside the ICU, 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of a calendar cut, and the overlap gap persists under a calendar split. The audits show which features and preprocessing choices to check; the evaluation protocol decides the consequences. I release the code, a library that runs the audits on any table with a unit column and a time column, and a guide to using the audits.
papers.summary: Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in intensive care records or hard drive failures, can score well by recognizing which unit a record came from or when it was recorded rather than by predicting the event. Two audits measure this before any prediction model is trained: one asks whether a classifier can tell that two records share a unit, the other which of two records from the same unit came later. Across seven public datasets in six domains, carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993, and on a 12-hour sepsis task it makes a model look 0.163 AUC better under patient overlap but only 0.046 better with held-out patients. Timing alone is a strong predictor: **hour of stay and measurement counts, with no clinical values, score 0.761 on held-out patients**, and code plus an audit library are released.

papers.title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization
papers.abstract: Decisions under uncertainty increasingly rest on fragmented evidence, such as samples from related but different populations, privacy-protected summary statistics, or complementary statistical descriptions of the same data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can fuse such evidence by constructing one ambiguity set per source and hedging against all distributions in the intersection of these sets. This fusion approach is less conservative than aggregating the sources into a single ambiguity set, but it is computationally demanding. Exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources, and even deciding whether the intersection is nonempty is NP-hard. We show that fusion DRO admits an exact reformulation in which the ambiguity sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers. Restricting these multipliers to affine decision rules yields upper bounds that decompose across the ambiguity sets, are exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references, and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations such as Minkowski sums and balls around mixtures. The approximations admit finite conic reformulations in important special cases and subgradient methods for weakly convex losses, which makes fusion DRO applicable to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments, the affine approximation stays close to the exact value wherever the latter is computable, scales far better than exact methods, and outperforms aggregation-based benchmarks out-of-sample.
papers.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can combine fragmented evidence by building one ambiguity set per source and hedging against every distribution in their intersection, which is less conservative than a single aggregated set but computationally hard, since exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources. The authors derive an exact reformulation in which the sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers, then restrict those multipliers to affine decision rules to obtain upper bounds that decompose across sets. These bounds are **exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations**, and subgradient methods extend them to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments the approximation stays close to the exact value, scales far better, and outperforms aggregation baselines out-of-sample.

papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
papers.summary: Publishing how a text watermark works also tells an attacker how to defeat it, either by rewording text to erase the mark or by learning the mark and forging it onto text the model never wrote. The authors study an attacker that reads the published design and picks whichever attack fits, erasing watermarks that are hard to learn and forging those that survive rewording, and every existing watermark they compare fails against it.
