Their proposed `KeyedLex` derives its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and its detector does not need to recover the key exactly. On both tested models it **loses about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds**, with no extra cost in text quality.

papers.title: Angular Interpolation in Sparse-View Low-Dose CT Reconstruction: Placement Effects and Data-Consistency Step-Size Scaling
papers.abstract: Dual-domain networks combine projection and image processing for sparse-view low-dose computed tomography (CT). We quantify the contribution of angular interpolation before learning and distinguish its roles in sinogram initialisation and the image residual base. On synthetic parallel-beam data, parameter-free interpolation reduces noise-free missing-view mean absolute error by 99.7% relative to zero filling at 60 views. Full-view filtered back-projection (FBP) of the jointly learned completed sinogram adds 1.27 dB of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) over interpolated FBP. In a data-consistency dual-domain network (DC-DuNet), a 2x2 configuration ablation controls branch width, depth and training schedule while varying these placements and their associated input channels. After 20 epochs, the PSNR contrasts are +1.98 dB for sinogram initialisation and -2.16 dB for the interpolated image base; the image-base ranking also reverses during training. The sinogram-initialised variant exceeds an image-only U-Net by 0.96 dB at 60 views and 10% dose, and by 1.28 dB on independently generated synthetic data. The U-Net leads at higher view counts and with a shared interpolated image base. Without retraining, the variant retains a 0.12 dB advantage on held-out CHAOS abdominal CT under simulated degradation; the image-base contrast rounds to zero. The implemented projection/backprojection pair has empirical dominant gain of approximately 0.85NK, where N is image-grid width and K acquired view count. These results distinguish interpolation placement from network architecture and support NK normalisation for step calibration.
papers.summary: Dual-domain networks for sparse-view low-dose computed tomography (CT) combine sinogram and image processing, and this study isolates how much angular interpolation contributes and where it should be placed. On synthetic parallel-beam data, parameter-free interpolation cuts noise-free missing-view error by 99.7% relative to zero filling at 60 views, and a controlled 2x2 ablation in a data-consistency dual-domain network (`DC-DuNet`) shows that **using interpolation for sinogram initialisation adds 1.98 dB of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) while using it as the image residual base costs 2.16 dB**. The sinogram-initialised variant beats an image-only `U-Net` by 0.96 dB at 60 views and 10% dose, though the `U-Net` leads at higher view counts, and it keeps a 0.12 dB edge on held-out `CHAOS` abdominal CT. The measured gain of the projection and backprojection pair supports normalising the data-consistency step size by image width times view count.

papers.title: Long-Horizon Planning with Latent World Models via Graph Anchors
papers.abstract:
Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its
  predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the
  goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure
  both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five
  environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two
  failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant
  goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent
  world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the
  shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's
  success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal
  fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
papers.summary: Planners for latent world models score a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image, and the authors show this distance fails in two ways: it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, and it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object so manipulation fails at contact. A ranking test on recorded data separates the two failures across five environments, six visual representations including `V-JEPA 2`, and nine `Meta-World` tasks. `Graph Anchors`, a training-free planner for frozen world models, builds a sparse graph over the model's training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead on the shortest path to the goal. On goals up to 400 steps away it raises `LeWM` success **from 13% to 85% on `PointMaze-Medium`**, from 8% to 87% on `PointMaze-Large`, and from 5% to 71% on `Push-T`.

papers.title: SMOTE 25 Years of Magic: What Has Been Done, What the Evidence Shows, and Whom It Reached
papers.abstract: Background. SMOTE was published in this journal in 2002 and reviewed here at its fifteenth anniversary in 2018. At twenty-five it is cited by more than 34,000 indexed works, half of them outside computer science. Objectives. To establish what the methods built on SMOTE change, how strong the evidence for them is, and whom the technique has reached. Methods. We audited a curated corpus of 76 papers, 37 of which propose a SMOTE-family generator, and tested its coverage with a systematic search of 22,426 records in the PRISMA 2020 format. From the corpus we collected 1,756 dataset entries, 1,511 published comparisons with SMOTE and the evaluation design of 71 studies; from the search we drew 300 applications of SMOTE at random. We used an agentic AI approach to extract, screen and code under our written rules, and we report how each step was checked. Results. Every variant re-decides some of the six decisions of the SMOTE rule, and 24 of the 37 are only ever run on two classes. In their own papers, proposed methods beat SMOTE in 79.0% of the decided comparisons, but independent studies find that the gains shrink with strong learners and tuned thresholds, and that resampling damages calibration. The corpus holds 52 of the 3,097 records that pass the screen and covers the early years closely, the recent ones thinly. The reach is very wide, but a benefit at the level of outcomes is undemonstrated, four harms are documented, and an estimated 37% of applications resample the whole data set before splitting it. Conclusions. For tabular classification, a new SMOTE variant should no longer count as a contribution in itself: a new generator should be tested one decision at a time against class weighting and a tuned threshold with a strong learner, with calibration reported. We close with a selection guide, a reporting checklist of fifteen items and a research agenda.
papers.summary: Twenty-five years after its publication, the `SMOTE` oversampling technique for imbalanced classification is cited by more than 34,000 works, and this review asks what its variants change, how strong the evidence is, and how it is used in practice. The authors audit a curated corpus of 76 papers, run a systematic search of 22,426 records, and sample 300 applications at random, using an agentic AI pipeline for extraction and coding under written rules. Proposed variants beat `SMOTE` in 79.0% of decided comparisons in their own papers, but independent studies find the gains shrink with strong learners and tuned thresholds and that resampling damages calibration, while **an estimated 37% of applications resample the whole dataset before splitting it**. The authors conclude that a new variant should no longer count as a contribution for tabular classification on its own, and provide a selection guide and a fifteen-item reporting checklist.

papers.title: Feasibility-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-CU and O-DU Mapping in 6G O-RAN
papers.abstract: This paper studies the mapping of the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the O-RAN central unit (O-CU) and O-RAN distributed unit (O-DU) onto virtual machines (VMs) in sixth-generation (6G) open radio access networks (O-RAN). The problem is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes the number of placed VNFCs and, secondarily, favors fewer active VMs and lower residual resource wastage. Although conventional optimization techniques can solve this problem, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for larger instances or when optimization must be repeated. To address this limitation, we explore two neural reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods: a deep $Q$-network (DQN) and a double deep $Q$-network (Double DQN). Whereas DQN uses the same target network to both select and evaluate the bootstrap action, Double DQN decouples these two operations to mitigate maximization-induced overestimation. We compare both methods against six baselines: random feasible placement, first-fit, first-fit decreasing, best-fit, a resource-wastage-aware heuristic, and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We conduct a controlled experimental evaluation across four problem sizes with $30$ independent instances each, together with capacity-stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation experiments. For the $16 \times 8$ VNFC-to-VM scenario, DQN and Double DQN achieve mean placed-VNFC fractions of $0.990$ and $0.996$, respectively. However, first-fit decreasing and the resource-wastage-aware heuristic match this placement quality with lower efficiency cost and lower decision time, whereas the MILP attains the lowest efficiency cost at a much higher runtime. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of neural placement for this static problem, without establishing superiority over conventional methods.
papers.summary: Placing the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the central and distributed units of a 6G open radio access network onto virtual machines is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes placed components and secondarily favors fewer active machines and less wasted resource. A deep Q-network (`DQN`) and a `Double DQN` are compared against six baselines, including first-fit heuristics and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver, across four problem sizes plus stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation tests. In the 16 by 8 scenario the two learned methods place 0.990 and 0.996 of components, but **first-fit decreasing and a wastage-aware heuristic match that quality at lower efficiency cost and decision time**, and the MILP solver achieves the lowest efficiency cost at much higher runtime. The authors report no superiority of neural placement over conventional methods for this static problem.

papers.title: PURA: Video Token Pruning via Unified Spatiotemporal Redundancy Assessment
papers.abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Video large language models are expensive at inference because of long visual token sequences, and existing compression methods often fix the order or ratio in which spatial and temporal redundancy are removed. `PURA` is a training-free pruning method that, for each token, builds spatial and temporal reference candidates, picks the one with the lowest representation error, and combines that error with token importance into a removal cost. A step called Coordinated Pruning groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches so tokens need not be removed one at a time. Across three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks, the authors report **a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency**.

papers.title: Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment
papers.abstract: This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.
papers.summary: Quantifying how well a system withstands and recovers from disruptions requires identifying resilience stages in its performance time series, which this work automates in a way intended to be independent of domain and threat type. Four classifiers, `Random Forest`, `Support Vector Machine`, `LightGBM`, and `XGBoost`, are trained to recognize the PARA stages (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt), and their predictions are then used to compute resilience metrics. On data from two network systems and an airport transportation system, **best F1-scores range from 74.3% to 99.4% across stages**, and the overall resilience metrics are estimated with mean absolute percentage error of 0.35-0.82% on the IEEE 802.11 and LTE networks and 1.65-9.56% for the airport.

papers.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
papers.abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.
papers.summary: Yandex describes an open mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and about 3 billion active per token, trained from scratch and released under Apache 2.0. The model combines `Kimi Delta Attention` with full attention, uses `Attention Residuals`, and is trained with the `Muon` optimizer on 17.5 trillion pretraining tokens followed by context-extension stages and a stage for reasoning and agentic interaction; the report covers data pipelines, architectural ablations, scaling-law experiments, and an auxiliary loss that stabilizes training. In zero-shot evaluation it reaches **88.7% pass@8 on `IMO-AnswerBench` and 82.9% pass@8 on `LiveCodeBench` v5-v6**, which the authors describe as leading among open base models of comparable size. On two newly released Russian factual benchmarks, `WikiWebFacts` and `HardMultiQA`, it scores 86.5% and 67.9%, ahead of the larger `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base` and `Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base`.

papers.title: Kant-Q: A Q-Learning Algorithm for Kantian Equilibrium in Symmetric Markov Games
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with one another, and many of these interactions are mixed-motive games, which have posed a persistent challenge for learning algorithms. Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are designed to reach Nash equilibria, yet in many such games these equilibria are Pareto-inefficient. We instead study Kantian equilibria, an economic solution concept in which each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt. In symmetric games, this corresponds to an optimal common policy. We propose Kant-Q, a Q-learning algorithm in which each agent learns action profiles where all agents play the same action. Each update is then a sample from a single-agent MDP, so Kant-Q inherits the convergence guarantees of standard Q-learning. We show that every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium. We also prove that all agents' Q-tables converge to the same limit, whose greedy policy is such an equilibrium, and that greedy play converges whenever the optimal common action is unique at every state. We further show that in a subclass of symmetric monotone games, the Kantian equilibrium is Pareto-efficient among pure strategy profiles and strictly individually rational. Empirically, on the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and the GovSim fishery with up to 200 agents, Kant-Q learns the Kantian equilibrium, while the baselines underperform. Since copies of the same AI system naturally face one another in symmetric games, these results suggest universalization as a design principle for cooperative AI-AI interaction.
papers.summary: Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms aim for Nash equilibria, which are often Pareto-inefficient in mixed-motive games. `Kant-Q` instead targets Kantian equilibria, where each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt, by having each agent learn Q-values only over action profiles in which everyone plays the same action, so each update is a sample from a single-agent decision process and standard Q-learning convergence guarantees carry over. The authors prove that **every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium and that all agents' Q-tables converge to a limit whose greedy policy is one**, and that in a subclass of symmetric monotone games this equilibrium is Pareto-efficient among pure strategy profiles. On the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and the `GovSim` fishery with up to 200 agents, `Kant-Q` learns the Kantian equilibrium while baselines underperform.

papers.title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
papers.abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.
papers.summary: Patient portal messages reveal how patients and healthcare providers communicate, but coding them by hand is labor-intensive. `EPPC-CARE` is an automated framework that identifies communication behaviors as triplets of supporting text span, broad category, and specific subcategory, extracting the components sequentially so each classification stays linked to its source text. Evaluated with six open-weight large language models on 5,516 reference annotations from 867 messages, it **improves triplet F1 over `EPPC-OASIS` by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%**. On a 100-message subset, its agreement with the reference standard was comparable to that of a human expert.

papers.title: HAS: Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling for Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multimodal language models cannot fit full-length videos in context and must sample frames, yet a single sampling principle serves poorly when some queries need a view of the whole video and others hinge on a short window. Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (`HAS`) first uses a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to pick backbone frames that are query-relevant and non-redundant. It then reads the temporal distribution of those frames to infer what the query needs and splits the remaining frame budget between local context around key moments and global context across the video. Added to three leading models, it reports **consistently better performance on `Video-MME`, `LongVideoBench`, and `MLVU`**.

papers.title: Recalling the Past to Answer the Present: Context-Aware Multi-Evidence Reasoning for Streaming Video Question Answering
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
papers.summary: Video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mostly test vision-language models (VLMs) offline, whereas streaming use requires answering context-dependent queries from evidence scattered across the video history. `StreamRecall` is a benchmark of 4,983 questions over 462 videos with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations, accompanied by an Evidence Utilization Cascade that diagnoses models through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. The authors also present `EviStream`, a training-free causal visual memory that keeps reasoning-critical evidence within a fixed key-value cache budget. Experiments show **substantial gaps between current VLMs and the demands of realistic streaming**.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Information Hiding in Semantic Communication
papers.abstract: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.
papers.summary: Hiding information inside semantic communication, where the goal is to convey meaning and not exact symbols, has lacked an information-theoretic treatment. Combining the Niu-Zhang semantic information theory with the Moulin-O'Sullivan hiding theory, the authors build a two-layer semantic and syntactic model with four distortion constraints and cast capacity as a Stackelberg game between hider and attacker, yielding a single-letter maximin expression. The resulting bounds show that **semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding**, and binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm a capacity loss when the semantic mapping is coarsened.

papers.title: On Utilization of Edge-AI for condition monitoring towards predictive maintenance: A use case in dairy processing using explainable AI
papers.abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are driving Industry 4.0, enhancing productivity, automation, and efficiency in manufacturing systems. This study develops an Edge-AI-based condition monitoring framework, as a step towards predictive maintenance, for a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant, using vibration data collected via a low-power IIoT sensor node and processed on an edge device.
papers.summary: Condition monitoring is studied as a step toward predictive maintenance for a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant. The authors develop **an Edge-AI framework that processes vibration data from a low-power Industrial Internet of Things sensor node on an edge device**, with explainable AI as part of the use case. The abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Investigating the efficacy of vortex beam speckle patterns for the recognition of atmospheric turbulence and fractional topological charge with a deep learning model
papers.abstract: Fractional topological charge (TC) enlarges the usable mode set of orbital angular momentum (OAM) links, but reading it reliably after atmospheric turbulence remains difficult. Interferometric and diffractive methods need an undistorted beam and a careful alignment, while most learned approaches treat integer or coarsely spaced charges and do not include turbulence. Here we ask whether the charge of a scalar vortex beam can be regressed directly from a single speckle image, and at which turbulence strength this stops working. We propagate vortex beams over 1500~m through 150 von K\'arm\'an phase screens, scatter them with a fixed random diffuser, and record $256\times256$, 16-bit speckle images for TC from 0 to 10 in steps of 0.01 and turbulence strengths $D/r_0$ from 0 to 50; the results reported here use a subset of 20\,000 images, and a data set of $10^{6}$ images is in preparation. A convolutional neural network estimates the TC and, through an auxiliary head, the turbulence category. On charges withheld from training, the mean absolute error is 0.031 without turbulence (with a common intensity scale) and rises to 0.78 at $D/r_0=10$ and 1.85 at $D/r_0=50$, against 2.5 for a constant prediction, and the turbulence category is identified correctly in 78\% of the images. The results show that, at the present training size, the charge is read accurately only without turbulence, and that the charge and the turbulence oth act on the speckle grain size, which may limit the readout. Experimental validation and the extension to vector vortex beams are left for future work.
papers.summary: Fractional topological charge (TC) expands the mode set available to orbital angular momentum (OAM) optical links, but is hard to read after atmospheric turbulence. The authors simulate vortex beams propagated over 1500 m through turbulence phase screens and a random diffuser, then train a convolutional neural network to regress the TC from a single speckle image and to classify the turbulence strength. On withheld charges, **mean absolute error is 0.031 without turbulence but rises to 0.78 and 1.85 at moderate and strong turbulence**, against 2.5 for a constant prediction, and the turbulence category is identified in 78% of images. The results use a 20,000-image subset, and the authors conclude that at this training size the charge is read accurately only without turbulence.

papers.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
papers.abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.
papers.summary: An evaluation of medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) finds they tend to trail frontier general-purpose models, that scaling model size mostly improves text ability and not visual perception, and that reasoning modes do not close the gap. The authors introduce `Sage-Med-Preview`, a 35B-parameter model with 3B activated parameters, trained on data curated from 322.7 million candidate records through medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Compared against 77 models on 238 clinical tasks, it scores **58.26% on average across 31 public multimodal benchmarks**, ahead of `Hulu-Med-235B-A22B` at 50.99% and `Intern-S2-Preview` at 52.24%, and approaches `GPT-6.2-Sol` on several tasks. Complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows are reported as remaining weaknesses.
papers.highlight_summary:
Medical multimodal LLMs still trail frontier general-purpose models, and scaling model size or enabling reasoning modes mostly improves text ability rather than visual perception. `Sage-Med-Preview` is a 35B-parameter model with 3B activated parameters, initialized from `Intern-S2-Preview`, that tests whether stage-specific data curation plus a progressive training curriculum can close that gap.

- The data pipeline assembles **322.7M** candidate records from over 200 public datasets, biomedical literature and more than 100 private resources, then filters them through separate six-step pathways into estimated retained pools of about 93.8M records for pretraining, 69.6M for supervised fine-tuning and 0.3M for reinforcement learning.
- Training runs continual pretraining on 83.8M records and mid-training on 28.1M, then three supervised fine-tuning stages (instruction alignment, task diversification, selective refinement), then `GRPO` reinforcement learning that samples prompts by policy-dependent difficulty and adds a separate teacher-forced reference replay loss.
- On the 31 public multimodal benchmarks it averages **58.26%**, ahead of `Hulu-Med-235B-A22B` at 50.99% and `Intern-S2-Preview` at 52.24%, and it beats `GPT-6.2-Sol` on comprehensive multimodal understanding (80.05% vs 76.81%) while reaching 30.74% ACC@.5 on `MedSG-Bench` grounding, the best among open-source models but well below the 64.25% of `GPT-6.2-Sol`.
- On unseen private multi-center tasks from 14 hospitals and institutions, it averages **57.72%** against 51.24% for `GPT-6.2-Sol` over the 11 scores that all 12 comparators completed, with no other comparator above 42.97%.
- Complex reasoning and multi-step workflows remain weak, with a 49.39% average on seven medical reasoning benchmarks and only 47.48% whole-case accuracy on `LiveClin`; in addition, the private PET/CT benchmark is not isolated from training data, curated coverage skews toward pathology, MRI and CT, and the newest proprietary models were evaluated on only a subset of benchmarks.

papers.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
papers.abstract:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
papers.summary: Hiring assistants that work across many sessions need to track how a recruiter's preferences and decision patterns evolve. The authors organize interactions in an episodic memory indexed with the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) and add `Procedure Memory`, which learns reusable decision procedures from those episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. OKF-indexed retrieval reaches preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 while using **69% fewer context tokens than full-history context**, and `Procedure Memory` cuts conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. On `PersonaMem-v2` the combined approach scores 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full history with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens, and `GPT-5.6 Luna` performs comparably to `GPT-5.4` at lower cost.

papers.title: Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning new ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of language models is widely believed to cause catastrophic forgetting, which recent work attributes to its off-policy nature. The authors show that the forgetting comes largely from tuning hyperparameters only for new-task performance: **a lower learning rate and batch size give similar gains with little to no forgetting**. With hyperparameters chosen jointly for gain and retention, plain SFT is competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (`SDFT`), an on-policy method designed to reduce forgetting, which is more robust to hyperparameters but also needs a retention-aware selection criterion.

papers.title: ChemoMAE: Self-Supervised Spectral Representation Learning Reveals Chemical Heterogeneity in Historical Wood
papers.abstract: In historical timber buildings, multiple environmental factors act over centuries on wood whose chemical composition varies across anatomical regions, producing complex patterns of degradation. Understanding how timber members degrade is important for the effective conservation and restoration of historical buildings, yet the mechanisms underlying these patterns remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we used self-supervised learning to establish a common basis for comparing specimens from timber members that differ in wood species and service history. We examined transverse sections of 49 wood specimens from several historical buildings in Japan using near-infrared hyperspectral imaging. ChemoMAE, a self-supervised Transformer, learns pixelwise spectral representations through masked denoising that exploits multicollinearity among spectral variables. Clustering these representations yields spatial maps without predefined chemical-state categories. Because anatomy and degradation can produce spatially continuous regions, we formulated Local Label Agreement (LLA) to quantify agreement among labels assigned to neighboring pixels. Using spectra alone, ChemoMAE yielded higher mean LLA than baseline methods on validation specimens. We then trained ChemoMAE anew and fitted cluster centers across all specimens. Spatial structures consistent with wood anatomy and the expected effects of surface exposure emerged in the resulting maps. By cross-referencing regional spectra and spatial distributions across specimens in light of wood anatomy, service histories, and prior studies, we proposed models of internal and surface degradation as mechanistic hypotheses. This exploratory AI for Science framework gives researchers a basis for linking latent patterns learned through self-supervision with domain knowledge when investigating how material states form.
papers.summary: Degradation in centuries-old timber is hard to study because wood chemistry varies across anatomical regions and specimens differ in species and service history. `ChemoMAE` is a self-supervised Transformer that learns per-pixel spectral representations from near-infrared hyperspectral images of 49 specimens from historical buildings in Japan, using masked denoising, and clustering those representations produces spatial maps without predefined chemical categories. Using a new metric called Local Label Agreement (LLA), which measures label agreement among neighboring pixels, **`ChemoMAE` achieves higher mean LLA than baseline methods** on validation specimens. The resulting maps match wood anatomy and expected surface-exposure effects, and the authors use them to propose hypotheses about internal and surface degradation.

papers.title: $\mu$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
papers.abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
papers.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) is often too slow to run online for nonlinear or high-dimensional systems. `μMPC` learns Koopman-linearized dynamics and precomputes finite-horizon control-to-output maps, leaving a quadratic program over actions only whose size does not depend on the lifted state dimension and which is solved with matrix-vector products and projections. Solve times are **as low as 23 microseconds on a desktop CPU** and 24 ms on a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller, with 4096-dimensional quadruped control in under 5 ms and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on a GPU. The authors report up to 108× faster constrained MPC and 1907× faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

papers.title: Learning from Crowds with Unsupervised Item Response Models
papers.abstract: Item Response Theory (IRT) is the study of tests, including the properties of both test items and test takers. Crowdsourced labelling can be cast as an unsupervised IRT problem: annotators play the role of test takers with varying ability, and annotation tasks play the role of items with varying difficulty. We evaluate unsupervised variants of standard logistic IRT models for latent trait recovery and label inference on six datasets with crowdsourced labels and known ground truths. Unsupervised IRT models can recover annotator and item traits (e.g., ability, difficulty and discrimination) reliably across most datasets when compared to supervised variants trained on the ground truth. IRT models seem to be more stable in label inference compared to most baselines, but might not be the best possible choice depending on the dataset. We further propose to use IRT models to inform classifiers during training and compare against existing crowd-learning methods. We find that crowd-learning methods can improve F1 over majority-vote baselines, but no method significantly improves both F1 and calibration. IRT-informed curriculum methods seem to preserve calibration better than other crowd-learning methods, but are not at the frontier regarding F1, and the best crowd-learning methods in terms of F1 seem to be miscalibrated.
papers.summary: Crowdsourced labelling can be framed as an unsupervised Item Response Theory (IRT) problem, with annotators as test takers of varying ability and annotation tasks as items of varying difficulty. The authors evaluate unsupervised logistic IRT models on six crowdsourced datasets with known ground truth, and find that they recover annotator and item traits reliably on most datasets and give stable, though not always the best, label inference. When IRT estimates are used to guide classifier training, **no crowd-learning method significantly improves both F1 and calibration**: IRT-informed curricula preserve calibration better, while the methods with the best F1 are miscalibrated.

papers.title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences
papers.abstract: As agents based on vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly interpret social-media content, errors in their analysis may lend credibility to rumors and amplify their spread. In this paper, we study the problem of visual cognitive collusion, in which coordinated posts combine authentic images and locally faithful captions to induce VLM agents to infer and accept attacker-chosen target claims through their own reasoning. To enable systematic evaluation of this cognitive threat, we introduce a new benchmark comprising 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight application domains. We further propose VisualMontage, a multi-agent framework for simulating such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. We evaluate this threat through extensive experiments across 12 vision-language models, examining modality effects, production-team components, and downstream defenses. Using identical attack feeds across models without victim-specific optimization, we demonstrate cross-model transferability, achieving mean attack success rates of 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models. Moreover, 92.65% of generated feeds pass independent model-based validity auditing. Even after downstream review, residual attack success rates range from 35.3% to 76.7% across the evaluated configurations. Our additional controlled comparisons further reveal that captions can improve model-rated posting naturalness while reducing attack success. Together, these findings reveal a novel cognitive threat in social-media interpretation and motivate safeguards that assess how authentic posts jointly shape agents' reasoning and conclusions.
papers.summary: Agents built on vision-language models (VLMs) that read social media can be led to accept false claims by coordinated posts that use only authentic images and locally accurate captions. The authors build a benchmark of 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight domains, and propose `VisualMontage`, a multi-agent framework that simulates such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment. Using identical attack feeds across 12 models with no victim-specific optimization, **mean attack success rates reach 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models**. Residual success remains between 35.3% and 76.7% after downstream review, and adding captions raises perceived naturalness while lowering attack success.

papers.title: Do We Really Need an LLM for Weight-Space Programming? A Deterministic Forward-Only Paradigm and Its Capability Boundaries
papers.abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.
papers.summary: Recent Weight-Space Programming work uses large language models to edit neural network weights with forward passes only, and the authors ask whether the language model is needed. Forward Weight-Space Programming (`FWSP`) is a deterministic pipeline of probing, localization, a set of editing operators, automatic routing, and paired verification, whose routing is correct 83.3% of the time versus 33.3% for a 27B LLM given the same tools. For reasoning models they add `Protected FisherGate`, a closed-form readout edit; on `DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B` a single frozen patch reaches **84.2% `HumanEval` pass@1 under a 1K token budget**, 14.6 points above budget forcing with 23.4% fewer tokens. Across thirteen models they also identify two limits of forward-only editing, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where LoRA adaptation is needed.

papers.title: Conditional Independence Graph Learning from Dependent Data Via Time-Delay Embedding
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of inferring the conditional independence graph (CIG) of a high-dimensional stationary multivariate Gaussian time series which could be short-range dependent (SRD) or long-range dependent (LRD). In a time series graph, each component of the vector series is represented by a distinct node, and associations between components are represented by edges between the corresponding nodes. We consider a time-domain approach based on time-delay embedding, casting the problem as one of multi-attribute graph estimation for random vectors where a vector is associated with each node of the graph. For an embedding dimension $d$, at each node the associated $(d+1)$-dimensional random vector consists of a time series component and its $d$ delayed copies, with integer delays up to $d \ge 1$. Graph estimation from dependent data has been investigated in the past using frequency-domain methods whose analysis is restricted to SRD data. We consider a penalized negative pseudo log-likelihood function with convex lasso or non-convex regularizations to estimate the CIG. Non-convex regularization functions are log-sum, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) and minimax concave penalty (MCP). We exploit an existing alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) approach to optimize the objective function. We establish sufficient conditions in a high-dimensional setting for consistency, local convexity when using non-convex penalties, and graph recovery, for both SRD and LRD series. We illustrate our approach with both synthetic and real-data examples. For a $p$-dimensional time series, the computational complexity of the ADMM algorithm is ${\cal O}((d+1)^3 p^3)$. Based on the numerical examples, a heuristic is suggested and illustrated for selection of $d$ which, in theory, should tend to infinity to infer the time series graph.
papers.summary: The task is to infer the conditional independence graph (CIG) of a high-dimensional stationary Gaussian time series, including long-range dependent series that existing frequency-domain analyses do not cover. The authors use time-delay embedding to attach to each node a vector of the series component and its delayed copies, turning the problem into multi-attribute graph estimation solved with a penalized pseudo-likelihood under lasso or non-convex penalties and an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver. They establish **sufficient conditions for consistency and graph recovery for both short-range and long-range dependent series**, and illustrate the method on synthetic and real data. The solver's cost grows cubically in both the series dimension and the embedding dimension.

papers.title: Automated Batch-Variable Selection for ComBat-Based Radiomic Harmonization
papers.abstract:
ComBat harmonizes multicentre radiomic features, but batch variables are usually chosen manually, without a standardized criterion across image acquisition parameters. We propose ParsiComBat, which selects acquisition parameters for ComBat, balancing batch-effect removal against feature-structure preservation and abstaining when technical variation is negligible.
  ParsiComBat ranks candidate acquisition parameters by batch effect, filters redundancy, and scores sequential ComBat corrections. We evaluated it in three experiments: in simulations, testing whether it recovered a known batch variable and abstained without one; in CT (NSCLC-Radiomics) and MRI (MAMA-MIA) cohorts, comparing batch-effect removal against manufacturer (manual), every feasible parameter (greedy) and AutoCombat; and in clinical prediction, internally and externally.
  In simulations, ParsiComBat identified the true batch variable in 92.9% of positive trials and abstained in 99.2% of null controls. In CT, correcting for reconstruction kernel reduced mean k-nearest neighbour batch-effect test from 0.276 to 0.032, almost matching greedy correction of six variables. In MRI, correcting for slice thickness and manufacturer reduced it from 0.680 to 0.325, slightly more than manual selection but less than greedy correction of seven variables. Removing technical variation did not improve clinical discrimination: no strategy, including raw features, differed significantly from ParsiComBat in area under the curve.
  ParsiComBat provides a data-driven framework that removes technical batch effects using minimal acquisition parameters, preserving feature structure and clinical discrimination. It selects variables verifiable against the acquisition protocol and abstains when no correction is needed, supporting transparent, reproducible multicentre radiomics.

papers.title: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
papers.abstract: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.
papers.summary: Security research on large language models delivered as cloud services is spread across fields with different threat models. The authors systematize it from a service perspective, breaking Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack with five trust boundaries, six adversary classes, and six security goals, then coding 120 studies and evaluating 50 defenses against common criteria. They find that **44.2% of studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%**. Defenses are tested on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware protections against the provider can be adopted by customers on their own.

papers.title: HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants
papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
papers.summary: Memory systems for long-running AI assistants are governed by a harness of code, prompts, and configuration that is still mostly tuned by hand. `HoMe` is an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively derives new candidate harnesses from any previously evaluated one, using session-level memory versioning and execution traces to trace shared failures back to specific sessions and harness components. It keeps evaluation cheap through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and reuse of constructed memory. Applied to the open-source memory system `ReMe` on `LongMemEval-S` and `BEAM`, with six candidate evaluations per benchmark, it finds harnesses that **improve end-task performance while consuming far fewer query-time tokens**.

papers.title: DecisionReplay: A Corpus and Offline Simulator for Ensembling Decision Models
papers.abstract: Comparing ensembles, routers and cascades requires the output of every model on every item, and its cost. Stored collections built for routing keep no per-option probabilities. We provide a dataset on which ensemble methods, routers and cascades are simulated quickly, without new model calls. DecisionReplay holds the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models, endpoints that return a probability for every answer option, on 35 benchmarks, with the token counts, billed cost and measured latency of every call, all released. A deterministic simulator replays any policy that selects, combines or cascades them. One well-chosen model per benchmark is hard to beat: pooling all models loses 2.7 accuracy points to it, and stacking gains 1.0 points at 3.4 times its cost. The models are wrong together: two that are both wrong choose the same wrong option in 72% of cases. The best router matches that model at 64% of its cost, and certified early exit cuts the cost of a stacked ensemble by 43% without changing an answer. DecisionReplay makes it cheap and fast to test whether a new method changes these results.
papers.summary: Comparing ensembles, routers, and cascades normally requires fresh model calls, and existing routing collections do not store per-option probabilities. `DecisionReplay` releases the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models on 35 benchmarks, along with token counts, billed cost, and latency for every call, plus a deterministic simulator that replays any selection, combination, or cascade policy offline. The data show that **one well-chosen model per benchmark is hard to beat**: pooling all models loses 2.7 accuracy points to it, and stacking gains 1.0 point at 3.4 times the cost. Models also fail together, picking the same wrong option in 72% of joint errors, while the best router matches the single best model at 64% of its cost.

papers.title: Predicting acute food crises and discovering actionable drivers with causal machine learning
papers.abstract: Acute food insecurity is driven by a compound of conflict, adverse climate events, displacement, and economic shocks. We enrich the open-access Harmonized Food Insecurity Dataset with driver variables (monthly, subnational, 80 countries, 2007--2024) and develop missing-data-resilient machine learning pipelines forecasting crisis occurrence at 3, 6, and 9-month lead times using both FEWS NET and, for the first time at scale, IPC/CH classifications. Pipelines, evaluated through nested cross-validation, outperform no-skill baselines by 15 to 50 percentage points in PR-AUC, with performance correlated with crisis prevalence rather than the classification system. TreeSHAP-based explainability reveals compound, geography-specific predictive signal profiles, with three recurrent forecasting archetypes. Comparing predictive importance against doubly robust causal estimates of actionable drivers, we find that acute conflict events, having the weakest predictive signals, emerge as primary causal drivers of crisis classification whilst agroclimatology is the sole dimension in which predictive importance and causal effect align.
papers.summary: Acute food insecurity arises from a mix of conflict, climate events, displacement, and economic shocks. The authors enrich the Harmonized Food Insecurity Dataset with monthly, subnational driver variables for 80 countries from 2007 to 2024 and train missing-data-tolerant models that forecast crises 3, 6, and 9 months ahead, beating no-skill baselines by 15 to 50 percentage points in precision-recall area under the curve. Comparing `TreeSHAP` feature importance with doubly robust causal estimates, they find that **acute conflict events carry the weakest predictive signal yet emerge as the primary causal driver of crisis classification**. Agroclimatology is the only dimension where predictive importance and causal effect agree.

papers.title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning agents for quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits, have states, actions, and networks that grow with the number of qubits, which blocks transfer between problem sizes. `LatentRL-QAS` uses a circuit variational autoencoder to map circuits on any number of qubits into one shared latent space, which the agent navigates instead of adding gates, and the space is refreshed with new discoveries and grown from solutions to smaller systems. On absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction, it discovers the five- and six-qubit states and **prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes**, while a baseline agent with a network 10 to 17 times larger fails on the same budget. The method stays robust under depolarizing noise well above IBM hardware error levels.

papers.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.
papers.summary: The question is how much model capacity a specialized language agent actually needs. `ZeroHero` trains small language agents with fewer than 50 million parameters from scratch: each is pretrained to imitate a large language model's successful trajectories, then post-trained on its own interactions with proximal policy optimization (PPO), with extra expert supervision on the reasoning text it generates. In three multistep environments, the agents **approach expert performance on `WebShop` and surpass their demonstration experts on `Crafter` training rollouts and held-out `Alfworld-Dialogue` tasks**.

papers.title: Carrying Feature Ablations Across Sparse Autoencoder Seeds
papers.abstract: A vision encoder turns an image into one vector per patch, refined layer by layer. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) writes each vector of one layer as a sum of learned directions, most with a coefficient of zero. Researchers call each direction a feature and edit the encoder by removing one feature. An SAE trained from another random seed learns different features. Earlier work matches the two SAEs' features one to one by how closely their directions agree. Matched features can point alike yet respond to different image parts, so removing them may change the encoder differently. We remove a feature and, separately, its match, then compare the changes in the encoder's output on the same held out images. When the second change nearly reproduces the first, we say the removal carries across seeds. A setting fixes a DINOv2 or SigLIP layer and its SAE feature count. At our tolerance, the removal carries for 12% to 70% of matched pairs across three settings. The share is 0% in two controls: an SAE whose directions stay random and, post hoc, matches shuffled among trained features. Post hoc, predicting which removals carry is more accurate with layer contributions than with directions. Some incorrect predictions remain. One persists on independent images. So pairs can be screened at the layer. Measuring the output detects errors this screen misses.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose a vision encoder's activations into features, but SAEs trained from different random seeds learn different features, and features matched by direction may not behave the same when removed. The authors ablate a feature and, separately, its matched counterpart from another seed, then compare the resulting changes in encoder output on held-out images. For `DINOv2` and `SigLIP` layers, **the ablation effect carries across seeds for only 12% to 70% of matched pairs** across three settings, versus 0% in two controls. Layer-level contributions predict which ablations carry more accurately than direction similarity, though some errors remain that only measuring the output detects.

papers.title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.
papers.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) methods that learn by reconstructing pixels spend representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. `VIBES` (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States) replaces reconstruction with an adversarial term requiring latent states to suffice for predicting rewards and the next latent state, and the authors show its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories whenever exact sufficiency is attainable. Used as a drop-in replacement for the model-learning component of `Dreamer`, it reaches **state-of-the-art performance on the `Distracting Control Suite`** and extends to manipulation in `Realistic ManiSkill`. It needs no image-specific augmentations and also works on high-dimensional vector-state tasks, shown on a 100-link swimmer robot.

papers.title: Motion Beyond Pixels: Learning Future Visual Representations for Object-Centric Dynamics
papers.abstract: Many embodied world models predict future states in latent spaces optimized for RGB reconstruction, which do not explicitly prioritize object-level semantics and geometry relevant to motion generation. We present MotionRep, a visual representation world model that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, coupling semantic and geometric information with object-centric dynamics.
