To make high-dimensional DINO features amenable to generative modeling, we introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact latents while preserving semantic and geometric information. Conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, a unified diffusion transformer predicts future visual representations and 3D object flow through joint attention. MotionRep employs asymmetric modality-specific noise schedules to keep the visual stream ahead of 3D object flow during joint denoising, allowing progressively refined future visual representations to guide flow generation. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes, while requiring only three denoising steps for inference. These results support predictive visual representations as an effective future-state space for object-centric dynamics modeling.
papers.summary: Embodied world models usually predict future states in latent spaces tuned for RGB reconstruction, which do not prioritize the object-level semantics and geometry that matter for motion. `MotionRep` instead uses a unified diffusion transformer to jointly generate future `DINO` representations and 3D object flow, conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, with a `DINO-VAE` compressing the features and asymmetric noise schedules keeping the visual stream ahead of the flow during denoising. On simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks it outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes while **requiring only three denoising steps at inference**.

papers.title: A Hard Background Pairing Transfers across Classifiers and Images
papers.abstract: An image classifier names the object in an image, and its accuracy is the share of images named correctly. A classifier that names a car on a road may miss the same car pasted onto clouds. Composite benchmarks measure such failures by pasting objects cut from photographs onto backgrounds from other photographs. A pairing puts every object label on a different background label, such as truck on sea. The pairing on which some classifiers do worst, their hardest pairing, makes a strict test, but may be hard only for them or only on the photographs used to choose it. We show that the hardest pairing of some classifiers stays hard for others and on new photographs. We split 40 ImageNet classifiers into halves balanced by reported ImageNet accuracy. One half picks its hardest pairing of 8 object and 8 background labels from Common Objects in Context (COCO). The other half, held out of the choice, compares that pairing with random pairings of the same objects and backgrounds. For the 14 held-out classifiers with little net accuracy change after pasting objects back onto their own backgrounds, mean accuracy on composites from new photographs falls from 50.3% over random pairings to 43.7% on the hardest pairing, 6.6 percentage points lower. A benchmark using these composites can compare this pool's held-out classifiers on the fixed and random pairings.
papers.summary: Composite benchmarks test image classifiers by pasting cut-out objects onto backgrounds from other photographs, and the object-background pairing that is hardest for one set of classifiers might be hard only for them or only for the photographs used to pick it. The authors split 40 `ImageNet` classifiers into two accuracy-balanced halves, let one half choose its hardest pairing of 8 object and 8 background labels from Common Objects in Context (`COCO`), and tested the other half on it against random pairings using new photographs. For the 14 held-out classifiers with little net accuracy change when objects were pasted back onto their own backgrounds, mean accuracy fell **from 50.3% on random pairings to 43.7% on the hardest pairing**, a 6.6 percentage point drop, indicating the difficulty transfers across classifiers and images.

papers.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.
papers.summary: `REE` (Research Entrance Exam) is a benchmark of 100 open-ended, expert-reviewed research problems across five scientific areas and 23 domains, built to measure whether autonomous agents can improve on established scientific methods. Each problem gives an agent up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and the result is scored on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. Two of the four frontier agents evaluated, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6.1 Sol`, **outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems** respectively, across all five areas. Both surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field.

papers.title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.
papers.summary: Instead of training a policy through reinforcement learning (RL), LLM-based coding agents here read an environment's source code as a readable world model and write executable decision rules directly, then refine them using online feedback or offline data. Across a range of decision-making benchmarks, the synthesized policies **match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience**. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access, and tests under challenging conditions, show the benefit of readable world models, and the resulting rules are interpretable and can be traced as they evolve through refinement.

papers.title: Multi-Party Authorization of Maintenance Prescriptions on a Permissioned Blockchain
papers.abstract: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, an equipment supplier's model may recommend an intervention that a plant schedules, a contractor executes, and a quality or safety function approves. A shared ledger records who submitted the prescription, yet cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule produced it. We require permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that calculation before releasing a work order. On a four-organization Hyperledger Fabric testbed using a public engine benchmark, this stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, whereas hash checks accepted four that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.
papers.summary: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, a shared ledger can record who submitted a maintenance recommendation but cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule actually produced it. The proposed scheme requires permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that calculation before a work order is released. On a four-organization `Hyperledger Fabric` testbed using a public engine benchmark, this **stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions**, whereas hash checks accepted four that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.

papers.title: Learning to Be Truncated: Preparing LLM Checkpoints for SVD Compression
papers.abstract: Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.
papers.summary: Compressing language models with singular value decomposition (SVD) usually needs fine-tuning or weight correction afterward, repeated for every compression ratio. `LLift` prepares a pretrained model once: it fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio with the original model as teacher, then merges the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the components left out of the training forward pass, so the same decompositions can be truncated at different ranks. On `LLaMA-7B`, **a single prepared model yields accuracy gains at three compression ratios** without per-ratio fine-tuning, and the gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. Gradient analysis provides local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can help compression at others.

papers.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
papers.abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.
papers.summary: Robot demonstrations synthesized in simulation look unlike real scenes, while purely generated video lacks physically consistent interactions and aligned action labels. `DemoFoundry` has coding agents reconstruct task-relevant geometry from a scene reference and write control programs that run in a physics simulator, producing proxy videos with aligned states and actions; a video renderer, trained on real-proxy video pairs that the agents also construct from existing robot episodes, then translates these into photorealistic observations. Automated task-execution checks select the successful trajectories, and no human demonstrations of the target task are required. Policies trained on the generated data outperform raw-simulation training and **approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations**.

papers.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action policies control robots efficiently but need new human demonstrations for unfamiliar settings, while reasoning agents can find solutions through robot-control APIs at a high cost in repeated deliberation. `RoboEvo^2` alternates two phases: in Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search code-based routes and consolidate verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and memory; in Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, the verified trajectories train the policy, with Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaching it to prefer successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. Without additional human demonstrations, standalone policy success on `LIBERO-PRO` rises **from 11.0% to 84.1%** and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5%, with similar gains and lower agentic costs on `RoboTwin C2R`. Further experiments report cross-embodiment harness transfer and 95.0% hybrid success on the `Unitree G1-D`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Vision-language-action policies need fresh human demonstrations to cope with unfamiliar scenes, while coding agents can reason their way to a solution but are slow and expensive to run on every task. `RoboEvo2` closes the gap by co-evolving the agent's harness (skills, memory, routing) and the policy in rounds, using the current policy's failures to drive both updates.

- In the Policy-to-Harness step (`P2H`), a `GPT-6 Astra` coding agent diagnoses each failed rollout, searches `Code`, `Code+ICL` and `Code+Policy` repair routes in parallel, keeps the verified success with the lowest normalized motion jerk, and merges compatible repairs into the skill library, routing rules and memory.
- In the Harness-to-Policy step (`H2P`), the policy is trained on verified trajectories plus Counterfactual Preference Distillation (`CPD`), a margin loss that favours the repair over the failed continuation from the same state relative to a frozen reference policy, with failure-aware task sampling and `EWC` to limit forgetting.
- With no extra human demonstrations, eight rounds on `LIBERO-PRO` lift standalone success from **11.0% to 84.1%** and hybrid success from **30.4% to 90.5%** while per-round API cost falls from 430.63 to 98.92 USD, and five rounds on `RoboTwin C2R` lift standalone from **46.0% to 77.5%** and hybrid from 48.8% to **87.4%**.
- On `RoboTwin C2R`, 2.5K clean plus 5K self-collected trajectories reach **77.5%** against 76.8% for conventional training on 27.5K, and on a real Unitree G1-D a `π0.5` policy trained on 120 auto-collected demonstrations scores **85.0%** against 80.0% for 200 teleoperated ones, with hybrid execution at **95.0%**.
- The evidence is thinner than the headline suggests: the real-robot test covers four tasks at 10 trials each with an operator resetting the scene after failures, the `LIBERO-PRO` baselines keep their original evaluation protocols, only the hybrid mode beats `EmbodiedRSI` (86.8%), and the loop depends on a proprietary coding agent.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation
papers.abstract: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $\epsilon$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.
papers.summary: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) covers standard reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration, but generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures, and existing methods either skip exploration, are limited to tabular settings, or lack efficient policy optimization. Working in finite-horizon episodic bilinear Markov decision processes, the authors estimate occupancy measures through low-dimensional feature expectations and propose a model-based framework called optimistic concave utility policy optimization (`OCUPO`). The on-policy version has a proven sample complexity on the order of epsilon^-4, and an off-policy version that reuses past trajectories through a backward feature regression subroutine achieves **sample complexity on the order of epsilon^-2**, up to a controllable projection error and under assumptions on the policy class. That dependence on epsilon matches standard reinforcement learning with linear function approximation, carries over to linear MDPs, and does not need the integral oracle used in prior work.

papers.title: Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers
papers.abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.
papers.summary: Generative video models lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional renderers, so it is hard to know which requests they will execute reliably. `NeurCo` (Neural Rendering Compiler) automatically probes a frozen video model to build a model-specific capability manual, expresses user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, and compiles it so that reliable requirements pass through unchanged while unreliable ones are rewritten or given alternative execution strategies. On `VComBench`, a new benchmark of 380 compositional multi-requirement tasks, requirement satisfaction rises **from 46.8% to 52.3% on `Wan`** and from 66.5% to 69.3% on `Minimax H3`, with further gains when combined with prompt enhancers. The analysis also finds model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism.

papers.title: Find the Clue, Not the Scene: Rethinking Reasoning for Entity Recognition in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting new entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.
papers.summary: Knowledge-based visual question answering requires recognizing the entity in an image and then recalling facts about it, and an analysis of four thinking vision-language models (VLMs) on `ViQuAE` finds that **76.3% of errors stem from misrecognizing the entity**, with 84.9% of those resolved once the entity name is supplied. Recognition turns out to depend on distinctive visual details that trigger recall, such as keys for Saint Peter, rather than on general scene descriptions. `ClueRL` extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) with an advantage localized to such clues in the thinking trace, and outperforms `GRPO` and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Though trained only on entity recognition, the gains carry over to knowledge-based question answering and general multimodal reasoning, raising `Qwen3.5-4B` by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the `ScienceQA` and `MMMU` subsets of `MMStar`.

papers.title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.
papers.summary: Non-invasive brain-to-text decoding must turn learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. `MEG2text` combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and language-model fusion over target words. On the word-ranking task of `LibriBrain100` it reaches **64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy**, 16.92 percentage points above the published `MEG-XL` across four corpora, with gains on each. Controlled comparisons attribute the improvement to both implementation corrections and the learned readout, and an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation.

papers.title: Evacuation Traffic Prediction for Dynamic Transportation Networks over Multiple Hurricanes: A Generalized Graph Learning Approach
papers.abstract: High traffic demand during hurricane evacuations causes severe congestion on major highways, leading to delays and safety risks for evacuees. Predicting evacuation traffic in real-time can significantly enhance evacuation management efforts. However, evacuation traffic is highly dynamic and uncertain due to evolving hurricane characteristics and diverse population response. Each hurricane has unique characteristics and evacuation contexts, resulting in different spatial-temporal traffic patterns. Moreover, the structure of detector-based transportation networks varies across multiple hurricanes. Hence, a model trained on the data from one hurricane may not generalize well for others. This study proposes a generalized dynamic graph learning framework using traffic detectors and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes. Leveraging the dynamic nature of transportation network, we develop a Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model that predicts evacuation traffic up to 6 hours in advance. For an unseen hurricane (Milton, 2024), the model shows strong generalizability, achieving an RMSE of 280.6 and R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction, and an RMSE of 459.8 and R2 of 0.89 for overall 6-hours prediction. We also introduce a modular training approach, where we evaluate performance improvements by sequentially incorporating data from multiple hurricanes. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models for overall 6-hour prediction horizons. Ablation experiments show an 8.4% improvement in RMSE for the proposed dynamic GCN-LSTM model compared to its static counterpart. Traffic management officials can use the developed model to understand future traffic conditions during hurricane evacuation in advance and take proactive measures to reduce delays during evacuation.
papers.summary: Traffic during hurricane evacuations varies with each storm, and the detector-based road network itself differs between hurricanes, so models trained on one storm tend not to generalize to another. Using detector and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes, the authors build a dynamic Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (`GCN-LSTM`) model that predicts evacuation traffic up to 6 hours ahead. On the unseen hurricane Milton (2024), it achieves **an R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction** (RMSE 280.6) and an R2 of 0.89 over the full 6-hour horizon (RMSE 459.8), outperforming baseline models. The dynamic graph formulation improves RMSE by 8.4% over a static counterpart.

papers.title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding
papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.
papers.summary: Turning poems into video requires handling compressed language, historical and cultural background, and metaphor rather than literal scene description. `PoVi` is both a benchmark and an agentic framework: it reconstructs a poem's meaning into an evidence-bounded representation, then progressively produces narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans before generating narration-aligned video. Across three planning backbones and four video generators it consistently improves over single-call generation, with **the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations**.

papers.title: A Failure-Driven Data Flywheel for Post-Training Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.
papers.summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely meet every behavioral requirement of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack data to fix the failures. The proposed data flywheel inserts task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes to create missing scenarios, evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement, and builds a failure map that directs larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. Applied to autonomous driving, five rounds of post-training raise the critical-phase collision-free rate for occluded-pedestrian emergence **from 0.261 to 0.579 for `AutoVLA` and from 0.390 to 0.765 for `ReCogDrive`**, with unnecessary braking never above 0.013, and stop-before-line rates at stop signs rise from 0.100 to 0.897 and from 0.000 to 0.667. On a full-scale vehicle with no real-world training, post-trained `ReCogDrive` achieves 4 of 5 safe passages versus 1 of 5 for the base model, though both models mainly learn anticipatory deceleration rather than braking after the pedestrian appears.

papers.title: Effect of class proportion shifts on classifier curvature
papers.abstract: Changing the class mix can alter mean loss without changing the classifier. To distinguish this reweighting from changes in the model itself, we studied ten-class CIFAR-10 classification in separate branches for two target classes, measuring the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to the output-layer parameters on fixed images of each target class. Across ten new initialisations, after 60 updates to the output layer with frozen features, the trace changed by -0.152% on average in branches where the target class share rose from 10% to 19%, and by +0.071% in branches where it fell to 1%, relative to each branch's initial trace. These changes do not isolate the effect of class share from that of the assigned training images. We developed a forecast based on initial class gradients after examining the first experiment's results and then tested it prospectively without modification. For direct increases from 10% to 19%, rather than increases after a deficit, its mean absolute error was 0.022 percentage points on the initial-trace scale, compared with 0.152 for a zero-change forecast and 0.104 for equally weighted gradients. Using the assigned class proportions improved the forecast of how much the trace would change.
papers.summary: Changing the class mix of training data can alter mean loss without changing the classifier, so the authors measure a property of the model itself: the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to output-layer parameters on fixed images of a target class in `CIFAR-10`. After 60 output-layer updates with frozen features, averaged over ten initialisations, the trace changed by -0.152% when the target class share rose from 10% to 19% and by +0.071% when it fell to 1%, though these changes do not isolate the effect of class share from that of the assigned training images. A forecast based on initial class gradients, tested prospectively without modification, had **a mean absolute error of 0.022 percentage points versus 0.152 for a zero-change forecast** and 0.104 for equally weighted gradients on direct increases from 10% to 19%.

papers.title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
papers.summary: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) trains one policy across several domains to expand agent capabilities without separate specialists or a distillation stage, but it is hard to keep stable, to allocate rollout compute well, and to extend to new domains. `Maco-RL` uses a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across task domains to balance gradient contributions and limit off-policy effects, plus Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS), which allocates compute among samples at different levels of mastery. On five benchmarks it raises the overall score of `Qwen3.5-27B` **from 43.6 to 54.2, then to 60.1 with continual expansion**, reaching the level of `Qwen3.8-27B`, which it improves by a further 5.7 points. It also outperforms single-task reinforcement learning while using less compute for policy updates.

papers.title: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling
papers.abstract: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.
papers.summary: Small proxy models are often used to choose training data for a larger target model, but the proxy can rank data differently from the target. The authors cast the problem as a multi-fidelity bandit in which each arm is a data intervention, the proxy reward is seen every round, and the target reward appears only on rare audits; the paired observations are used to correct the proxy per arm, audits are spent only on uncertain decisions, and the audit budget is paced across training. They prove that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret, that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary, and that a sliding-window policy achieves regret on the order of the square root of (number of change points × T × log T) under abrupt changes. In a proof of concept on `CivilComments-WILDS` with `BERT-Small` guiding `BERT-Large`, spreading audits over training improves **worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points** at the same audit count.

papers.title: From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.
papers.summary: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) keep gaining new entities whose histories start empty and remain sparse and bursty, and existing methods either transfer patterns without catalog-wide event memory or rank unseen answers poorly because of asymmetry between endpoint roles. `INSPIRE` (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning) first trains a shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog with coordinated masking, then freezes it and trains a lightweight evidence adapter combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics. On four benchmarks built from the `ICEWS` and `GDELT` event datasets, it improves mean reciprocal rank on emerging entities **by 16.73% to 88.83% over the strongest baselines**, and the adapter alone adds 8.28% to 32.63% over the corresponding first-stage predictors. The evaluation is also broken down by endpoint role and by cohorts of emerging answers tracked over time.

papers.title: Spec2Weights: Certifying Networks that a Language Model Writes from a Specification
papers.abstract: A language model can write the weights of a small MLP, CNN, RNN or GNN from a plain-language specification, with no data and no gradient step. We ask when such a network can be proved exact in the float32 arithmetic it actually runs in. A float-safety lemma makes exhaustive float32 enumeration a proof for any summation order, and a layered error bound covers networks whose weights are not short binary fractions. With dynamic programming, template checks, an SMT proof, breadth-first search and induction for weight-tied recurrences, this certifies 12 of 15 written networks (one after a single constant fix) on every input of a stated domain (up to $10^{16}$ inputs, or every graph or grid up to a size bound), in a minute of CPU or less each. The certificates also say where a network stops being exact: the shortest-path network is exact iff the distance is at most 4,096 and fails at the predicted hops. Thirty new specifications were each written by a fresh session of one model family (Claude Opus 5.5). Twenty-five first submissions are certified exact for any summation order; the five tax schedules stay within \$0.11 of the true tax at every whole dollar in one fixed float32 run. An open 27B model passes 23 of the 30, and 25 with more thinking and code execution, so the method transfers in part. We also prove two limits of learning from examples: input coordinates never active in training cannot be learned from more in-range data, and Luhn-type checksums have exponentially small target-dependent gradient variance across their family. Tuned gradient descent on the same architectures agrees with both, which cover two of our five failure classes.
papers.summary: A language model can write the weights of a small MLP, CNN, RNN or GNN directly from a plain-language specification, with no data or gradient steps, and the question here is when such a network can be proved exact in the float32 arithmetic it actually runs in. The authors combine a float-safety lemma, a layered error bound, dynamic programming, template checks, an SMT proof, breadth-first search and induction to certify networks over entire stated input domains of up to 10^16 inputs, in a minute of CPU or less each. Of 30 new specifications written by fresh sessions of `Claude Opus 5.5`, **25 first submissions are certified exact for any summation order**, and an open 27B model passes 23 to 25 of the 30. They also prove two limits of learning from examples, covering input coordinates never active in training and Luhn-type checksums, which tuned gradient descent confirms.

papers.title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.
papers.summary: Alzheimer's diagnosis draws on clinical, biospecimen and imaging tests that few patients complete in full, and existing methods either drop missing modalities or train on a single estimate of them. `Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers` has the model fill in missing modalities itself, one at a time and several times over, while an imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each fill and a diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. On the `Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative` cohort it outperforms prior baselines, and on two external cohorts **its calibration error is level with the lowest even after every method is recalibrated**. Adding the teachers to three of the baselines improves each of them.

papers.title: Robust Recourse under Causal Graph Ambiguity
papers.abstract:
Causal algorithmic recourse recommends actions to reverse unfavorable decisions by modeling how interventions change an individual's features. Existing methods typically assume one causal graph that describes the system and account for uncertainty in the causal mechanisms. However, there usually exist several graphs that fit the same data but can predict different effects for the same action. Certain actions may achieve recourse across multiple graphs, but as the set of potential graphs grows, a single best action may become infeasible.
  We propose Worst-Case Recourse and Graph-Weighted Recourse to find a low-cost action that succeeds across all candidate graphs or a specified fraction of graph weight, respectively. Assuming a set of plausible graphs, for each graph we fit Gaussian process structural equations and assess success using the posterior mean--standard-deviation criterion. We use gradient-based search to determine minimal cost actions and check the validity of the actions on fresh posterior samples. In synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, relaxing robustness, the requirement that an action succeed under every candidate graph, can increase the number of valid recommendations for recourse and lower costs of actions for both methods. In the 20-node GP benchmark, relaxation increases the number of factual instances offered recourse (coverage) from 341 to 436 out of 1,000, while the number of true successes, actions that flip the decision under the generating model, falls from 251 to 184, illustrating the coverage--validity trade-off. Accounting for graph ambiguity can help decision-makers recommend actions that remain effective even when the causal mechanisms of the system are not fully known.
papers.summary: Causal algorithmic recourse recommends actions to reverse an unfavorable decision, but usually assumes a single causal graph even though several graphs can fit the same data and predict different effects. `Worst-Case Recourse` and `Graph-Weighted Recourse` search for low-cost actions that succeed under every candidate graph or under a specified fraction of graph weight, using Gaussian process structural equations per graph and gradient-based search. On a 20-node benchmark, relaxing the robustness requirement **raises the number of instances offered recourse from 341 to 436 of 1,000 while true successes fall from 251 to 184**, illustrating a trade-off between coverage and validity.

papers.title: LiDAR Intensity Reconstruction with Limited Real Data: An Architecture Benchmark under Fixed-Epoch Training
papers.abstract: Physics-derived simulation can supplement scarce real-world LiDAR intensity measurements, but its effectiveness depends on the learning architecture and the amount of real training data available. We benchmark nine neural architectures for LiDAR intensity reconstruction from depth, semantic labels, incidence angle, and material reflectance, using real SemanticKITTI and synthetic VoxelScape range-image data. All models follow a fixed 20-epoch protocol; this controls the number of training passes, not the computational cost across architectures. We report mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity (SSIM), inference timing, and spectral-energy agreement. We also evaluate four selected architectures with fixed-size training mixtures containing 0\%, 1\%, 5\%, 10\%, 20\%, 50\%, or 100\% real frames. With real-only training, UNet-V2 achieves the best reported reconstruction metrics (MAE 0.234, MSE 0.140, PSNR 8.64 dB, and SSIM 0.647), followed by a denoising diffusion model (DDPM). In several mixtures containing 1--10\% real data, DDPM achieves lower error and higher image-quality metrics than the evaluated deterministic alternatives, whereas UNet-V2 leads with 100\% real data. Spectral analysis additionally reveals architecture-dependent discrepancies across frequency bands. These findings characterize reconstruction trade-offs under the stated data mixtures and fixed-epoch protocol, without establishing compute-matched superiority or isolating the diffusion objective from backbone differences.
papers.summary: Nine neural architectures are benchmarked on reconstructing LiDAR intensity from depth, semantic labels, incidence angle and material reflectance, using real `SemanticKITTI` and synthetic `VoxelScape` range images under a fixed 20-epoch protocol. Four of the architectures are also trained on mixtures containing between 0% and 100% real frames. With real-only training `UNet-V2` gives the best metrics (mean absolute error 0.234, structural similarity 0.647), whereas **a denoising diffusion model (`DDPM`) does better in several mixtures with only 1-10% real data**. The authors note that the protocol fixes training passes rather than compute, so the results do not establish compute-matched superiority or isolate the diffusion objective from backbone differences.

papers.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.
papers.summary: `Chorus` adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to a transformer's input and attention, and the question studied is how much backbone capacity those tables actually replace. Models from 16M to 349M parameters are trained on 1.34 billion tokens of pre-1918 Polish, and each `Chorus` model is matched to the plain model with the same held-out loss. With tables about as large as the backbone, `Chorus` matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M, so **each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters**. Tuning the learning rate separately for each model type cuts the measured gain by about a third at 47M, and the results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.

papers.title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
papers.abstract: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.
papers.summary: Metanetworks, models that take other neural networks' weights as input, have mostly been limited to small MLPs and CNNs because graph metanetworks process every neuron and weight and so scale with parameter count. Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (`H-GMNs`) use the input architecture's hierarchy of neurons, layers and blocks to coarsen and refine the graph with pooling and un-pooling layers that preserve permutation symmetry, and a new graph construction extends them to Transformers. Evaluated on new `ResNet-18` and `ViT` model zoos of up to 86M parameters across Lipschitz bound, generalisation and robustness prediction, backdoor detection and pruning, they are more sample-efficient than flat and non-equivariant alternatives. **Their cost stays nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows**, allowing deeper processing where flat graph metanetworks run out of memory.

papers.title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
papers.abstract: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.
papers.summary: Noisy parity fitting is NP-hard in the worst case, and the question addressed is whether extra observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. For uniformly sampled entries of a rank-one sign tensor of fixed order k at least 3 with independent errors, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, the authors show that **O(n/(log n)^(1/(k-2))) further readings suffice with high probability for exact optimization in O(n log^2 n) worst-case work**. The leading coefficient is shown to be sharp for weak recovery by shallow local estimators, and the analysis also characterizes the number of tied optima and the sharp radius of local verification.

papers.title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
papers.abstract: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.
papers.summary: Evaluations of action-conditioned world models assume that actions are encoded at rollout time exactly as they were in training, and an audit of Navigation World Models (`NWM`) finds three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs without retraining **reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%**, measured with `DreamSim` on the `RECON` navigation dataset, changes the ranking of checkpoints, and removes or reduces the measured advantage of two alternative models. Fixing only the normalization offset makes error worse, which shows that interacting mismatches must be checked together. The authors release `ActRosetta`, a tool that checks and where possible repairs action encoding, while noting that its diagnostic coverage is limited and improved control remains unproven.

papers.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
papers.abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.
papers.summary: Answer accuracy in embodied question answering mixes together what a memory retains, reading errors and question priors, so the authors define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from a scene graph alone. In a simulated multi-room pipeline the baseline graph recovers only 24.1% of visible object types, and four targeted repairs double recall, **raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%** and lift retrained accuracy from 71.4% to 75.9%. Better object F1 can nonetheless lower answerability, a question-type prior beats the reader on every predicted graph, and in one real-video test graph memory lowers accuracy. The findings are described as exploratory.

papers.title: BRIAR: Martingale Belief Smoothing on Bifurcation-Guided Reasoning Trees
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has rapidly advanced long-chain reasoning, yet standard policy optimizers distribute rollout compute and gradient credit blindly across a trajectory. On hard problems, an early misstep derails the remaining trace, whereas on solvable problems, the policy keeps generating redundant verification long after the answer is already determined. We trace both pathologies to a single structural fact: under an on-policy verifier, the true prefix pass probability $V^\pi(u)$ along a reasoning trace forms a $[0,1]$-bounded Doob martingale whose learnable credit variance is strictly conserved and bounded above by $V^\pi(u)(1-V^\pi(u))$, vanishing at both the derailed ($V^\pi\to 0$) and absorbed ($V^\pi\to 1$) boundaries. We introduce BRIAR (Bifurcation-guided Rollout and Inference on Adaptive Reasoning trees), a tree-structured RLVR framework built directly around this martingale geometry. First, BRIAR expands discourse-aligned reasoning trees along an upper-confidence outcome-bifurcation frontier, steering rollouts away from absorbed rumination and toward unresolved decision points. Second, it models latent node values with boundary-scaled heteroscedastic edge variances and computes exact global posteriors in linear $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$ time via two-pass Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) tree belief smoothing, eliminating $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$ matrix inversions while gating out spurious boundary noise. Third, BRIAR detects minimal absorbed frontier nodes and applies zero-sum log-length centered suffix advantages strictly post-absorption, leaving pre-absorption derivations provably invariant.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) spreads rollout compute and gradient credit evenly along a reasoning trace, even though early missteps derail hard problems and solved problems keep generating redundant verification. The authors attribute both to one fact: the probability that a trace prefix eventually passes the verifier is a bounded martingale whose learnable credit variance vanishes once a trace is either derailed or certain to succeed. `BRIAR` builds reasoning trees that direct rollouts toward unresolved decision points, **computes exact posteriors over node values in time linear in tree size** using two-pass Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, and applies length-based advantages only after the answer is already determined. The abstract presents the framework and its theoretical properties without reporting experimental results.

papers.title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context
papers.abstract: Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98--100\% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory's gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60\% of the gain on one planted family, 48\% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61\% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47\%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them.
papers.summary: The study measures how much a stated mathematical theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of `Qwen3-14B` **raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83** and cuts median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help; the gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow. To separate induction from recall, unpublished theorems are planted in custom probability families, where a strong open model that explores with code recovers 60%, 48% and almost none of the oracle gain on three families. Merging several induced notes recovers 61% of the gain on the classic family, above the 47% of the best single note.

papers.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is expensive for long-horizon agents because every update needs fresh environment rollouts, and prefix replay from stored histories reduces that cost but misses student-induced histories and uses fixed position-based replay schedules. `CARE-OPD` has the teacher complete trajectories that the student started, gates updates on response-level confidence, and uses downstream execution evidence to choose which turns to replay. It outperforms online OPD and earlier prefix replay baselines on software engineering and deep research tasks. On `SWE-bench Verified` it **reaches 59.5% task success while cutting end-to-end training time by 45%** and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

papers.title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
papers.abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.
papers.summary: A common scoring system based on token readouts is introduced to compare weight-, activation- and output-based model diffing methods for detecting backdoors inserted during fine-tuning. The authors also improve weight and activation methods by decoding through the `J-lens` and its refinement the `J++-lens`. The strongest single method, the weight difference decoded through the base model's `J++-lens`, **ranks a token naming the backdoor in its top ten in 11 of 12 settings**. Output and activation methods such as `ADL` and `Diff Mining` break when the backdoored model is penalised for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, while permuting hidden units or training only certain layers hides the backdoor from weight-based methods, so no single method resists both attacks.

papers.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
papers.abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.
papers.summary: Preference-aligned LLMs can collapse onto a narrow set of high-reward responses, which limits creative generation that needs quality, novelty and diversity together. `SEPO`, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization, evolves system prompts, greedily selects a behaviorally distinct set under a quality constraint, and samples one prompt uniformly per response at inference time. Across four creative tasks and three open-weight models it **ranks first in 8 of 12 settings** on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two.
