On a 1-5 LLM-judged scale, average diversity rises from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling, with quality falling from 3.72 to 3.30.

papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
papers.summary: LLM agents with external memory often retrieve the correct memory yet still answer against it or apply it to the wrong question, which the authors call use-time memory hallucinations and trace to conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory. Across five open models these take three forms: ignoring the memory (up to 46% of queries), misapplying it to unrelated entities (up to 24%), and confusing versions of revised facts (53%). `TASK` memory pairs a text note with a removable knowledge edit that supplies an in-model address and a pair of steering vectors that decide per query whether the model adopts the memory. On frozen models under a pre-registered protocol it **cuts memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells**, beats `BM25` retrieval on a 300-memory library by 16.4 points, and adds 7.5 points of multi-hop accuracy on `MQuAKE`.

papers.title: InterConRank: Joint Node Centrality in Interconnected Heterogeneous Networks
papers.abstract: Two nodes with identical connections within their own layer can differ in importance if their neighbors in another layer occupy different positions in the network. We introduce InterConRank, a centrality algorithm that computes a separate node ranking for each layer of an interconnected network. Directed dependencies specify which layers supply scores to each receiving layer. InterConRank normalizes each type of link separately and updates all layers together, so a score can cross into a layer in one iteration and propagate along its internal links in the next. We prove convergence of this joint update and evaluate the resulting rankings on four scholarly networks. On all four networks, InterConRank gives the highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations for nodes in the collaboration layer.
papers.summary: In interconnected multi-layer networks, two nodes with identical connections within their own layer can differ in importance depending on where their neighbors in other layers sit. `InterConRank` computes a separate ranking for each layer, with directed dependencies specifying which layers supply scores to which, each link type normalized separately, and all layers updated together. The authors prove that this joint update converges. On four scholarly networks it **gives the highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations** for nodes in the collaboration layer.

papers.title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.
papers.summary: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) can fail silently when the deployment distribution shifts. `CALD` (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement) is an unsupervised monitor that finetunes the decoder to maximize disagreement with its own test-batch predictions while staying accurate on an in-distribution anchor set, then uses the resulting anchor loss as an alarm signal that needs no test labels. The authors prove the post-finetune anchor loss has strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift, which yields a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets on both `TabPFN` and `TabICL`, it **matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts while raising fewer false alarms on benign shifts**.

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.
papers.summary: LLMs lower an attacker's cost to scan and adapt, and the authors argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes rather than by realism or detection. They propose giving each recognized adversary its own persistent, isolated fake environment kept consistent with that adversary's past actions, with the language model only rendering explicit state rather than storing it, and formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER) relating adversary effort burned to defender resources spent. The idea is instantiated in an SSH honeypot pairing `Cowrie` with a local LLM. Only the defender side is measured so far: across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations **cut per-session defender cost by around 63%** against a naive all-LLM decoy, while per-adversary state and adversary-side cost are specified but not yet evaluated.

papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding on natively sparse-attention models still relies on drafters that keep their own context cache or read the target's cache without a per-query choice of positions, costing memory, prefill time and concurrency. `DFly2` is a block-parallel drafter in which each draft layer reads the key-value cache of its paired target layer at the positions that layer's sparse indexer already selected, so it runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On `DS-V4.1-Flash`, `GLM-5.3-Flash` and `Hy4 flash` it accepts more tokens per step than `DFlash` and `DSpark`, with **the margin over the stronger baseline widening from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones**. At high concurrency and matched per-user decode speed on `DS-V4.1-Flash`, throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K-context sets.

papers.title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL
papers.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.
papers.summary: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often produces groups in which every sampled trajectory fails on long-horizon agent tasks, leaving no reward-based gradient. Instead of supplying full solutions from a stronger model, `SPLICE` has a proposal model pick a splice point in a failed current-policy trajectory and generate several bounded options from there, estimates each option's value with repeated current-policy continuations, and fits the policy to a return-weighted local target. Across two policy families on `SWE-bench Verified` and `BrowseComp-Plus`, it beats `GRPO` and full-trajectory guidance in all four settings, **improving over `GRPO` by 2.8 to 9.8 percentage points**. On initially failed software engineering tasks it raises the graduation rate by 10.8 points while using less proposal-model computation.

papers.title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets
papers.abstract: In a Houston 2024 replay, replacing a fixed 20 percent battery reserve with a county-risk threshold raises observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0 percent to 86.5 percent and adds USD 10.2 in modeled annualized margin per home (paired 95 percent interval: USD +1.7 to USD +21.7). The paired coverage-gain interval includes zero. This is a conditional simulation result, not measured company reliability. Residential batteries face this tradeoff because market discharge consumes energy also needed for household outages. We release HomeFleet-ERCOT, combining observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs. We compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs; ten promise-cost candidates span 31.1 percent-96.3 percent backup coverage. Of these, 10 have lower modeled margin than fixed 20 percent, and 3 also have lower coverage. Chronological, geographic, fleet, and storm tests examine transfer. An alert charging override has a conditional energy-and-power sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5 percent of 41 county mass-outage episodes provide enough continuous warning for every battery preset. Synthetic tests include short, missed, and false warnings, load uplift, capacity loss, and dropout. A static AC audit retains existing feeder violations; aging comparisons expose model sensitivity. The released benchmark, controllers, and checkpoints provide a reproducible basis for comparing these tradeoffs. This work supports the design of residential battery programs that assess market value and household backup service together.
papers.summary: Residential batteries that discharge into electricity markets use up energy a household may need during an outage, so operators must choose how much to hold in reserve. The authors release `HomeFleet-ERCOT`, a benchmark combining observed Texas prices and county outages with simulated homes, and compare fixed reserves, a county-risk threshold, independent-home optimization, and 21 proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) training runs. In a Houston 2024 replay, the county-risk threshold raises five-hour backup coverage from 75.0% to 86.5% and adds about USD 10.2 in modeled annual margin per home, though the coverage-gain interval includes zero and **all ten `PPO` candidates earn lower modeled margin than the fixed 20% reserve**. An alert-triggered charging override has a conditional sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5% of 41 mass-outage episodes gave enough continuous warning for every battery preset.

papers.title: Comparative Study of Deep Learning Architectures for Brain Tumour Classification
papers.abstract: Accurate and early classification of brain tumours from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for treatment planning, yet many published deep learning studies are trained and tested on small, single-source datasets, reporting accuracies that may not hold outside these datasets. This study compares six deep learning architectures for four-class classification (healthy, meningioma, glioma and pituitary tumour): a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), an attention-based CNN, ShuffleNet, and EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50 and Xception augmented with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The models were trained on a corpus assembled from four publicly available MRI datasets. Because these datasets carry no patient identifiers, a leakage-aware pipeline was developed that removes exact duplicates using MD5 hashing (550 images) and near-duplicates using perceptual hashing (8,024 images), and assigns visually similar images to the same fold during 5-fold group cross-validation. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test on a fully held-out dataset was used to measure cross-dataset generalisation. Under a conventional random split, ShuffleNet achieved 97.1% accuracy with 1.2M parameters. Under leakage-aware group K-fold cross-validation, ShuffleNetV2 (98.41%) and EfficientNet-B0 (98.23%) were statistically indistinguishable (paired t-test, p = 0.19), and both significantly outperformed the custom CNNs. On the held-out dataset, accuracy dropped for every model: EfficientNet-B0 generalised best (78.4%), while ShuffleNetV2 fell to 66.2%. Glioma-meningioma confusion was the dominant error mode, and Grad-CAM maps showed that predictions were driven by tumour regions. These results indicate that in-distribution accuracy alone overstates real-world performance and that leakage-aware and cross-dataset evaluation should be reported alongside it.
papers.summary: Published brain tumour classifiers for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often trained and tested on small single-source datasets, which can inflate reported accuracy. Six architectures, including a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN), `ShuffleNet`, and `EfficientNet-B0`, `ResNet-50` and `Xception` with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (`CBAM`), are compared on a corpus built from four public datasets, using a leakage-aware pipeline that removes exact and near-duplicate images via hashing and keeps similar images in the same cross-validation fold. Under leakage-aware cross-validation `ShuffleNetV2` and `EfficientNet-B0` reach about 98%, but on a fully held-out dataset in a leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) test **accuracy drops to 78.4% for `EfficientNet-B0` and 66.2% for `ShuffleNetV2`**. Confusion between glioma and meningioma was the dominant error.

papers.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.
papers.summary: Language models used to simulate users for training and evaluation data tend to produce monolingual, stylistically flat prompts that do not resemble real user messages. `PersonaFactory` is a pipeline that generates structured user personas and rewrites existing prompts from each persona's point of view, yielding **a bank of over 740,000 synthetic personas and roughly 1.24 million persona-styled conversations across 85 languages**. The structured, attribute-based style representation gives per-axis control and better intent preservation than free-text persona descriptions at comparable style fidelity, and human experts rated the conversations as plausible. Models trained on the augmented data match the original data on capability benchmarks and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.

papers.title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning policies often receive conflicting feedback that is localized in space or time, such as favoring speed in open areas and precision in tight gaps, and neural networks blend these signals across shared parameters. `Split-RL` is a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels from heuristics, sensor events, or rule-based systems during tree construction to route conflicting updates into disjoint regions of the state space. The authors show theoretically how aggregating gradients early loses objective-specific information and characterize when their split score isolates the conflicts. In constrained and offline settings, the method **meets the episodic cost budget while keeping competitive reward** and reaches near-expert performance on mixed offline datasets across dataset sizes.

papers.title: Guidance as Variance Matching
papers.abstract: Guidance repels the prediction of a diffusion model away from a weaker reference prediction. It substantially improves sample quality, but its mechanism remains poorly understood. We first find that, at the scales used in practice, guidance does not improve the prediction of the posterior mean (the model's training target); it makes the prediction worse, while samples improve. Second, posterior-mean predictions have less variance than the data, and we find that guidance restores it. We introduce variance-matched guidance: a closed-form rule that picks the guidance scale by matching the variance of the guided predictions to that of the data. Without tuning, it recovers the hand-picked scales of eleven widely used models across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation; to our knowledge, no previous explanation of guidance predicts them. Applied per noise level, it yields a schedule without tuned hyperparameters that users prefer to hand-crafted ones on SD 3.5 Medium. Third, we offer an interpretation of the mechanism behind guidance: each model makes a random error in predicting the posterior mean, and guidance rescales the difference of these errors into a sample with the posterior's covariance, which improves sampling. This view also suggests two new hypotheses that our experiments support: guidance can work with negative scales, and guiding a model with its own checkpoint needs a larger scale than guiding it with an independently trained model.
papers.summary: Guidance in diffusion models pushes a prediction away from a weaker reference prediction and improves samples, but why it works is not well understood. The authors find that at practical scales guidance makes the prediction of the posterior mean worse, while restoring the variance that posterior-mean predictions lack relative to the data. They derive variance-matched guidance, a closed-form rule that sets the guidance scale by matching the variance of guided predictions to that of the data, and it **recovers the hand-picked guidance scales of eleven widely used models without tuning** across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation. Applied per noise level it gives a schedule that users preferred to hand-crafted ones on `SD 3.5 Medium`, and the accompanying error-rescaling interpretation predicts that negative scales can work.

papers.title: Barron Smoothness for Layers in Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: In order to bound approximation errors for deep neural networks, we split the problem into two steps: First the selection of optimal infinite width limits for each layer and second an optimal discretization of all layers to obtain finite sized networks. We show that in expectation, the latter problem is equivalently characterized by a layer wise generalization of Barron norms. Moreover, we provide an analysis of the optimization landscape and show that local minima are characterized by an equidistribution principle akin to similar ideas in adaptive spline and finite element approximation.
papers.summary: Bounding approximation error for deep neural networks is split into two steps: choosing an optimal infinite-width limit for each layer, then discretizing all layers into a finite-size network. The authors show that, in expectation, **the discretization step is characterized by a layer-wise generalization of Barron norms**. An analysis of the optimization landscape shows that local minima follow an equidistribution principle similar to those in adaptive spline and finite element approximation.

papers.title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.
papers.summary: World-action models, which jointly predict future observations and actions for robot control, can fail when camera input is corrupted. `HOG-WAM` adds prediction of future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as an auxiliary training signal, using a diffusion transformer (DiT) module that reads RGB features through asymmetric attention and is removed at inference so the `FastWAM` architecture is unchanged. It achieves the highest success among compared policies under all four corruptions in `RoboTwin-Plus`, with mixed-noise success rising from 78.86% to 82.86%, and small gains on `LIBERO Plus`. On four real Franka tasks, **average success rises from 40% to 59% with clean observations** and from 17% to 24% with noisy ones.
papers.highlight_summary:
World-action models that learn by predicting future RGB frames tie their features to colour, texture and lighting, which makes the resulting policies fragile under visual corruption. `HOG-WAM` adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients as a training-only structural target, so the RGB representation used for control is also shaped by where object boundaries will be.

- An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer predicts future HOG rasters (computed deterministically from clean demonstration frames and encoded by the same frozen VAE as RGB) and reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, so its loss updates the RGB backbone while actions never depend on HOG tokens; the module is dropped at inference, leaving the `FastWAM` architecture and parameter count unchanged.
- On `RoboTwin-Plus`, the authors' four-corruption extension of `RoboTwin 2.0`, mixed-noise success rises from 78.86% to **82.86%** and the corruption mean from 87.02% to **88.58%**, while clean scenes stay flat (92.08% vs 91.88%) and the three photometric corruptions each gain under one point.
- On `LIBERO Plus`, overall success moves from 74.49% to **75.26%**, with sensor noise up from 74.14% to **78.89%** and camera viewpoint up 4.07 points, but background and lighting regress by 2.70 and 2.54 points, and a paired bootstrap over source tasks excludes zero only for sensor noise.
- Across four real Franka tasks, macro-average success rises from 40% to **59%** under clean observations and from 17% to **24%** under noise, at 25 trials per task, model and condition; block stacking (32% to 80%) drives most of the clean gain, and neither policy completes cylinder insertion under noise.
- Replacing RGB with HOG as both input and target drops `LIBERO Plus` success to **66.80%**, supporting HOG as complementary supervision; caveats are that every result comes from a single trained checkpoint per model, `RoboTwin` scene seeds are unpaired across policies, and the auxiliary module adds training compute and parameters.

papers.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.
papers.summary: Video generation models are increasingly tested as visual reasoners that must produce a video carrying out a task from a first frame and a prompt, but this route has not been compared with a symbolic one under identical conditions. Here a coding agent receives the same first frame and prompt and writes a program that renders the answer video, scored by the same rule-based evaluator on the 500-instance `VBVR-Pro-Bench`. `Codex` with `gpt-6-astra`, `Claude Code` with `Fable 5.1`, and `Gemini CLI` with `Gemini 3.1 Pro` **score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model**, while the best of 23 open-weight models, `GLM-5`, reaches 0.572. The authors also distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs that operate on hard-coded values.

papers.title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
papers.abstract: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.
papers.summary: A network's initialization sets up a geometry over the input data that shapes which examples are treated as similar and what gradient descent learns first, which the authors treat as an optimization prior. They ask whether this prior can be borrowed from a different architecture by aligning a target network's representational geometry to that of a randomly initialized guide network before training, with no labels, no learned features, and no gradients to the guide. Aligning shallow networks to deeper ones and coarse-resolution networks to fine-resolution ones **improves the target network's downstream performance in both cases**. The authors conclude that the optimization behavior associated with an architecture can be separated from its physical structure and changed at initialization.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-UAV Data Harvesting Under Variable Team Sizes and Agent Loss
papers.abstract: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.
papers.summary: Teams of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can collect data from wireless sensors in areas without communication infrastructure, but multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies trained for a fixed team size are costly to retrain and fragile when an agent fails. `F-MADDPG` is a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (`MADDPG`) that handles varying numbers of sensors and UAVs and the permanent loss of agents mid-mission. Compared with a multilayer perceptron `MADDPG` baseline, it learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster on average, and stays effective after agent losses. Sampling team sizes by inverse cardinality beats uniform sampling, while **exposing agents to failures during training gives no consistent benefit**.

papers.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Emotionally supportive interactions require large language models not only to avoid overtly harmful content, but also to recognize vulnerability-related risk, regulate their relational stance, preserve user agency, and provide context-appropriate support. Existing safety benchmarks often measure isolated violations, leaving unclear what underlying response competence their scores represent. We introduce VulnSafe, a Chinese capability assessment centered on Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC). VARC organizes relational safety into five complementary constructs: Risk Perception, Safety Preservation, Autonomy Protection, Supportive Response, and Boundary Management. Following an evidence-centered design, 41 scenarios elicit construct-relevant behavior through 2,050 balanced prompts and scenario-specific scoring rubrics. The assessment further separates proactive should-do behavior from prohibitive should-not behavior. Across eight representative LLMs, results show distinct competence profiles and larger disparities than prohibitive requirements. VulnSafe therefore makes relational safety interpretable as a multidimensional model capability rather than as refusal compliance alone.
papers.summary: Safety benchmarks for emotionally supportive conversations mostly count isolated violations, leaving unclear what underlying competence a score reflects. `VulnSafe` is a Chinese-language assessment built around Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC), which covers five constructs: Risk Perception, Safety Preservation, Autonomy Protection, Supportive Response, and Boundary Management. It uses 41 scenarios with 2,050 balanced prompts and scenario-specific rubrics, and separates proactive should-do behavior from prohibitive should-not behavior. Across eight language models, the results show distinct competence profiles, with **larger gaps between models on proactive requirements than on prohibitive ones**.

papers.title: LoopTitan: What Does Parameter Revisit Buy a Mixture-of-Experts?
papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.
papers.summary: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures reuse layer parameters across depths and have been reported to beat standard MoE models at matched parameter, compute, and cache budgets, but those gains mix parameter revisiting with other design choices. Using matched controls without revisiting, the authors find that **parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing**: most of the gain comes from network shape and the rest from a residual scale, which they prove acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers and which stops helping under the `Muon` optimizer. When compute is added at fixed parameters, a deeper standard MoE without revisiting obtains 90.2% of the gain of an extra visit under `Muon`. They propose `LoopTitan-Base` as a stronger MoE baseline that matches the best looped recipe, and release 17 pretrained models with a pre-registered experiment record.

papers.title: The Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark: Do Language Models Know the Foundations of Early-Grade Literacy?
papers.abstract: Many languages of instruction in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are poorly represented in the data used to train language models. Before these models can support early-grade literacy in such languages, we need to know whether they hold the linguistic knowledge of each language that literacy teaching relies on. To test this, we present the Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark and the reproducible, largely automated pipeline that turns curriculum documents, teacher guides and pupil books into a vetted question set organised on a fixed grid of nine linguistic domains and seven grade levels. The pipeline combines LLM-driven source survey, feature consolidation, item generation and quality control with an item-selection step inspired by item response theory and a final expert review. We instantiate it for Kiswahili (Kenya; 135 items) and English (United Kingdom; 137 items) and evaluate 121 and 119 models respectively. Frontier models exceed 90% accuracy in both languages, but accuracy falls steeply for smaller and cheaper models, and more so in Kiswahili. The two best models under 10 billion parameters reach 91.7% and 73.0% in English but only 51.9% and 40.7% in Kiswahili, and the mean accuracy of models deployable on mobile and tablet hardware is 47% in English against 24% in Kiswahili. The models most practical for low-resource classrooms are therefore the least capable in the languages they would serve. We release a 20-item sample per language, all pipeline prompts, open-source code, and a public leaderboard. This is the first rung of a three-level evaluation ladder for measuring and generating decodable text to support foundational literacy.
papers.summary: Many languages of instruction in low- and middle-income countries are poorly represented in language model training data, raising the question of whether models hold the linguistic knowledge that early-grade literacy teaching depends on. The `Linguistic Knowledge Benchmark` is built by a largely automated pipeline that turns curriculum documents, teacher guides, and pupil books into vetted questions across nine linguistic domains and seven grade levels, instantiated for Kiswahili (135 items) and English (137 items) and run on roughly 120 models each. Frontier models exceed 90% in both languages, but smaller models fall off sharply, especially in Kiswahili. **Models deployable on mobile and tablet hardware average 47% in English against 24% in Kiswahili**, so the models most practical for low-resource classrooms are the weakest in the languages they would serve.

papers.title: Routeability Before Routing: Routeability Audit Protocol (RAP) and RouteabilityBench for Audited LLM Model Selection
papers.abstract: LLM routing aims to choose, for each prompt, which model in a portfolio is most likely to answer correctly. This only makes sense when the benchmark contains enough prompt-specific variation for different models to be best on different inputs. On coarse-scored LLM benchmarks, however, many models often tie for the best score, and the single best model may already leave little room for improvement. We therefore propose a routeability-first audit, instantiated as RAP and RouteabilityBench, a runnable claim-verification package. The audit is retrospective: it runs once the benchmark-portfolio score matrix exists and before router comparisons are interpreted as general evidence, rather than certifying a portfolio that has not yet been evaluated. Across four benchmarks and 66 LLMs, generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, dimensionality reduction, selective abstention, clustering, and stronger regressors do not consistently outperform the single best model. The clearest positive evidence is concentrated in portfolio-dependent Omni-MATH settings, while GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval show different ways in which routing can remain hard or predictor-sensitive. Our practical recommendation is that routing gains should be reported together with routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, portfolio construction details, and family-corrected statistical tests.
papers.summary: Routing each prompt to the model in a portfolio most likely to answer it correctly only helps when different models are actually best on different inputs, yet on coarsely scored benchmarks many models tie and the single best model leaves little headroom. The authors propose a routeability-first audit, the Routeability Audit Protocol (`RAP`) with `RouteabilityBench`, which is run on an existing benchmark-by-model score matrix before router comparisons are interpreted. Across four benchmarks and 66 models, **generic routing enhancements such as larger embedding sets, clustering, selective abstention, and stronger regressors do not consistently beat the single best model**. Positive evidence is concentrated in some `Omni-MATH` portfolios, and the authors recommend reporting routing gains alongside routeability diagnostics, tied-best analysis, and family-corrected statistical tests.

papers.title: Gradient TD($\lambda$) for Non-Linear Function Approximation
papers.abstract: Temporal difference (TD) learning is central to reinforcement learning. Many methods use semi-gradient TD, which may diverge, or develop algorithms with mean-squared Bellman or TD-error objectives that are difficult to analyze. Gradient TD algorithms overcome these challenges by using projection of the value function and present convergent off-policy algorithms. However, the algorithm for $\lambda$-return was limited to linear function approximation. Here, we extend the same to non-linear function approximation, which is desirable since many strong modern function approximators are complex and non-linear. Recent works have derived similar algorithms with a generalized projected Bellman error objective. Alternatively, we continue working with the projected Bellman error.
papers.summary: Semi-gradient temporal difference (TD) learning can diverge, and gradient TD methods address this with convergent off-policy algorithms based on a projected value function. The existing gradient TD algorithm for the λ-return applied only to linear function approximation. The authors **extend it to non-linear function approximation** while keeping the projected Bellman error objective, in contrast to recent work that uses a generalized projected Bellman error.

papers.title: Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models
papers.abstract: World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.
papers.summary: World models used for planning are only trustworthy within their experience, and epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal meant to mark where that experience ends. A controlled study compares post-hoc uncertainty estimates (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) on `LeWorldModel`, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with no decoder, and `DreamerV3`, a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that reconstructs observations, tracing a state perturbation through each model in ten simulated visual-control environments. **The RSSM attenuates the perturbation before it reaches the uncertainty estimate**, because its recurrent update averages over context and its reconstruction objective weights entities by pixel area, whereas the JEPA passes the change through. This produces gaps on five downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning.

papers.title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.
papers.summary: Distilling a large language model into a smaller student can degrade trustworthiness even when task performance holds, and repair is difficult because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable and direct preference optimization can alter inherited capabilities. The proposed repair framework uses the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF), estimating the needed curvature from a surrogate proxy dataset and adding an odds-ratio objective so preferred and dispreferred response pairs can be used while constraining changes to the model. Across several distilled models, the authors report that **trustworthiness regressions improve by up to 8% with less than a 1% loss in perplexity**.

papers.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
papers.abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.
papers.summary: The advice encoded in proverbs has rarely been quantified, so the authors analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs using large language models validated against human judgments. They map proverb topics, measure how prescriptive each is, and score recommendations along dimensions of judgment and behavior. Most proverbs are prescriptive and concern matters under individual control, and when they take a consistent stance they **favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice**, with a moderate lean toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions with real trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs give contradictory advice.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.
papers.summary: Risk-sensitive offline reinforcement learning is studied in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov decision processes under recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), covering both the risk-averse and risk-seeking settings of the risk parameter β. The authors introduce a model-based algorithm, ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (`ERM-VI-LCB`), and derive a PAC-type sample complexity bound for learning a near-optimal policy from a fixed dataset. A matching lower bound shows that **exponential dependence on |β|/(1−γ) is unavoidable in the worst case**.

papers.title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.
papers.summary: The structure of a knowledge base behind a language model application determines how well it can retrieve and connect information, and this work studies learning that structure from questions and expected answers. `Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent` diagnoses mismatches between expected answers and responses from the current knowledge base, proposes a structural edit to a graph schema or set of linked documents, rebuilds, and keeps the edit if the loss decreases; `Schema Descent` is the graph-schema instance. On large documents made of bundled research papers, updated knowledge cards and schemas score higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions, with schema gains on every document. On human-written questions, however, **mean F1 rises for schemas but falls for cards**, indicating the learned structures serve the kind of question they were trained on.

papers.title: Probing Visual Idiosyncrasies in Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models turn short text descriptions into images, and the leading models now produce images of comparable visual quality. Whether their outputs still carry model-specific characteristics matters for attribution, for model comparison beyond aggregate quality, and for evaluations that assume anonymity. We ask whether images from frontier T2I models can still be classified by source, and which visual properties make this possible. Here we show that a standard ResNet-50 identifies the source of an image among HiDream-O1-Dev, FLUX.2-dev, HunyuanImage-3.0, and Qwen-Image-2512, the four highest-ranked open-source models on the Text-to-Image Arena, with 100.00% accuracy on held-out prompts. Human participants reach only 62.61% on the pairwise version of this task, so the distinguishing cues are not visually obvious. They are also not tied to a particular classifier and survive severe image corruptions and out-of-distribution prompts. We trace them to visual idiosyncrasies at three levels. Low-level texture statistics alone let a lightweight multi-layer perceptron match ResNet-50. Object layout, depth, and albedo estimated from the images each carry a source signal. Image captions reveal model-specific preferences in style and background that the prompts never specify. A one-sentence hint about these cues raises human accuracy by 9.03 percentage points. These idiosyncrasies make source classification a tool for measuring similarity between models and between real and generated images, and they caution against assuming anonymity in human preference evaluation of T2I models.
papers.summary: Leading text-to-image (T2I) models now produce images of similar quality, raising the question of whether their outputs can still be told apart by source. A standard `ResNet-50` identifies which of `HiDream-O1-Dev`, `FLUX.2-dev`, `HunyuanImage-3.0`, and `Qwen-Image-2512` produced an image with **100.00% accuracy on held-out prompts**, while humans reach only 62.61% on the pairwise version of the task. The cues survive severe image corruptions and out-of-distribution prompts, and are traced to low-level texture statistics, object layout, depth and albedo, and model-specific style and background preferences that the prompts never specify. The authors caution against assuming anonymity in human preference evaluations of T2I models.

papers.title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.
papers.summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) on time series reasoning usually present events in chronological order and already matched to the series, so it is unclear whether models actually use timestamps. The authors treat timestamps as indices linking observations and external events to shared world states, and build a diagnostic protocol that separates timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that **accuracy stays high when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed**, while breaking event-series alignment causes systematic failures. Without dates, models rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps.

papers.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for deep research agents score report quality along several dimensions but do not directly measure which research directions a report covers and how deeply. `DRBench Pro` builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia, samples subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics, and scores breadth across major directions and depth along knowledge chains, combining them by geometric mean. It contains 144 cases across 24 domains with 44,102 rubrics. Across 16 deep research agents, the best reaches **57.04% overall coverage**, and rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations.

papers.title: From Prediction to Decision: Decision-Focused Fine-Tuning of Autoregressive Tabular Transformers for Cost-Sensitive Financial Events
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on tokenized tabular event streams are a simple and strong baseline for predicting financial events such as fraud. Yet institutions do not act on probabilities; they act on decisions whose consequences are asymmetric and heteroscedastic: the cost of a missed high-value fraud and that of a wrongly declined small purchase are not the same. The standard bridge is post-hoc Bayes-optimal thresholding of calibrated probabilities under a cost matrix. We ask whether fine-tuning the model to the decision objective can do better. We fine-tune the same pretrained model so that its restricted softmax over label tokens (already a distribution over business actions) maximizes expected utility under an institution-specified, amount-scaled cost matrix. Because the reward is a known function of (action, outcome, amount) and the outcome is observed in the data, the expected-utility objective and its gradient are available in closed form. This is example-dependent cost-sensitive learning whose per-example loss is linear in the predicted probability, with no sampling, critics, or advantage estimation. A KL anchor to the pretrained model and an auxiliary language-modeling term preserve calibration and the generative event model. A sampled, group-normalized (GRPO-style) variant provides the extension point to trajectory-level rewards.
papers.summary: Fraud and other financial event predictors output probabilities, but institutions act on decisions whose costs are asymmetric and scale with transaction amount. Instead of thresholding calibrated probabilities after the fact, the authors fine-tune a pretrained autoregressive tabular transformer so that its softmax over label tokens maximizes expected utility under an institution-specified, amount-scaled cost matrix. Because the reward is a known function of action, outcome, and amount, **the objective and its gradient are available in closed form, with no sampling, critics, or advantage estimation**. A KL anchor to the pretrained model and an auxiliary language-modeling term preserve calibration, and a group-normalized `GRPO`-style variant extends the approach to trajectory-level rewards.

papers.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines
papers.abstract: The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.
papers.summary: The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation bring AI models into scope and call for re-identification testing, but do not specify how such tests should be designed, validated, or weighed as evidence. The authors describe a framework built around a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), distinguishing forms of release and formal, empirical, and indirect evidence. They raise seven open questions and examine them for model weight release, airlock review, and regulatory sandboxes, noting that a failed re-identification attempt may only mean the test was too weak. They call for **re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods with stated detection limit, bias, and uncertainty**.

papers.title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
papers.abstract: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
papers.summary: `BOP-Refer` is a benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects, built from 9 `BOP` datasets by pairing images with human-verified referring expressions and deriving ground-truth boxes from 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. An evaluation of 17 vision-language models (VLMs) from the Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families finds that the best, `Gemini 4 Carbon`, reaches **72.6% average precision in 2D but only 12.4% in 3D**, despite more lenient 3D overlap thresholds. Predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target in the image but off in depth by more than the object's size, pointing to metric scale estimation as the main source of error.

papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
papers.summary: Training-free token merging reduces the cost of vision transformer encoders for video object segmentation, but it merges uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. The authors give a frozen `DINOv3` encoder inside a `Cutie` segmenter a focus map that keeps full resolution where objects are expected, using velocity-shifted and block-matched masks plus a camera-compensated surprise check, and merges coarsely elsewhere. On `LVOS V2` it beats the `ALGM` merging baseline by **+2.76 J&F at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs**, about 1.0 point below the dense encoder. The authors report that the lower counted compute did not reduce startup-inclusive step time, and that protecting only the previous mask matches the accuracy at higher FLOPs.

papers.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.abstract: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training.
