Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, and existing offline speedup methods assign predefined factors to whole segments even when parts of a segment need precise alignment. `RePace` measures how each candidate speedup factor shortens a recorded movement and changes the resulting observation-action training pairs, then has a pretrained language model use the task instruction, visual context, and original motion to pick a speedup profile for the full episode. It **outperforms acceleration baselines in overall task execution efficiency on `LIBERO` and `RoboCasa-Kitchen`**. On three real tasks with a Franka Research 3 arm, it matches or exceeds the baselines in success rate while finishing successful trials faster.

papers.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed in telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support, where the data is unusually sensitive and longitudinal. This survey reviews the associated risks and safeguards and contributes **a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics to use cases**. It also outlines open research challenges including longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.

papers.title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
papers.abstract: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.
papers.summary: Merging serialized RDF knowledge graphs produces spurious ordering conflicts while missing semantic ones. The authors implement a three-way merge in a production multi-agent store in which a conflict exists only where a `SHACL` shape bounds a slot's cardinality and both sides' changes cannot fit within it; everything else is unioned, and contended slots go to a person. On synthetic data the operator raised **33 conflicts, all true positives, where a baseline based on `Quit Store`'s context-overlap rule found the same conflicts but asked 845 questions**, with no triples lost or fabricated. A replay of production incidents shows a limit: different names for the same entity remain invisible, with 0 of 93 alias repairs detected, and the authors restrict their claim to cardinality conflicts in one deployment.

papers.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
papers.abstract: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.
papers.summary: Coding agents produce larger patches than developers, which is often read as over-editing, but size alone does not show whether the extra edits are needed. Delta Residue Attribution (`DRA`) replays agent trajectories, traces each block of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts it, and reruns the task tests to decide whether it is necessary; it is applied to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 models on `SWE-bench Verified` and `DeepSWE`. The extra edits on `SWE-bench Verified` are mostly tests (61%) and documentation (13%), and **agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers'**, though 11% of agent code units there are still unneeded and most of those change behavior. Pruning with `DRA` using only tests visible to the agent removes most unneeded code (67% recall, 46% precision) while 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task.

papers.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
papers.abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.
papers.summary: Vision models can over-rely on scene context, predicting objects from their typical neighbors instead of their own features, which the authors call typicality bias. They quantify it with normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs and introduce `STRANGE-Bench`, a photorealistic, layout-controlled synthetic benchmark spanning 17 tiers from typical to never-co-occurring pairs. Across specialist and open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised models, vision-language models, and multimodal large language models, **gaps of 5-11 percentage points persist when objects appear outside their typical company** and do not consistently shrink with scale. Their Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (`AAS`) rule for paste-based augmentation reduces the gap by up to 1.6 points on `COCO` splits and 23.0 points on `STRANGE-Bench` without hurting overall performance.

papers.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
papers.abstract: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.
papers.summary: Greedy decision trees can split on feature values or on proximity to exemplar instances, and no single split type has proven universally best. The authors propose a hybrid tree that mixes feature-based and case-based splits throughout, along with a selective case-based split that searches for the most informative subset of features to define each exemplar comparison. On a range of tabular datasets, the method **outperforms standard decision trees and performs on par with ensemble methods while producing shallow trees**.

papers.title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
papers.abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/\rho$, and its yield stress $\sigma_Y/\rho$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.
papers.summary: From a single real video of an object being dropped, `PhysReader` estimates a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness, and its yield stress when the impact causes plastic deformation, using a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. The authors find that synthetic validation ranks input types in the wrong order: **tracklets lifted to 3D are the most accurate input in simulation but the least accurate on real drops, while short 2D optical-flow tracklets transfer best**, and better depth does not fix the 3D failure. `PhysReader` therefore reads video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. On the new `PhysReader-Real` set of 16 everyday objects with tensile-test-checked reference materials, it is closer to the references than all other inputs and baselines except a per-scene optimizer that takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

papers.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
papers.abstract:
This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.
  Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .
papers.summary: Processing raw Earth observation imagery at scale is constrained by data volume, so the authors test whether Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) tasks can run directly on compressed embeddings from the geospatial foundation model `TerraMind`. Linear and non-linear probes on embeddings of `Sentinel-1` synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images detect vessels with a **ROC-AUC of 0.95**, localize vessels longer than 100 m with a median error of about 300 m, and classify vessel type with 62% accuracy for the majority classes, though that result is highly correlated with vessel length. A new dataset of about 2,000 `Sentinel-1` images paired with manually verified, temporally aligned AIS vessel signals is released for use with the `NeuCo-Bench` framework.

papers.title: $\mu$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
papers.abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $\mu$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $\mu$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.
papers.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must handle interdependent requests from several people while respecting each person's authority, privacy, and task constraints. `μ-Bench` evaluates this in closed-loop, full-duplex interaction, with simulated participants acting from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions across 800 cases in 20 domains. Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold together, and Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, **proprietary systems peak at 62.24% tool-free and 65.44% tool-augmented success while open-weight models stay below 20%**, and larger groups consistently degrade success.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
papers.summary: Looped Transformers gain expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, at a cost in efficiency. The Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (`MoLT`) uses attention keys and values as memory that can be selectively reused across depths and loops, with variants that either keep the residual stream or restart from embeddings to enable parallel training and single-traversal decoding; a U-shaped version, `U-MoLT`, separates memory construction from prediction readout. In 400B-token pretraining, `U-MoLT` outperforms `OLMo3` at 700M and 1.5B dense and 3B mixture-of-experts scales, with **1.7x token efficiency in validation cross-entropy at 700M**. Continued pretraining of `Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base` lowers cross-entropy on all 11 domains, and at inference a hybrid decoding mode matches non-looped `OLMo3` latency on roughly 113M-parameter models.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped Transformers gain expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops but pay for it in compute. `MoLT` rethinks what is passed between loops, using attention keys and values (KV) as a memory that is selectively reused across depths and loops through `MoLA` (Mixture-of-Loops Attention).

- `MoLT-R` keeps the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity, while `MoLT-KV` restarts each loop from the embeddings and reads current-loop KV plus preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions only, which removes same-position cross-loop dependence.
- Paired with loop forcing for parallel training, `MoLT-KV` supports single-traversal decoding beyond the training loop horizon, and the U-shaped `U-MoLT` separates memory construction from prediction readout so unused decoder traversals can be skipped without changing predictions.
- In 400B-token pretraining, `U-MoLT` beats `OLMo3` at 700M and 1.5B dense and 3B MoE scales, with **1.7x** validation cross-entropy token efficiency at 700M and, for the 3B MoE model, **0.75** lower 10-domain perplexity and **+2.1 points** 10-task accuracy.
- In 100B-token continued pretraining of `Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base`, the `U-MoLT` adaptation lowers cross-entropy on **all 11 domains** against a matched baseline, with **1.4x** mean token efficiency.
- Latency parity with non-looped `OLMo3` (**996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms** using `MoL-Hybrid-2`) is reported only for S-size (~113M) models, so the abstract leaves open whether inference cost stays matched at the 700M–3B scales where the quality gains are shown.

papers.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.
papers.summary: Post-training large language models for math often depends on reasoning traces whose final answers pass a verifier, but such traces are rare for hard problems under independent Monte Carlo sampling. Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (`DART`) starts from a rejected trace, splits it into steps, ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty, and generates deliberately distinct alternatives for the top-ranked steps using reference-answer guidance before completing the traces. On `DeepMath-103K` problems unsolved by greedy decoding, it **recovers 37% more problems than Monte Carlo sampling at a matched number of generated traces**, with a 30% lower cost per accepted trace. Post-training `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` on the mined traces gives the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations on `MATH-500` and `AIME`.

papers.title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.
papers.summary: Pathology foundation models are usually compared on downstream task performance, which does not show what biology they represent. `BioScore` uses spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as a reference: a sparse autoencoder splits an encoder's patch embeddings into features, which are clustered into groups, and the score measures how specifically a group tracks the expression of each of 52 marker-gene-defined cell identities. Among 8 pathology models and 3 natural-image models, **every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299-0.371 versus 0.214-0.232)**, with three tiers separated among the pathology models. The benchmark needs no labels yet ranks encoders as a supervised probe does.

papers.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
papers.abstract:
AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
  The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.
papers.summary: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are typically evaluated on transcripts generated by attack policies standing in for real dangerous behaviour. Using an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study, the authors find that the **measured false negative rate ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across optimisation levels of a single reinforcement-learning attack method**, and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best level. All attacks were developed against proxy monitors and transferred to the held-out `GPT-5.4` target monitor. The authors argue that evaluations using only basic attacks can give false confidence, and that reading results as evidence about deployment requires a separate argument for why the proxy transcripts are informative.

papers.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
papers.abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
papers.summary: The study tests whether letting a multimodal model generate a helper image improves its answers to visual questions: the model describes the helper it needs, an image generator produces it, and the model then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, **generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points**, with declines on nine of ten tasks, and the unified models `BAGEL` and `Janus-Pro-7B` each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On `VSTAR`, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits give mixed results, with `ChartQAPro` and `MathVista` staying below their no-generation baselines while `ERQA` gains three points after ten edits.

papers.title: Tokenisation is not in APX
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.
papers.summary: The computational hardness of finding an optimal tokeniser is analysed in terms of approximability, asking whether a polynomial-time algorithm can at least get within a constant factor of the best achievable objective (the property that defines the APX complexity class). The authors prove that **unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate the optimal tokeniser within any constant factor**. The result covers both direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under either a compression or a unigram log-likelihood objective, and for binary or larger alphabets. They also show that direct tokenisation is APX-hard even over unary alphabets, which rules out a polynomial-time approximation scheme there.

papers.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.
papers.summary: End-to-end learned radio links replace separate modulation, coding, and detection with an autoencoder (AE) trained jointly at the transmitter and receiver, but systems trained only on an additive white Gaussian noise channel degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. The proposed transfer-learning procedure starts from the noise-only pretrained system and fine-tunes a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the rest, with layer selection posed as a budget-constrained optimization problem. The authors report that **partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the bit error rate (BER) of fully retrained models**. A layer-wise study shows this also cuts training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters.

audio.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Medical AI models that read both scans and text still trail the best general-purpose models. Making them bigger mostly helps with text, not with seeing. The authors built Sage-Med by carefully filtering a huge pool of medical data and training in stages. On unseen tasks from real hospitals, it averaged about 58 percent, ahead of a leading proprietary model. But multi-step reasoning stays weak. It matters because careful data and staged training, not just size, can narrow the gap.
